rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/.x:
Originally considered a less-orthodox defence in the Queen's Gambit, this opening has stood as an entire opening system in its own right for decades.

The idea behind this defence is straightforward: instead of locking in the light squared bishop on c8, why not support the center with the c-pawn instead? Black tends to be more active in this variation than the QGD.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nc3
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.x:
This move develops a piece and bears more pressure on d5. Due to this, it also makes 3...Bf5 a grave mistake due to 4. cxd5 cxd5 5. Qb3, winning a pawn. If then 5...Qb6, 6. Nxd5! Qxb3 7. axb3 wins the d pawn. If instead 5...Nf6 to protect the d-pawn, 6. Qxb7 Nbd7 7. Nf3 Rb8 8. Qxa7 wins two. In general, if Black can safely play Bf5 and e6 in the Slav, Black equalizes. The c3-knight also bears pressure on e4, allowing for a potential e4 pawn-push in the future.

/3...Nf6/ is Black's most common reply by far. White's play typically transposes into a semi-slav with 4. Nf3, although some unique lines exist where Nf3 is delayed or not played at all.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6
rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2P.x:
Black develops a knight to f6, and puts pressure on the e4-square. From here White has multiple good responses, although 4. Bf4 and 4. Bg5 should be avoided as Black can play 4...dxc4 and retain the pawn without giving White any compensation.

/4. Nf3/ develops the White's knight to f3, increasing control over the d4 and e5 squares. This is considered the mainline and it gives Black many responses to choose from.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/4. Nc3
rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP.x:
White develops his other knight onto the c3 square where it increases the pressure on d5 and also exerts control over the e4 square. Although this knight is sometimes developed onto the d2 square by Nbd2, the c3 square is slightly preferable since it does not block in white's bishop on c1.

This is an important branching point. While all of Black's responses belong to the "Slav" family of openings, the arising positions are generally very different from each other.

/4...e6/ leads to the Semi-Slav defence. Black keeps their light-squared bishop inside of the pawn chain for the time being, but intends to free it with the pawn breaks c5 or e5.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Nf3/4...e6
rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP.x:
A highly theoretical opening. Black willingly keeps the light-squared bishop behind the pawn-chain, intending to free it later with either the e5 or c5 pawn breaks. In response, White has two main options with very different playstyles.

/5. Bg5/ leads to sharp, tactical positions, where Black can choose to play the Botvinnik variation 5...dxc4 or the Moscow or Anti-Moscow.

/5. e3/ leads to calmer, more positional variations. White will generally decide whether to go into the mainline Meran with 6. Bd3 or avoid it with one of the many Anti-Meran variations.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N2N2/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Nf3/4...e6/5. Bg5
rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N2N2/.x: This super-sharp move is often today a true gambit. White intends to offer the c-pawn as a real sacrifice. Here Black can try the solid 5...Nbd7, which leads into the Queen's Gambit Declined (Cambridge Springs Variation), the sharp Botvinnik Variation (5...dxc4 6. e4 b5 7. e5 h6 8. Bh4 g5 9. Nxg5! hxg5 10. Bxg5 with tremendous complications), or the even sharper Anti-Moscow variation, 5...h6 6. Bh4 dxc4 7. e4 g5 8. Bg3 b5.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/6B1/2pP4/2N2N2/PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Nf3/4...e6/5. Bg5/5...dxc4
rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/6B1/2pP4/2N2N2/PP.x:
Welcome to the Botvinnik Slav, the highway of wild variations, where crazy tactical complications fill the board.

Black boldly accepts the gambit pawn, but their material advantage is only temporary. White's main response is /6. e4/, establishing a large center and planning to continue with e5. The resulting positions will be very chaotic and theoretical, making it very dangerous for an unprepared player.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/6B1/2pPP3/2N2N2/P.x: White claims the entire center, while revealing the f1 bishop's attack on the c4 pawn. Black must fortify the c4 pawn with /6...b5/.

rnbqkb1r/p4ppp/2p1pn2/1p4B1/2pPP3/2N2N2/.x: Black fortifies the c pawn, but allows White to continue with /7. e5/. While this may look scary, Black does have a way out.

rnbqkb1r/p4ppp/2p1pn2/1p2P1B1/2pP4/2N2N2.x: White pushes forward the e pawn, attacking the pinned knight. Black can still save the knight by playing /7...h6/, kicking away the bishop.

rnbqkb1r/p4pp1/2p1pn1p/1p2P1B1/2pP4/2N2N.x:
This is the only move for Black to not lose a piece. White's main response is /8. Bh4/, retreating the bishop and retaining the pin.

The alternatives to 8. Bh4 give Black relatively little problems. If White tries 8. exf6? Black gets a comfortable position up a pawn after 8...hxg5 9. fxg7 Bxg7.

8. Bxf6?! is also dubious at best and allows Black to quickly equalize. Since White has given up the dark-squared bishop, Black can combat White's remaining bishop by putting the majority of their pawns on light squares.

rnbqkb1r/p4pp1/2p1pn1p/1p2P3/2pP3B/2N2N2.x: White retains the pin on Black's knight, threatening to take it with the pawn. Black must respond adequately with /8...g5/, removing the bishop from the diagonal.

rnbqkb1r/p4p2/2p1pn1p/1p2P1p1/2pP3B/2N2N.x: Black blocks the vision of White's dark-squared bishop in order to save the knight. It seems that White's attack is finally over but /9. Nxg5/ continues the attack, temporarily sacrificing the knight for two pawns to win it back later.

rnbqkb1r/p4p2/2p1pn1p/1p2P1N1/2pP3B/2N5/.x:
White sacrifices their knight temporarily. Black should simply recapture with /9...hxg5/.

/9...Nd5/? doesn't work because of White's response 10. Nxf7! and Black can't avoid losing material.

rnbqkb1r/p4p2/2p1pn2/1p2P1B1/2pP4/2N5/PP.x:
White recaptures the pawn, reestablishing the pin on the knight. Black can't avoid White gaining his piece back and should continue development. /10...Nbd7/ is the usual reply, representing the starting point of the Botvinnik variation.

/10...Be7/ is another option, although it leads to many trades resulting in a very simplified position, which usually isn't the goal of players going into the Botvinnik.

r1bqkb1r/p2n1p2/2p1pn2/1p2P1B1/2pP4/2N5/.x:
Black defends the knight on f6 again to prevent 11. Bxf6 forking the queen and the rook.

This is the first big branching point in the Botvinnik variation. White has two main options.

/11. g3/, the Lilienthal variation, delays capturing the knight on f6 and prepares to fianchetto White's light-squared bishop.

/11. exf6/ takes the hanging knight immediately. While it often transposes back into the Lilienthal, it gives Black more options to deviate from the Lilienthal.

r1bqkb1r/p2n1p2/2p1pn2/1p2P1B1/2pP4/2N3P.x:
White prepares to fianchetto the light-squared bishop.

Blacks main response is /11...Bb7/, fighting for the a8-h1 diagonal.

/11...Rg8/ is a sideline, preparing to exchange the rook for White's powerful dark-squared bishop. White ends up having a rook, a pawn and open lines on the kingside for the two pieces.

rnbqkb1r/pp3pp1/2p1pn1p/3p2B1/2PP4/2N2N2.x: This move invites White into either the positional Moscow variation after /6. Bxf6/, or the tactical Anti-Moscow variation after /6. Bh4/.

rnbqkb1r/pp3pp1/2p1pn1p/3p4/2PP3B/2N2N2/.x:
White has decided to enter the Anti-Moscow variation of the Semi-Slav, a tactically rich and theoretically heavy opening.

Black's main move is /6...dxc4/, taking the pawn that White has declined to defend.

rnbqkb1r/pp3pp1/2p1pn1p/8/2pP3B/2N2N2/PP.x: Black takes White's offered pawn, but in doing so has relinquished control of the center allowing /7. e4/.

rnbqkb1r/pp3pp1/2p1pn1p/8/2pPP2B/2N2N2/P.x:
White takes control of the center, opening up the light-squared bishop to recapture the c pawn.

The immediate /7...b5/ allows White to play 8. e5, transposing into the Botvinnik variation.

Black's main response is to first play the in-between move /7...g5/, forcing White to drop back the dark-squared bishop to g3.

rnbqkb1r/pp3p2/2p1pn1p/6p1/2pPP2B/2N2N2/.x:
Black attacks White's bishop again, forcing it to retreat to g3.

Unlike the Botvinnik variation, /8. Nxg5/? is a blunder in this position. After the sequence 8. Nxg5 hxg5 9. Bxg5 Black can defend the knight and break the pin with 9...Be7 and simply move the knight after e5.

rnbqkb1r/pp3p2/2p1pn1p/6p1/2pPP3/2N2NB1/.x:
White retreats their bishop to g3.

Black's pawn on c4 is still hanging, so they should defend it with /8...b5/.

rnbqkb1r/p4p2/2p1pn1p/1p4p1/2pPP3/2N2NB1.x:
Black defends the c pawn. This is the starting point of the Anti-Moscow variation.

White's main move is /9. Be2/, preparing to castle short and start an attack on Black's king, which is still stuck in the center.

An immediate 9. a4 to try and strike back at the defended pawn is a mistake, although it's commonly played at amateur level. 9... b4 gives Black strong initiative. Amateurs frequently deepen the hole by playing 10. e5, but now after 10...bxc3, 11. exf6 is too slow and White has collapsed.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2PP4/2N1PN2/P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Nf3/4...e6/5. e3
rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2PP4/2N1PN2/P.x:
This move protects the c4-pawn with the light-squared bishop, but keeps the dark-squared bishop behind the pawn-chain. Play is usually very positional compared to the 5. Bg5 lines.

Black's main idea is to take the c4-pawn once White develops their bishop to d3, gaining important tempi while expanding on the queenside. Since White has yet to place the bishop on d3, Black's main response is /5...Nbd7/, waiting for White to develop the bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2PP4/2N1PN2.x:
This is a waiting move: Black is waiting for White to develop the light-squared bishop with /6. Bd3/. Black does so in order to win some important tempi on White's bishop to make space for Black's light-squared bishop on b7. This is called the Meran variation.

White doesn't have to follow this plan however. White can play /6. Qc2/, the Anti-Meran, to avoid this line and make Black's development of the light-squared bishop more difficult.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2PP4/2NBPN2.x:
White intends to enter the Meran variation. However, Black gets the final say in this matter.

After /6...dxc4/ Black has officially entered the Meran variation, forcing White to move the bishop again to recapture the pawn.

If Black doesn't want to play the theoretical Meran, they can avoid it with /6...Bd6/.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/8/2pP4/2NBPN2/P.x:
Black captures the c4 pawn with a tempo on White's bishop, forcing White to move it again.

/7. Bxc4/ is the only sensible move.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/8/2BP4/2N1PN2/P.x:
White recaptures the pawn.

/7...b5/ is the most proper response, justifying the loss of control over the center by making the b7-square available for the light-squared bishop while gaining a tempo.

r1bqkb1r/p2n1ppp/2p1pn2/1p6/2BP4/2N1PN2/.x:
Black expands on the queenside and makes the b7-square available for their bishop while gaining a tempo on White's bishop.

White should retreat the bishop, there are three viable options:

/8. Bd3/ is the main line, returning the bishop to the square it was originally positioned on. From this square, it supports the e4 pawn-push and glances at Black's kingside.

/8. Be2/ is a more passive option. It can't be attacked as easily on e2 as on d3, but its also not as active in the attack.

r1bqkb1r/p2n1ppp/2p1pn2/1p6/3P4/2NBPN2/P.x:
White returns the bishop to its original position, from where it supports the e4 pawn push. This is considered to be the main line.

The classical response by Black is /8...a6/, protecting the b4-pawn in order to be able to free the light-squared bishop with c5 later. This does allow White to take control of the center with the immediate 9. e4, after which some very complicated positions can arise.

A slightly more modern and nowadays more popular response is /8...Bb7/, the Wade variation. This makes the immediate 9. e4 less desirable for White, who usually responds by castling kingside immediately.

r1bqkb1r/3n1ppp/p1p1pn2/1p6/3P4/2NBPN2/P.x:
Black protects the b-pawn so they can play 9...c5 without blundering a pawn.

Foreseeing this plan, White should play actively and take over the center with /9. e4/, preparing to open up the center with either 10. d5 or 10. e5 and opening up the dark-squared bishop.

Less provocative setups have been tried as well. At the amateur level /9. O-O/ is very popular, but this poses no problems for players with the black pieces at all, since they score quite well in this line.

Another move that is played often is /9. a4/. White does better than after 9. O-O, but has lost quite a bit of initiative.

r1bqkb1r/3n1ppp/p1p1pn2/1p6/3PP3/2NB1N2/.x:
White strikes in the center, opening up the dark-squared bishop in the process.

Black's main move is /9...c5/, looking to break up White's center immediately. This move is played in the vast majority of games, and is Black's best option to open up the light-squared bishop and fight for an advantage.

A very rare sideline is /9...b4/, the Pirc variation. This is the only other move (according to chess engines) that doesn't give White a winning advantage, since it gains a tempo on White's knight.

r1bqkb1r/3n1ppp/p3pn2/1pp5/3PP3/2NB1N2/P.x:
Black strikes back at White's center, opening up the light-squared bishop.

This is the main branching point of the mainline Meran, since White has to choose between one of two pawn breaks: e5 and d5.

/10. e5/ is the Old variation.

/10. d5/ is Reynold's variation.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2PP4/2N1PN2.x: With this move, White decides to avoid the theory-heavy Meran. After Black's usual response /6...Bd6/ White will have a wide range of choices.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/2pP4/2N5/PP2PPPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nc3/3...dxc4
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/2pP4/2N5/PP2PPPP/.x: This move captures the gambit pawn. Since White's knight on c3 is exposed to attacks by Black's b-pawn, Black can often safely over-extend with moves like a6 and b5 to keep a hold of the c-pawn in this line. This move is lesser seen than the main line 3...Nf6. From here, White has several replies:

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/2pP4/2N1P3/PP3PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nc3/3...dxc4/4. e3
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/2pP4/2N1P3/PP3PPP.x:
This is considered to be the best move for White:

* Keeps the e4-square free for the c3-knight to retreat to in case of a b7-b5-b4 advance.
* Gains control of the centre with pawns on e3 and d4.
* Prepares to capture the c4 pawn with Bxc4.

Black should prevent the capture of the c-pawn with /4...b5/. This usually leads to very complicated variations on the queenside where White attempts to undermine Black's defence of the c-pawn with moves like a4. If White can successfully recapture the pawn, White should be better.

rnbqkbnr/p3pppp/2p5/1p6/2pP4/2N1P3/PP3PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nc3/3...dxc4/4. e3/4...b5
rnbqkbnr/p3pppp/2p5/1p6/2pP4/2N1P3/PP3PP.x:
This guards c4 and is the best move. The queenside weaknesses are not a problem, as the knight on c3 is vulnerable to b-pawn attacks with ...b4. Note that 5. Nxb5?, trying to exploit the long diagonal to destroy Black's queenside, is a mistake, and gives up the advantage to Black. A common motif in these positions is for Black to play b5 in order to boot the knight, often giving up the c4-pawn in the process.

When your opponent has a space advantage, you want to use pawn breaks to break up their pawn chains. /5. a4/ is the most effective way to do that. The alternative 5. b3?! Qa5 results in Black being able to put a lot of pressure on White's queenside.

rnbqkbnr/p3pppp/2p5/1N6/2pP4/4P3/PP3PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nc3/3...dxc4/4. e3/4...b5/5. Nxb5
rnbqkbnr/p3pppp/2p5/1N6/2pP4/4P3/PP3PPP/.x:
This clever attempt to win material is a huge mistake, providing Black with a huge advantage.

Black should undoubtedly continue with 5...cxb5, taking the offered piece. Now 6. Qf3 is White's only way to try to capitalise on their sacrifice, threatening to take the rook on a8. Black does have a few ways out.

rnbqkbnr/p3pppp/8/1p6/2pP4/4P3/PP3PPP/R1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nc3/3...dxc4/4. e3/4...b5/5. Nxb5/5...cxb5
rnbqkbnr/p3pppp/8/1p6/2pP4/4P3/PP3PPP/R1.x:
This move bravely accepts White's bold sacrifice. Conventional chess wisdom says "The best way to refute a gambit is to accept it". Therefore, if black would have declined the gambit, white would successfully rip black's queenside apart and Black would just be worse. Now, white's queen will get trapped on a8.

Of course, the only way to try to regain the material is with 6.Qf3.

rnbqkbnr/p3pppp/8/1p6/2pP4/4PQ2/PP3PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nc3/3...dxc4/4. e3/4...b5/5. Nxb5/5...cxb5/6. Qf3
rnbqkbnr/p3pppp/8/1p6/2pP4/4PQ2/PP3PPP/R.x: This move tries to regain the material, hopefully with interest. Now, we come to a cross, where two moves lead to a clear black advantage. The first idea is to cut Black's losses to a piece while maintaining the queenside. This can be achieved simply by Nc6, when after Qxc6+ Bd7 Black's queenside holds. The other, more dramatic plan is to imprison white's queen on a7 at the cost of a rook. This is achieved by Qc7! Qxa8 (Now, cut off the long diagonal so the Queen can't escape with her capture) Bb7! Qxa7 (Now, cut off c5 and a3 and the queen will get trapped) e5! (e6 is also good). Now, the center is opening, and Nc6 is threatened. White will have to lose material in order to save his queen.

rnbqkbnr/p3pppp/2p5/1p6/P1pP4/2N1P3/1P3P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nc3/3...dxc4/4. e3/4...b5/5. a4
rnbqkbnr/p3pppp/2p5/1p6/P1pP4/2N1P3/1P3P.x: This move tries to attack Black's queenside and lure it to it's doom. b4 is almost universally played after this, as if Qa5, the queen is exposed. b4 tries to boot the knight into oblivion and disrupt White's queenside.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/2pPP3/2N5/PP3PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nc3/3...dxc4/4. e4
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/2pPP3/2N5/PP3PPP/.x:
White uses the fact that the capture has left the e4-square undefended and expends their centre, revealing an attack from the light-squared bishop on the c4 pawn.

Black generally holds onto their pawn with /4...b5/, preparing to push b5-b4 if White challenges their pawn with a2-a4.

/4...e5/ was the first main line, but players with White have shown that it is not to be feared, scoring very well against it.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/2PP4/5N2/PP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nf3
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/2PP4/5N2/PP2PPP.x:
With the most common move in the Slav, 3. Nf3, White develops their knight and exerts more control over the e5-square. Similar to 3. Nc3, Black should avoid 3...Bf5 as 4. cxd5 cxd5 5. Qb3 effectively wins a pawn. However, unlike 3. Nc3, 3...dxc4 should also be avoided as White is better after 4. e3 and 5. a4 since White will win back the pawn as the knight on f3 is not vulnerable to a b5-b4 pawn push. As such, Black only has 2 main responses.

/3...Nf6/ is by far Black's most common reply, and play from White typically transposes into a Semi-Slav with 4. Nc3, although some unique lines exist such as 4. e3, the Quiet Slav, where Nc3 is delayed or not played at all.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2PP4/5N2/PP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nf3/3...Nf6
rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2PP4/5N2/PP2P.x:
Black begins development of his minor pieces with 3...Nf6, which is invariably the best square for this knight, as it exerts control over the e4 square and adds protection to the d5-pawn.

White can respond to this move in a variety of ways:

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p1b2/2PP4/2N2N2/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/4. Nc3/4...Bf5
rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p1b2/2PP4/2N2N2/.x: This move looks natural, but it allows the annoying cxd5 cxd5 Qb3, losing a pawn if the bishop does not retreat to c8.

rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p1p2n2/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/4. Nc3/4...a6
rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p1p2n2/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/P.x:
The move 4...a6 introduces the Chebanenko (or Chameleon) Slav. Though it seems a small move, it prepares ideas of ...b5 (either to attack White's c4 pawn or to shore up Black's after ...dxc4) and eases the problems of developing Black's light-squared bishop, as now Qb3 can be met with ...Ra7.

The weakening of the b6 square, however, invites White to simply push - /5. c5/ is the most common response, gaining space on the queenside. In the resulting positions, it is very common for Black to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop, where it is a lot more useful by eyeing White's center.

rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p1p2n2/2Pp4/3P4/2N2N2/P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/4. Nc3/4...a6/5. c5
rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p1p2n2/2Pp4/3P4/2N2N2/P.x:
White plays 5. c5 to control the weak b6 square and forestall any ...dxc4 or ...b5 ideas. If White can make this space advantage permanent, they will have a very comfortable game, so Black needs to start planning a pawn break on either b6 or e5. To support this, the main move is /5...Nbd7/, developing the queen's knight to its best available square and preparing whichever break Black chooses.

The main alternatives are /5...Bf5/, developing the bishop before it gets blocked in by ...Nbd7, and /5...g6/, preparing a fianchetto.

5...Bg4 is also played occasionally, with the idea of pressuring the e5 square indirectly, but there is no reason White cannot simply occupy it at once with 6. Ne5.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/8/2pP4/2N2N2/PP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/4. Nc3/4...dxc4
rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/8/2pP4/2N2N2/PP2P.x: Black finally takes the sacrificial pawn with dxc4. Despite being known as the "Pure Slav," this move has about half the popularity of 4...e6, the Semi-Slav. The idea of this move is to threaten a pawn advance onto White's queenside. White can choose to either allow the queenside expansion and gambit the c-pawn, or they can prevent it and give Black time to develop the light-squared bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/8/P1pP4/2N2N2/1P2.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/4. Nc3/4...dxc4/5. a4
rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/8/P1pP4/2N2N2/1P2.x:
The advance of the a-pawn prevents Black from playing 5...b5, which in turn leaves the c4 pawn available for capture. This is White's most popular and ambitious response. Over the last century, there have been four major lines played by Black.

/5...Bf5/, the Czech variation, is by far the most testing and theoretical line. The bishop eyes at the center and makes it harder for White to play e4.

/5...Bg4/ is the Steiner variation. It is played quite often at the amateur level, but requires Black to understand the positions well to be played successfully. White's knight isn't pinned and can move to e5 with a tempo on the bishop.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1pP4/2N2N2/1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/4. Nc3/4...dxc4/5. a4/5...Bf5
rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1pP4/2N2N2/1.x:
Black develops their light-squared bishop. This is possible now because the threat of Qb3 is no longer present thanks to the pawn on c4.

White should try to regain their pawn, which can be done in two ways.

/6. e3/ is the Dutch variation. This is the classical main line. White tries to capture the pawn with 7. Bxc4 and continues the game by castling and preparing to play e4.

/6. Ne5/ is the central variation. Instead of recapturing the pawn with the bishop, White tries to do so with their knight instead. This is White's most ambitious option and leads to sharper positions.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/4Nb2/P1pP4/2N5/1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/4. Nc3/4...dxc4/5. a4/5...Bf5/6. Ne5
rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/4Nb2/P1pP4/2N5/1P.x:
White places their knight into the center to recapture the pawn on c4 while leaving the diagonal for the dark-squared bishop open. There are two theoretical responses for Black.

/6...Nbd7/ is the main move, letting White take on c4 and preparing to either put the knight on b6 or to play e5.

/6...e6/ is the Wiesbaden variation. This line involves White attempting to gain a lot of initiative and Black preventing it by sacrificing a piece for three pawns, generally leading to an endgame where Black tries to march an army of pawns down the board.

r2qkb1r/pp1npppp/2p2n2/4Nb2/P1pP4/2N5/1P.x: This is a simple developing move. White's only real follow-up is 7. Nxc4, keeping the knights in the center and recapturing the c4 pawn.

r2qkb1r/pp1npppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1NP4/2N5/1P2.x:
White recaptures the c4 pawn.

Black can now choose to either enter the Carlsbad variation with 7...Qc7 or to transfer the knight to b6 with 7...Nb6.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/1np2n2/5b2/P1NP4/2N5/1P2.x:
Black intends to trade off White's active knight. This move poses an immediate threat, so White's options are fairly limited.

/8. Ne5/ puts the knight back in the centre and declines the trade. This is the main line.

8. e3 intends to recapture the knight with the bishop.

8. Ne3 retreats the knight with a tempo on the bishop. The knight is not entirely misplaced here, since White's idea is to clamp down the d5-square and develop the light-squared bishop to g2 instead.

r3kb1r/ppqnpppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1NP4/2N5/1P2P.x:
Black develops the queen to c7 in order to prepare e5. This will likely lead to the Carlsbad variation.

White's main response is 8. g3 preparing to develop the dark-squared bishop to f4 where it can put pressure on the knight after 8...e5 9. dxe5 Nxe5. This also prepares to fianchetto the light-squared bishop.

r3kb1r/ppqnpppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1NP4/2N3P1/1P.x: This move prepares to develop both bishops; the dark-squared bishop to f4 and the light-squared bishop to g2. This move doesn't deter Black from playing /8...e5/ which has been prepared with Black's previous moves.

r3kb1r/ppqn1ppp/2p2n2/4pb2/P1NP4/2N3P1/1.x:
Black finally pushes the e pawn forward, releasing the dark-squared bishop and fighting for the center.

If White ignores the pawn and prepares to castle with 9. Bg2, Black can start building pressure with 9...Rd8, aiming at White's queen, and 10...Be6 pressuring the knight (if 9...O-O-O then 10. a5! followed by 11. Qa4 starts a nasty attack on the queenside).

Therefore, White's best option is 9. dxe5, exchanging pawns in the center.

r3kb1r/ppqn1ppp/2p2n2/4Pb2/P1N5/2N3P1/1P.x: White exchanges the pawns in the center. Black doesn't have many valid options other than 9...Nxe5, recapturing the pawn.

r3kb1r/ppq2ppp/2p2n2/4nb2/P1N5/2N3P1/1P2.x:
The central pawns have been exchanged. White can, and should, play 10. Bf4, developing the bishop and pinning the knight on e5. This also justifies White's previous move 8. g3.

White's knight on c4 is hanging, so there isn't many alternatives. 10. Nxe5? doesn't develop any of White's pieces and allows Black to quickly catch up in development.

r3kb1r/ppq2ppp/2p2n2/4nb2/P1N2B2/2N3P1/1.x:
This move pins the knight on e5 to the black queen, which is its only defender at the moment. Moving the knight isn't an option, so the only move to add another defender is 10...Nfd7.

10...Bd6?? fails to defend the knight because it loses a piece. The d6 square is attacked by both the c4 knight and the queen on d1 and only defended by Black's queen on c7.

r3kb1r/ppqn1ppp/2p5/4nb2/P1N2B2/2N3P1/1P.x: This move defends the pinned knight. White no longer has any moves to increase the pressure on the e5 knight, so play usually continues by developing the light-squared bishop with 11. Bg2.

White develops the light-squared bishop and prepares to castle short.
From this position, two moves have been played historically: f6 and g5.

11...f6 is the old mainline, defending the knight.

11...g5 is the most popular line nowadays and is considered the best move for Black.

r3kb1r/ppqn2pp/2p2p2/4nb2/P1N2B2/2N3P1/1.x:
This is the old mainline. Black protects the knight with a pawn in order to protect the knight.
The usual continuation after f6 is 12. O-O Nc5 13. Ne3 Bg6 14. b4.

r3kb1r/ppqn1p1p/2p5/4nbp1/P1N2B2/2N3P1/1.x:
11...g5 is the most popular line nowadays and is considered the best move for Black. Because the kingside pawn structure is significantly weakened, Black will usually resort to castling queenside.

12. Bxg5?? would blunder 12...Nxc4. The bishop can't stay on the same diagonal as the black queen, so some pieces have to be traded.

12. Bxe5 allows Black to secure the bishop pair after 12...Nxe5 but White gets compensation after 13. Qd4 f6 14. O-O-O preventing Black from castling queenside.

r3kb1r/ppqn1p1p/2p5/4nbp1/P4B2/2N1N1P1/1.x:
White decides to exchange the bishop pair with Black. After 12...gxf4 13. Nxf5 both sides will have one bishop left.

There are no alternatives to 12...gxf4, as they all lose material or give White a lot of initiative.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/4Nb2/P1pP4/2N5/1P.x:
Black prepares to develop their dark-squared bishop to b4 where it stands uncontested thanks to White's move 5. a4.

If White tries to recapture the c4 pawn immediately with 7. Nxc4?! Black can strike back 7...c5, putting pressure on White's centre and garnering an advantage in development.

The only move that preserves White's advantage is /7. f3/, trying to play e4 on the next move. This threat cannot be stopped by Black, who has to play for piece activity, potentially sacrificing a piece to destroy White's centre.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/4Nb2/P1pP4/2N2P2/.x:
White doesn't capture the c4-pawn. Instead, they prepare 8. e4, which comes with tempo on Black's bishop. With the support of the f-pawn, Black can't stop e4 from being played, so they must find an advantage by different means.

/7...Bb4/ is the main line. This move removes the knight's defence from e4 and has the idea of sacrificing the light-squared bishop on e4 in exchange for three pawns.

7...c5 tries to disrupt White's centre. After 8. e4 both 8...cxd4 and 8...Bg6 have been tried, but results have generally been favourable for White. This variation was also played in games 3, 5 and 8 of the 2010 World Chess Championship.

rn1qk2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/4Nb2/PbpP4/2N2P2/1.x:
Black makes use of the weakened b4-square, pressuring the knight on c3 and gaining a bit more control over e4.

The main line continues with /8. e4/, also known as the Sharp line. Black has to sacrifice their light-squared bishop for three pawns if they want to retain any winning chances.

/8. Nxc4/ is White's main alternative, avoiding many of the complications that ensue from 8. e4. The position branches out after Black castles.

8. Bg5 is a rare continuation that has lost it's popularity over time. Usually Black responds with 8...h6, which gives their light-squared bishop a nicer square to go to if e4 happens.

rn1qk2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/4Nb2/PbpPP3/2N2P2/.x:
White takes over the centre, attacking Black's bishop and opening up an attack on the c4-pawn. Retreating the bishop would be a mistake, since this gives White the full centre without any compensation.

Sacrificing the knight with 8...Nxe4? doesn't work, since after 9. fxe4 Qh4+ White can move their king to safety on the kingside. If 9. fxe4 Bxe4 Black doesn't have any pressure on the c3-knight, so 10. Be3 keeps everything held.

Thus, 8...Bxe4! is the main move to not have a passive position. White doesn't have much better than 9. fxe4, after which 9...Nxe4 threatens 10...Nxc3 11. bxc3 Bxc3+ 12. Bd2 Qxd4 to pick up a fifth pawn for the piece. White has two options in this position.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1pP3N/2N5/1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/4. Nc3/4...dxc4/5. a4/5...Bf5/6. Nh4
rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1pP3N/2N5/1P.x:
White immediately goes after Black's light-squared bishop. The usual response is 6...e6, opening up the dark-squared bishop and preparing to recapture with the e-pawn.

6...Bc8 has also been tried, retreating the bishop to its home-square and arguing that the knight on h4 is misplaced. In practice, Black scores poorly in this line.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1pP4/2N1PN2/.x:
White opens up the light-squared bishop in order to recapture the pawn on c4. In doing so, the movement of the dark-squared bishop is temporarily restricted in the hopes to open it up later with e4.

6...e6 is played almost every time, looking to develop the dark-squared bishop to the b4-square, which has been weakened by White's choice to prevent b5 with 5. a4.

/6...Na6/ is a rare sideline called the Lasker variation, where Black tries to place their knight on b4, instead of the dark-squared bishop.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/n1p2n2/5b2/P1pP4/2N1PN2/.x: This move has a similar idea to the Smyslov variation: to bring the knight to the outpost on b4. White can continue playing in their usual fashion: 7. Bxc4 Nb4 8. O-O e6 9. Qe2, after which White will be able to play e4 without any issues. 9. Ne5 transposes to a line that can be reached from the Krause attack with 6...Na6, as can be seen in Carlsen - Vladimir, 2008.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/P1pP4/2N1PN2/.x:
Black prepares to develop the dark-squared bishop to the b4-square, which was weakened by White's move 5. a4.

White can now simply recapture the c-pawn with /7. Bxc4/.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/P1BP4/2N1PN2/.x:
White reclaims their lost pawn. Black should follow up with /7...Bb4/, pinning White's knight and putting it on a square where it can't be kicked out by pawns.

/7...Nbd7/ is also possible, but will most likely transpose back into the main line.

rn1qk2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2/1.x:
Black develops the bishop to its most natural square.

White should simply castle kingside /8. O-O/ to get out of the pin and start preparing e4.

White castles their king to safety to unpin the knight and to start preparing e4.

Black can now choose to either play /8...Nbd7/ or /8...O-O/. Play is very likely to transpose, but different deviations from the main line are possible depending on which move Black plays first. The main difference is that after 8...O-O, Black has many possibilities of fully preventing e4, while after 8...Nbd7 trying to do so is more dangerous for Black.

In both positions, White is likely to play Qe2, preparing e4. There is, however, another option.

r2qk2r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2/.x:
White chooses to develop their knight instead of castling. This move prevents White's knight from jumping to e5 and chasing away the bishop.

White does still have the option of /9. Nh4/, transposing into the Bled attack and claiming the bishop pair.

More common, however, is /9. Qe2/, preparing e4 and going into the main line.
White prepares to push e4. Unlike after 8...O-O, Black has no real way of preventing this. /9...O-O/ transposes to the main line, while /9...Bg6/ still gives Black room for deviation.

r2qk2r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pnb1/8/PbBP4/2N1PN2/1.x: Black prophylactically retreats the bishop so that /10. e4/ doesn't come with tempo. This allows for Black to win a pawn at the cost of giving White a big initiative.

r2qk2r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pnb1/8/PbBPP3/2N2N2/1.x:
White takes up the full center. If Black simply plays /10...O-O/ we are once again following the main line.

One thing that sets this position apart from 8...O-O 9. Qe2 9...Bg6 is that White was actually able to play e4. Black can take the pawn but it is not free. 10...Bxc3 removes an important defender of e4. After 11. bxc3 Nxe4 12. Ba3! Black is up a pawn, but White has prevented them from castling king-side. Black will have to castle queen-side, where White has the open b-file and the far-advanced a-pawn.

If Black gets greedy and tries to win more pawns with 12...Nxc3? White is quick to get the upper hand after 13. Qb2!, forking the knight and the pawn on b7.

r2q1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pnb1/8/PbBPP3/2N2N2/.x:
Black retreats the bishop, keeping an eye on e4. White must either protect or push the pawn.

/11. Bd3/ defends the pawn and threatens to trade off the light-squared bishops after 12. e5.

11. e5 immediately chases away the knight, but is likely to transpose to the lines with 11. Bd3.

r2q1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2.x: This move develops the knight to it's most natural square, but also invites White to play /10. e4/. This move also sets up Nb6, attacking the light-squared bishop and uncovering the black queen's attack on the d4-pawn. This tactic can cost White a pawn if they are not careful with their pawn-advance.

rn1q1rk1/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2/.x:
Black quickly castles their king to safety. This gives Black the option of playing 9...Bg6, which prevents 10. e4 and results in positions where White doesn't get as much central control.

White's main option is still /9. Qe2/, threatening to play 10. e4.

White can also opt for /9. Nh4/, transposing into the Bled attack.
White is threatening to play 10. e4 with a tempo on the bishop. If Black allows this, they will have to fend off White's king-side attack, which comes in very quickly.

rn1q1rk1/pp3ppp/2p1pnb1/8/PbBP4/2N1PN2/1.x:
Black prevents e4 tactically. By retreating the bishop, 10. e4? is no longer played with tempo and in response Black plays 10...Bxc3! 11. bxc3 Nxe4 .

Instead, White should chase Black's light-squared bishop with /10. Ne5/.

Some players have played 10. Rd1?! in this position, since this move is played anyways. But this is inaccurate, because 10...Nbd7 now prevents the knight from jumping to e5 and trading off the bishop. While chess engines evaluate 10. Rd1 as approximately equal, Black outperforms White in practice.

r2q1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBPP3/2N2N2.x:
White has been building up to this move for a while. This central expansion hits Black's light-squared bishop with tempo. Black has two squares to retreat the bishop to.

/10...Bg6/ lets the bishop keep an eye on the e4-pawn, which must now either be pushed to e5 or protected by White's bishop.

/10...Bg4/ immediately pins White's knight on f3, making the e5 pawn-break possible and also allowing various tactics revolving around the d4-pawn unless defended again.

r2q1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pnb1/8/Pb1PP3/2NB1N2.x: /11...Bh5/ sidesteps the discovered attack and pins the f3 knight.

r2q1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/7b/Pb1PP3/2NB1N2.x: White can finally go through with their plan of taking over the center with /12. e5/.

r2q1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/4P2b/Pb1P4/2NB1N.x:
White finally takes over the centre, with tempo on Black's knight.

Black's main response is 12...Nd5, trying to trade it off for White's c3 knight. Nearly all games continue 13. Nxd5 cxd5 14. Qe3. White unpins their knight and prepares Ng5 to start an attack on Black's king-side. Black has a few possible responses.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/8/P1pP2b1/2N2N2/1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/4. Nc3/4...dxc4/5. a4/5...Bg4
rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/8/P1pP2b1/2N2N2/1.x:
Instead of the usual 5...Bf5, Black opts to put the bishop on g4, harassing White's knight. However, because the e-pawn hasn't advanced, the knight isn't actually pinned to the queen, so White can play 6. Ne5 with a tempo on the Bishop.

After the bishop retreats with 6...Bh5, White has the option to go for either 7. f3, preparing e4, or 7. g3, preparing to fianchetto.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/n1p2n2/8/P1pP4/2N2N2/1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/4. Nc3/4...dxc4/5. a4/5...Na6
r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/n1p2n2/8/P1pP4/2N2N2/1P.x:
Black develops the knight to a6 in order to later transfer it to b4, which was weakened by White's move 5. a4. This does however give White time to occupy the center with 6. e4, or to support the d-pawn with 6. e3.

Regardless of whether White pushes the e-pawn one or two squares, Black's response is going to be 6...Bg4, pinning the knight on f3 to the white queen. This is different from the Steiner variation, where the knight isn't actually pinned and can move to e5, gaining a tempo on the bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/8/2pPP3/2N2N2/PP3.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/4. Nc3/4...dxc4/5. e4
rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/8/2pPP3/2N2N2/PP3.x:
White occupies the center with their pawns. In doing so, Black gets the chance to hold onto the c4-pawn with the move b5, expanding on the queenside.

The main line continues 6. e5 Nd5 7. a4 e6 8. axb5 Nxc3 9. bxc3 cxb5 after which Black has to ward off White's attack on the kingside. In practice, Black scores well in this line. This is also backed by computer evaluations, which tend to prefer Black.

A better try for White is to play 6. Be2, where White tries to castle quickly and chip away at Black's queenside pawns with moves like b3.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2p2np1/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/4. Nc3/4...g6
rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2p2np1/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/P.x:
Black intends to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop.

White has the option of transposing into an exchange variation with /5. cxd5/. This is quite a popular way to meet the Schlechter at the master level, since 4...g6 isn't a very useful move for Black in the exchange variation.

Apart from that, White can try to develop the dark-squared bishop outside of the pawn-chain with /5. Bf4/ or /5. Bg5/. More popular, however, is /5. e3/, preparing to develop the light-squared bishop and defending c4.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2PP4/5N2/PPQ1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/4. Qc2
rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2PP4/5N2/PPQ1.x:
This move is a proper sideline of the Slav defence. White defends the c4-pawn and prepares e4 at the same time. Despite defending c4, it does not prevent its capture: 4...dxc4 is the main move in this position.

After 4...dxc4 5. Qxc4 Black can safely develop the light-squared bishop before playing ...e6. White usually employs a kingside fianchetto. Qb3 is usually met with ...Qb6, recapturing with the a-pawn to open up the a-file if White takes.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3P4/3P4/5N2/PP2PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/4. cxd5
rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3P4/3P4/5N2/PP2PP.x:
After this move, the tension in the center is relieved, often allowing Black equality. Because of this, this variation often ends in a draw.

Black's only decent move is to complete the exchange of pawns with 4...cxd5. After the exchange, Black will find it difficult to win unless White is overly ambitious.

The most draw-ish line of them all is the symmetrical line. Black keeps copying White and both sides exchange minor pieces: 4...cxd5 5. Nc3 Nc6 6. Bf4 Bf5 7. e3 e6 8. Bd3 Bxd3 9. Qxd3 Bd6 10. Bxd6 Qxd6 11. O-O O-O . Most players agree to a draw in this or any of the following positions.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2PP4/4PN2/PP3.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/4. e3
rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2PP4/4PN2/PP3.x:
White plays the quiet move 4. e3, introducing more positional play as white is yet to commit the b1-knight to c3. As such, the position remains flexible for both sides and a variety of openings can occur.

Black's most common responses are /4...Bf5/ and 4...e6, with the latter frequently transposing back into a mainline Semi-Slav defence. However, White can avoid such a Semi-Slav transposition on move 5 with a variety of options, such as Bd3, b3, Nbd2, and Qc2 rather than Nc3. Other responses from Black include /4...a6/, /4...g6/, and /4...Bg4/, all of which are frequently played.

White tends to score similarly in this quiet variation compared to the mainline Slav variations.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p1b2/2PP4/4PN2/P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/4. e3/4...Bf5
rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p1b2/2PP4/4PN2/P.x:
Black makes use of the opportunity to develop the light-squared bishop. They don't have to be afraid of 5. cxd5 cxd5 6. Qb3 Qc7 since the f6-knight prevents Qb3 from being an effective fork of the b7 and d5 pawns.

White's most promising response is /5. Nc3/, developing the pieces actively and putting more pressure on d5.

The most popular alternatives are 5. cxd5, transposing into the exchange variation where White's dark-squared bishop is stuck behind the pawns, and 5. Bd3, trading off the light-squared bishops.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2PP2b1/4PN2/P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/4. e3/4...Bg4
rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2PP2b1/4PN2/P.x:
Black develops the bishop to g4, pinning the f3 knight to the queen. White will generally want to get rid of this pin quickly, and has many ways to do so.

/5. h3/ immediately asks Black the question of whether they want to exchange their bishop for the knight. Both 5...Bh5 and 5...Bxf3 are viable options. After 5...Bh5 White will usually strike back with g4 soon.

5. Nc3 doesn't address the pin yet, but White will likely play h3 soon, often transposing into lines where White begins with h3 instead.

5. Qb3 breaks the pin by moving away the queen, threatening to take the b7 pawn. After either 5...Qb6 or 5...Qc7 White has the looming threat of playing Ne5 with tempo on Black's bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/2PP4/5N2/PP2PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nf3/3...e6
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/2PP4/5N2/PP2PP.x:

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3P4/3P4/8/PP2PPPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. cxd5
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3P4/3P4/8/PP2PPPP/R.x:
After this move, the tension in the center is relieved often allowing Black equality due to the symmetrical position. Because of this, this variation often ends in a draw.

Black's only good move is to complete the exchange of pawns with /3...cxd5/, and accept a symmetrical position. However, Nf6!? might be interesting as the position transposes to QGD, Marshall defence, Tan Gambit although this is rarely seen in high-level games. 3...Qxd5?! should be avoided as 4. Nc3 gains a lot of tempo, and allows White a crushing spacial advantage in the center.

After 3...cxd5, either side will find it difficult to win unless the other is over-ambitious.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/3p4/3P4/8/PP2PPPP/RNB.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. cxd5/3...cxd5
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/3p4/3P4/8/PP2PPPP/RNB.x:
This is Black's best option, accepting a symmetrical position.

While normal development moves will suffice, White can try to make it harder for Black to get the light-squared bishop out by delaying the combination of Nf3 and e3, which would allow Black to pin the knight to the queen with Bg4.

The most popular continuation for White is the combination of Nc3, Bf4 and e3. Usually White starts with /4. Nc3/ which is more flexible than the immediate, but totally viable, /4. Bf4/.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/3p4/3P4/2N5/PP2PPPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. cxd5/3...cxd5/4. Nc3
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/3p4/3P4/2N5/PP2PPPP/R.x:
White doesn't reveal their intentions yet and simply develops the knight to its most natural square, putting pressure on d5.

Black's main response is /4...Nf6/, overprotecting the d5 pawn and developing the kingside.

Black can also play /4...Nc6/, often transposing to the same lines as 4...Nf6. However, this move does give White additional options. One of those options being 5. e4, which would have been prevented by 4...Nf6, transposing into a position resembling the French defence.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/3p4/3P4/2N5/PP2PPPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. cxd5/3...cxd5/4. Nc3/4...Nf6
rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/3p4/3P4/2N5/PP2PPPP.x:
The most common move for Black. White now has to reveal their opening plan.

/5. Bf4/ is the most common move, delaying Nf3 and developing the bishop.

/5. Nf3/ is the second-most common move. This allows a completely equal position and is often used if playing for a draw, especially the variation 5...Nc6 6. Bf4 Bf5 7. e3 e6 8. Bd3 Bxd3 9. Qxd3 Bd6 10. Bxd6 Qxd6

/5. f3/ is the Boor attack, a rare sideline where White tries to take over the center by preparing e4.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pP4/8/PP2PPPP/RNB.x:
The Queen's Gambit Accepted has a rich heritage in chess, both sides played by many of the world champions through the years. It is not really much of a gambit since White can recover the pawn immediately with 3. Qa4+, though unless White wants the queen placed on c4, this is unnecessary.

Black does better not to hold on to the pawn. Attempts to immediately support it with either 3...b5 or 3...Be6 are not advisable. 3...b5 is countered by 4. a4, threatening Black's pawn chain at its base, and 3...Be6 allows 4. e4, with White grabbing a large share of the center and threatening a later d5 to kick away the bishop.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pP4/2N5/PP2PPPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...dxc4/3. Nc3
rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pP4/2N5/PP2PPPP/R.x: Two players have labeled this move misguided, as the knight is vulnerable here to a b7-b5-b4 advance. It also doesn't control d4 or e5, two important squares in Queen's Gambit Accepted positions. The most common and highest-scoring response for Black is to follow up with 3...a6, preparing a future ...b5 thrust which will introduce the idea of attacking the knight with ...b4, whilst also claiming that Black can keep ahold of the pawn with suitable defence. This usually leads to a firefight on the queenside, with a4 usually being played sooner rather than later by White in order to disrupt Black's defence of the c-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1p1pp/8/5p2/2pP4/2N5/PP2PPPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...dxc4/3. Nc3/3...f5
rnbqkbnr/ppp1p1pp/8/5p2/2pP4/2N5/PP2PPPP.x: This move is too weakening. It weakens the entire e-file, and the c4-g8 diagonal. In Match 1, Game 8, Labourdonnais-McDonnell, McDonnell played f5 and lost quickly.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pP4/5N2/PP2PPPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...dxc4/3. Nf3
rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pP4/5N2/PP2PPPP/R.x: This is the classical continuation. White pursues its development and increases control over the e5 square. Black's main reply is 3...Nf6.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/2pP4/5N2/PP2PPPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...dxc4/3. Nf3/3...Nf6
rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/2pP4/5N2/PP2PPPP.x: Black develops and prevents White from establishing a pawn center with e4.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/2pP4/4PN2/PP3PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...dxc4/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/3. e3
rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/2pP4/4PN2/PP3PPP.x: #REDIRECT Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...dxc4/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/4. e3

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/2pP4/4PN2/PP3PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...dxc4/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/4. e3/4...e6
rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/2pP4/4PN2/PP3PPP.x:
This move prepares to release the f8-bishop into action. The light-squared bishop is supposed to go to b7, but sometimes has to settle for the passive d7-square.

White should follow up on their previous moves and capture the pawn on c4 with /5. Bxc4/.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/2BP4/4PN2/PP3PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...dxc4/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/4. e3/4...e6/5. Bxc4
rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/2BP4/4PN2/PP3PPP.x:
White recaptures the pawn while developing the light-squared bishop. This also allows White to quickly castle kingside.

Black should try to stay active and strike at the center with /5...c5/.

Black could also play /5...a6/, trying to get in 6...b5 with a tempo on White's bishop. The move a6 is also part of the main line and therefore likely to transpose with 6. O-O c5.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2p5/2BP4/4PN2/PP3PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...dxc4/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/4. e3/4...e6/5. Bxc4/5...c5
rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2p5/2BP4/4PN2/PP3PP.x:
Black strikes back at the center, potentially leaving White with an isolated queen's pawn after ...cxd4.

White's main option is /6. O-O/, getting their king out of the center.

An alternative is /6. Qe2/, the Furman variation. This supports the advance of the e-pawn and enables dxc5 without trading the queens.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pP4/4P3/PP3PPP/RN.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...dxc4/3. e3

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pPP3/8/PP3PPP/RNB.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...dxc4/3. e4
rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pPP3/8/PP3PPP/RNB.x: In this line, white moves immediately to reclaim the "gambit" pawn. The rationale is simple. In most lines of the QGA, white allows black to play ...Nf6 which usually means white has to play f2-f3 in preparation for e3-e4. By playing e2-e4 now, white establishes broad control of the center without losing time. This also has the potential advantage of allowing the c1-bishop to develop unhindered. Also, black is forced to choose a central strategy now or else face being dominated by white's center and development. Black is no worse in these lines, though, than in the classical QGA's, and can obtain counterplay in these lines as well as the others.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/2pPP3/8/PP3PPP/RN.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...dxc4/3. e4/3...e5
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/2pPP3/8/PP3PPP/RN.x:
This is the most common and ambitious reply by Black. This move attacks White's centre and opens up the dark-squared bishop.

There is only one move that preserves White's advantage, that being /4. Nf3/, attacking e5 and defending d4.

4. Bxc4? doesn't work due to 4...Qxd4! 5. Qxd4 exd4 6. Nf3 c5 and Black is able to build a fairly stable centre.

4. dxe5? also does not work due to 4...Qxd1!, forcing a trade of queens with Kxd1, and although material is even, White is exposed in the center and loses castling rights.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/.x: With 2...e6, Black declines the Queen's Gambit in the traditional fashion. 2...e6 bolsters the d5 pawn and opens a diagonal for the development of Black's dark-squared bishop. However, 2...e6 also blocks the c8-h3 diagonal for Black's light-squared bishop. Finding a way to productively develop this piece is a perennial challenge for Black players in the QGD.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1bppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...Be7
rnbqk1nr/ppp1bppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.x:
Black stops White from playing the immediate 4. Bg5, practically forcing White into one of three options:

/4. Nf3/, simply developing the knight. This is the most common and flexible response, since White doesn't reveal anything about their setup yet. If Black plays 4...Nf6 then 5. Bg5 transposes back into the main lines.

/4. Bf4/ develops the bishop to f4 instead. White intends to enter the Harrwitz attack.

/4. cxd5/ transposes into an exchange variation where Black has already played Be7, preventing White from usefully developing the bishop to g5.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N5/PP2.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Bg5
rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N5/PP2.x: With 4. Bg5 White pins Black's knight against the black queen.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N5/PP2.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Bg5/4...Be7
rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N5/PP2.x:
Black unpins the knight and prepares to castle short.

White's two main responses /5. e3/ and /5. Nf3/ are very likely to transpose, so the order doesn't particularly matter.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N1P3/P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Bg5/4...Be7/5. e3
rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N1P3/P.x: With the dark-squared bishop developed, White can safely create a dark-squared pawn-chain.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N1PN2.x:
White proceeds with normal development. Black now has two options.

* Go into the classical variation with /6...Nbd7/.
* Go for either Lasker's defense or the Tartakower variation with /6...h6/.

r1bq1rk1/pppnbppp/4pn2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N1PN2.x:
With this move Black enters the Classical variation. This is an older and well-studied variation that has stood the test of time, as it is still played to this day. Due to its age, White has developed many responses to it over time.

* /7. Rc1/ is the main line, developing the rook to the to-be-opened c-file.
* /7. Qc2/ is the Rubinstein attack. White develops the queen to watch over the b1-h7 diagonal. 
* /7. cxd5/ releases the tension from the center and transposes into an exchange variation.
* /7. Bd3/ is the Botvinnik variation, in which Black gains a few tempi on White's bishop with 7...cxd5 and, later on, Nb6.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bpp1/4pn1p/3p2B1/2PP4/2N1PN.x:
Black pushes the bishop away, likely intending to go for either the Tartakower or Lasker's defence.

Apart from White's main option /7. Bh4/ they can also avoid these theoretical lines by playing /7. Bxf6/.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bpp1/4p2p/3p4/2PPn2B/2N1PN2.x:
Black centralizes the knight, opening up an attack on White's dark-squared bishop.

The mainline continues by trading the dark-squared bishops and later the knights as well.

rnbq1rk1/p1p1bpp1/1p2pn1p/3p4/2PP3B/2N1P.x: 7...b6 enters the Tartakower defence, where Black hopes to develop the light-squared bishop. While it looks like Black intends to fianchetto the bishop, this isn't necessarily true. If White tries to blunt the a8-h1 diagonal immediately with 8. cxd5, Black will nonetheless be able to develop the bishop: 8. cxd5 Nxd5 9. Bxe7 Qxe7 10. Nxd5 exd5 and Black can now put the bishop somewhere on the c8-h3 diagonal instead (usually going to e6).

r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/4pn2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N5/PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Bg5/4...Nbd7
r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/4pn2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N5/PP.x: With 4...Nbd7, black intends to play the Cambridge Springs Defense, which continues 5. Nf3 c6 6. e3 Qa5. The Cambridge Springs Defense is a solid line of the QGD and is often played both in the amateur level (because of the easier to understand theme) and the grandmaster level. This move also sets a trap that has ensnared quite a few players. White can continue 5. cxd5 exd5, resulting in a position that resembles the QGD Exchange variation (which is fine for both camps), as long as he/she doesn't play 6. Nxd5??. While it superficially appears to win a pawn (because the black knight is pinned), black can capture with his knight with 6... Nxd5!.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/1bPP4/2N2N2/PP2.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Nf3/4...Bb4
rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/1bPP4/2N2N2/PP2.x:
The mainlines continues either

* /5. Bg5/ h6 (Moscow variation)
* /5. Bg5/ dxc4 (Vienna variation)

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p4/2PP1B2/2N2N2/P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Nf3/4...Be7/5. Bf4
rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p4/2PP1B2/2N2N2/P.x:
White develops the bishop to f4. This just looks like a standard developing move, but it is extremely aggressive. With the bishop on f4 instead of g5, White avoids piece exchanges, and often castles queenside while Black castles kingside, leading to sharp opposite-side castling positions.

Black has nothing better to do than castle.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p4/2PP1B2/2N1PN2.x:
Blackburne Variation

After the developing move 6. e3, Black has 3 choices:

-She can take advantage of the Bishop being on f4 instead of g5, which doesn’t pressure the d5 pawn, and play 6...c5 without fear of being forced into an IQP structure. However, this line is entry to the rabbit hole and leads to very complicated positions.

-6...Nbd7 is a more solid choice and avoids the complications of the main line. However, it allows 7. c5 resulting in white having a pleasant space advantage.

-6...b6 is the most solid way for Black to play, resulting in positions resembling the Tartokower Defense.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/4pn2/2pp4/2PP1B2/2N1PN2.x:
6...c5

Black immediately strikes the White centre with ...c7-c5. This takes advantage of the Bishop being on f4 instead of g5, which applies less pressure on d5. To demonstrate, after 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. Nf3 Be7 5. Bg5 O-O 6. e3 h6 7. Bh4, 7...c5 can be met with 8. Bxf6 Bxf6 9. cxd5 exd5 10. dxc5, and Black is left with a suboptimal isolated queen’s pawn structure.

White’s only move is the Botvinnik exchange: 7. dxc5, forcing the black bishop on e7 to waste a tempo. 7. cxd5 can be met with ...Nxd5, and 7. Bd3 or 7. Be2 can be met with ...dxc4, which all allow black to equalise comfortably.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/4pn2/2Pp4/2P2B2/2N1PN2/.x:
7. dxc5

White captures the c-pawn with 7. dxc5, forcing the black bishop on e7 to waste a tempo with 7...Bxc5. Note that 7...dxc4 leads to a favorable endgame for white after 8. Bxc4 Qxd1+ 9. Rxd1, where white enjoys more active pieces.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/4pn2/2bp4/2P2B2/2N1PN2/P.x:
7...Bxc5

Black recaptures the pawn. Now White can play the unambitious 8. cxd5 and saddle black with an isolani, or continue going down the rabbit hole with the mainline 8. Qc2, where the queen points towards the black kingside. It should be noted that 8. a3 transposes into the mainline.

8. Qc2

White activates the queen, who points towards the black kingside. Black develops with 8...Nc6

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2bp4/2P2B2/2N1PN2.x:
8...Nc6

Black simply develops. White continues with 9. a3, an important move to control b4 and prepare b2-b4.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2bp4/2P2B2/P1N1PN.x:
9. a3

This move is important to control the b4 square and support b2-b4. Black is forced to play 9...Qa5, which prevents b4 by pinning the a3 pawn to the rook and pins the c3 knight to the king. This also supports ...Nb4.

r1b2rk1/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/q1bp4/2P2B2/P1N1PN.x:
9...Qa5

This move is forced, pinning the a3 pawn to the rook, preventing b2-b4 and supporting ...Nb4 ideas. White has a sideline and 2 mainline moves.

10. Nd2 is the sideline, avoiding the complications of the mainlines. As Nb3 is threatened, black responds with ...Be7.

The mainlines 10. Rd1 and 10. O-O-O are not for the faint of heart, as they lead to wild, extremely complicated positions.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2pp4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Nf3/4...c5
rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2pp4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.x:
Unlike the regular Tarrasch, in the Semi-Tarrasch Defense Black does not accept an isolated pawn, since he intends to recapture on d5 with the knight (as after 5.cxd5, 5...exd5 has long been known to be dubious after 6.Bg5), but he cedes a spatial advantage to White.

After 4...c5, White usually plays 5.cxd5 Nxd5 6.e3 or 6.e4, which leads to different types of middlegame play and has attracted the interest of strong players with both colors since the early twentieth century.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/2pP4/2N2N2/PP2PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Nf3/4...dxc4
rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/2pP4/2N2N2/PP2PP.x:
4...dxc4 is a very aggressive response by Black leading to very double-edged positions. Black gives up some central control, allowing for White to build up a big center that Black tries to tear down later.

5. e4 is White's main response, taking up the entire center and preparing to recapture the pawn with the bishop.

5. e3 is the quiet variation. Positions often resemble those of the Queens Gambit accepted with 3. Nf3.

5. Qa4+ is a sideline with positions similar to the Semi Slav defence.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/2pPP3/2N2N2/PP3P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Nf3/4...dxc4/5. e4
rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/2pPP3/2N2N2/PP3P.x:
White takes up the center and opens up the light-squared bishop to recapture the pawn on c4.

Black can choose to go into the sharp mainline with 5...Bb4 or to hang onto the pawn a little longer with 5...b5.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/1bpPP3/2N2N2/PP3P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Nf3/4...dxc4/5. e4/5...Bb4
rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/1bpPP3/2N2N2/PP3P.x:
Black pins the c3 knight, removing the only defender of the e4 pawn.

6. Bg5 is White's main response, pinning the f6 knight to the queen which indirectly defends the e4 pawn.

6. Bxc4 is a sideline, letting Black take the e4 pawn for faster development.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/6B1/1bpPP3/2N2N2/PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Nf3/4...dxc4/5. e4/5...Bb4/6. Bg5
rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/6B1/1bpPP3/2N2N2/PP.x: White pins the f6 knight, indirectly defending the e4 pawn. Black's main option is 6...c5 striking at White's center.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3p4/3P4/2N5/PP2PPPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. cxd5/4...exd5
rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3p4/3P4/2N5/PP2PPPP.x:
4...exd5

With this move, Black frees up his light squared bishop, which was originally blocked with the move 2...e6. In addition, the classic Carlsbad pawn structure is entered, in which White has a pawn majority in the centre, and Black has a pawn majority on the queenside.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2pp4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...c5
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2pp4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.x:
Black aggressively attempts to gain space in the center, with the caveat of a potentially isolated pawn on d5 after a few pawn exchanges. The isolated queen's pawn is one of the reasons many players prefer to play the Semi-Tarrasch instead.

White has the options of taking on d5, taking on c5 and protecting the pawn.

/4. cxd5/ is considered to be the main line, making sure the c3 knight won't be pushed around by Black's pawns and trying to create an isolated queen's pawn to play against.

/4. e3/ is White's main sideline, which equalizes for Black quite quickly. After both sides have developed the knights the position is completely symmetrical.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2pP4/3P4/2N5/PP2PPPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...c5/4. cxd5
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2pP4/3P4/2N5/PP2PPPP.x:
White captures the d5 pawn in an attempt to give Black an isolated queen's pawn. Black has two viable responses:

/4...exd5/ is the main line, replacing the captured pawn to control the center.

/4...cxd4/ is the Schara gambit, luring White's queen into the center in order to develop quickly with tempo on the queen.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/3P4/3p4/2N5/PP2PPPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...c5/4. cxd5/4...cxd4
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/3P4/3p4/2N5/PP2PPPP/.x:
Instead of the usual 4...exd5 Black opts to gambit a pawn for rapid development.

The immediate /5. Qxd4/ runs into many tempo gaining moves, the first of which is 5...Nc6, making use of the fact that the pawn is pinned. The line continues 6. Qd1 exd5 7. Qxd5 and black can choose to play 7...Be6 going into the Von Hennig gambit, trading White's queen which was moved three times in the opening already.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/8/2pp4/3P4/2N5/PP2PPPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...c5/4. cxd5/4...exd5
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/8/2pp4/3P4/2N5/PP2PPPP/R.x:
Black recaptures on d5, keeping a pawn in the center.

White usually continues developing the knights and preparing to fianchetto the light-squared bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...c6
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.x:
In this position, by delaying Nf6, Black keeps many opportunities open. They can keep on playing in the normal Queen's Gambit Declined (QGD) fashion with 4...Nf6 (whether White plays e3 or Nf3), or can try other options.

/4. Nf3/ can lead to regular QGD games or alternatively the Noteboom variation: 4...dxc4. Here, Black aims to get two passed pawns on the flank in exchange for White's big center. The middlegame is critical, but if Black survives, the endgame will be in their favor.

On the other hand /4. e3/ can lead to a stonewall defense position with 4...f5, where Black's usual plan is a quick attack on the king side and can often involve a rook lift to f6.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...c6/4. Nf3
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.x: White develops the knight and leaves the opening choice to Black. The move /4...Nf6/ transposes into the Semi-Slav defence, while /4...dxc4/ enters the sharp Noteboom variation.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/2pP4/2N2N2/PP2PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...c6/4. Nf3/4...dxc4
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/2pP4/2N2N2/PP2PP.x:
With this move Black enters the aggressive Noteboom variation.

White can attempt to win back the pawn like in the Alapin Slav with /5. a4/ but Black can take advantage of that move with 5...Bb4. After 6. e3, attacking the pawn, Black can defend it with 6...b5, making use of the fact that after 7. axb5 cxb5 White's knight on c3 is still pinned and can't capture the pawn on b5.

White's other option is to try to win back the pawn with the immediate /5. e3/ but Black will respond with 5...b5, defending the pawn. After 6. a4 Black has successfully provoked White into weakening the b4-square, where Black will once again place the dark-squared bishop, transposing into the previous line.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/2PPP3/2N5/PP3P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...c6/4. e4
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/2PPP3/2N5/PP3P.x: This move controls the center and creates a huge pawn roller. Black's c8-bishop will be blocked and inactive for some time. However, White will have to sacrifice a pawn in a few moves if they want to fight for the edge. Black hasn't moved a single piece yet and put all their central pawns on light squares. White quickly got e4 in.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/2PPN3/8/PP3PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...c6/4. e4/4...dxe4/5. Nxe4
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/2PPN3/8/PP3PPP/R.x: Any move other than 5...Bb4+ is generally unfavorable for Black.

rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/1bPPN3/8/PP3PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...c6/4. e4/4...dxe4/5. Nxe4/5...Bb4
rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/1bPPN3/8/PP3PPP/.x:
This move is Black's best option to fight for an advantage. It forces White to either gambit the d4 pawn for activity, or to retreat the knight back to c3, "losing" a tempo in the process.

/6. Bd2/ is the main move, blocking the check and attacking Black's bishop at the same time. This does however block the white queen from defending the d4 pawn, allowing 6...Qxd4, which gambits the pawn in exchange for quick development and active pieces.

/6. Nc3/ is the Forgotten variation, a sideline where White holds onto the d4 pawn, keeping material equal.

rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/1bPPN3/8/PP1B1PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...c6/4. e4/4...dxe4/5. Nxe4/5...Bb4/6. Bd2
rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/1bPPN3/8/PP1B1PP.x: This move blocks the check and attacks Black's bishop, but loses sight of the d4-pawn. /6...Qxd4/ picks up the gambitted pawn and threatens the knight on e4.

rnb1k1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/1bPqN3/8/PP1B1PP.x: Black takes the gambitted pawn and will be up material for the time being. This opening doesn't come without compensation for White. After /7. Bxb4/ White will have dominance over Black's weakened dark squares.

rnb1k1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/1BPqN3/8/PP3PPP/.x: White takes Black's dark-squared bishop. White's dark-squared bishop is now placed on a very active diagonal, cutting through d6, e7 and f8. Black should play 7...Qxe4+ to not be down a piece.

rnb1k1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/1BP1q3/8/PP3PPP/.x:
Black recaptures the piece. This is the starting point of the Marshall gambit. White has two main ways of blocking the check, both leading to complex positions where White has to find a way to convert their lead in development into a tangible advantage. White should generally avoid trading pieces, especially queens, as any endgame will favour Black.

/8. Be2/ is the main line, blocking the check with the bishop. This leaves the g2-pawn undefended, but taking it would be unwise, since it allows White to develop even more quickly with Bf3, Ne2 and then Rg2 comes with tempo.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/6P1/PP2PP1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. g3
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/6P1/PP2PP1.x:
White prepares to fianchetto their bishop. White chooses a Catalan-style set up, an approach that combines c4 and d4 with a king's side fianchetto.

This is a less common move order. Black usually develops their knight next, 3...Nf6, and the same Catalan position is reached as if the game had played out in the order 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 e6 3. g3 d5.

r1bqkb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/8/2BP4/4P3/PP3PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. e3/2...Nf6/3. c4/3...dxc4/4. Bxc4/4...Nc6
r1bqkb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/8/2BP4/4P3/PP3PP.x:
This move is the main move and where is diverged most of the lines of the Kurtz opening, some like the main line, the Benz Variation, the Silent Game, etc.

It is a door for a big center attack, and White does everything to stop 5... e5.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.x:
White offers their e4 pawn in exchange for quick development and open lines. At the professional level this move is considered somewhat suspect, but Black must be careful if they choose to take the pawn as there are many traps in this opening.

2...dxe4 accepts the gambit.

Black has three ways to decline the gambit.
*2...e6 transposes to the French Defence
*2...c6 transposes to the Caro-Kann Defence
*2...Nc6 transposes to the Nimzowitsch Defence
*2...c5 is a largely unexplored countergambit.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2pp4/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.x:
An unusual countergambit to the Blackmar-Diemer or Smith-Morra gambits. It superficially resembles a reversed Albin countergambit, but with White to move.

White can capture either of the pawns and come out ahead.

If 3. dxc5 dxe4 leads to a queen trade. Most common in amateur games is 3...d4?, which seems to take space but just leaves the pawn stranded after 4. Nf3 (preventing ...e5) Nc6 5. c3. 3...Nf6 is an improvement.

If 3. exd5 Qxd5 then 4. Ne2 is best to defend the d-pawn (if 4. Nf3 then ...Bg4, pinning the knight, cannot be met with f3) 4...Nf6 5. Nbc3 Qd7 6. d5. Otherwise this probably leads to a queen trade too, e.g. 4. Nc3 Qxd4 5. Qxd4 cxd4 6. Nb5 Na6.

rn1qkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/5b2/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2PPP.x: Bf5 defends the pawn on e4 and develops the queenside bishop, with intentions of keeping the pawn as it is a thorn to White who can't play Nf3 or Bd3, otherwise the knight/bishop will be taken by the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2p5/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. e4/2...dxe4/3. Nc3/3...c5
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2p5/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2PPP/.x: This rare and rather unknown countergambit adds pressure to White's d-pawn. The name of this opening is the Reversed Albin Countergambit as it resembles an accepted Albin Countergambit with colors reversed and an extra knight on c3. This is sometimes considered slightly dubious or bizarre, but it is nonetheless playable.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1p1pp/8/5p2/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. e4/2...dxe4/3. Nc3/3...f5
rnbqkbnr/ppp1p1pp/8/5p2/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2PPP.x: Instead of opting for the standard 3...Nf6 or even 3...Bf5, Black chooses to defend their e4 pawn with their f-pawn, an opening named the Netherlands Variation. This is inferior to other ways of defending the pawn as it weakens the kingside and creates a hole on e5.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P1P2/8/PPP1P1PP.x: This dubious attack controls e5 once more, with the f-pawn. The name of the opening is the Mason Attack. Although it is not fully sound, it is playable and White scores quite well after the main line, 2...Nc6 3. Nf3 Nf6 4. e3, and White controls lots of the dark squares. However, this slightly weakens the kingside and creates a permanent hole on e5.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P2P1/8/PPP1PP1P.x:
Called the Zürich gambit, this very unsound and dubious move gambits the g4 pawn. Moving the g-pawn so early weakens White's kingside and is generally not advised.

Black should take with 2...Bxg4 as it is simply a free pawn. Black simply wins a pawn and White doesn't have much compensation except the hope that the semi-open g-file will one day be useful for attacking Black's kingside. White may continue with 3. Bg2, then Nf3 or h3.

Declining the gambit, e.g. 2...Nc6?!, gives White the chance to defend the pawn with 3. h3 (not 3. f3?? allowing 3...Qh4+!) or they could play 3. Bg2 to insist on gambitting the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/3p4/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.x:
As with many of Black's off-beat 1st move alternatives, this move does not hold independent status as it usually transposes into other mainstream openings. It is certainly not a bad move on Black's part, but it does allow White to transpose into the Pirc or Modern defence by playing 2. e4, so Black must enjoy playing these defences or should shy from this move.

White's options are many. Here are the three most popular:
* 2. e4, Pirc or Modern transposition. 
* 2. c4, allowing 2... e5! Otherwise, heading for various queen's pawn games (e.g. King's Indian defence). 
* 2. Nf3, keeping the options open while controlling the e5 square.
