rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4p3/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/.x:
=Rat Defence=

The Rat Defence is a solid option for black in the Old Indian. It mainly challenges white’s center and fights for development. White may take the pawn with 3. dxe5.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4P3/2P5/8/PP2PPPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d6/2. c4/2...e5/3. dxe5
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4P3/2P5/8/PP2PPPP/R.x:
=Rat Defence=
At this point, black has 2 main options. /3...dxe5/, the best move according to the engine; and /3...Nc6/, the Lisbon Gambit.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2np4/4P3/2P5/8/PP2PPPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d6/2. c4/2...e5/3. dxe5/3...Nc6
r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2np4/4P3/2P5/8/PP2PPPP/.x:
=Rat Defence=

Nc6 is the key move to the Lisbon Gambit. White can greedily capture another pawn with /4. exd6/, but must play accurately.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.x:
Black offers their e-pawn. The Englund gambit is considered unsound: against best play, Black will not get enough compensation for the pawn. It is therefore rare in tournament chess, but it is not uncommon in amateur games where Black wants an open, tactical game with sharp traps and practical chances.

2. dxe5 to accept the gambit capitalises on Black's dubious move. White challenges Black to find compensation. The main line continues with 2...Nc6 3. Nf3 Qe7 4. Bf4, and Black invites White to blunder with the manoeuvre ...Qb4+ &...Qxb2, but if White plays carefully this is toothless. 2...d6, letting the pawn go in return for an open centre and development, is the main side line.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/3P4/5N2/PPP1PPPP.x:
= 2. Nf3 - Reversed Alekhine =
This move may seem like a good response, and also is similar to Alekhine defense but from white side. However black can just push the pawn further and force the knight to move (if you don't want to lose it of course).

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/3Pp3/5N2/PPP1PPPP/.x:
= 2... e4 - Reversed Krebs =
Of course black pushes further, forcing white to lose tempo and move the knight. White has a few responses to this:

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/3Pp3/8/PPP1PPPP/RN.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...e4/3. Ng1
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/3Pp3/8/PPP1PPPP/RN.x: Due to the lack of good options, White decides to retreat the knight, losing tempo. This shows that playing Nf3 earlier was a mistake. Black will play /4...d5/ to solidify their control of the center.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4N3/3Pp3/8/PPP1PPPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...e4/3. Ne5
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4N3/3Pp3/8/PPP1PPPP/.x:
= 3. Ne5 (?!) - Reversed Mokele Mbembe =
White hops the knight into opponent's territory, which is not a good move, of course. It is easily kickable, which only helps black to develop pieces and makes position worse for white because they lose more and more tempo.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/3Pp3/8/PPPNPPPP/RN.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...e4/3. Nfd2
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/3Pp3/8/PPPNPPPP/RN.x: This is the only move that makes sense. You seem to retreat the knight to a safe place and also attack undefended pawn in hope to develop normally. But black has an interesting response - e3 (!?) - they sacrifice their semi-isolated pawn for good. It's forced to either take it or move the knight once again. But every one of them is bad - if you take it you think you just got a free material (even chess engines don't like it), but in exchange you ruin your kingside, your pawn structure,open your king for attacks and block your center pawn. If you move your knight, black just takes pawn on f2 and then you're unable to castle anymore.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/3Pp3/8/8/PPP1PPPP/RN.x: White avoids ...exd4 by pushing their pawn to d5. This is a mistake only in that it does not punish Black for their mistake. The Englund gambit is bad for Black, but if White does not know the refutation they may choose this line to avoid complications.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4P3/8/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.x:
White captures the free pawn. This is theoretically the best variation for White. Black can try several approaches to entrap White:

2...Nc6 is the main line. Black starts efforts to recover the pawn. After 3. Nf3 Qe7 White can let Black have it back (4. Nc3 Nxe5 5. Bf4 Nxf3+ 6. gxf3 d6 7. e4) for a lead in development and space. More common is 3. Bf4 and Black swings over to take the b-pawn: 4...Qb4+ 5. Bd2 Qxb2. So long as White avoids a couple of traps (6. Bc3?? is fatal, as is 6. Nc3 Nb4 7. Rb1??) White comes out ahead in position.

rnbqk1nr/pppp1ppp/8/2b1P3/8/8/PPP1PPPP/R.x:
Black develops the bishop to pressure f2.

This usually leads to the Derek Wu trap, where Black pretends to blunder a pre-move (it therefore is best kept for online blitz or bullet), where, after 3. Nf3 Black plays 3...d6 and premoves 4. Ne7: so after 3...d6 4. exd6 Ne7? White is lulled into a false sense of security. However the obvious move 5. dxe7?? blunders 5...Bxf2+! deflecting White's king from defence of the queen.

Otherwise, the game can continue 3. Nf3 Nc6 and transpose into the Felbecker Gambit (usually reached after 2...Nc6 3. Nf3 Bc5).

3. Nc3, another natural developing move, also acts to defang the trap by adding another defender to the queen.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4P3/8/8/PPP1PPPP/RN.x: Black argues that by play 2...d6 and gambiting the pawn, they will have enough compensation because of their earlier kingside development and open centre. However, if White plays carefully, they will be ahead throughout the game because of their central pawn on e2. This doesn't mean, though, that Black shouldn't play this gambit. If White isn't careful, Black can gain an extraordinary kingside attack because of Black's extra tempo in development.

rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/5p2/4P3/8/8/PPP1PPPP/RN.x:
Black offers a second pawn with 2...f6. Although it looks like a weakening move, White must be careful to avoid falling into potential traps.

White can capture the pawn with 3. exf6, but Black gains a lead in development in exchange after re-capturing with the knight.

Alternatively, White can give back the pawn by playing 3. e4. Note that Black cannot immediately capture the e5 pawn as 3...fxe5?? loses to 4. Qh5+.

= Soller Gambit Accepted =
Taking the pawn is a slight inaccuracy and not recommended, as it plays into Black's gameplan and allows them to easily develop their knight. White still has the advantage, though they must be careful not to fall for any of Black's traps. Black could continue by developing their bishop to c5, threatening the f7 pawn and laying down a nasty trap. After 4. Bg5 Bc5 5. Nf3 Ne4!!, it looks like Black blundered their queen, but 6. Bxd8?? results in White getting checkmated by Bxf2#

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/3P4/4P3/PPP2PPP/.x: White declines the gambit by supporting the pawn. This position looks similar to the French defense, as the name suggests. The winrate according to the lichess database is: 50% win rate to 47% loss rate, and a 3% draw rate.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/4p3/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.x:
1...e6 is the Horwitz defence. Black plays something less committal without showing their hand, and waits to see how White wants to approach the game. This can transpose into a myriad of different openings.

Uniquely, this is an invitation for White to transpose into a French defence with 2. e4.

2. c4 is the most common reply, where White keeps the game in Queen's pawn territory. Black can then transpose into a Dutch defence with 2...f5, an Indian defence with 2...Nf6, or a Queen's gambit declined with 2...d5. 2...Bb4+ is known as the Keres or Kangaroo defence.

rnbqk1nr/pppp1ppp/4p3/8/1bPP4/8/PP2PPPP/.x:
= Keres Defence =

The Keres Defence is a chess opening that begins with the moves 1. d4 e6 2. c4 Bb4+. It is also known as the Kangaroo Defence or Franco-Indian Defence. The opening is named after Estonian grandmaster Paul Keres.

After the opening moves, White has several options to respond, including 3. Bd2, 3. Nd2, and 3. Nc3. If white plays 3. Nc3, the game might transpose into a Nimzo-Indian Defence or a Bogo-Indian Defence.

The standard reply today is 3. Bd2. Black can continue with 3...Bxd2+ into a line of the Bogo-Indian, and 3...a5 will also usually transpose to a Bogo-Indian when White plays Nf3. Alternatively, Black can allow White to play e4: 3...Qe7 4.e4 d5.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.x:
This is the Dutch defence, the fourth most common way to meet 1. d4. Black controls the central e4 square with their flank f-pawn.

Because it does not develop or prepare to develop a piece (cf. 1...Nf6 and 1...d5 respectively), 1...f5 is less popular than Black's other options to control e4. In addition, moving the f-pawn so early, before Black has castled, is not for the faint of heart because it weakens Black's kingside. An illustration of this is the classic beginner's trap in the Hopton attack: 2. Bg5 h6 3. Bh4 g5 3. Bg3 f4 (thinking to trap the bishop) 4. e3 fxg3?? 5. Qh5#.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5pB1/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/.x:
White develops the Bishop so as to hinder Black's development. The bishop pins Black's e-pawn, and in the event of ...Nf6 White will be happy to trade the bishop for the knight and upset Black's pawn structure.

Therefore Black usually postpones the development of their knight and chooses whether they wish to fianchetto or to drive the bishop off first.

r1bqkbnr/ppppp1pp/2n5/5pB1/3P4/8/PPP1PPP.x: A rare sideline in Hopton attack. Black did not wish to develop their king's knight, 2...Nf6, because White would be happy to trade it off, so instead they developed their other knight. Usually in the Hopton attack, Black doesn't play ...Nc6 because they want to support d5 with c6 (the main line is 1. d4 f5 2. Bg5 g6 3. Nc3 Bg7 4. e3 d5 5. h4 c6). Though White is better by engine, the inaccuracy is not immediately punishable by White.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp2p/6p1/5pB1/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP.x:
Black prepares to fianchetto their bishop. This will allow them to develop their knight and, if White captures it, recapture with the bishop instead of doubling their pawns.

One way for White to play this is to keep the position closed with ideas of e3, h4, and Nf3. Typically both sides castle short. 
This leads for more positional grinds.

After 2. Nc3 Bg7, White can open the position with 3. e4 fxe4 5. Nxe4 or keep the position closed with with 3. e3. Black may adopt a move order with 2...d5 followed by 3...Bg7 to discourage White from playing e4.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/3P4/2N5/PPP1PPPP.x: The Raphael Variation, characterized by 2. Nc3, aims to control e4, the square Dutch players want to control. Although this is a sideline, it is principled as it develops a piece and controls a key central square.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/3P4/7N/PPP1PPPP/.x:
A rare but respectable sideline where White chooses to develop their knight to the edge of the board. Despite going against common opening principles, this move is sound.

2...Nf6 is the most common move, continuing with the plan of controlling e4 alongside the f-pawn. The game can progress many ways, but the most common is the Blackburne variation, 3. g3 e6 4. Bg2, where the knight doesn't block the kingside bishop's sight, and is essentially similar to a Bladel but from the White side.

2...e6 usually leads to the same line, just from a different move order, through 3. g3 Nf6 4. Bg2.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/3P4/3Q4/PPP1PPPP.x:
A rarer line. White develops their queen aggressively to an active square and attacks the vulnerable f5 pawn.

2...e6 is the most common way of defending the pawn and the second most common move. Black goes into a Stonewall setup and makes the queen seem misplaced. However, the unique line that can arise from 2. Qd3 is 3. g4!?, the tricky Manhattan gambit.

2...Nf6!? is the most popular move, the so-called Pretzel gambit. Black ignores that their pawn is hanging and hopes that kicking the queen around after 3. Qxf5 d5 is sufficient compensation.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP.x:
2...Nf6 is the normal variation of the Dutch Defence. It is a natural developing move. As well as helping to control the centre, the knight is valuable in controlling h5. Black weakened the e8-h5 diagonal when they moved their f-pawn.

White has several ways to continue:

3. Nc3 is the queen's knight variation. White develops the knight to its most active square to control e4.

3. g3 is the fianchetto variation, where White prepares to control the long diagonal with their king's bishop.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...f5/2. c4/2...Nf6/3. Nc3
rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.x:
3. Nc3 develops a piece and increases White's control over the e4 and d5 squares.

3...e6 leads to the Classical or Stonewall systems.

3...d6 prepares to develop the king's bishop to b4, pinning White's knight.

3...g6: prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop instead.

Preparing to fianchetto the queen's bishop, 3...b6, is uncommon.

rnbqkb1r/p1ppp1pp/1p3n2/5p2/2PP4/2N5/PP2.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...f5/2. c4/2...Nf6/3. Nc3/3...b6
rnbqkb1r/p1ppp1pp/1p3n2/5p2/2PP4/2N5/PP2.x:
Black prepares ...Bb7, to exert long term pressure on the long light square diagonal and further control e4.

This move order makes it harder for White to play g3 and Bg2, as Black's bishop gets to contest the diagonal first. A continuation is 4. Nf3 to prepare g2, and 4...e6 5. g3 Bb7 6. Bg2 Bb4.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp2p/6p1/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/.x:
A dynamic choice, the Dutch with g6 is a Leningrad setup. The pawn structure is practically always g6-f5-d6. Black plays in this system, with only a few rare exceptions, his bishop to g7, knight to f6, and castles quickly.

Leningrad Dutch main line is, with possible changes in move order: 1. d4 f5 2. c4 Nf6 3. g3 g6 4. Nf3 Bg7 5. Bg2 d6 6. 0-0 0-0 7. Nc3 Qe8 (Diagram).

rnbqkbnr/ppppp2p/6p1/5p2/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...f5/2. c4/2...g6/3. Nc3
rnbqkbnr/ppppp2p/6p1/5p2/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.x:
A natural move, White develops a their queen's knight to control the centre. At the moment White's options are still open and they may choose whether to play in the modern way with g3 and Bg2, or in the traditional way with e3 and Be2.

3...Nf6 is the main move here, usually followed by 4...Bg7, or in the order 3...Bg7 followed by 4...Nf3. White may continue with Nf3, g3, etc, or with the aggressive 4. h4! intending h5 and h6 if possible, though this attack doesn't work as well as if White had tried it on turn turn.

An unusual option, which Black enabled by having played 2...g6 before developing their knight, is 3...Nh6!?, the Bladel variation.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp2p/6pn/5p2/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...f5/2. c4/2...g6/3. Nc3/3...Nh6
rnbqkb1r/ppppp2p/6pn/5p2/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.x:
3...Nh6!? is an offbeat continuation in the Dutch defence. Black develops their knight to the edge of the board. 3...Nf6 would be more active, but ...Nh6 is just about getting the knight out of the way. It at least helps Black get ready to castle, and keeping the f6 square clear of pieces means both ...Bg7 will exert immediate pressure and (so long as Black can castle and open the f-file) so will Black's rook on f8. Black may later reroute their knight to f7 or f5.

White may choose to continue with their typical development plans, e.g. 4. Nf3 with g3 and Bg2 or e3 and Be2.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/3P4/5P2/PPP1P1PP.x: A rare and abnormal sideline in the Dutch Defence. The main idea is quite straightforward: push e4 to control the center and challenge Black's f5 pawn. However, it blocks the natural developing square for the g1 knight and opens the e1-h4 diagonal. Sometimes, White can gambit a pawn on e4 for quick development and lines.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/3P4/6P1/PPP1PP1P.x:
This is considered to be the main line of the Dutch defence at the highest level of play.
The moves /2...Nf6/ 3. Bg2 are played virtually every game, and it is from there that the positions start to branch out.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/3P2P1/8/PPP1PP1P.x:
The idea of 2. g4?! is straight forward enough: deflect Black's f-pawn from control of e4, and perhaps White can get in the move e4 themselves soon, so building a strong, spacious centre with both d and e pawns. Against best play the gambit doesn't work out that way and White doesn't get complete compensation for the pawn.

2...fxg4 accepts the gambit. Though this loses control of the e4 square, it transpires that White can't make much of 3. e4?! anyway. (If 3. e4 (discovering an attack on g4 with the queen) d5 both discovers a defender of g4 in the form of the bishop and attacks e4. Black is up a pawn and better. If 4. exd5? Qxd5 comes with an attack on White's rook.)

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/3P4/7P/PPP1PPP1/.x:
The Korchnoi attack is a theory based, sound, aggressive way to play against the Dutch. This Attack has been named after the Russian Grandmaster, Viktor Lvovich Korchnoi.

Viktor Lvovich Korchnoi (Russian: Виктор Львович Корчной, IPA: [vʲiktər lʲvovʲɪtɕ kɐrtɕˈnoj]; 23 March 1931 – 6 June 2016) was a Soviet (before 1976) and Swiss (after 1980) chess grandmaster (GM) and chess writer. He is considered one of the strongest players never to have become World Chess Champion.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/3P4/7P/PPP1PPP.x:
The most common and best response to the Korchnoi Attack, however White can spring a trap with a surprising gambit.

3. g4 is the Janzen-Korchnoi Gambit, which can set up a trap if accepted with 3...fxg4: 4. hxg4 Nxg4 5. Qd3! Nf6?? 6. Rxh7!! Rxh7?? 7. Qg6#. However, if Black knows the correct responses, it can be neutralized.

A sounder response is 3. Nf3, however it doesn't lead to the fun Janzen-Korchnoi positions, instead developing the kingside knight and aiming for a relatively normal game.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/8/6p1/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/R.x: Perhaps the worst possible reply to 1. d4 is 1...g5??. Against 1. e4, 1...g5? is bad because it fails to contest White's centre and weakens Black's kingside. Against 1. d4 it has the added disadvantage of sacrificing the pawn immediately.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp2p/5p2/6B1/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/.x:
f6 seems like a relatively decent, if strange move by Black at first, kicking out the bishop and preparing for an advance to e5. However, this move weakens the king, as well as blocks development of the knight and the queen to f6. This can be abused by White with the move e4!, which makes the bishop poisoned, takes control of the center, and threatens to attack with the queen.

White always goes Qh5 after a few moves to either checkmate the king or force it to move away. This is not a good situation for Black to be in at all, with little development chances, being attacked, and a weak kingside.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/4P3/PPPP1PPP/RNB.x:
An irregular opening, considered somewhat passive, as although White opens lines for their bishop and queen to enter the game, Black is given the opportunity to take over the centre with ...e5 and ...d5.

Black may play any number of moves to stake a claim in the centre: 1...Nf6, 1...e5, 1...d5, 1...c5 are all reasonable. 1...g6, intending ...Bg7, or 1...Nf6 followed by 2...g6, is a typical approach to meet lots of transpositions equally.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/8/4P3/PPPP1PPP/R.x:
Black takes space in the centre.

If White responds 2. d4, a reversed French defence position is arrived at, more usually seen in the Englund gambit declined with e3.

2. e4?! appears to reach the usual position seen after 1. e4 e5, the Open game--except this time it's Black to move.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.x:
Play reaches the same position as after 1.e4 e5, the Open game, but with Black to move. This is an irregular way to play where White concedes the first move advantage, perhaps because they really wanted to play the Black side.

From here any of the typical Open game positions can be reached, but with colours reversed.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.x:
Best by test.
— Bobby Fischer

1. e4, the King's Pawn Opening, is the most popular first move at all levels of the game. 1. e4 opens lines to develop the queen and the king's bishop. It also fights for control of the centre.

r1bqkbnr/pppppppp/n7/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RN.x:
A rare and weak response to 1. e4. The knight develops to a square that doesn't control the centre and as such, it's a wasted opportunity.

This allows White to take the full centre with 2. d4. The most serious line is 2...c6, which transposes to the De Bruycker line of the Caro-Kann defence. 2...c5!? (defended by the knight on the rim) 3. Nf3 cxd4 leads to an unusual sort of Sicilian.

r1bqkbnr/pppppppp/2n5/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.x:
In the "maverick" Nimzowitsch defence, Black postpones contesting the centre with pawns, usually to strike back after White has expanded some more.

Although Black's knight "sees" d4, it doesn't prevent White from achieving the two pawn centre because after 2. d4, White's queen can see d4 too. Black then has three main approaches:

r1bqkbnr/pppppppp/2n5/1B6/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.x: The Pseudo-Spanish Variation is an offbeat sideline in the Nimzowitsch Defence. The main idea is to put pressure on the c6 knight, similar to the Ruy Lopez. This also invites a transposition into the Ruy Lopez after 2...e5 3. Nf3.

r1bqkbnr/pppppppp/2n5/8/4P3/2N5/PPPP1PPP.x:
This somewhat uncommon response to the Nimzowitsch transposes to the Vienna Game with 2...e5.

If Black wishes to avoid transposing, 2...Nf6 3. d4 d5 reaches the Vehre variation otherwise seen in the move order 1. e4 Nc6 2. d4 d5 3. Nc3 Nf6.

2...e6 leads to something like the French defence (the Lichess.org and Chess.com opening books call it the "French connection"), though Black's knight on c6 prevents ...c5, a usual idea in the French.

r1bqkbnr/pppppppp/2n5/8/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.x:
White develops their knight to its most active square, and offers to let Black transpose into the Open Game. This avoids the original positions resulting from lines like 2. d4 d5 3. e5 Bf5.

To keep things in original territory, Black may play 2...d6, the Williams variation, or 2...f5?!, the Colorado gambit.

Black can transpose into the Open Game, usually reached after 1. e5 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6, with 2...e5, but other transpositions are inferior because of the placement of Black's knight.

r1bqkbnr/ppp1pppp/2np4/8/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PP.x:
= Nimzowitsch Defence, Williams Variation =
At this point, White can build a large pawn center with /3. d4/. Black can attempt to control the center with pieces with either /3...Bg4/, allowing 4. d5 Ne5 5. Nxe5, or /3...Nf6/

r1bqkbnr/ppppp1pp/2n5/5p2/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.x:
Black strikes at White's centre with a flank pawn. At the cost of weakening their king, they hope to deflect White's e-pawn from control of d5, so that Black may play ...d5 themselves. This gambit is considered dubious, for even though Black can usually recover the material and has two centre pawns for White's one, their kingside is too weak.

3. exf5, accepting the gambit, is the main move, after 3...d5 White is best advised to allow Black to recover the material, 4. d4 Bxf5.

r1bqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3Pn3/4p3/2N5/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nc3/3...dxe4/4. d5/4...Ne5
r1bqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3Pn3/4p3/2N5/PPP2PPP.x:
Following 4...Ne5, White could recapture the gambitted central pawn with 5. Nxe4, but following 5...e6! Black is guaranteed good development and almost certain equality.

A more critical response is 5. Bf4, threatening the knight on e5. 5...Ng6 is forced, due to the fact that 5...Qd6?? loses to 6. Nb5! Nf3+ 7. Qxf3!!, and after 6. Bg3, 6...f5 is critical, although largely unexplored.

White can avoid these lines with 5. Qd4, also forcing 5...Ng6. This line is more aggressive, and Black must be careful, but Black can probably equalize.

r1bqkbnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3pP3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6/2. d4/2...d5/3. e5
r1bqkbnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3pP3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP.x:
White advances the e pawn to avoid the pawn trade. This is considered main option for White.

Black usually now plays 3...Bf5 4. c3 e6. In the resulting position, Black has achieved a superior French defence (1. e5 e6) structure, with their bishop developed outside of their pawn chain, but at the cost of their knight on c6 preventing them from playing ...c5 to start counterplay against White's centre.

White has a good position and a slight advantage. These positions are complex and unique, with a slight advantage for White but Black has the ability to play for a win.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP.x:
The Kennedy variation is a sideline in the Nimzowitsch defence. Black has two attackers on d4 and so threatens to take it next turn.

White has three ways of dealing with the central tension: to push the pawn, take first, or defend the pawn. Both pushing the pawn or taking on e5 are very good for White, and the most testing replies, though defending the pawn may allow a transposition to a more familiar position.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.x:
With this aggressive pawn advance, White looks to open up the centre.

3...exd4 is played almost every time. It releases the central tension and leads to a very open game, with a lot of space for both players.

3...Nxd4, the Lolli variation, is playable. White can trade on d4, 4. Nxd4 exd4 5. Qxd4, taking advantage of the fact Black has traded their knight to centralise their queen, or play 4. Nxe5, threatening Qxd4.

A few tries have been made with 3...d6, transposing into a Philidor defence, but this affords White a range of good options: 4. d5, kicking the knight and expanding in the centre is the most straight-forward, or 4. Bb5 transposing into an Old Steinitz Spanish.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n1p3/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP.x: In this position, 3. Nf3 is the most common move. The pawn structure will soon resemble the Advance Variation of the French Defence.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.x:
1...Nf6 makes an immediate attack on the e4-pawn. The main idea of the Alekhine is to provoke White to advance and push pawns, which Black can pick at later. This leads to an asymmetric and unbalanced game and aggressive tactical opportunities.

2. e5 is the main move. White takes more space and kicks Black's knight, usually to d5. White is able to keep taking space in the centre: they must weigh taking more space against developing their minor pieces. Meanwhile, Black hopes that White's pawn centre will be overextended and so possible to exploit later in the game.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2B1P3/8/PPPP1PPP.x:
White leaves the e4-pawn undefended. Though they can recover the pawn tactically with Bxf2+ this riposte from White is not as dangerous as it looks and Black ends up with a superior position.

2...Nxe4 takes the hanging pawn. To recover the material, White has a flashy manoeuvre where they sacrifice the bishop and trade for Black's knight. 3. Bxf7+ Kxf7 4. Qh5+ (4. Qf3+?? Nf6 }) Kg8 5. Qd5+ e6 6. Qxe4. However, White has given up their space advantage, while Black's king is quite safe and they have easy development. 6...d5 7. Qe2 e5! (sacrificing the e-pawn to open their bishop and develop with tempo) 8. Qxe5 Nc6. Black is far ahead in development.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/8/2B1n3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.x: White's only way to recover the pawn is 3. Bxf7+. Black can take the bishop but White wins the knight in trade through the sequence 1. e4 Nf6 2. Bc4 Nxe4 3. Bxf7+ Kxf7 4. Qh5+ Kg8 5. Qd5+ e6 6. Qxe4 d5 7. Qe3 e5 .

rnbq1b1r/pppppkpp/8/8/4n3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.x: White can take the knight in trade for their bishop through the manoeuvre 4. Qh5+ 5. Qd5+ 6. Qxe5, and material will be equal.

1.e4 Nf6 2. Bc4 Nxe4 3. Bxf7+ Kxf7 4. Qh5+ Ke6?!

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/4P3/2N5/PPPP1PPP.x:
White defends e4 while developing a piece. This is solid but less testing than 2. e5.

This allows Black to play 2...e5 and transpose into a Vienna game.

However, if Black thinks White is too eager to avoid the Alekhine's defence then they may avoid transposing with 2...d5, the Scandinavian variation.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/4P3/2N5/PPPP1P.x:
Black attacks e4. Surely White cannot drop the pawn, so they have two main options. Both are relatively drawish.

After 3. exd5 Nxd5 4. Nxd5 Qxd5, Black has a strong centralised queen and easy development, leaving equality or a slight advantage to Black.

After 3. e5 Nfd7 and White may defend their e5 pawn or trade it. 4. d4 and the position resembles the Steinitz French, except Black can delay playing e6 until after they have developed their bishop (4...c5 5. f4 cxd4 6. Nb5 Nc6 7. Nf3 Ndb8 8. Nbxd4 Bg4 9. h3 Bxf3 10. Nxf3 e6 ). If exchanging the pawns instead, 4. Nxd5 Nxe5 comes with tempo on White's knight. If 3...d4 then a cascade of trades leads to a drawish position.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/4P3/2N2N2/PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/4P3/2N2N2/PP.x:
The position is now completely symmetrical, leading to a somewhat drawish position.

There are a range of moves played here, but by far the main tries are 4. Bb5, developing the bishop and pressuring the centre, and 4. d4, opening the centre and transposing into a variation of the Scotch game.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/4P3/8/8/PPPP1PPP/R.x:
Black's knight is under attack.

2...Nd5 is the most popular and best move.

2...Ng8?!, the Brooklyn variation, surely does not stand up to scrutiny. Black wants to start the game over, but White has used the tempo to seize the centre and is prepared to develop all their pieces.

2...Ne4?! is called Mokele Mbembe. White is likely to gain more tempo on, or even trap, the knight that has strayed to their side of the board.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/3nP3/8/8/PPPP1PPP/RN.x:
Black's knight, under attack, moves to a safer square, but may soon move again.

3. d4 is the most intuitive move. This reinforces White's advanced but weak pawn, and opens lines for White to develop. After 3...d6, chipping away at the end of White's pawn chain, White has the choice either to seize as much space as possible, 4. c4 Nb6 then 5. f4 dxe5 6. fxe5 Nc6, the four pawn attack, or 5. exd6 exd6, the exchange variation; or to focus on not falling behind in development, 4. Nf3 Bg4 5. Be2 e6 6. O-O Be7 7. c4 Nb6 8. Nc3 O-O 9. Be3 Nc6.

3. c4, the two pawns attack keeps attacking the knight. After 3...Nb6, 4. d4 d6 transposes or 4. c5 is the Lasker variation.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/3nP3/8/N7/PPPP1PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nf6/2. e5/2...Nd5/3. Na3
rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/3nP3/8/N7/PPPP1PPP/R.x: White develops their knight to the rim: perhaps with the intention of Nc4.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/3nP3/8/2N5/PPPP1PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nf6/2. e5/2...Nd5/3. Nc3
rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/3nP3/8/2N5/PPPP1PPP/.x:
White offers Black the trade of knights. After 3...Nxc3 4. dxc3 White has open lines for their pieces to develop, but is unable to support their e5-pawn with their d-pawn.

3...e6, allowing White to trade into Black, and 3...Nb6 have also been tried.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/3nP3/2P5/8/PP1P1PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nf6/2. e5/2...Nd5/3. c4
rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/3nP3/2P5/8/PP1P1PPP/.x:
White kicks the knight immediately.

3...Nb6 is its best retreat. Then White may play 4. d4 and often reach a position otherwise reached from the main line 3. d4. 4...d6 5. exd6 reaches the exchange variation; 4...d6 5. f4 transposes into the four pawns attack.

4. c5, chasing the knight again but giving up control of d5, is the Lasker variation. The game may continue 4...Nd5 5. Bc4 e6 6. d4 b6 7. cxb6 axb6 .

3...Nb4?! and the knight may find itself being kicked around again into irrelevance. 4. d4 and 4...d6 fails to 5. Qa4+. 4...c5 5. d5 d6 6. a3 N4a6

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/1n6/4P3/2P5/8/PP1P1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nf6/2. e5/2...Nd5/3. c4/3...Nb6
rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/1n6/4P3/2P5/8/PP1P1PPP.x:
White may now play 4. d4 to sure up their centre. This is the main move and reaches positions familiar from the 3. d4 move order, where often White plays c4 as well. 4...d6 5. exd6 reaches the exchange variation; 4...d6 5. f4 transposes into the four pawns attack.

4. c5 stays in original territory. This is the Lasker variation. White chases the knight again but it usually returns to plant itself on the newly minted outpost on d5, 4...Nd5. 5. Nc3 e6 6. Nxd5 exd5 7. d4 to close up the outpost might be sensible, or the game may continue 4...Nd5 5. Bc4 e6 6. d4 b6 7. cxb6 axb6 =.

4. b3 is the Steiner variation.

4. a4!? is the Tate variation.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/1n6/4P3/P1P5/8/1P1P1PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nf6/2. e5/2...Nd5/3. c4/3...Nb6/4. a4
rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/1n6/4P3/P1P5/8/1P1P1PP.x:
A rare move.

White's immediate threat is to play a5! and trap Black's knight, so Black needs to either prevent a5 (by playing 4...a5 themselves) or give their knight an escape square (4...d6 or 4...d5).

An idea for White is then to use the a3 square to lift their rook (5. Ra3).

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/1n6/4P3/2PP4/8/PP3PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nf6/2. e5/2...Nd5/3. c4/3...Nb6/4. d4
rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/1n6/4P3/2PP4/8/PP3PPP/.x:
Black would now like to carry on with their development, but they find White's pawn chain to be stifling. The main move is 4...d6, because Black is left with little other choice.

They cannot play 4...Nc6?, because 5. d5! Nxe5 6. c5 Nxd5 (6...Nbc4 7. Qd4!) 7. Qxd5 , and 4...Na6?! is grim, little better than not developing the knight at all.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/1n1p4/4P3/2PP4/8/PP3PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nf6/2. e5/2...Nd5/3. d4/3...d6/4. c4/4...Nb6
rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/1n1p4/4P3/2PP4/8/PP3PP.x:
Black threatens 5...dxe5 6.dxe5 Qxd1+ 7.Kxd1, shattering White's pawns and preventing castling. This is a common position in Alekhine's defence that may arise from the 3. d4 or 2. c4 move orders by transposition.

White has two main choices.

5. f4, the four pawns attack, is the maximalist approach. White wishes to recapture on e5 with the pawn (5...dxe5 6. fxe5) and keep their smothering pawn chain alive. 5...dxe5 is the main move, or Black can start with 5...Bf5, the Trifunovic variation (...dxe5 fxe5 normally follows later). Uncommon moves include 5...g6, the fianchetto variation and 5...g5, the Cambridge gambit.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/4P3/2P2n2/8/PP1P1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nf6/2. e5/2...Nd5/3. c4/3...Nf4
rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/4P3/2P2n2/8/PP1P1PPP.x:
= Alekhine's Defence: The Squirrel =

Black saves their Knight, which was attacked by the pawn on c4. Even though the knight moves forward, this move is not seen as best because the Knight is unstable on f4 and will likely have to move again to a worse square to save itself.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/3nP3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nf6/2. e5/2...Nd5/3. d4
rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/3nP3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/R.x:
Black's knight is safe for now, which gives them the opportunity to start the counterattack on White's advanced pawns.

3...d6 is the main move. This threatens ...dxe5 and opens a line for Black's bishop to develop. This is the best direction to develop the bishop in because Black anticipates that White may kick their knight again soon, and they certainly don't want to play ...b6 & ...Bg7 and take away the knight's retreating square. The main responses are 4. c4 Nb6 5. f4, the four pawns attack, where White intends to recapture on e5 with the f-pawn, and 4. Nc3, intending to recapture on e5 with the knight.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/3p4/3nP3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nf6/2. e5/2...Nd5/3. d4/3...d6
rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/3p4/3nP3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP.x:
Black threatens ...dxe5 and opens a line for their bishop to develop.

White's next move makes a decision about how they would like to take back on e5 after ...dxe5.

4. Nf3 is the modern variation. This develops a piece and prepares to answer 4...dxe5, called the Larsen variation, with 5. Nxe5. In the main line, Black first pins the knight, 4...Bg4, and leaves the tension while both sides develop. Eventually White usually initiates the trade. 5. Be2 e6 6. O-O Be7 7. c4 Nb6 8. Nc3 O-O 9. Be3 Nc6 10. exd6 cxd6 (see diagram).

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/3p4/3nP3/3P4/5N2/PPP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nf6/2. e5/2...Nd5/3. d4/3...d6/4. Nf3
rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/3p4/3nP3/3P4/5N2/PPP2P.x:
White develops a piece and prepares to recapture on e5 with their knight. Black still lacks space. They must avoid passive play at all costs, which would allow White to crush them quickly.

4...dxe5, the Larsen variation, resolves the centre tension immediately. White can retake 5. Nxe5, and from e5 they have a powerful knight that cannot be easily dislodged.

4...Bg4 is the main line. This pins the knight and reduces White's control over the centre.

If 5. h3, the Panov variation, Black is happy to trade 5...Bxf3 6. Qxf3 dxe5 (simultaneously defending the knight on d5) 7. dxe5 e6 , material is equal but Black has weakened White's centre.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/3p4/3nP3/3P2b1/5N2/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nf6/2. e5/2...Nd5/3. d4/3...d6/4. Nf3/4...Bg4
rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/3p4/3nP3/3P2b1/5N2/PPP.x:
4...Bg4 is the main line: this pins the knight so prevents it from recapturing after ...dxe5.

If 5. h3, the Panov variation, then Black is happy to trade the bishop for the knight. 5...Bxf3 6. Qxf3 dxe5 (simultaneously defending the knight on d5) 7. dxe5 e6 , and while material is equal, Black has weakened White's centre.

5. Be2 is the main line. This unpin the knight to resume control of e5.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/3np3/3P4/5N2/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nf6/2. e5/2...Nd5/3. d4/3...d6/4. Nf3/4...dxe5
rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/3np3/3P4/5N2/PPP2PPP.x: Black initiates the trade of pawns. Consistent with 4. Nf3, recapturing with the knight, 5. Nxe5, is the preferred move.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/3nN3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nf6/2. e5/2...Nd5/3. d4/3...d6/4. Nf3/4...dxe5/5. Nxe5
rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/3nN3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/R.x:
White retakes the pawn with their knight. e5 is a good square for this knight. It exerts crushing control over the light squares. With inaccurate play Black can easily go wrong, (e.g. 5...g6 6. Bc4 Nb6?? 7. Bxf7#). Therefore, Black would like to dislodge this troublesome knight and greatly free their position. How are they to do so?

Black cannot kick it away yet. 5...f6? 6. Qh5+! g6 7. Nxg6 hxg6 8. Qxh8 . They cannot trade it away yet either. 5. Nc6? or 5. Nd7?, thinking to trade off the knight, is too costly. One line is 5...Nd7? 6. Nxf7 Kxf7 7. Qh5+, with a double attack on Black's knight on d5. 7...g6 8. Qxd5 .

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/3p4/3nP3/2PP4/8/PP3PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nf6/2. e5/2...Nd5/3. d4/3...d6/4. c4
rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/3p4/3nP3/2PP4/8/PP3PPP.x:
White grabs even more space and kicks the knight away. Doing so now, before any trades of the e-pawn, prevents 4...Nf6.

Of the available squares, only b6 and b4 are not defended. However, 4...Nb4?? loses due to 5. Qa4+!, forking the knight, and Black must lose a piece. If 5...N4c6 to block the check, the knight is pinned and falls to 6. d5. 5...N8c6 to block the pin runs into 6. d5 too. A tricky line is 5...N8c6 6. d5 b5! 7. cxb5 Nd4, where 8. Qxb4?? Nc2+! wins Black the queen. White must start with 8. Na3 to control c2 before picking up the knight.

Therefore, 4...Nb6 is the best move.

r1bqkb1r/ppp1pppp/1nn5/4P3/2PP4/4B3/PP4P.x:
=Alekhine Defence=
With this move, White defends the d4-pawn with the bishop while not allowing the ...Bg4 pin. Black now almost always plays 7...Bf5, since that is the only logical square for the bishop. Then White plays 8.Nc3 and then Black plays 8...e6, and now White plays 9.Nf3 when Black has a choice between several moves.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/3nP3/8/6P1/PPPP1P1P/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nf6/2. e5/2...Nd5/3. g3
rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/3nP3/8/6P1/PPPP1P1P/.x: This opening line is uncommon among master games (it has only been played around a hundred times) so it doesn't have any theory attached. The extremely basic idea is that it opens up the g2 square for the bishop, which attacks the knight on d5 if it is left undefended. This can be used to regain the tempo that is commonly lost by playing g2 in other openings.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/4P3/4n3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.x:
This knight sally, unsupported and into its opponent's side of the board, is unusual. White is likely to at least gain tempo on the knight, and possibly trap it.

3. d4 takes the centre uncontested and supports the e5-pawn. It threatens f3 to trap the knight (e.g. 3...d6? 4. f3). 3...e6, the Vavra defence, defends 4. f3? because Black can answer it 4...Qh4+! 5. g3 Nxg3 (the h-pawn is pinned to the rook). 4. Bd3 is natural, but there is a better line in the surprising 4. Nh3!, where 4...d5 5. f3 Qh4+? 6. g3 Nxg3 7. Bg5! (defended by the knight) Qh5 8. hxg3. 4. Nh3 sets off a race for the g5 square. 4...h6 5. Qg4 d5 6. f3 Ng5 7. Nxg5 hxg5 8. Bxg5 f6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/4P3/8/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.x:
Black retreats their knight from White's advancing pawn. A generous assessment is that Black may continue as in the main line Alekhine (...d6, ...Bg4 etc.) with the knowledge that White doesn't have the option to play c4 with tempo, and play to undermine White's centre. Of course, the trade off is that Black has undeveloped their only developed piece, and it will take a while to get it into the action again (perhaps to g6 or f5 via e7).

3. d4 is White's best move.

rn1qkbnr/1bpppppp/p7/8/1pPPP3/1QN5/PP3PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...a6/2. d4/2...b5/3. c4/3...Bb7/4. Nc3/4...b4/5. Qb3

rnbqkbnr/p1pppppp/8/1p6/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.x:
Black gambits a pawn after 1. e4. White, can take the pawn with 2. Bxb5. What White doesn't know that after Bxb5, Black will start attacks on the kingside, in the middlegame.

Having opened the b7 square, Black can fianchetto 2...Bb7 to attack White's centre from afar. (cf. the Owen's defence, 1...b6.) One devious try for Black is to take advantage of having brought White's bishop away from defence of the g2 square. 1. e4 b5?! 2. Bxb5 Bb7 3. Nc3 f5?! 4. exf5 and Black thinks ...Bxg2?! wins the rook in the corner. Unfortunately, Qh5+ and Black's king proves to be too weak.

rnbqkbnr/p1pppppp/8/1B6/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.x:
White accepts the gambitted pawn and develops their bishop to boot.

Black can play 2...Bb7, consistent with having moved their b-pawn, and pressure White's centre. Now or at some point later they may wish to play ...a6, kicking the bishop, and otherwise play in the manner of an Owen's defence or a Queen's Indian, with ...e6, ...Bb4, ...Nf6, and ...O-O, aiming for ...d5 to break in the centre.

Black can also play 2...a6 which is the mainline, which attacks the bishop to go back to a less active square, so Black can gain a very little tempo back by developing the bishop afterwards.

rn1qkbnr/pbpppppp/8/1B6/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.x:
Black fianchettos their bishop and attacks White's e4 pawn.

White has 3. Nc3 or 3. d3 to defend it.

rn1qkbnr/pbpppppp/8/1B6/4P3/2N5/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b5/2. Bxb5/2...Bb7/3. Nc3
rn1qkbnr/pbpppppp/8/1B6/4P3/2N5/PPPP1PPP.x:
White defends their e4 pawn while developing a piece. White is still winning but there is potential for traps and sharp play.

Typical moves include:

rn1qkbnr/pbppp1pp/8/1B3p2/4P3/2N5/PPPP1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b5/2. Bxb5/2...Bb7/3. Nc3/3...f5
rn1qkbnr/pbppp1pp/8/1B3p2/4P3/2N5/PPPP1P.x:
Black offers the f-pawn hoping to tempt White's e-pawn away, thereby opening the long diagonal controlled by Black's bishop on g7.

This is doubly "hope chess", in that Black hopes White will not play (the best move by engine) 4. d3, but also, in that if White accepts the pawn 4. exf5!? Black is still losing and ...Bxg2 doesn't work anyway: 4. exf5!? Bxg2 5. Qh5+! g6□ 6. fxg6 Bg7 (6...Bxh1?? g7#!) 7. Qg5 Bxh1 8. gxh7 Rxh7 9. Bd3!.

rnbqkbnr/p1pppppp/1p6/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.x:
A very rare and uncommon response to the King's pawn game It may transpose to an English opening or other lines.

It is offbeat in that Black allows White to play 2. d4 and easily control the centre. Black usually fianchettos the light-squared bishop to b7, and may plan to assault White's big centre with ...c5.

rnbqkbnr/p1pppppp/1p6/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.x:
A principled move, White takes space with both centre pawns. Both of their bishops are ready to enter the game. This position may arise out of either 1. e4 b6 or 1. d4 b6.

2...Bb7 completes the fianchetto and puts pressure on e4.

The alternative 2...Ba6?!, known as the Guatemala defence, is considered weak as White emerges with an advantage after 3. Bxa6 Nxa6.

rn1qkbnr/p1pppppp/bp6/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.x: Black offers White the trade of bishops, 3. Bxa6 Nxa6. Black is left with weak light squares on the queen's side and their knight is misplaced on the rim. Black has spent time they can ill afford.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.x:
1...c5 is the Sicilian defence, a counter-attacking, asymmetric opening. Black controls the d4 square with a flank pawn, asserting that trading their flank c-pawn for White's d-pawn will surely be to their advantage, as it will leave them with two central pawns to White's one. Black would love to one day achieve d5, and exploit the c-file should it open.

The main approach for White is the Open Sicilian: 2. Nf3 intending to bust open the position with 3. d4. This is the most testing approach, but as it is also normally what Black is most prepared for, a number of other approaches, the "anti-Sicilians", are also popular.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/2B1P3/8/PPPP1PPP.x:
This is a mistake that allows clear equality. Black's best answer is 2. ...e6 followed by d5 at some point which easily removes White's bishop and gives Black a tempo and clear centre.

For example: 1. e4 c5 2.Bc4 e6 3. Nc3 Nc6 4. Nf3 Nf6 5. O-O d5 6. exd5 exd5 7.Bb3

Black needs to play Nc6 before d5, otherwise the king will be exposed on the a4-e8 diagonal, and therefore inviting a check from White's light square bishop.

It is analogous to some lines in the Italian Game but Black has played the move c5 which helps prevent d4 and makes b3 a less attractive place for the White Bishop (because of c4).

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2np4/2p5/2B1P3/2P5/PP1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Bc4/2...d6/3. c3/3...Nc6
r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2np4/2p5/2B1P3/2P5/PP1P.x:
The Camelot Defence is a modern response
on facing the Bowlder Attack.

While Black continues with 2...d6 part of the mainline from the Open Sicilian White now opens up the d1-a4 diagonal 
after playing 3...c3 allowing the Queen to join the Bishop's attack from b3 after the 4th move.

Black ignores this threat and continues with 3...Nc6 
therefore developing his Knight.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPPKPPP/R.x: Ke2 is considered to be a very dubious move. This is the Sicilian variation of the Bongcloud Attack. The problems with 2. Ke2? are that the King move prevents castling to protect the King, endangers the King, ignores development and the center, and blocks the Queen and Bishop, which are the two pieces that are free after 1. e4. All that being said, it can be used as a surprise to unseat Black, as many novices may be unable to cope with the unfamiliar board positions of the Bongcloud Attack. However, if it has been encountered before, it usually results in a defeat for White.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/2N5/PPPP1PPP.x:
2. Nc3 is the chief "Anti-Sicilian", the main sideline to 2. Nf3. White avoids opening the position (for now at least) and avoids the more theoretical main lines that follow 2. Nf3 and 3. d4. White may yet open the position, but White's second move suggests the possibility of playing in a closed, manoeuvring way instead.

There are several approaches for White to keep the position closed:

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/4P3/2N5/PPPP1P.x: Most of the time in the Sicilian, White puts their knight on c3. White may yet play d4, but for the moment the question is yet to be answered. White's second move of 2. Nc3 suggests the possibility of NOT playing d4 (avoiding the exchange), and playing a closed position instead of the slashing, attacking types of positions that are more common to the Sicilian Defence. Leads to 3. g3 g6 4. Bg2 Bg7 5. d3 d6

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/4PP2/2N5/PPPP2.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nc3/2...Nc6/3. f4
r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/4PP2/2N5/PPPP2.x: With 3. f4, white starts the Grand Prix attack, a sharp and aggressive weapon against the Sicilian. Instead of trying to control the center with d2-d4 or develop the minor pieces, white controls the center with the f-pawn and launches a pawn storm directly against the kingside. Black may choose to fianchetto the bishop or start attacking on the queenside (A choice made easier by the pawn on c5). In general, players castle on opposite sides and attack the other side with pawns and bishops, trying to weaken each other's kings. Black can also strike back at the center with an early 3...d5.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.x:
White increases their control of the d4 square: the conventional plan is to follow with 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 and open the position.

Black's attention must now turn to their development: determining how to release their bishops, or first developing their knight. The main lines are 2...d6, accounting for almost half of games, and 2...Nc6 and 2...e6, each about half as popular as 2...d6.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.x:
Black develops the knight to its natural square c6, where it controls the centre. This move is sometimes called the old Sicilian. Black forestalls a decision on a pawn move for a little longer: if they get to play ...d5 in one move later, they will have saved a tempo by not playing 2...d6.

3. d4 continues with the open Sicilian plan to open the position. After 3...cxd4 4. Nxd4, the most common lines include 4...g6, the accelerated dragon, 4...e5, the Kalashnikov, or 4...Nf6 5. Nc3 where 5...e5 is the Sveshnikov and 5...d6 is known as the classical Sicilian.

3. Bb5 is the Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo attack, and is the major side line to the open Sicilian.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/1Bp5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5
r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/1Bp5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1.x:
This is the chief alternative 3. d4. White's bishop on b5 pressures Black's knight and therefore its control of the centre.

By prioritising the development of their kingside, White is ready to castle with plans of d3 (now that the light square bishop has been developed outside of the pawn chain) or d4 (supported by Re1 and c3). In general White is happy to trade the bishop for the knight if they can leave Black with doubled pawns: they may do so immediately or wait until provoked.

Black's main two options are 3...g6 and 3...e6.

r1bqkbnr/1p1ppppp/p1n5/1Bp5/4P3/5N2/PPPP.x: This move attacks the bishop but since White wanted to trade it off anyway, this effectively wastes a move.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/4P3/2N2N2/PPPP.x:
White develops their knights to their most active squares. White usually intends to put their knight on c3 eventually: by playing it, now White waits to open the centre with d4 until they have more information about how Black intends to play. This move suggest the possibility of not playing d4, and instead playing a closed position.

3...e5 is the main move. This capitalises on White's hesitation and prevents White from getting to play d4 after all. 4. Bc4 is the main continuation, as now Black's cannot play ...e6 to limit the bishop, and the position resembles an Italian game where Black has somehow gotten in c5.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2np4/2p5/4P3/2N2N2/PPPP.x: This is a non-committal move. Black retains flexibility to wait and see if White opens the game with d4 or not.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/4P3/P4N2/1PPP1.x:
The delayed Mengarini Variation (French Wing Variation) is a variation of the Sicilian Defense where White plays a move that delays development for an interesting idea: playing the move b4. The move a3 itself is not the best choice since it does not control the center and does not develop any pieces.

Black can respond in several ways, including /3...g6/ to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop, /3...Nf6/, /3...d6/, and /3...e5/.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/4P3/2P2N2/PP1P.x: The Opening Line 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 Nc6 can transform from the Old Sicilian to the Alapin variation with 3. c3. The ideas of this line are the same as the regular Alapin.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4
r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.x:
White takes space in the centre. White invites Black to take the d-pawn. Black can hardly allow White to advance to d5, taking more space and displacing their knight.

3...cxd4 eliminates the pawn and White can recapture 4. Nxd4. White's advantage is that they now have open lines for all their pieces to develop. Black's advantage is that they have both central pawns to White's one.

3...Nxd4?! is legal but barely warrants mentioning. 4. Nxd4 cxd4 5. Qxd4 only gives White a helping hand with their attack.

3...e6? to increase control of the d5 square does not prevent White from playing d5.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...cxd4
r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP.x:
Black captures White's d-pawn and reduces White's control of the centre. They are now playing with two centre pawns to White's one.

4. Nxd4 recaptures the pawn. White now has opened lines for their bishops to develop and join the attack. Their knight on d4 may subsequently move to b3, where it assists in the defence of their king following queen's side castling and is out of the way of a king's side pawn storm.

4. c3 is also in keeping with the position. This is a gambit that transposes into the Smith-Morra gambit if accepted. White sacrifices a pawn or two to extend their development lead.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4
r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.x:
White recaptures the pawn. They have open lines for their pieces to develop. Black has the positional advantage of two centre pawns to White's one.

The two knights are at a standoff. Neither wants to take first: if Black trades knights, 4...Nxd4!?, after 5. Qxd4 White will have better control of the centre and Black cannot easily chase away the white queen. If White elects to trade, say 4...Nf6 5. Nxc6!? bxc6, Black has brought in another pawn to help control the centre and support playing d5.

The main moves here are 4...Nf6, 4...e5, and 4...g6.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2np1n2/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP2P.x:

Next White looks to develop their bishops.

6. Bc4 is the Sozin attack. Black usually plays 6...e6, and the line continues 7. Be3 Be7 8. Qe2 a6 9. O-O-O O-O. 6...Qb6 is an alternative.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1np1n2/1N2p1B1/4P3/2N5/.x: The primary purpose of 7...a6 is to drive the knight on b5 away from its strong position. The knight on b5 threatens to jump to c7, which would be a fork on Black's king and rook, and puts pressure on d6. By pushing the a-pawn, Black gains space on the queenside, which can support further pawn advances like ...b5, potentially leading to active counterplay on that side of the board. Forcing the knight to retreat diminishes White's immediate threats and allows Black to better organize their pieces. The knight typically moves to a3, where it is less active compared to b5.

r1bqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/2n1p3/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nc6
r1bqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/2n1p3/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP.x:
4...Nc6 in the e6 Sicilian is the Taimanov, named for Russian GM Mark Taimanov who popularised the opening in the 1960s.

While Nc6 doesn't make a threat on e4, 5. Nc3 is White's usual response all the same. After, Black's principal options are 5...Nf6, the Four Knights Sicilian, or 5...Qc7, the Bastrikov variation.

With 5...Qc7, Black wants to focus on their queenside development first: a6, b5, Bb7 and Rc8, with the dark-square bishop developing to e7 or b4. White's plans include the English Attack (with Nc3, Be3, Qd2 and O-O-O), or Nc3, Be2 and O-O.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppp1p/2n3p1/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...g6
r1bqkbnr/pp1ppp1p/2n3p1/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP.x:
Black wants to play a Dragon Sicilian set-up, with ...Bg7, ...Nf6, and ...O-O. This is "accelerated" over the conventional Dragon because Black has not played ...d6. They have prioritised developing their pieces and will have saved a tempo if they play ...d5 in one move.

This system specifically defangs the Yugoslav attack, the most punishing attack against the Dragon Sicilian. (Briefly, because it allows Black to play ...d5 one move earlier, opening the position before White has had a chance to long-castle and form a battery on the d-file.) The trade off is it allows White 5. c4, a line the conventional Dragon move order avoids.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppp1p/2n3p1/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...g6/5. Nc3
r1bqkbnr/pp1ppp1p/2n3p1/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP2P.x:
Avoiding 5. c4, White develops their knight to its natural square. This is slightly less common than 5. c4.

5...Bg7 is essentially the only move and the line continues 6. Be3 Nf6. There White has some choice but almost always picks 7. Bc4 to control d5, where White intends to castle long and attack on the king's side. Less common sidelines include 7. Be2 and O-O, or 7. Nxc6 intending 8. e5, or 7. f3?!, which is an error.

r1bqk2r/pp1pppbp/2n2np1/8/3NP3/2N1B3/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...g6/5. Nc3/5...Bg7/6. Be3/6...Nf6
r1bqk2r/pp1pppbp/2n2np1/8/3NP3/2N1B3/PPP.x:
Black develops their knight to its natural square where it controls the centre, and prepares to castle.

7. f3?! is the most common move in amateur games, but it is inaccurate. White thinks to play in the manner of the Yugoslav attack, where f3 is necessary to defend e4 and control g4, preventing ...Ng4 and freeing the queen to move to d2. However, in this line, after 7...O-O 8. Qd2, Black has 8...d5!. Compared to the regular dragon, Black saved a tempo by skipping ...d6 and so played ...d5 one turn earlier, before White has had the chance to long castle. White doesn't have the time to deliver their crushing kingside attack and Black has achieved equality.

r1bqk2r/pp1pppbp/2n2np1/8/2BNP3/2N1B3/PP.x:
This is the main line. White develops their bishop and increases control of d5 before playing f3. This prevents Black's rejoinder 8...d5, that otherwise equalises against the move order 7. f3 O-O 8. Qd2.

After 7...O-O, the main move, White must first move their bishop again, 8. Bb3, before continuing with f3 (controlling g4), Qd2, and O-O-O. Otherwise, 8. f3?! is answered with 8...Qb6!, 8. Qd2? with 8...Ng4!, exposing an attack on d4 while attacking White's dark square bishop.

7...Qa5!? is a sideline. This compels White to give up on the idea of long castling.

r1bq1rk1/pp1pppbp/2n2np1/8/2BNP3/2N1B3/P.x:
Black castles. White would like to continue their plan to long castle and assault Black's king side, but again they must take additional time to prepare it. Otherwise...

8. Qd2? to make way for long castling is answered with 8...Ng4!. This uncovers an attack on the knight on d4 while also attacking White's dark square bishop, which is a valuable piece needed to contest Black's bishop's control of the dark squares. To save the bishop, White is compelled to initiate the trade of knights themselves, 9. Nxc6 dxc6 10. Qxd8 (10. O-O-O?! Qxd2 11. Rxd2 Nxe3 loses the bishop pair anyway; 11. Bxd2?? hangs 11...Nxf2 with a fork) 10...Rxd8 11. Bg5 and Black stands better.

Nf3 d6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6. In a sense this is just a shake-up in move order, an "accelerated Najdorf".

rnbqkbnr/1p1ppppp/p7/2p5/4P3/2P2N2/PP1P1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...a6/3. c3
rnbqkbnr/1p1ppppp/p7/2p5/4P3/2P2N2/PP1P1.x:
3. c3 prepares to play d4 and dominate the centre. This is a sort of improved Alapin Sicilian: White argues that Black has wasted time with ...a6 compared to the conventional Alapin, and so allowed White to develop their knight for "free".

3...d5, the regular Alapin move, is most common. After 4. exd5 Qxd5 White does not have the option of Nc3 to kick away the queen, and Black has avoided White achieving a two-pawn centre.

3...e6 preparing 4...d5 is possible, leading to an advance French defence structure. 4. d4 d5 5. e5

rnbqkbnr/p2ppppp/1p6/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PP.x:
Black prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop.

White's best move is 3. d4 which continues 3...cxd4 4. Nxd4 Bb7.

Once fianchettoed, Black must be mindful of the danger to their weak light squares. They may be exploited by a well-timed Bb5 or Nb5, especially should Black play ...d6. e.g. 5. Nc3 Nc6 6. Be3 Nxd4 7. Bxd4 d6??, White can win a queen with 8. Bb5+! (see diagram).

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2pp4/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.x:
A move that has some popularity with beginners only, who want to open the centre immediately.

Something like a delayed Scandinavian defence, the forcing sequence is 3. exd5 Qxd5 4. Nc3 (White gains time on Black's queen). Unable to move to a5, as the main line of the Scandinavian, the queen returns to 4...Qd8.

Black has lost time and White is ahead in developing their minor pieces. Black has half-opened their d-file, so White should play 5. d4, or they will find it difficult to later: 5. Bc4? Nc6 and Black controls d4 three times to White's twice.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PP.x: With 2...d6, Black opens the c8-h3 diagonal for his light-squared bishop and defends the c5. ...d6 controls the e5 square, so Black can develop ...Nf6 safely in the future, without any worry of White playing e5. This is the modern, main way for Black to play the Sicilian. The Sicilians with ...d6 include many of the most popular and most theoretical lines in modern chess, including the Najdorf and dragon variations.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/1Bp5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bb5
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/1Bp5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.x:
3. Bb5+ is the Moscow variation. White develops their bishop with a tempo. White's kingside is now developed, so they are ready to castle. One plan for White is to set up a Maróczy bind, where they control d5 with pawns on both e4 and c4, and not wishing to have the king's bishop stuck behind the c4 pawn, they exchanging it first. Alternatively, they may plan to play for the centre with c3 and d4, Ruy López-style.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/2p5/2B1P3/5N2/PPPP1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/2p5/2B1P3/5N2/PPPP1.x:
3. Bc4, "Italian" variation

A trendy continuation, leading to structures resembling the Giuoco Pianissimo or the Ruy Lopez. White usually develops with d2-d3, c2-c3, O-O, Re1, and plays a2-a4 or Bb3 to prevent the bishop from being exchanged off, and prepares Nbd2-Nf1-Ng3 manoeuvres.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/2p5/4P3/2N2N2/PPPP1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Nc3
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/2p5/4P3/2N2N2/PPPP1.x: 3. Nc3 is a flexible choice, which leaves Black with the decision making process. White can still go for the Open Sicilian with d4 break, or a closed setup with g3, or something like the canal attack or rossolimo with Bb5.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/2p5/3PP3/5N2/PPP2PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/2p5/3PP3/5N2/PPP2PP.x:
White plays 3. d4, inviting Black to trade a pawn and open the position.

3...cxd4 is the main move. Black captures towards the centre with a flank pawn, breaking up White's two pawn centre. Once White recaptures 4. Nxd4, Black has two central pawns to White's one, and a semi-open c-file to use. White meanwhile has opened attacking lines: both bishops have access to the game, and their queen has the semi-open d-file.

The game usually continues 4...Nf6 (attacking e4) 5. Nc3, and from there, Black can choose their flavour of ...d6 Sicilian, including the Najdorf (5...a6), classical (5...Nc6), or dragon (5...g6) Sicilians.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/2P5/4P3/5N2/PPP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nf6/4. dxc5
rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/2P5/4P3/5N2/PPP2P.x:
dxc5 seems like an enticing move for white for a queen exchange and displacing black's king but is easily diffused in this line with Nxe4.

Nc3 is currently the preferred white move in the main line, however Bb5 or Bg5 are widely accepted but less played through openings.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP/.x:
With 3...cxd4, Black breaks up White's two-pawn centre and achieves a majority of central pawns and a semi-open c-file, expecting the pawn to be recaptured on the next turn.

While White could play in a gambit-fashion with 4. c3, transposing to a delayed Smith Morra gambit, in the large majority of cases, White recaptures the pawn.

4. Nxd4 is the main move, centralizing the knight, which eyes key squares such as b5 and f5. This was one of the main purposes of 2. Nf3, allowing White to recapture this d4-pawn with the knight rather than the queen, thus saving valuable tempi.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.x:
White recaptures the pawn, and centralises their knight. Their knight is active and centralised, and they have the space advantage and open lines to develop both of their bishops. Black meanwhile has the advantage of having both d- and e-pawns.

If White were to move again, they would love to play the move 5. c4. The structure with pawns on c4 and e4 is called te "Maróczy bind" and makes it very hard for Black to achieve ...d5. Then White could play Nc3 without blocking the progress of their c-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nf6
rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/.x:
Black starts the development of their pieces, whilst also attacking the e4 pawn. When Black played 2...d6, they controlled the e5 square, thus preventing White from playing e5 and kicking away this knight. As the e4 pawn is hanging, White does not have time to play 5. c4?, setting up the Maroczy Bind, as 5...Nxe4 would follow, in which White is down a pawn for no compensation.

As a result, White must find a way to defend against this threat.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP2PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nf6/5. Nc3
rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP2PP.x:
White defends their e-pawn while developing a piece.

Time has come for Black to make an important strategic choice. The four main variations are:

5...Nc6, developing their forces, is the classical Sicilian.

5...e6, the Scheveningen variation, prepares to develop the bishop to e7 and castle. This produces a solid pawn structure but Black's queen's bishop is shut in, for the moment at least.

5...g6, the dragon variation, prepares to develop the bishop to g7 instead, where it puts pressure on the long diagonal.

5...a6, the Najdorf variation, starts to take the control of the queen's side.

rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p2p1n2/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nf6/5. Nc3/5...a6
rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p2p1n2/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP2P.x:
Black plays 5...a6 and controls the b5 square. This is prophylaxis, removing White's options of Ndb5 or Bb5+, and supports further queenside expansion with ...b5 and ...b4 in the future, which could become dangerous for White should they castle queenside.

Flexibility is a key to this opening: Black chooses to develop their knight to d7 or c6 in some lines; their bishops to b7 or e6 and e7 (if the e-pawn is advanced) or g7 (after ...g6) in different lines.

5...a6 prepares 6...e5, kicking the knight to b3, because the intermezzo 7. Bb5+ is prevented. However, it doesn't make any immediate threats, therefore White has a large variety of ways to continue:

rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p2p1n2/8/2BNP3/2N5/PPP2.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nf6/5. Nc3/5...a6/6. Bc4
rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p2p1n2/8/2BNP3/2N5/PPP2.x:
6. Bc4

White develops her light-squared bishop to c4, entering the Fischer-Sozin attack. Pioneered by Fischer who extensively developed the theory of it, taking inspiration from Sozin's 6. Bc4 againt the Classical Sicilian, this move was at one point White's main weapon of choice against the Najdorf. However, it then fell out of favor as ways for Black to effectively equalise against it have been found, while the English Attack's true potential to pose problems for black was discovered. Recently, it has made a resurgence with modern lines that have strong practical value.

rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p2p1n2/8/3NP3/2N1B3/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nf6/5. Nc3/5...a6/6. Be3
rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p2p1n2/8/3NP3/2N1B3/PPP.x:
6. Be3 is the English attack. White has an idea to castle long and storm Black's kingside with their pawns.

6...e5 is the main line. This drives off White's knight to b3, but weakens d5 which White will try to use as an outpost.

6...Ng4 is the Anti-English. Black tries to avert White's plans of a kingside attack by trading off White's important dark square bishop. Whereas in the Yugoslav attack against the Dragon Sicilian, 6. Be3 Ng4?? is a mistake on account of 7. Bb5+! Nc6 8. Nxc6 bxc6 9. Bxc6+ Bd7 10. Bxa8, the difference in the Najdorf is that Black has played ...a6, so White does not have the resource Bb5+, therefore ...Ng4 is safe.

rnbqkb1r/4pppp/p2p1n2/1p6/3NP3/2N1B3/PPP.x:
6...b5?, apparently a natural move to expand on the queenside as prepared by ...a6, is a mistake on account of 7. Nd5!.

7. Nd5! appears to give up White's e-pawn. However, 7...Nxe5?? falls into a common amateur trap. After 8. Nxb5! (threatening Nc6+) axb5 9. Bb6 Black's queen is trapped. If 9...Qd7 10. Bxb5 Qxb5 11. Nc7+ forks the queen.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p2p1n2/4p3/3NP3/2N1B3/PP.x:
6...e5 is the most popular and most unbalancing response to the English attack. The pawn drives off the White's well-placed knight from d4 to a more passive square. Although this creates an outpost on d5, Black is saying, basically, that it is irrelevant to the play on the wings, while White is saying that Black will be lost if d5 is occupied.

White must save their knight, usually to 7. Nb3, and Black's main move is 7...Be6, increasing their control of d5. White's plans include playing f3, Qd2, long castling, and storm on the kingside with pawns.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p2p1n2/4p3/4P3/1NN1B3/PP.x:
White saves their knight. Black now needs to develop their pieces.

They usually begin 7...Be6, which increases their control of the d5 square, a potential outpost for White, while eyeing White's queenside (where Black anticipates White may castle). White continues 8. f3, preventing ...Ng4 and preparing to attack on the kingside with a brute-force pawn storm and long castling. This might take the form 8...Be7 9. Qd2 O-O 10. O-O-O Nbd7 11. g4. If Black obstructs those plans, as with 8...h5 to prevent g4, White switches tack to prioritise the skirmish for d5 and fight in the centre instead.

7...Be7 is another move-order, and is good as long as Black intends to follow up with ...Be6.

rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p2p1n2/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP2P.x: The Freak Attack is a very recent and upcoming response to the Najdorf. White's idea is to prepare a quick g2-g4, in style of the Keres Attack, combined with h4 and f4 causing problems to black's kingside. It also allows the bishop to develop to h3 in the future. Even though Rg1 looks absurd at first glance, it is a totally sound option according to the strongest engines. It is also a great surprise weapon - Theory is still developing on it and engine lines are still not sure how to proceed.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/3ppn2/8/2BNP3/2N5/PPP2PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nf6/5. Nc3/5...e6/6. Bc4
rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/3ppn2/8/2BNP3/2N5/PPP2PP.x:
White enters the Sozin Attack, a direct and aggressive system named after Russian master Veniamin Sozin. By placing the bishop on c4, White eyes the vulnerable f7 square and sets the stage for a fast kingside assault. This move fits perfectly against the Scheveningen setup, where Black’s e6 pawn can make the light squares around the king more tender.

Typical ideas for White include Qe2, Bb3, 0–0, and f4–f5, often leading to sharp play. In response, Black must tread carefully—failing to play ...Be7 and ...0–0 promptly can invite devastating attacks. The Sozin is a favorite of players seeking initiative and imbalances, and was famously wielded by Bobby Fischer with great success.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP2P.x:
Black prepares to fianchetto their dark-square bishop. From g7 this bishop will exert considerable pressure over the centre and facilitate a queen's side attack. However, 5...g6 weakens Black's kingside pawn structure and encourages White to pursue a king's side attack of their own.

6. Be3 is the main move. This usually leads to the Yugoslav attack, where White castles queen's side and tries to pawn storm on the king's side. Because both players are attacking on opposite wings, there is no time to be lost for either side and subtle manoeuvring will tend to take a back seat to sharp tactics.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP1B.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nf6/5. Nc3/5...g6/6. Be2
rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP1B.x: This variation is a variation of the Sicilian tradition of the dragon. White wants to make a great defence in kingside.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/8/3NP3/2N1B3/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nf6/5. Nc3/5...g6/6. Be3
rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/8/3NP3/2N1B3/PPP.x:
White develops their bishop. This prepares to castle queenside and usually leads to the Yugoslav attack.

6...Bg7 is the most logical and main line continuation, developing the bishop as prepared by ...g6 and preparing to castle.

6...Nc6 is an alternative. This is really a waiting move where Black delays committing their bishop. 7. f3 h5 is the Hungarian variation, and Black has the idea of meeting 8. Qd2 with 8...Nxd4 9. Bxd4 Bh6! 10. Be3 Bxe3 11. Qxe3, trading off the minor pieces and so easing the discomfort of being down on space.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/8/3NP3/2N1B3/PPP2.x: 7. f3 is the main move. This controls the g4-square and so denies Black ...Ng4, therefore allows White to play Qd2 next and castle long (the Bb5+ idea, which refuted 6...Ng4??, is less powerful now that Black's king can access f8). The pawn on f3 also supports the e4 pawn, liberating the knight from that duty, and can support a king-side pawn storm (g4, h4, g5, h5).

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/8/3NP3/2N1BP2/PPP.x:
White's f-pawn defends e4, freeing the c3-knight from the duty, and controls the g4-square. This prevents ...Ng4, which Black was threatening to play and game time on White's bishop. The pawn on f3 is critical for supporting a king's side attack with g4, h4, and h5 in the future, where White aims to take advantage of the "hook" in the Black king's side, the g6 pawn.

7...O-O is the main move, which gets the king to safety, and aims to setup a sharp and exciting game involving opposite-sides castling.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p2p1/8/3NP1n1/2N1B3/PP.x:
Black attacks White's bishop, but falls into a common amateur trap.

White's queen attack's Black's knight, but it is currently guarded by their light square bishop. 7. Bb5+ cuts off that protection.

If Black blocks the check with 7...Nd7, their bishop no longer guards g4. If 7...Bd7, the bishop becomes pinned and so also does not guard g4.

If 7...Nc6, White can trade knights, 8. Nxc6 (attacking the queen) bxc6, and 9. Bxc6+ forks the king and rook.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/8/3NPP2/2N5/PPP3.x: This move has a few ideas connoted to it. The primary idea is to push e5, since this pawn idea gains central influence and is now prepared by f4. White can also look to put the knight back onto f3 and play the position like a Grand Prix attack, with future ideas of swinging the white queen onto the kingside through the e1-h4 diagonal. Against some sidelines, white can also consider castling long!

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/8/3QP3/5N2/PPP2PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Qxd4
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/8/3QP3/5N2/PPP2PPP/.x:
White recaptures on d4 with their queen. This is an irregular continuation that avoids the main line Open Sicilians.

Usually it is considered unprincipled to develop one's queen early because it can be a target affording the enemy valuable tempo. However, here White argues that their queen is hard for Black to exploit because they have played ...d6.

After 4...Nc6, attacking the queen, White pins and trades off the knight with 5. Bb5 Bd7 6. Bxc6. Then, the usual continuation is 6...Bxc6 7. Nc3 Nf6 8. Bg5 e6 9. O-O-O Be7 10. Rhe1 O-O.

rnbqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/8/2p1p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.x:
Sorry, but JalalaVeryBad.―Anish Giri

In the Jalalabad variation, Black responds to e4 with both e5 and c5 (in either the move order 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 c5? or 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 e5?). This gives up Black's central e-pawn. This is not considered sound.

After 3. Nxe5, Black can play 3...Nc6, offering to trade knights and take the game in a Stafford gambit-style direction, or 3...Qe7 looking to recover the pawn.

3...Nc6 offers to trade knights. 4. Nxc6 dxc6 and the position resembles a Stafford gambit where Black is down a tempo, having played c5 instead of Nf6. There is no immediately threat to e4 and the position is a lot less precarious for White.

rnbqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/4p3/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.x: Black opens up the a3-f8 diagonal for their dark squared bishop, while also controlling the d5 square for a second time. This prepares to play ...d5 and recapture with a pawn, gaining further central control.

rnbqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/4p3/2p5/4P3/1P3N2/P1PP.x:
This opening has some very interesting ideas. With this move White prepares to fianchetto the dark squared bishop to b2 but depending on what Black plays next White's ideas aren't really clear.

Black can continue with the usual Taimanov or Kan setup and Black can also play the /4...d5/ pawn break, but the most played move in the chess database right now is /4...b6/.

rnbqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/4p3/2p5/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6/3. d4
rnbqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/4p3/2p5/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.x:
White plays 3. d4, inviting Black to trade a pawn and open the position.

3...cxd4 is the main move. Black captures towards the centre with a flank pawn, breaking up White's two pawn centre. Once White recaptures 4. Nxd4, Black has two central pawns to White's one, and a semi-open c-file to use. White meanwhile has opened attacking lines: both bishops have access to the game, and their queen has the semi-open d-file. After the trade of pawns is complete, Black then has a choice of ...e6 Sicilians, the most popular of which are the Kan (4...a6), Taimanov (4...Nc6), four knights (both ...Nc6 and ...Nf6), or Kveinis (4...Qb6) variations.
