r1bqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/2n1p3/1N6/4P3/8/PPP2PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nc6/5. Nb5
r1bqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/2n1p3/1N6/4P3/8/PPP2PP.x:
With 5. Nb5 White moves to exploit Black's dark square weaknesses. When Black played 2...e6, they left a hole on the d6 square.

White has two attackers on d6 and Black only one defender, the bishop, so 5...a6? allows 6. Nd6+ Bxd6 7. Qxd6 ∓. White gets the bishop pair and their Queen is all up in Black's business.

5...d6 is the only way for Black to add a defender, allowing the black queen to see d6. White can then follow with 6. c4 or 6. Bf4. White will have to spend some tempo retreating their knight to somewhere safer, before or after it is kicked by a6. White chooses either knights on a3 and c3, or c3 and d2.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2npp3/1N6/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nc6/5. Nb5/5...d6
r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2npp3/1N6/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/.x:
Black prevents White's knight coming in to d6.

White can then follow with 6. c4 or 6. Bf4.

6. Bf4 acts to provoke 6...e5, weakening the d5 square and leading the game into a Kalashnikov-style Sicilian, with Black's pawns on e5 and d6. After 6...e5 the bishop falls back to 7. Be3. Then Black typically looks to kick White's misplaced knight, 7...a6, or develop while attacking White's e4 pawn, 7...Nf6.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2npp3/1N6/2P1P3/8/PP3PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nc6/5. Nb5/5...d6/6. c4
r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2npp3/1N6/2P1P3/8/PP3PPP.x:
White sets up the Maroczy bind structure to control d5. Between their c and e pawns, and having induced Black to play d6 and restrict their own dark square bishop, they hope to keep Black's position cramped, hampering their development, and that this will make up for the loss of tempo White incurred in moving their knight multiple times in the opening.

If 6...a6 straight away, Black kicks White's knight and they are forced to move it again: usually to c3.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2nppn2/1N6/2P1P3/8/PP3PP.x:
6...Nf6 develops while threatening White's e4 pawn.

White can defend with 7. N1c3, developing their second knight and intending their other knight to retreat to a3, or 7. N5c3, leaving their knight on b1 undeveloped for now.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2nppn2/1N6/2P1P3/2N5/PP3.x:
7. N1c3 defends White's e4 pawn while developing their knight.

Black usually continues 7...a6, compelling White to retreat to the passive a6 square. However, at least from there White will overprotect the c4 pawn and keep d5 in sight of their queen.

Black can delay a6 until after they have castled: 7...Be7 8. Be2 9. O-O O-O 10. a6.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1nppn2/1N6/2P1P3/2N5/PP.x:
7...a6 kicks White's knight.

Its available squares are d4 or a3.

The most common move is 8. Na3. This places a knight on the rim, but at least it overdefends c4 in case Black hopes to make use of the half-open file and play ...Rc8 one day.

8. Nd4 reduces White's control of d5, and allows Black to untangle with 8...d5 9. cxd5 exd5 10. exd5 Nxd5 11. Nxc6 bxc6 (see diagram). The position is equal but now open, and White is no longer able to keep Black suffocating in their side of the board as they had hoped.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1nppn2/8/2P1P3/N1N5/PP3.x:
White saves their knight with 8. Na3.

The position is looking cramped for Black. Those pawns on c4 and e4 prevent them from playing d5 and gaining more space. Meanwhile, Black's pawns on d6 and e6 prevent Black from developing their bishops very actively.

They have three typical continuations.

Black still has their bishops to develop, so option one is to develop their light-square bishop, in which case first Black must play 8...b6 to make room to fianchetto it.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1n1pn2/3p4/2P1P3/N1N5/P.x:
Black challenges White in the centre to open up the position.

White has four attackers to Black's three defenders. However, after 9. cxd5 exd5 10. exd5, Black intends to play 10...Nb4, bringing another attacker.

r1b1kbnr/ppqp1ppp/2n1p3/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP2P.x:
Black chooses to develop their queen to a safe square where it has good scope.

6. Be3 is the most common move. White develops their bishop to an active square where the knight on d4 is defended from any potential ...Nxd4 exchanges that may happen in the future. White may be preparing to castle long, 6...a6 7. Qd2 Nf6 8. O-O-O, or is overdefending their knight so that they may play 7. Bd3 and castle short.

6. Be2 develops the king's bishop without obstructing the queen's defence of d4, and prepares to castle short, 6...a6 7. O-O.

6. Nxc6 does not wait to exchange knights. White decides that it is finally time to settle the trade offer by accepting.

rnb1kbnr/pp1p1ppp/1q2p3/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Qb6
rnb1kbnr/pp1p1ppp/1q2p3/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP.x:
The rare and razor-sharp Kveinis (or Kveinys) variation has often been considered inferior to other variations of the French Sicilian, but statistics show it scores the best of any of Black's turn four moves at the club level, and respectably well at grandmaster level, too. It is especially efficacious as a surprise weapon in blitz and bullet games.

...Qb6 pressures b2, White's knight on d4, and beyond it the weak f2 square. Much of the variation's club-level success comes from White underestimating ...Bc5, where Black stacks power against f2. For example, 5. c4? Bc5! and Black threatens to win the knight. 6. Be3 Nc6 (increases pressure on d4) 7. Nxc6? Bxe3 8. fxe3 Qxe3+ .

rnbqkbnr/1p1p1ppp/p3p3/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...a6
rnbqkbnr/1p1p1ppp/p3p3/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/.x:
The Kan is a highly dynamic opening. Black intends to put their pawns on light squares and control the dark squares with their pieces. For now they take a "wait-and-see" approach, developing only after White has committed their pieces.

rnbqkbnr/1p1p1ppp/p3p3/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP2PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...a6/5. Nc3
rnbqkbnr/1p1p1ppp/p3p3/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP2PP.x: fi:Shakkiaapinen/Peli/1. e4/1...c5/2. Rf3/2...e6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Rxd4/4...a6/5. Rc3

rnbqkbnr/pp1pp1pp/8/2p2p2/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.x: Black offers the f-pawn, hoping to deflect White's e-pawn from control of d5. However, it comes with severe trade-offs. Moving the f-pawn opens the a2-g8 and e8-h5 diagonals, and if White accepts the pawn Black may find their unable to play ...d5 anyway, due to the weaknesses of the e6 and e5 squares. Therefore the gambit is not considered sound.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppp1p/6p1/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.x:
Black prepares to fianchetto their king's bishop, ...Bg7. This is the start of the Hyperaccelerated Dragon.

In the Accelerated Dragon, Black usually plays 2...Nc6 before preparing to fianchetto their bishop. This allows White the option of 3. Bb5, the Rossolimo attack. With the move order 2...g6, Black hopes to sidestep that line.

The main continuation is the usual Open Sicilian plan: 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4, and 4...Nc6 transposes to the Accelerated Dragon, Rossolimo successfully avoided. White can continue with 5. Nc3, the conventional Open Sicilian move, or 5. c4, the tricky Maróczy bind, which clamps down on the d5 square with both e- and c-pawns.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppp1p/6p1/2p5/2P1P3/5N2/PP1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...g6/3. c4
rnbqkbnr/pp1ppp1p/6p1/2p5/2P1P3/5N2/PP1P.x:
= Sicilian - Hyper-Accelerated Dragon, Maróczy Bind =

The Maróczy Bind Variation of the Hyper-Accelerated Dragon is a variation where white advances the c4 before playing Nc3, this also helps controlling the d5 square, after black fianchettos the bishop on g7, white will play Nc3 and d4, build a big and stable center, Similar to the Staunton-Cochrane Sicilian where white play e4, c4, and aims for d4.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppp1p/6p1/2p5/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...g6/3. d4
rnbqkbnr/pp1ppp1p/6p1/2p5/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.x:
White plays 3. d4, the classic Open Sicilian move, to open up the centre while opening lines for their bishop and queen to develop. White is playing to maximise their activity.

This gives White pawns on both d4 and e4 controlling great tracts in the middle of the board, so the main move is 3...cxd4 to break up White's powerful two-pawn centre, and after White recaptures, Black will have a central pawn majority and use of the half-open c-file. White can then retake the pawn with either 4. Nxd4, the conventional Open Sicilian move, or 4. Qxd4, which is an effective sideline against the Hyperaccelerated Dragon.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppp1p/6p1/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...g6/3. d4/3...cxd4
rnbqkbnr/pp1ppp1p/6p1/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP.x:
Black takes the d-pawn. This was the idea behind 1...c5: White can retake and Black has a central pawn majority (both d- and e-pawns). In exchange, White gets open lines for development.

There are two ways to retake the pawn.

4. Nxd4 is natural. 4...Nc6 transposes into the accelerated dragon Sicilian and Black has successfully avoided facing the Rossolimo variation through the hyperaccelerated move order.

From there, the main continuations Black faces are 5. c4 or 5. Nc3. 4...Bg7 5. c4 Nc3 transposes. 4...Nf6 first, attacking e4, encourages 5. Nc3 so as to avoid facing 5. c4, though White can always play 5. f3 to keep the option of c4. 4...Nf6 5. e5? loses the pawn to 5...Qa5+.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppp1p/6p1/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...g6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4
rnbqkbnr/pp1ppp1p/6p1/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.x:
White recaptures according to the standard open Sicilian plan.

Black can now transpose into the accelerated dragon with 4...Nc6. This is the main idea behind this move order: to reach the accelerated dragon while avoiding facing the Rossolimo sideline. White may play with 5. Nc3 or 5. c4, the Maróczy bind.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/1P2P3/8/P1PP1PPP.x:
2. b4 marks the Sicilian Wing Gambit. There are other wing gambits like this using the b-pawn (for instance, the Evans Gambit); however, this wing gambit is the most common one. The b-pawn push tries to undermine Black's c-pawn control of d4.

This gambit is unsound at the top level, and Black can safely accept it. However, it is common in amateur play.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/8/1p2P3/8/P1PP1PPP/R.x:
Black bravely accepts the gambit. Since the gambit is of questionable soundness, it is best to accept it.

One trap: a3 d5! (Countering in the center) exd5 Qxd5 axb4?? (White, in his eagerness to regain the pawn, forgot a simple tactic), Qe5+ wins the rook on a1.

The recommended refutation is to counterattack in the center at the right time.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/8/1p2P3/P7/2PP1PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. b4/2...cxb4/3. a3
rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/8/1p2P3/P7/2PP1PPP/R.x: This move hopes for bxa3, when White would have good compensation after Bxa3 due to his development and open queenside files. However, d5! is very strong. exd5 is usually played and is the best move. Black is better.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/3p4/1p2P3/P7/2PP1PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. b4/2...cxb4/3. a3/3...d5
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/3p4/1p2P3/P7/2PP1PPP/.x: This is the antidote to the Wing Gambit. Black counterattacks in the center and prevents axb4 due to dxe4, winning a central pawn. White cannot win the pawn back with 4. exd5 Qxd5 5. axb4?? due to 5... Qe5+.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/2P5/PP1P1PPP.x:
This is one of the main "anti-Sicilians", a way for White to avoid the theory-dense open lines following 2. Nf3.

2. c3 supports pushing the pawn to d4. If 2...Nc6!?, which is a common amateur try, 3. d4 cxd4 4. cxd4 and White has achieved a two-pawn centre. When they played 1...c5, Black had hoped for an edge by taking central pawn with a less-important flanking c-pawn, but this disappeared when White was able to recapture with their own flank pawn. The line continues 4...d5 5. exd5 (5. e5?! allows Black to play ...Bf5 and ...e6, for an improved French defence structure) Qxd5 6. Nf3 e5 7. Nc3 Bb4 8. Bd2 Bxc3 9. Bxc3 e4 10. Ne5 Nxe5 11. dxe5 Ne7

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/2p5/4P3/2P5/PP1P1P.x:
3.e5 immediately pressures the Black knight, and is by far the most popular response. It also continues White’s assault on the centre, and aims to reinforce with d4.

3.d3 and 3.d4 are playable, but more passive. d3 aims to protect the e pawn, while d4 simply continues with White’s original plan of controlling the d4 square - the goal of the Alapin opening.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/8/2pnP3/8/2P5/PP1P1PPP.x: This is obviously the only good move, as 3...Ne4?? 4.d3! forfeits the knight, whilst 3...Ng8? is way too passive and forfeits two tempi. White usually plays 4.d4 or 4.Nf3. If White played 4.Bc4, or 4.g3, Black is fine after e6 and eventually d6.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/8/2pnP3/3P4/2P5/PP3PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. c3/2...Nf6/3. e5/3...Nd5/4. d4
rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/8/2pnP3/3P4/2P5/PP3PPP.x: This move gains central space and connects with the e-pawn. White has created a pawn chain in the center and is now threatening c4 followed by d5, when Black would really suffocate by his lack of central space. This pawn controls White's center.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/8/2p1P3/4n3/2P5/PP1P1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. c3/2...Nf6/3. e5/3...Ne4
rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/8/2p1P3/4n3/2P5/PP1P1P.x: This is a mistake because after 4.d3! white wins the knight.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p1P3/8/2P5/PP1P1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. c3/2...Nf6/3. e5/3...Ng8
rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p1P3/8/2P5/PP1P1PPP.x: This retreat is just too cowardly and timid. Black has lost two tempi moving the knight to g8 from f6. After d4, White has a huge center and initiative. 3...Nd5 is much better, since the knight is well placed there. It is usually unwise to move a piece back to it's original square in the opening.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2pp4/4P3/2P5/PP1P1PPP.x:
Black is threatening to take on e4. White's best option is to take first, with 3. exd5.

After 3. exd5 the main line continues 3...Qxd5, the Barmen variation, and White doesn't have Nc3 to kick the queen away. After 4. d4, it is possible for Black to win a pawn and go into an endgame, however White has adequate compensation and better practical chances. A more common plan is to leave White with an isolated queen's pawn position and control d5 with ...e6 and ...Nf6.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2pP4/8/2P5/PP1P1PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. c3/2...d5/3. exd5
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2pP4/8/2P5/PP1P1PPP/R.x:
The natural move; eliminating the tension in the center, while bringing Black's queen to a more vulnerable position.

Although White cannot immediately attack the Queen because of the pawn on c3, in some lines the Queen can be pinned to a captured pawn on d4 (eg. 4. d4 cxd4 5. Nf3), or become a target later down the line with moves such as c4. However, the Black Queen on d5 is often one of Black's biggest assets, as it assists in ideas such as Bg4 and is exceedingly hard to kick out before White castles.

3. exd5 is the most common move after 2...d5, followed by 3. d3 and 3. e5.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.x:
White opens up the centre immediately. This is an uncommon but tactical sideline to avoid the conventional Open Sicilian. Today it is played with the idea of sacrificing a pawn for development and open lines.

Black should play 2...cxd4, which was why they played 1...c5 in the first place.

In the 19th century, 2. d4 was played with the idea of opening the centre and recapturing the pawn immediately: 2...cxd4 3. Qxd4!?. This is sometimes seen today, but it allows Black to develop with tempo on the queen (3...Nc6) for an even game. White has to move their queen again and suddenly their development advantage, and the whole reason for opening the centre in the first place, disappears.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/8/3pP3/8/PPP2PPP/RNB.x:
Black takes the pawn. The trade of a c- for d-pawn gives Black a central pawn majority.

Though White could take it back with 3. Qxd4?!, this allows Black to push the queen around and play 3...Nc6 with tempo.

Instead the main move is 3. c3, the Smith-Morra gambit. After 3...dxc3 White can retake while developing their knight.

An alternative is 3. Nf3, the Morphy gambit. White prepares to recapture with the knight. If Black tries to holds onto the extra pawn with 3...e5, White's best continuation is 4. c3 leading to something similar to the Smith-Morra, where Black has a hole on d5 and a backward d-pawn. Otherwise, this can transpose into an Open Sicilian after (e.g.) 3...d6 4. Nxd4.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. Nf3
rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP/R.x:
Rather than recapture the pawn with their queen, which would allow White to gain tempo with ...Nc6, White prepares to recapture with their knight.

This looks to transpose into a regular open Sicilian. Black may play whatever move they would have played after 2. Nf3 (3...d6, 3...Nc6 etc.) and allow the transposition.

However, the way to "punish" White for the irregular move order is 3...e5, securing the pawn. 4. Nxe5?? fails to 4...Qa5+!. White's best continuation is 4. c3, the Andreaschek gambit, reaching a position similar to the Smith-Morra gambit when declined with ...e5.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/8/3QP3/8/PPP2PPP/RNB.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. Qxd4
rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/8/3QP3/8/PPP2PPP/RNB.x:
= Smith-Morra Gambit =
This move is not the best. Even though it regains the pawn, black can simply harass White's queen with 3...Nc6.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/8/3pP3/2P5/PP3PPP/RN.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3
rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/8/3pP3/2P5/PP3PPP/RN.x:
White offers a pawn for quicker development and open c- and d-files.

3...dxc3 accepts the gambit, and White can recapture with 4. Nxc3. Black is now a pawn up, but in return White has a lead in development. They are ready to develop both their bishops, but Black will have to make two more pawn moves before they can get their bishops out. The game usually continues 4...Nc6 5. Nf3 e6 6. Bc4, where Black reaches the first major branching point in theory.

Accepting is the main move, and the choice of chess engines (who are fearless). However, White gets good compensation for the pawn and attacking chances, so it is not uncommon to decline it.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/8/4P3/2Pp4/PP3PPP/RN.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...d3
rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/8/4P3/2Pp4/PP3PPP/RN.x:
Players have played this move a bit, but it is too passive. Black does not need to decline White's gambit. After c4 followed by Bxd3, White has a and a spatial plus.

However, this move is very much playable, and even poses some specific benefits over 3...d5: specifically, it allows Dragon players to continue going for their fianchetto plans, and Najdorf/Kan/O'Kelly players to continue with their flexible ideas and setups, allowing lower-level players to still stick to their prep more or less.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/8/4P3/2p5/PP3PPP/RNB.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3
rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/8/4P3/2p5/PP3PPP/RNB.x:
Black accepts the gambit by taking another pawn.

4. Nxc3 retakes the pawn while developing a piece. White's advantage is that they have managed to move both their e- and d-pawns, meaning they are ready to develop both their bishops without making any more pawn moves, without Black having had time to develop anything. All they had to give up was their central d-pawn: Black's advantage is that they are a pawn up and have both d- and e-pawns on the board.

Offering up another pawn, e.g. 4. Bc4? cxb2 5. Bxb2 à la the Danish gambit is considered to give up too much material for the compensation on offer, but it is aggressive and may still be played especially at shorter time controls.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/8/4P3/2N5/PP3PPP/R1B.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3
rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/8/4P3/2N5/PP3PPP/R1B.x:
White is now ready to develop all their minor pieces to natural squares. Their next few moves are straight-forward developing moves: Nf3, Bc4, O-O. Meanwhile, Black will still have to make some pawns moves before they can catch up.

Black has a few different moves that are mainly just changes in move order, but 4...Nc6 seems to be the most flexible starting point, as it is a good developing move that controls d4 and e5: (if 4...Nf6?! instead then 5. e5 is a free tempo move to embarrass Black).

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/8/4P3/2N5/PP3PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6
r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/8/4P3/2N5/PP3PPP/R.x:
Black gets the development of their pieces underway and starts to control the centre and the d4 and e5 squares. Control of e5 prevents White pushing a pawn there, at least for now, and control of d4 means Black has the option of developing their king's bishop with ...e6 and ...Bb4 without allowing Qd4 to attack b4 and the g7-pawn.

5. Nf3 is White's main move, followed by 5. Bc4 to develop and to prepare to castle kingside. (White surely doesn't want to castle queenside into the open c-file open.)

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/8/4P3/2N2N2/PP3PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3
r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/8/4P3/2N2N2/PP3PPP.x:
White continues development. They plan to follow up with 6. Bc4 and 7. O-O.

Black usually wants to start thinking about a pawn move:

5...e6 is the main move. This opens a line for the king's bishop to develop. Since Black expects 6. Bc4, ...e6 has the added advantage of relieving the bishop's pressure on f7. After 6. Bc4, the game reaches the main tabiya of the Smith-Morra accepted, where Black's main choices are 6...a6, playing in the style of the Paulsen, 6...d6, playing in the style of the Scheveningen, 6...Qc7, the Siberian variation, or 6...Bb4, the pin variation.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2np4/8/4P3/2N2N2/PP3PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3/5...d6
r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2np4/8/4P3/2N2N2/PP3PPP.x:
Black adds control of e5. This also allows their queen's bishop to move off the back rank, though if Black is intending to develop their bishop in that direction they will have to play precisely.

After 6. Bc4, Black isn't quite ready to develop their knight or bishop for tactical reasons. Black's main choices are to transposes into the Scheveningen structure with 6...e6, or prepare to develop their knight and bishop with the move 6...a6, leading to a classical structure.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2np4/8/2B1P3/2N2N2/PP3P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3/5...d6/6. Bc4
r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2np4/8/2B1P3/2N2N2/PP3P.x:
White's bishop pressures Black's vulnerable f7 pawn. The strength of the bishop's pressure can be seen in a number of traps Black can fall into with imprecise play. Black can blunt its attack by pushing the pawn ...e6, though the question is, now or later?

6...e6 is the most straight forward and main move. This reaches a Scheveningen structure, transposing into the line 5...e6 6. Bc4 d6. This only requires a small amount of patience: Black will eventually play ...e5 and the bishop is still allowed into the game.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppp1p/2n3p1/8/4P3/2N2N2/PP3P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3/5...g6
r1bqkbnr/pp1ppp1p/2n3p1/8/4P3/2N2N2/PP3P.x:
Black prepares to fianchetto their bishop, playing in the style of the accelerated dragon Sicilian. This is a playable but sharp line, and Black needs to be accurate to hold the position.

6. Bc4 develops the bishop, prepares to castle, and places pressure on f7. 6...Bg7 and White has the interesting move 7. e5. The e-pawn is not in fact hanging because of tactics emerging from White's bishop (7...Nxe5?! 8. Nxe5 Bxe5 9. Bxf7+ Kxf7 10. Qd5+ Kg7 11. Qxe5+ Nf6 ). While it is on e5, it prevents Black's knight from developing to f6, and if Black removes it with 7...d6 8. exd6 they may not recapture the pawn yet because of 8...exd6? 9. Nb5!.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/8/4P3/2P5/P4PPP/RNBQ.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. bxc3
rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/8/4P3/2P5/P4PPP/RNBQ.x:
White forgets why they offered the pawn sacrifice 3. c3 in the first place. Slavish adherence to the rule of "capture towards the centre" has lead them here, down a pawn, with isolated a- and c-pawns, nothing developed, and with their knight unable to reach c3.

Black should have an easy game.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4PP2/8/PPPP2PP/R.x:
With 2. f4 White begins an aggressive attack against Black's kingside. This is the McDonnell attack, aka a(n accelerated) Grand Prix.

2...d5, the Tal gambit, lets Black thwart the attack before it gets started. If White declines with 3. e5, Black can play Bf5 and e6, achieving a superior French defence structure without the lousy French bishop. If White accepts, 3. exd5, Black can recover the pawn and get a development lead: 3...Nf6 4. Nc3 Nxd5 5. Nxd5 Qxd5.

For this reason the attack is often played in the move order 2. Nc3 followed by 3. f4, the (conventional) Grand Prix, where if e.g. 2. Nc3 Nc6 3. f4 e5 can be met with Nxe5.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2pp4/4PP2/8/PPPP2PP/R.x:
2...d5 is the Tal gambit.

3. exd5 is the main move. Rather take back immediately, 3...Qxd5, which allows 4. Nc3 to develop with tempo, Black's usual idea is to gambit it: 3...Nf6, threatening d5, allows White the time to defend the pawn with 4. c4?!, but after 4...e6 5. dxe6 Bxe6 Black has a development lead and the initiative and compensation for the pawn.

3. e5 is the usual way to decline the gambit. Though White has a king's side space advantage, this is thought to favour Black, who will be able to develop their queen's bishop before playing ...e6, reaching a "superior" French defence structure.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.x:
1...c6 is the Caro-Kann. Black prepares to play 2...d5, with the c pawn ready to take back should White take it.

In the traditional Open Game (1. e4 e5), many of the major threats that Black faces target their weak f7-square with White's bishop positioned on c4. Black often can consider this threat resolved if they succeed in pushing their queen's pawn to d5, controlling c4. So, by achieving d5, Black makes their kingside safer.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/4P3/2N5/PPPP1PPP.x:
This is a flexible alternative move order in the Caro-Kann, where White has not committed the pawn to d4 yet.

After 2...d5 (near enough the only move, contesting the centre as Black prepared to do on move one), White may still play 3. d4 and transpose into the more common 2. d4 & 3. Nc3 Caro-Kann. However, the plan usually is to play 3. Nf3, the two knights attack. 3. Qf3 is the unusual Goldman variation.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/4P3/2N5/PPPP1PP.x: After 2...d5, White usually continues with 3. Nf3, entering the Two Knights Attack. If 3. d4 is played, the position transposes to the Classical Variation of the Caro-Kann.

r1bqkb1r/pp1npppp/2p5/8/3PQ3/5N2/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. Nc3/2...d5/3. Nf3/3...dxe4/4. Nxe4/4...Nf6/5. Qe2/5...Nxe4/6. Qxe4/6...Nd7/7. d4
r1bqkb1r/pp1npppp/2p5/8/3PQ3/5N2/PPP2PPP.x:
=Caro–Kann Defence: Two Knights Attack=
The most natural move in this position is /7...Nf6/, attacking the white queen.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/3PP3/2N5/PPP2PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nc3

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.x:
White develops a knight. This is a fairly unusual move sometimes played by Bobby Fischer. It usually is just a move-order difference.

After Black plays 2...d5 (which, as after 2. d4, is almost always the move) this usually transposes to the:

* Exchange Caro-Kann, after 3. exd5 cxd5 4. d4 Nc6 (normally seen in the move order 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 cxd5 4. Nf3 Nc6).
* Two knights attack, after 3. Nc3 (normally seen in the move order 2. Nc3 d5 3. Nf3).

Two unique lines are 2...d5 3. exd5 cxd5 4. Ne5!?, the Apocalypse attack, and 2...d5 3. d3, offering to go into a queenless middlegame.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PP.x:
Black plays the usual Caro-Kann move, 2...d5, supported by the pawn on c6.

White may continue:

3. exd5, which after 3...cxd5 4. d4 Nc6 transposes into an exchange variation, normally seen in the move order 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 cxd5 4. Nf3 Nc6. Alternatively, 4. Ne5!? is the Apocalypse attack.

3. Nc3, which transposes into the two knights attack otherwise seen in the move order 2. Nc3 d5 3. Nf3.

3. d3 is the endgame offer line otherwise seen in the Breyer variation (1. e4 c5 2. d3). After 3...dxe4, 4. dxe4 Qxd1+ 5. Kxd1 goes into a queenless middlegame, or 4. Ng5!? goes into a sharp gambit.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/4P3/2N2N2/PPPP1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. Nf3/2...d5/3. Nc3
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/4P3/2N2N2/PPPP1.x: #REDIRECT Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. Nc3/2...d5/3. Nf3

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/4P3/3P1N2/PPP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d3/2...d5/3. Nf3
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/4P3/3P1N2/PPP2P.x:
This variation is called the Endgame offer because, more often than not, the players will now trade their pawns and queens.

3...dxe4, eliminating the tension, is the most common move. After 4. dxe4 Qxd1+ 5. Kxd1 the endgame is reached. White still has an opportunity to avoid the endgame with 4. Ng5!?, a trappy line similar to the Tennison gambit in the Scandinavian defence.

If Black wishes to keep the queens on the board, they may want to remove their queen from the d-file (3...Qc7) before taking or just leave the central tension: 3...Bg4 and 3...g6 (intending 4...Bg7) have both been played.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/4P3/1P6/P1PP1PPP.x:
White's response to the Caro-Kann is a fianchetto of the dark-squared bishop. This move is rarely played today, but was used with success by World Champion Max Euwe, who won against Richard Reti in 1920.

Black will almost always continue with the usual 2...d5.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/2P1P3/8/PP1P1PPP.x: With pawns on c4 and e4, White locks down d5 square. This is a rare, aggressive sideline against the Caro-Kann. It is "accelerated" over the regular Panov where White plays c4 only after 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 cxd5. This can lead to very different positions. A difference is that, in the accelerated Panov, White leaves their pawn on d2 until after they have castled, so they may place their knight on c3 without it becoming pinned.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/3P4/8/8/PP1P1PPP/RNBQ.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. c4/2...d5/3. exd5/3...cxd5/4. cxd5
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/3P4/8/8/PP1P1PPP/RNBQ.x:
Black is down a pawn.

4...Qxd5!?, retaking immediately, has been played but concedes the initiative back to White. 5. Nc3 develops with tempo and the line continues 5...Qd8 6. d4 e6 7. Nf3 Nf6 8. Bd3 Be7 9. O-O O-O.

4...Nf6 is the main move. This prepares to recapture the d-pawn with the knight. White either concedes the pawn back straight away, 5. Nc3 Nxd5, or attempts to hold onto it with the intermezzo 5. Bb5+!?, intending 5...Bd7 6. Bc4. This brings a defender to the pawn while also cutting the number of attackers (Black's bishop on d7 prevents their queen from seeing d5). Better for Black is 5...Nbd7, which can answer 6. Bc4 with 6...Nb6!.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/4P3/3P4/PPP2PPP/.x: The unambitious Breyer variation of the Caro-Kann. 2. d3 prepares to recapture the pawn on e4 and may lead to an early endgame, or, if White wants to keep queens on the board, a King's Indian Attack-style position (see diagram).

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/4P3/3P4/PPP2PPP.x: Black plays 2...d5, supported by the pawn on c6. The main choice White faces is whether to allow a queen trade or not.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/4p3/3P1N2/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d3/2...d5/3. Nf3/3...dxe4
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/4p3/3P1N2/PPP2PPP.x:
Black takes the pawn.

4. dxe4, the most common move, leads to a queen trade and an even position after 4...Qxd1+ 5. Kxd1.

White's other option is 4. Ng5!?. This is a sharp line where White sacrifices a pawn. After 4...exd3 5. Bd3 White gets compensation with a lead in development. White has the possibility of attacks on f7 or h7, and it is easy for Black to misstep.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/6N1/4p3/3P4/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d3/2...d5/3. Nf3/3...dxe4/4. Ng5
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/6N1/4p3/3P4/PPP2PPP.x:
White gambits their d-pawn while targeting Black's weak f7-pawn.

The most critical line is to accept the gambit with 4...exd3 and Black is up material but must be careful not to fall into any traps. After 5. Bxd3, White threatens attacks on h7 and f7. If Black is not careful and plays a natural move like 5...Nf6?? they are soon lost: 6. Nxf7! (forking queen and rook) Kxf7!? 7. Bg6+ hxg6 8. Qxd8 wins Black's queen for two minor pieces.

Alternatively Black may find declining the gambit to be more straight-forward: e.g. 4...e5 5. Nxe4 or 4...Nf6 5. Nxe4 Nxe4 6. dxe4 Qxd1+ 7. Kxd1.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pNp1/2p4p/8/8/3B4/PPP2PPP/RN.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d3/2...d5/3. Nf3/3...dxe4/4. Ng5/4...exd3/5. Bxd3/5...h6/6. Nxf7

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.x:
White plays the principled move: if your opponent allows you to put two pawns in the centre, then put two pawns in the centre.

Black responds 2...d5. Black threatens to take on e4 if White leaves their e-pawn where it is. As d5 is supported by Black's c-pawn, Black is very happy to answer 3. exd5 (the exchange variation) with 3...cxd5, functionally having traded White's central e-pawn for Black's peripheral c-pawn. Therefore, White's most common responses are 3. e5, protecting the pawn by moving it out of harms way, or 3. Nc3, preparing to recapture it.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/n1p5/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/.x:
2...Na6!? is the De Bruycker defence. Black delays playing d5 to first develop their knight.

Having played c6, the usual square for Black's queenside knight is unavailable. Although a6 (being on the rim) is grim, via a6 the knight can reach c7, where it is more active.

Using two tempi to develop the knight this way is an unusual continuation: in the Caro-Kann, Black usually just develops the knight a bit later when they can do so in one move: either to c6 (if it becomes available again, as in the Exchange Caro-Kann) or d7.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/B1p5/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...Na6/3. Bxa6
r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/B1p5/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/.x:
White snap off Black's knight, thinking if 3...bxa6? they have ruined Black's pawn structure with doubled, isolated pawns on the a-file.

However, because Black has already opened up their queen with c6, they have the reply 3...Qa5+ 4. Nc3 Qxa6, and Black picks up the bishop pair without spoiling their pawns.

r1b1kbnr/pp1ppppp/B1p5/q7/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...Na6/3. Bxa6/3...Qa5
r1b1kbnr/pp1ppppp/B1p5/q7/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP.x: Black gives a check and attacks the bishop, intending to capture it with the queen. White will most likely block the check using /4. Nc3/.

r1b1kbnr/pp1ppppp/B1p5/q7/3PP3/2N5/PPP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...Na6/3. Bxa6/3...Qa5/4. Nc3
r1b1kbnr/pp1ppppp/B1p5/q7/3PP3/2N5/PPP2P.x: White blocks the check by developing a knight. Black plays /4...Qxa6/ next.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/.x:
This is the main line of the Caro-Kann defence, a semi-open game that tends to contain lines with minor piece play.

Black's threatens to capture ...dxe4. White has four main plans to deal with the central tension: close the centre, capture first, or prepare to recapture with knight or pawn.

3. e5 is the advance variation. White closes the centre and takes more space. This is the modern-day main line at all levels. The main line continues 3...Bf5 4. Nf3 e6 5. Be2, and Black either plays for an early ...c5 pawn break or contents themselves with developing in a cramped position. White has a choice of several sharp sidelines, including 3. Nc3 & 4. g4, sometimes called the Shirov attack.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nc3/3...dxe4
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2PPP/.x:
Black has taken White's e-pawn and denied them the classical two-pawn centre. By taking the pawn, Black frees up the space it controlled and creates new possibilities for their piece development.

4. Nxe4, recapturing the pawn is the natural and most common response, which usually leads to one of three main lines, 4...Bf5, the classical variation, 4...Nd7, the Karpov variation, or 4...Nf6 5. Nxf6+ exf6, the Tartakower variation.

White may choose to gambit the pawn with 4. f3 or 4. Bc4 for a development advantage. White doesn't receive full compensation for the pawn, but the lines can be sharp.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/3PN3/8/PPP2PPP/R1.x:
4. Nxe4 is an obvious recapture. This is the traditional treatment of the Caro-Kann and may arise from either the 3. Nc3 or 3. Nd2 variations.

Black has three main alternatives.

4...Bf5 is the classical variation. The bishop ends up controlling the long diagonal first from g6 via the manoeuvre 5. Ng3 Bg6, then from h7 after 6. h4 h6 7. Nf3 Nd7 8. h5 Bh7.

4...Nf6, developing the knight instead, leads to 5. Nxf6+ exf6, the Tartakower variation. This is perfectly playable but Black has to accept doubling their pawns.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/5bN1/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/.x:
= Caro-Kann Defense: Ng5 =
Unusual move to play with white. Knight escapes from the bishop's vision, but it is near the opponent's side.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p3b1/6N1/3P4/8/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nc3/3...dxe4/4. Nxe4/4...Bf5/5. Ng5/5...Bg6
rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p3b1/6N1/3P4/8/PPP2PPP.x:
= Caro-Kann Defense: Ng5 - Bg6 =
Bishop retreats to not to be endangered again in the future. The most common response to Ng5.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p3b1/6N1/3P4/5N2/PPP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nc3/3...dxe4/4. Nxe4/4...Bf5/5. Ng5/5...Bg6/6. N1f3
rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p3b1/6N1/3P4/5N2/PPP2P.x: White plays Nf3 and is about to counterattack. However, black rarely understands and notices it. There are a few popular replies to this, but black usually responds with h6, trying to kick out the knight, who's been a pain in the neck for a while.

rn1qkbnr/pp2ppp1/2p3bp/6N1/3P4/5N2/PPP2P.x: Black pushes the pawn to kick out the knight. The Knight should now be rerouted to a better square via Nh3-f4.

rn1qkbnr/pp2ppp1/2p1N1bp/8/3P4/5N2/PPP2P.x: Like the Alien Gambit, the Martian Gambit leads to an interesting and very exciting game. White plays Ne6, which is considered a blunder by Stockfish. However, in a real game, the move does pretty well. It ruins the kingside, doubles Black's pawns, and what is most important, helps the knight on f3 to deploy on e5 and control king's escape squares. But don't fret, Black has various responses to this gambit.

rn1qkbnr/pp2p1p1/2p1p1bp/8/3P4/5N2/PPP2P.x: Black recaptures the "free" knight. But actually it's not completely free, and black will pay even more for thinking less.

rn1qkbnr/pp2p1p1/2p1p1bp/4N3/3P4/8/PPP2P.x: Knight lands on e5, controlling black king's escape squares. Because of doubled pawns, black side has turned into bipolar world - Queenside and Kingside, when the last one has been ruined. Best response as black would be Be4, but the most popular is Bf7?, which at the first sight helps to defend the king, but later causes only more problems. The main counterattack for white is usually either Bc4, but sometimes you can attack right after that with Qh5+.

r1bqkbnr/pp1npppp/2p5/8/3PN3/8/PPP2PPP/R.x: By developing his Knight rather than the Bishop, Black aims to trade for White's central Knight, without compromising his pawn structure.

r1bqkbnr/pp1npppp/2p5/8/3PN3/8/PPP1QPPP/.x:
This is an unusual looking move, but it creates a subtle mate threat. Black can fall into it very easily in amateur play, and so this move is recommended. 
Black can get mated in one move if he makes an error.

If black plays correctly, it is easier for him to equalize. Black can get mated on move 5.

r1bqkbnr/pp1npppp/2p5/6N1/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nc3/3...dxe4/4. Nxe4/4...Nd7/5. Ng5
r1bqkbnr/pp1npppp/2p5/6N1/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/.x: This is an interesting move, with chances to blow Black off the Board. Even Kasparov got blown with a crushing knight sacrifice.

r1bqkbnr/pp1nppp1/2p4p/6N1/3P4/8/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nc3/3...dxe4/4. Nxe4/4...Nd7/5. Ng5/5...h6
r1bqkbnr/pp1nppp1/2p4p/6N1/3P4/8/PPP2PPP.x:
This move seems logical, as Nxf7 doesn't work. However, White can get a slight edge with Ne6! and can win quickly if Black makes a blunder.
A grandmaster lost to this trap. The e8-h5 diagonal is slightly weakened, and so is f7. The main line is Ne6! Qb6 (Wisely avoiding fxe6?? Qh5+ g6 Qxg6#) Nxf8 Nxf8 with two Bishops and a slight edge.

r1bqkbnr/pp1nppp1/2p1N2p/8/3P4/8/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nc3/3...dxe4/4. Nxe4/4...Nd7/5. Ng5/5...h6/6. Ne6
r1bqkbnr/pp1nppp1/2p1N2p/8/3P4/8/PPP2PPP.x: This is a sharp and surprising move, but it takes advantage of the weaknesses created by h6. This is one of the points of Ng5, to open of the h5-e8 diagonal.

r1bqkb1r/pp1npppp/2p2n2/8/3PN3/8/PPP1QPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nc3/3...dxe4/4. Nxe4/4...Nd7/5. Qe2/5...Ngf6
r1bqkb1r/pp1npppp/2p2n2/8/3PN3/8/PPP1QPP.x:
This move looks like simple development, yet black is now doomed to a mate in 1. Can you see it?. This trap has ensnared countless amateurs.
Much better is 5...Ndf6.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/8/3PN3/8/PPP2PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nc3/3...dxe4/4. Nxe4/4...Nf6
rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/8/3PN3/8/PPP2PPP/.x:
Nf6 is played at all levels, bit is slightly more common in amateur play, and offers a trade of knights.

This move challenges white's strong e4-knight but allows white to double black's pawns with the main move, 5. Nxf6+.

Other moves also exist. /5. Qd3/ defends the knight and sets up a trap, 5...Bf5?? 6. Nxf6+! exf6 7. Qxf5!.

/5. Bd3/ is the Alekhine Gambit. White gives up their d-pawn in exchange for development after 5...Qxd4 6. Nf3.

Some players have also tried /5. Ng5/, with the intention of entering the Alien Gambit, a dubious but scary knight sacrifice on f7, first played by Witty Alien, a streamer from Bulgaria.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/6N1/3P4/8/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nc3/3...dxe4/4. Nxe4/4...Nf6/5. Ng5
rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/6N1/3P4/8/PPP2PPP.x:
This move is not good for White; moving an already-developed piece, the queen knight, for a third time. Black already has an advantage.

However, many players with White, especially followers of Witty Alien or even Eric Rosen, usually have a sneaky idea with this move; after the natural 5...h6 by Black, White intends to sacrifice the knight for the f7 pawn with 6. Nxf7??, entering the dubious but incredibly scary Alien Gambit.

rnbqkb1r/pp2ppp1/2p2n1p/6N1/3P4/8/PPP2PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nc3/3...dxe4/4. Nxe4/4...Nf6/5. Ng5/5...h6
rnbqkb1r/pp2ppp1/2p2n1p/6N1/3P4/8/PPP2PP.x:
= Caro-Kann Defense, Classical Variation: 5...h6 =
Black naturally looks to kick the knight away with h6. Best in this position is 6. N5f3, retreating the knight to safety. However, this move of 5...h6 actually encourages many players, especially followers of chess content creator Witty Alien, to play 6. Nxf7??, the dubious but scary Alien Gambit.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pNp1/2p2n1p/8/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/.x:
= Caro-Kann Defense: Alien Gambit =
White grabs the f7 pawn with 6. Nxf7?, entering the dubious but incredibly scary Alien Gambit, popularized by YouTuber Witty Alien! This gambit is losing for White and can be punished with careful play; as such, it is mostly used in Bullet and Blitz.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p2n2/4p3/3PN3/3Q4/PPP2P.x:
This move appears to completely free Black's position and equalize the game, but it really loses time in a wide open position and falls behind in development. This puts Black in a critical position. This also gives black an opportunity to fall for a brilliant mating attack that was played in the game Reti-Tartakower, 1910. It is rarely a good idea to open up the position if you are behind in development, and Black is doing just this here.

Better is to trade knights on e4 and then move the other knight to d7. He can then play for the freeing...c5, ...e5, or attack the queen with ...Nf6 After this mistake, black loses time and development.

rnbqkbnr/pp2p1pp/2p2p2/8/3PN3/8/PPP2PPP/.x: The f6 Caro-Kann is a rare line that weakens the kingside and hinders the development of the king's knight, but prepares an e5 push.

rnbqkbnr/pp2p1pp/2p2p2/8/3P4/6N1/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nc3/3...dxe4/4. Nxe4/4...f6/5. Ng3
rnbqkbnr/pp2p1pp/2p2p2/8/3P4/6N1/PPP2PPP.x: Ng3 is an interesting but important move that allows the e5 pawn push, but gains a huge lead in development after 5...e5 6. Nf3.

rnbqkbnr/pp2ppp1/2p4p/8/3PN3/8/PPP2PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nc3/3...dxe4/4. Nxe4/4...h6
rnbqkbnr/pp2ppp1/2p4p/8/3PN3/8/PPP2PPP/R.x:
Black prepares an escape square for their c-bishop's later use. This is usually perceived as passive and is thus rarely seen at higher levels.

5. Nf3 is the main move. White develops their knight to its more natural square, ignoring Black's strange pawn move h6.

5. Bc4 is another good move, developing the bishop to an active square with good scope, and maybe even preparing Bxf7+ sacrifices to exploit the weakened kingside h6 caused.

5. Ng3 is playable. White stops the bishop from coming to f5 so it doesn't gain tempo on the knight nor does it get a chance to go to the newly opened h7.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/3PP3/8/PPPN1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nd2
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/3PP3/8/PPPN1PPP.x:
White prepares to recapture on e4 with their knight while keeping the option of c3.

This move is intended to avoid the Gurgenidze system, 3. Nc3 g6, where Black will fianchetto their king's side bishop.

Here, 3...g6 may be answered 4. c3, mitigating the pressure Black's bishop will be able to impose on the long diagonal.

This encourages the main move, 3...dxe4, and after 4. Nxe4 this transposes into the same line as if 3. Nc3 dxe4 4. Nxe4 had been played.

A minor sideline is /3...Qb6/, the Edinburgh Variation. Black develops their queen and attacks the undefended d4 pawn, though this can be answered with 4. c3.

rnb1kbnr/pp2pppp/1qp5/3p4/3PP3/8/PPPN1PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nd2/3...Qb6
rnb1kbnr/pp2pppp/1qp5/3p4/3PP3/8/PPPN1PP.x:
This is a minor sideline of 3. Nd2, where Black attacks the undefended d4 pawn.

4. c3 is the main and best move. White defends their pawn with another pawn, forming a solid b2-c3-d4 pawn chain.

4. Ngf3 is another good move. White develops their g-knight to its most active square and defends the d-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/3Pp3/8/PPPN1PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nd2/3...dxe4
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/3Pp3/8/PPPN1PPP/R.x: 4. Nxe4, retaking the pawn and defending d4, transposes into the main line 3. Nc3 variation of the Caro-Kann.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3pP3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. e5
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3pP3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/.x:
3. e5 closes the centre and gains space. This is one of the most popular and serious lines against the Caro-Kann.

Black has two main responses: 3...Bf5 and 3...c5.

A common idea is to achieve a pawn break with ...c5, attacking the base of White's pawn chain. However, If ...c5 there is a possibility of dxc5, and if so Black would ideally to recapture while developing their bishop. That requires moving the e-pawn, however.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3pPb2/3P4/8/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. e5/3...Bf5
rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3pPb2/3P4/8/PPP2PPP.x:
This is the main continuation to the advance variation. Black develops their bishop so that they may continue ...e6 to unleash their other bishop without restricting this one. The development of the bishop outside of the pawn chain is the key positional advantage difference between the Caro-Kann and the French.

White's choice here is between patient development and positional play, and attempting to capitalise on Black's bishop, which is unsupported and potentially vulnerable on f5.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3pPb2/3P4/8/PPPN1PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. e5/3...Bf5/4. Nd2
rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3pPb2/3P4/8/PPPN1PP.x:
4. Nd2 is an uncommon sideline in the Caro-Kann advance variation. This is a positional approach. Rather than develop the knight to c3, White plans to route it via d2 to b3, where it will control c5, and White retains the option of playing pawn to c3 or c4.

4...e6 5. Nb3 is the main continuation. On b3 the knight controls c5, so if 5...c5 6. dxc5 Bxc5 7. Nxc5 Qa5+ 8. c3 Qxc5 9. Be3 Qc7 10. f4, White gets the bishop pair and some space advantage. Instead, Black may postpone the pawn break and the line may continue 5...Nd7 6. Nf3 Ne7 7. Be2 Nc8 8. O-O Be7.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3pPb2/3P2P1/8/PPP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. e5/3...Bf5/4. g4
rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3pPb2/3P2P1/8/PPP2P.x:
=Caro-Kann Defence - Bayonet Attack=
This aggressive move forces Black to choose a retreat square for the bishop. While occasionally played for surprise value, the move weakens White's kingside and offers Black good chances. Black's best response is Be4!, inducing White to play f3 before retreating the bishop. Play might continue 4...Be4 5. f3 Bg6 6. e6! Qd6 7. exf7 Bxf7 8. Nc3 Nd7 9. f4, with rough equality.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2ppP3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. e5/3...c5
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2ppP3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/R.x:
This is Black's second most common option, after 3...Bf5. It is an attack on the base of White's pawn chain.

After 4. dxc5, Black can eventually recover the pawn with ...e6 and ...Bxc5, though there is usually no hurry and it's not in White's best interests to hold onto the c-pawn too tightly. One line is 4...Nc6 (the e5-pawn is now loose) 5. f4 e6 6. Be3 d4 7. Bf2 Bxc5.

4. Nf3 allows 4...cxd4 and prepares to recapture the pawn with the knight. 5. Nxd4 Nc6 (e5 is loose) 6. Nxc6 bxc6 7. Bd3 prevents Black from developing their light-square bishop actively.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/3p4/3P4/3B4/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. exd5/3...cxd5/4. Bd3/4...Nc6
r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/3p4/3P4/3B4/PPP2PPP.x:
Black attacks the d-pawn. 5. c3 is probably the most sound response, and the most-commonly played.

Black is fine after 5. Nf3 or 5. Be3, although 5. Nf3 has a poor record and allows Black to play 5...Bg4, freeing the weak light-squared bishop, and White has to play 6. c3 anyway. 5. Ne2 at least prevents it.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/3PP3/5P2/PPP3PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. f3
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/3PP3/5P2/PPP3PP.x:
White bolsters their e-pawn and hopes to obtain a full pawn centre and a half-open f-file should Black take on e4. It has been used by Alexander Morozevich, ranked number two in the world in July 2008, with success.

The most common responses are the more adventurous 3...dxe4, and the more solid 3...e6.

3... e6 can lead to original positions, or transpose to the Steinitz Variation of the French Defence with the moves 3...e6 4. Nc3 Nf6 5. e5 Nfd7 6. f4 c5.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/3Pp3/5P2/PPP3PP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. f3/3...dxe4
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/3Pp3/5P2/PPP3PP/R.x:
A perfectly playable variation for Black, but they must know the lines to avoid certain pitfalls. White will have multiple opportunities to strike at f7 if Black goes wrong.

White almost always recaptures with fxe4.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/3PP3/8/PPP3PP/RNB.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. f3/3...dxe4/4. fxe4
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/8/3PP3/8/PPP3PP/RNB.x: Black has only one acceptable response here; 4...e5. Anything else gives White serious initiative.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p5/4p3/3PP3/8/PPP3PP/RN.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. f3/3...dxe4/4. fxe4/4...e5
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p5/4p3/3PP3/8/PPP3PP/RN.x: Striking back in the centre, and threatening both to take the pawn, as well as Qh4+. Nf3 is the only move for White that both avoids disaster and maintains the pressure.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p5/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP3PP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. f3/3...dxe4/4. fxe4/4...e5/5. Nf3
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p5/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP3PP/.x: White threatens Black's pawn on e5. Black mostly responds by pinning the knight with Bg4.

rn1qkbnr/pp3ppp/2p5/4p3/3PP1b1/5N2/PPP3P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. f3/3...dxe4/4. fxe4/4...e5/5. Nf3/5...Bg4
rn1qkbnr/pp3ppp/2p5/4p3/3PP1b1/5N2/PPP3P.x: 6. Bc4, attacking f7, is the most common response, and it's the line that forces Black to walk a tightrope to avoid tactical disaster. If Black knows the theory, the line leads to complete equality. 6. c3 is probably the best objective try for White against knowledgeable Black opponents.

rn1qkbnr/pp3ppp/2p5/4p3/2BPP1b1/5N2/PPP3.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. f3/3...dxe4/4. fxe4/4...e5/5. Nf3/5...Bg4/6. Bc4
rn1qkbnr/pp3ppp/2p5/4p3/2BPP1b1/5N2/PPP3.x: If Black sleepwalks into a response such as 6...Nf6, White will strike with Bxf7. 6...Nd7 is the only response that maintains equality.

r2qkbnr/pp1n1ppp/2p5/4p3/2BPP1b1/5N2/PPP.x: White usually castles here, to maintain the pressure on f7. 7. c3 is also commonly played, aiming for a different threat, Qb3, directed at both f7 and b7.
Once again Black has to be careful. Developing the dark-squared bishop, for example, walks into 8. Bxf7. 7...Ngf6 is the only response, blocking the discovered attack on f7 from the rook.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p2n2/4p3/2BPP1b1/5N2/P.x: White's two main responses, 8. c3 and 8. dxe5, both create tactical threats. 8. c3 threatens 9. Qb3, with overwhelming pressure on f7, while 8. dxe5 forces Black to respond correctly to win the pawn back.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p2n2/4P3/2B1P1b1/5N2/P.x: Black cannot recapture with Nxe5, as White escapes the pin with Qxd8. 8...Qb6 and 8...Bxf3 are the only responses that allow Black to recapture on e5.

r2qkbnr/pp1n1ppp/2p5/4p3/2BPP1b1/2P2N2/P.x:
c3 creates a different threat, that of Qb3, with the queen adding to the pressure on f7 as well as targeting b7. Black cannot play passively, and a move like 7...Nf6 leaves Black in a world of trouble after 8. Qb6.

Black can respond with 8...b5, either chasing the bishop from the diagonal, or blocking the queen from b6. This comes at the cost of queenside weaknesses that White can later target with moves such as a4.

8...Bh5 also holds, perhaps with a later Qc7 and O-O-O, where Black is happy to give up the f7 pawn for a solid position or good counterplay.

8...Bd6 is another playable tactical line, that can give up the b and c pawns, but provides Black with sufficient compensation.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/3PP3/5P2/PPP3P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. f3/3...e6
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/3PP3/5P2/PPP3P.x: White's typical response is 4. Nc3, and this can transpose into a Steinitz Variation of the French Defence with the moves 4. Nc3 Nf6 5. e5 Nfd7 6. f4 c5.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/3PP3/2N2P2/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. f3/3...e6/4. Nc3
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/3PP3/2N2P2/PPP.x:
This can transpose into a Steinitz Variation of the French Defence with the moves 4. Nc3 Nf6 5. e5 Nfd7 6. f4 c5.

If Black wants to avoid this, 4... Bb4, pinning the knight, is a good alternative.

rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/1b1PP3/2N2P2/P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. f3/3...e6/4. Nc3/4...Bb4
rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/1b1PP3/2N2P2/P.x: Black asks the question of how White is going to continue developing. There are quite a few alternatives here. White may try to get in 5. Bf4, Qd3 and O-O-O, or 5. Ne2, shoring up c3 and d4.

rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/1b1PPB2/2N2P2/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. f3/3...e6/4. Nc3/4...Bb4/5. Bf4
rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/1b1PPB2/2N2P2/.x: 5...Ne7 is the most common reply here. Leaving the knight on b8 allows Black to attempt to solve the problem of the weak light-squared bishop by placing it on a6, protected by the knight.

rnbqk2r/pp2nppp/2p1p3/3p4/1b1PPB2/2N2P2/.x: Moving the queen to d3, or even d2, aims to allow White to quickly castle kingside.

rnbqk2r/pp2nppp/2p1p3/3p4/1b1PPB2/2NQ1P2.x: Black can now attempt to activate the light-squared bishop with b6. This also discourages White from castling immediately, as 7...Ba6 could then force the trade of the problematic light-squared bishop.

rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/1b1PP3/2N2P2/P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. f3/3...e6/4. Nc3/4...Bb4/5. Ne2
rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/1b1PP3/2N2P2/P.x: 5...Nf6 is playable, but the knight can be more vulnerable to attack on f6, so 5...Ne7 is more commonly-played.

rnbqk2r/pp2nppp/2p1p3/3p4/1b1PP3/2N2P2/P.x: White typically plays 6.a3 here, chasing the bishop, or hoping to lure Black into mistakenly exchanging the strong black bishop for the knight on c3, and freeing up e2 to allow White's light-squared bishop to be developed.

rnbqk2r/pp2nppp/2p1p3/3p4/1b1PP3/P1N2P2/.x:
Black certainly doesn't want to exchange the strong black bishop for the knight on c3, and free up e2 to allow White's light-squared bishop to be developed.

Black could continue after 6...Ba5 by developing the knight to d7, castling, and then attempting to break in the centre.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.x:
Black takes on White's centre head on. They are determined to disrupt White's centre and immediately open up the board, even if they have to give up their own hopes of big centre and some tempo to do it.

White could trade the pawn, defend it, or gambit it. 1...d5 is a very forcing response: almost invariably White captures, their plans derailed.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.x:
White sacrifices their e-pawn in the hopes of a potential lead in development. The Tennison gambit may arise out of the Scandinavian defence or Zukertort opening.

2...dxe4, accepting the gambit, is usual and most critical. This attacks White's knight, so 3. Ng5, counter-attacking the e-pawn and pressuring f7 is the main move. White can leverage this pressure into a lead in development before recovering the pawn, or lay a number of traps for Black, especially if they get too invested in holding onto the extra pawn. Black is typically advised to accept the gambit then give the pawn back with 3...e5.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/4p3/5N2/PPPP1PPP/R.x:
Black accepts the pawn and attacks White's knight.

3. Ng5 is the usual square. From here, White's knight attacks e4 and pressures f7, the most vulnerable square in Black's position. Black is objectively better, but the position is notorious for traps against an unsuspecting Black player, which Black may avoid by giving the pawn back, 3...e5.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/6N1/4p3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. Nf3/2...dxe4/3. Ng5
rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/6N1/4p3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.x: From g5 White's knight attacks e4 and pressures f7, the most vulnerable square in Black's position.

rn1qkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/5bN1/4p3/8/PPPP1PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. Nf3/2...dxe4/3. Ng5/3...Bf5
rn1qkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/5bN1/4p3/8/PPPP1PPP/.x:
Black defends the e4 pawn with their bishop.

This is considered the most accurate move against 3. Ng5, though not the most common. White usually plays 4. Nc3, adding pressure onto the e4 pawn. Black then usually defends with 4...Nf6, where White can either develop their bishop with 5. Bc4 or attack the pawn again with 5. Qe2!?. If 5. Qe2!? is played, Black should give the pawn back with 5...Nc6. But a common trap Black players fall for is the Brigg's trap, where they hold on to the pawn and instead blunder 6. Qb5+!. Black will then be forced to either give up material or get checkmated:

rn1qkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/5bN1/4p3/2N5/PPPP1PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. Nf3/2...dxe4/3. Ng5/3...Bf5/4. Nc3
rn1qkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/5bN1/4p3/2N5/PPPP1PP.x:
White attacks Black's e4 pawn with their knight, the most commonly played move.

4...Nf6 is the most common reply, defending the pawn with their knight. White can then choose between the normal 5. Bc4, developing their bishop, or 5. Qe2?!, setting up a trap if Black plays 5...Qd4??.

4...Qd4?! defends the pawn with the queen. This may transpose into the 4...Nf6 5. Qe2?! trap if after 5. Qe2?! 5...Nf6?? is played, or can go into another trap that can happen after 5. d3 exd3? 6. Bxd3, where if 6...Bxd3?? is played, 7. Qf3! and Black cannot defend both f7 and b7 at the same time.

4...Nc6 gives the pawn back peacefully and develops the knight.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/6N1/4p3/8/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. Nf3/2...dxe4/3. Ng5/3...Nf6
rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/6N1/4p3/8/PPPP1PPP.x:
Black defends their pawn with their knight.

Although this isn't the most accurate move (3...Bf5 is better), this is the most popular move and still playable for Black as long as they don't fall for a well-known trap. White usually plays 4. d3, forcing Black to react to the pawn being attacked again and may lead to a trap.

4. Nc3 is playable, but 4...Bg4 attacking the queen on d1 can prove quite annoying, and there are not as many traps as there are with the move 4. d3.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/4P3/3P4/PPP2PPP/.x:
This is a timid reply, usually played only for surprise value or by beginners.

White's e-pawn is defended but it's not ideal: after 2...dxe4 White's d-pawn is pinned to their queen. So, 3. dxe4 Qxd1+ 4.Kxd1 and White has lost castling rights. One alternative for White is to gambit their central pawns instead: 3. Nc3 transposes into the Dunst-Perrenet gambit, where 3...exd3 4. Bxd3 and White has better piece activity, but it is scant compensation for the loss of both central pawns.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3pP3/8/8/PPPP1PPP/RN.x:
While advancing the e-pawn to gain space looks somewhat natural, it is rarely seen by masters and never by players above 2500.

Black has a number of ways to equalize quickly but the most common plan is to develop the light-squared bishop to f5 or g4 and then play ...e6. This results in a position similar to the French defence, but with the improvement that they have already developed their bishop outside of the pawn chain.

2...c5, controlling d4, is most common and this move has scored very well for Black. White may play 3. d4 anyway or prepare it with 3. c3, or abandon d4 and play 3. f4.

2...Bf5 also equalizes.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3P4/8/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.x:
After 2. exd5, Black can recapture the pawn.

2...Qxd5 retakes the pawn immediately. This is the main line, also known as the classical line. Black regains the pawn but allows White to develop with tempo against the queen: 3. Nc3 and the black queen must move again, usually to 3...Qa5. 3. Nf6 is also tried, with the idea of retaining the option of pushing both c4 and d4 and taking over the centre.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3P4/8/8/PPPP1PPP/R.x:
Black elects to play 2...Nf6 instead of the traditional reply, 2...Qxd5. This allows Black to develop a piece before recapturing the pawn. By taking the time to develop another attacker on d5, Black intends to win it without losing tempo.

Now if 3. Nc3!?, Black can trade off the knights 3...Nxd5 4. Nxd5 Qxd5 and centralise their queen without the loss of tempo associated with 2...Qxd5 3. Nc3. (5. c4?! runs into the same issues as 2...Qxd5 3. c4.)

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3P4/2P5/8/PP1P1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Nf6/3. c4
rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3P4/2P5/8/PP1P1PPP.x:
As Black didn't recapture the d-pawn straight away, White defends it, hoping to stay up the material.

Black has two main options: to chip away at the pawn chain with 3...c6 or 3...e6.

After 3...c6, White could trade 4. dxc6?! Nxc6. However, although White is up a pawn, this helps Black to develop and Black is thought to have full compensation.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3P4/2P5/8/PP1P1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Nf6/3. c4/3...e6
rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3P4/2P5/8/PP1P1PPP.x:
With 3...e6 Black offers White a pawn.

If White accepts, 4. dxe6, Black can recapture 4...Bxe6. In exchange for being down a pawn, Black has two minor pieces developed and, by removing the pawn that was guarding c6, will have an easier time developing their knight. Black's game is then to make use of their development lead and the open lines in the middle of the board to press their attack.

Declining the gambit is less common but playable. After 4. d4 exd5 White has given back the pawn they won on move two and the game is even.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4Pn2/8/2P5/8/PP1P1PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Nf6/3. c4/3...e6/4. dxe6
rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4Pn2/8/2P5/8/PP1P1PPP/R.x:
With 4. dxe6 White accepts the pawn. Black can recapture the pawn while developing their bishop, and though they will be a pawn down, they will have two minor pieces developed already while White has none. Black hopes to transform their development lead and the open lines in the middle of the board into a successful attack.

After 4...Bxe6, developing the bishop, 5. d4 is the main move. White takes control of the centre and prepares to develop their queenside pieces. Then, the main move is 5...Bb4+, though 5...Nc6? is a trap for the unwary.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3P4/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Nf6/3. d4
rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3P4/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/.x:
With 3. d4, White focuses on controlling as much of the centre as they can, and opens lines to develop their queen and queen's bishop.

This offers back the pawn, and Black's main continuation is to take it with 3...Nxd5, the Marshall variation. White usually plays Nf3 and c4, securing control over the centre and Black can end up cramped. If 3...Qxd5 instead, play may transpose into the Scandinavian main line after 4. Nc3 Qa5.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3P4/3P2b1/8/PPP2PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Nf6/3. d4/3...Bg4
rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3P4/3P2b1/8/PPP2PP.x:
Black develops their bishop with tempo on White's queen. White will have the time to secure their pawn on d5 and so hold on to the extra material, but Black hopes instead to gain the advantage in piece development and activity.

White's first priority must be to parry the threat of ...Bxd1. There are several ideas: 4. Be2, 4. Ne2 or 4. Nf3, and 4. f3. Additionally, White may play the intermezzo 4. Bb5+.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3q4/8/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.x:
Black retakes the pawn immediately.

3. Nc3 is White's usual continuation. White develops a knight tempo on the queen, and Black must pick a safe square to where their queen will be safe: typically Qa5 or Qd8.

3. Nf3 is also tried. White's idea is to delay playing Nc3, realising that they may pick up the tempo on Black's queen later. Without playing Nc3 yet, White has the idea of taking over the queenside by putting both c and d pawns in the centre (Nc3 would obstruct the c pawn's way to c4). 3...Bg4 is the typical move, then 4. Be2 Nc6 5. d4 O-O-O.

3. d4 first is similar to the 3. Nf3 lines, transposing after 3...Nc6 4. Nf3 Bg4 5. Be2 O-O-O. White keeps the option of c4.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/3q4/8/8/2N5/PPPP1PPP/R.x: #REDIRECT Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qd6

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3q4/8/8/PPPPKPPP/RNB.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Ke2
rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3q4/8/8/PPPPKPPP/RNB.x:
This move is interesting, as it is a blunder that allows 3...Qe4#.

According to GM Ben Finegold, there was a rule in chess over 150 years ago that forced the player to move the king instead if they happened to make an illegal move. One such occasion happened in the 1800s. After 2...Qxd5, the player with the white pieces wanted to play 3.Nc3, but accidentally moved the bishop, 3.Bc3, which is an illegal move. The player was then forced to play 3.Ke2??, as it was the only legal move for the king, thus getting checkmated.

1. e4 d5 2. exd5 Qxd5 3. Ke2??

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/4q3/8/PPPPKPPP/RNB.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Ke2/3...Qe4
rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/4q3/8/PPPPKPPP/RNB.x:
This happened because white blundered with 3. Ke2??, which allowed a shocking mate with 3...Qe4#.

1. e4 d5 2. exd5 Qxd5 3. Ke2?? Qe4#

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3q4/8/2N5/PPPP1PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3
rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3q4/8/2N5/PPPP1PPP/R.x:
White develops with tempo against Black's queen. Black's queen now must find a safe square: ideally one from which she may not be kicked again straight away.

3....Qa5 is the mainline. From a5 the queen cannot be attacked immediately, she can pin the knight should White dare to advance their d pawn, and she can later move to b6 to target the b2 pawn. From a5 she supports e5. This is considered the sharpest variation.

The principal alternatives are 3...Qd8 and 3...Qd6.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/q7/8/2N5/PPPP1PPP/R1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5
rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/q7/8/2N5/PPPP1PPP/R1.x: Black moves the queen to a5. This is a good square for the queen: it can't be easily attacked again, it supports Black playing ...e5, and will pin the knight if White advances their d pawn. Later it can move to b6 to target the b2 pawn.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/q7/1P6/2N5/P1PP1PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5/4. b4
rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/q7/1P6/2N5/P1PP1PPP/.x:
White gambits a pawn for tempo. The gambit is nearly sound (with best play Black is equal or slightly better) but there are several sharp lines.

After 4...Qxb4, there are two tries for White. 5. Rb1 Qd6 6. Nf3 and White has developed three pieces and has control of the half-open b-file, and its up to White to prove they can capitalise on this in the middle game.

The other try is 5. Nb5, threatening Nxc7+. 5...Qa5 6. Bc4 sets a trap, where the natural move 6...c6?? loses the queen for two minors: 7. Bxf7+ Kxf7 8. Qh5+ g6 9. Nd6+ exd6 10. Qxa5.

Declining the gambit with 4...Qb6 avoids complications, but by letting White off the hook they don't have to prove their sacrifice was worth it.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/1q6/8/1P6/2N5/P1PP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5/4. b4/4...Qb6
rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/1q6/8/1P6/2N5/P1PP1PPP.x: While declining the gambit isn’t unsound, it is far less ambitious than accepting it. White continues to develop normally. Black shouldn’t take the b-pawn because that will give White a favourable version of the Leonhardt Gambit accepted, where she enjoys an extra tempo.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/1q6/2N5/P1PP1PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5/4. b4/4...Qxb4
rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/1q6/2N5/P1PP1PPP/R.x:
The Black queen greedily takes the pawn, accepting White's challenge. White now has an open b-file, so she continues with 5. Rb1.

5. Nb5?! has been tried by some mavericks, setting up some deadly traps.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/1N6/1q6/8/P1PP1PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5/4. b4/4...Qxb4/5. Nb5
rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/1N6/1q6/8/P1PP1PPP/R.x:
5. Nb5?!

The white knight leaps to b5, eyeing the c7 square and a fork of the black queen and rook. Black can avoid White's tricks with 5...Na6 or 5...Qc5. The most ambitious and popular move however, is 5...Qa5

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/qN6/8/8/P1PP1PPP/R1B.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5/4. b4/4...Qxb4/5. Nb5/5...Qa5
rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/qN6/8/8/P1PP1PPP/R1B.x: It appears as if Black has solved her problems—her queen covers the c7 square and escapes the b-file, where she could be a target for attack. However, this is merely entry to the rabbit hole. White continues with 6. Bc4, which looks like a simple developing move, but comes with a trick. this could possibly Win Blacks Queen with the correct Moves

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/qN6/2B5/8/P1PP1PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5/4. b4/4...Qxb4/5. Nb5/5...Qa5/6. Bc4
rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/qN6/2B5/8/P1PP1PPP/R.x:
6. Bc4

It looks like White simply develops her bishop to c4. 6...c6 looks like an amazing move! You attack the annoying knight on b5 and give your queen an escape square in c7 just in case. Surely nothing can go wrong.

Right?

It turns out, 6. Bc4 has a threat of Bxf7!! followed by Qh5+ and then Nd6+ winning Black's Queen! That is why 6...Nf6 is black's best move here, you cover the h5 square and avoid white's tricks.

rnb1kbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/qN6/2B5/8/P1PP1PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5/4. b4/4...Qxb4/5. Nb5/5...Qa5/6. Bc4/6...c6
rnb1kbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/qN6/2B5/8/P1PP1PPP/.x:
6...c6??

What a fool, Black must have thought. You let me threaten your pest on b5 and grant my queen an escape square?

White plays 7. Bxf7!, knowing Black has missed her threat.

rnb1kbnr/pp2pBpp/2p5/qN6/8/8/P1PP1PPP/R1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5/4. b4/4...Qxb4/5. Nb5/5...Qa5/6. Bc4/6...c6/7. Bxf7
rnb1kbnr/pp2pBpp/2p5/qN6/8/8/P1PP1PPP/R1.x:
7. Bxf7

White sacrifices her bishop, drawing Black's king out into the open. Black usually accepts the sacrifice, it looks like a free bishop, right?

7...Kd8 avoids black’s threats, but white still has an advantageous position after 8. Nc3 due to the weakness of the black king. And let’s be real, anyone who saw the threat of 6. Bc4 would not have played 6...c6 in the first place.

rnb2bnr/pp2pkpp/2p5/qN6/8/8/P1PP1PPP/R1B.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5/4. b4/4...Qxb4/5. Nb5/5...Qa5/6. Bc4/6...c6/7. Bxf7/7...Kxf7
rnb2bnr/pp2pkpp/2p5/qN6/8/8/P1PP1PPP/R1B.x:
Black accepts the bishop sacrifice. But then, 8. Qh5+

and Black realises she has fallen into a trap.

rnb2bnr/pp2pkpp/2p5/qN5Q/8/8/P1PP1PPP/R1.x:
8. Qh5+

Black has been greedy with 6...c6 and will pay dearly for it. White will play 9. Nd6+ or 9. Nd4+, which is a discovered attack on Black's queen.

/8...Kf6/ keeps the queen, but after 9. Bb2+ Black might as well be down one, since White has a monstrous attack.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/2q5/8/8/2N5/PPPP1PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qc6
rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/2q5/8/8/2N5/PPPP1PPP/R.x: Black blundered. While moving out of the knight's attack and preventing the development of the bishop to c4, this allows for the Queen to be immediately pinned to the king with Bb5 with support from the c3 Knight, leading to the additional threat of a king-rook fork on the c7 square if the bishop is taken.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/2q5/1B6/8/2N5/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qc6/4. Bb5
rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/2q5/1B6/8/2N5/PPPP1PPP.x:
There is no way for black to save their queen now, unless white fails to (re)capture.

Qxb5 allows the knight to recapture, immediately threatening a king-rook fork on the c7 square.

Bd7 aims to compensate, because after 4... Bd7, 5. Bxc6 Bxc6, black immediately threatens to regain some compensation by capturing the g2 pawn and the h1 rook, though this is easily refuted with Nc3.

Nf6 and recapturing with Nxc6 allows black to gain compensation through two tempos, allowing black the initiative, albeit without a queen.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/8/2N5/PPPP1PPP/R1B.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qd8
rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/8/2N5/PPPP1PPP/R1B.x:
Black un-develops their queen. Back on d8 she is very safe but has limited scope, and Black will have to spend some more time developing her again later.

White now has a free hand to continue development. The main move is 4. d4, taking space in the centre and allowing the queen's bishop into the game. The main line continues 4...Nf6 5. Nf3 Bg4 6. h3 Bxf3 7. Qxf3 c6 (7...Qxd4?? allows 8. Qxb7 winning Black's rook).

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3q4/2P5/8/PP1P1PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. c4
rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3q4/2P5/8/PP1P1PPP/R.x:
With 3. c4?! White thinks to gain space in the centre while gaining tempo on Black's queen. White gets to play another pawn move in the opening but without losing tempo, and this way, they think, they can develop Nc3 without blocking in the c-pawn and let both knight and pawn get to where they'd like to go.

However there are drawbacks to this approach. For one thing, playing c4 with tempo means Nc3 isn't played with tempo, and Nc3 would have also developed a piece.

For another, playing in this order makes it harder for White to achieve d4, which takes control of the centre while moving the pawn out of the way of both bishops:

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/3p4/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.x:
The Pirc defence is a hypermodern response to 1. e4 where, rather than fill the centre with pawns, they look to exert pressure on the centre from afar with their pieces.

In the Pirc, Black would like to control e4 with their knight from f6. However, were they to play ...Nf6 immediately then White could kick it with e5!. 1...d6 controls e5 and so prepares for Black to play ...Nf6 safely. Black also intends ...g6 and ...Bg7 to project pressure over the centre from the long diagonal.

As Black hasn't contested the central squares yet, 2. d4 is nearly almost played, and White often builds a huge centre with f4 as well: the main line is 2. d4 Nf6 3. Nc3 g6 4. f4, the Austrian attack.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/3p4/1B6/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.x:
= 2. Bb5 =

This does not do much, as Black can easily counter with 2...c6, forcing White to retreat the bishop.
However, the check might have a psychological impact on Black.
