r1bqkb1r/2pp1ppp/p1n2n2/1p2p3/4P3/1B3N2/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Ba4/4...Nf6/5. O-O/5...b5/6. Bb3
r1bqkb1r/2pp1ppp/p1n2n2/1p2p3/4P3/1B3N2/.x:
The move ...b5 is seen at some point in most variations of the main line Ruy Lopez, so Black has a few transpositional possibilities here: 6...d6 or 6...Be7 will probably end up in the standard Closed Variation (5...Be7 6. Re1 b5) and 6...Nxe4 almost certainly leads back to the Open Variation.

Basically, replacing ...Be7 with ...b5 means that Black has retained the option of setting up bishops at b7 and c5. The two independent moves, therefore, are the Arkhangelsk 6...Bb7 and the Møller 6...Bc5. They may transpose into each other.

r2qkb1r/1bpp1ppp/p1n2n2/1p2p3/4P3/1B3N2/.x: Black elects to fianchetto his light-square bishop in order to gain pressure against White's kingside and center. This has the added benefit of defending the rook on a8, thereby taking some of the sting out of a future a4 thrust by White. However, the activity of Black's fianchettoed bishop can be countered by White overprotecting e4. Thus the most common reply by White in recent years has been 7. d3, after which Black typically develops his other bishop to either e7 or c5. The latter leads to positions which can also be reached from the Neo-Arkhangelsk (6...Bc5), though 6...Bb7 7. d3 Bc5 is the more common order.

r1bqk2r/2pp1ppp/p1n2n2/1pb1p3/4P3/1B3N2/.x: Black wagers that his dark-square bishop is more active here, while his light-square bishop may yet wish to develop along either diagonal. Transpositions to the Old Arkhangelsk (6...Bb7) are common, but there are independent lines involving ...Bg4 as well. White's main ideas in the position are a4, attacking the weak b5 pawn at once, c3 followed by d4, gaining central space and taking a tempo off Black's c5 bishop, or some combination. Also played, but less critical, are 7. Nc3 and 7. d3. The central fork trick 7. Nxe5 leaves white without the prospect of greater central control than his pawn on e4 can provide.

r1bqkb1r/1ppp1ppp/p1n2n2/4p3/B3P3/2P2N2/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Ba4/4...Nf6/5. c3
r1bqkb1r/1ppp1ppp/p1n2n2/4p3/B3P3/2P2N2/.x: c3 is a thematic move in the Spanish to prepare d4. In this position it allows 5...Nxe4 and 6. O-O? is too slow to recover the pawn. White may play 6. Qe2 Nc5 7. Bxc6 dxc6 8. d4 (the e5-pawn is pinned) Ne6 9. Nxe5 instead.

r1bqkb1r/1ppp1ppp/p1n2n2/4p3/B3P3/3P1N2/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Ba4/4...Nf6/5. d3
r1bqkb1r/1ppp1ppp/p1n2n2/4p3/B3P3/3P1N2/.x: White doesn't want to attack immediately with O-O, c3, and d4. They instead want to attack after building an impregnable fortress that offers no chances for counterplay. Though passive and harmless-looking, this move defends the e4-pawn and makes Bxc6 followed by Nxe5 a reality. Black must therefore either defend e5 or run off White's a4 bishop. Simplest is 5...b5, which removes the threat of Bxc6 but loosens Black's queenside pawns, inviting a later a4 thrust by White. Black can instead solidify their crucial e5 pawn with 5...d6, but this pins the c6 knight and restricts the f8 bishop.

r1bqkb1r/2pp1ppp/p1n2n2/1p2p3/4P3/1B1P1N.x: This retreats the bishop to the only good square. It puts it on a good square where it controls the a2-g8 diagonal.

r1bqkb1r/1ppp1ppp/p1n2n2/4p3/B2PP3/5N2/P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Ba4/4...Nf6/5. d4
r1bqkb1r/1ppp1ppp/p1n2n2/4p3/B2PP3/5N2/P.x:
The Mackenzie variation is an attacking sideline. It seems a mite uncivilised to open the centre so early, but White hopes to generate opportunities along the e-file before Black gets safely castled and avoid facing the more theoretical Closed Spanish positions. The game frequently transposes into an Open Spanish.

White threatens to take on e5 or play d5. Black has a choice of pawn captures.

5...Nxe4 transposes into the mainline of the Open Spanish after 6. O-O.

r1bqkbnr/2pp1ppp/p1n5/1p2p3/B3P3/5N2/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Ba4/4...b5
r1bqkbnr/2pp1ppp/p1n5/1p2p3/B3P3/5N2/PPP.x:
Black drives White's bishop away. Black ends White's pressure on their knight, therefore ends the possibility of Bxc6 and makes their e5 pawn more secure.

While ...b5 is a common move in Ruy Lopez at some point, it is unusual to play it immediately on move four, because Black's e5 pawn was still defended tactically (Bxc6 dxc6 Nxe5 Qd4! forks White's knight and e4 pawn).

5. Bb3 is the only move. White preserves their bishop and gets the free tempo to move it onto the dangerous a2-g8 long diagonal, eying Black's vulnerable f7 pawn.

r1bqkbnr/2pp1ppp/p1n5/1p2p3/4P3/1B3N2/PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Ba4/4...b5/5. Bb3
r1bqkbnr/2pp1ppp/p1n5/1p2p3/4P3/1B3N2/PP.x:
White saves their bishop and now pressures Black's vulnerable f7 pawn.

5...Bb7, taking advantage of having moved the b-pawn to increase the pressure on e5, was the continuation preferred by Horatio Caro and common in the late 19th/early 20th centuries. Developing the kingside bishop instead in the manner of the Classical defence, 5...Bc5 aka the Graz variation, was also common.

5...Na5 is the Norwegian variation: Black wants to hunt down White's bishop and get the bishop pair. This is the main continuation today in tournament games.

r1bqkbnr/2pp1ppp/p7/np2p3/4P3/1B3N2/PPPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Ba4/4...b5/5. Bb3/5...Na5
r1bqkbnr/2pp1ppp/p7/np2p3/4P3/1B3N2/PPPP.x:
Black hunts down White's bishop, arguing that the advantage of the bishop pair is worth giving White a tempo to develop.

White can't preserve their bishop. They're not in time to play 6. c3? to give it an escape square, and if 6. Bd5? c6 and the bishop again has nowhere to go. So, White instead can thank Black for the extra tempo, focus on development, and retake when the time comes.

Though Black seems to have left their e-pawn hanging, as is often the case in the Ruy Lopez it is not so simple. 6. Nxe5?! Nxb3 7. axb3 Qg5! 8. Nf3 Qxg2 (recovers the pawn) 9. Rg1 Qh3 10. Rg3 Qe6 .

r1bqkbnr/2pp1Bpp/p7/np2p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Ba4/4...b5/5. Bb3/5...Na5/6. Bxf7
r1bqkbnr/2pp1Bpp/p7/np2p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.n: Ruy Lopez Opening: Morphy Defense, Caro, Norwegian, Nightingale Gambit|
r1bqkbnr/2pp1Bpp/p7/np2p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.x:
6. Bxf7+!

As we can see here, White played the unexpected move 6. Bxf7+!, sacrificing the Bishop to abuse the position of Black after 6...Kxf7 7. Nxe5 7...Kf6 8.Qh5 8...c6 9.Qf7+! & White has a huge advantage. This is known as the Nightingale Gambit. This is by far the most aggressive & sharp move after 5...Na5.

r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1np4/4p3/B3P3/5N2/PPPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Ba4/4...d6
r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1np4/4p3/B3P3/5N2/PPPP.x: Much of the play and counterplay in the beginning of the Spanish opening revolves around White creating threats to play Nxe5, Black defending against them, and White finding new ways to reinvigorate the threat. By defending e5 with a pawn, 4...d6 defuses the threat for good.

r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1np4/4p3/B3P3/2P2N2/PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Ba4/4...d6/5. c3
r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1np4/4p3/B3P3/2P2N2/PP.x: One of the main lines against the Deferred Steinitz! White prepares to build an ideal pawn center with c3, looking for d4. Black has several ways to combat this move.

r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1np4/4p3/B2PP3/5N2/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Ba4/4...d6/5. d4
r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1np4/4p3/B2PP3/5N2/PPP.x:
5. d4?! is premature.

After 5....b5!, Black unpins their knight and brings another attacker to d4 with tempo. 6. Bb3 Nxd4 and White has lost an important centre pawn. (If 6. d5? to counterattack the knight, 6...bxa4 7. dxc6 Ne7 and White has only opened up the b-file for Black's rook. Black will win the pawn on c6 shortly.)

r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1np4/4p3/B3P3/5N1P/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Ba4/4...d6/5. h3
r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1np4/4p3/B3P3/5N1P/PPP.x:
This move will most likely see a surge in popularity in order to directly discourage Black from playing the Octopus Defense, a scary hypermodern attack against the Ruy Lopez. 5. h3 also prevents Black's idea of Bg4 to pin the f3 knight.

However, 5. h3 is not a good move, since it does not fight for the center or focus on development. Black immediately equalizes and then some after 5...b5! 6. Bb3 Na5, hunting down White's light-squared bishop in similar fashion to the Norwegian Variation of the Ruy Lopez.

r1bqkbnr/1ppp2pp/p1n5/4pp2/B3P3/5N2/PPPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Ba4/4...f5
r1bqkbnr/1ppp2pp/p1n5/4pp2/B3P3/5N2/PPPP.x:
Black offers the f-pawn in a bid for central control. This is not as popular as ...f5 on the third move, but delaying it until after playing ...a6 leads to some important differences which an unprepared player may not appreciate.

First among the differences is that d4!, which against the turn three Schliemann is a mistake, is the critical move.

r1bqkbnr/1ppp1ppp/p1B5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Bxc6
r1bqkbnr/1ppp1ppp/p1B5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1.x:
White chooses to trade off Black's knight for a bishop. This reduces Black's control of the centre, and alleviates the risk that White's bishop may become trapped on the queenside. Black gets the bishop pair, but at the cost of doubled pawns.

4...dxc6 is the main move. Taking back this way, though it takes a pawn away from the centre, opens lines for Black's queen and queen's bishop to enter the game. Black's e5 pawn is still defended tactically for now: Nxe5 may be met with ...Qd4!, forking the knight and e4 pawn. So, before White can win it they must defend e4: either 5. O-O intending Re1, or 5. Nc3. An alternative is 5. d4, attacking e5 and opening the centre.

r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1p5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Bxc6/4...dxc6
r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1p5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.x:
Black takes the bishop and opens lines for their pieces.

If White takes the e5 pawn, 5. Nxe5?, Black can win it back tactically with ...Qd4!. Therefore White must first defend e4, so as to reinforce the threat. Black can functionally end the threat with ...f6, after which if White continues to pressure with d4, most of the lines lead to an early endgame. White's belief is that, once they have traded down, they will have the advantage in the endgame because Black is hampered with doubled pawns.

r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1p5/4N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Bxc6/4...dxc6/5. Nxe5
r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1p5/4N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.x:
Taking the e5 pawn is a poor move because of the reply 5...Qd4!, forking the knight at e5 and the pawn at e4.

5...Qd4 6. Ng4 Qxe4+ Ne3 and Black gets the pawn back. Any other move for the knight affords Black the opportunity for further damage: 6. Nf3 Qxe4+ 7. Kf1 (7. Qe2 Qxe2+ 8. Kxe2) and White also loses the power to castle.

r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1p5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Bxc6/4...dxc6/5. O-O
r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1p5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.x:
Castling reinvigorates the threat of Nxe5, because the tactic ...Qd4 to recover the pawn will fail to Nf3 Qxe4 Re1! pinning Black's queen to the king. Therefore, Black must prevent Nxe5.

5...Bg4 accomplishes this by pinning the knight. Because White has castled and Black has not, this bishop can be difficult to dislodge. 6. h3 h5 is the Alapin gambit: if White takes then they can face trouble on the open h-file, e.g. 7. hxg4 hxg4 8. Nxe5 (g-pawn threatened to take knight) Qh4! is mate in 3 (9. f4 g3 10. Qh5 Rxh5 11. Re1 Qh1#).

Guarding the pawn is the other approach:

r2qkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1p5/4p3/4P1b1/5N2/PPPP1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Bxc6/4...dxc6/5. O-O/5...Bg4
r2qkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1p5/4p3/4P1b1/5N2/PPPP1.x: This aggressive move pins the f3-knight and is a good way to stop the threat of Nxe5. But this also has a hidden sting to it! The 'Obvious' h3 allows a hidden trap!

r2qkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1p5/4p3/4P1b1/5N1P/PPPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Bxc6/4...dxc6/5. O-O/5...Bg4/6. h3
r2qkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1p5/4p3/4P1b1/5N1P/PPPP.x: This move looks natural, forcing Black's hand, but there is a surprising option for Black! /6...h5/ is a surprising move that forces White's hand instead.

r2qkbnr/1pp2pp1/p1p5/4p2p/4P1b1/5N1P/PPP.n: Ruy Lopez, Exchange Variation, Alapin Gambit
r2qkbnr/1pp2pp1/p1p5/4p2p/4P1b1/5N1P/PPP.x: After h5, black sacrifices the bishop for the betterment of Black's position. 7. hxg4? is bad because after 7. ...hxg4! the knight on f3 is attacked, and moving the knight is even worse. For example, after 8. Nxe5??, white captures the pawn, but after 8. ...Qh4! the checkmate in four moves is unavoidable. White can also try 7. c3 with the idea of playing d4, but 7. ...Qd3 stops it. 8. hxg4, hxg4. 9. Nxe5, there is a move Bd6, attacking the knight. 10. Nxd3 and then, there is 10. ...Bh2+ and you repeat moves. And white can also play 7. d4 with the idea of developing queenside pieces.

r1bqkbnr/1pp3pp/p1p2p2/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Bxc6/4...dxc6/5. O-O/5...f6
r1bqkbnr/1pp3pp/p1p2p2/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1.x:
Black defends their hanging e5 pawn.

6. d4 is the main move. Black is behind in development and at best still three moves from castling, so it's incumbent on White to strike fast and open the centre. Black wishes to avoid dxe4 fxe4 Nxe4, so the main continuation is 6...exd4 7. Nxd4. After 7...c5 8. Nb3 Qxd1 9. Rxd1 this goes into an endgame. An alternative is 6...Bg4 to pin the knight. If 7. dxe4 there may still be a queen trade, but otherwise White can keep a centre with 7. c3.

r1bqkbnr/1pp3pp/p1p2p2/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Bxc6/4...dxc6/5. O-O/5...f6/6. d4
r1bqkbnr/1pp3pp/p1p2p2/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2.x:
White opens up the center with this move and attacks the e5-pawn.

Black has two main moves, he can either take the d4-pawn with 6...exd4, or pin the knight with 6...Bg4.

r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1p5/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Bxc6/4...dxc6/5. d4

r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1p5/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Bxc6/4...dxc6/5. d4/5...exd4
r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1p5/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP.x:
= Ruy Lopez: Exchange Variation =
The best move for white here is 6.Qxd4. This leads to 6.- Qxd4 7.Nxd4. This line is thought to slightly favor black.
6.Nxd4?! is bad because of 6.- c5! and after 7.Nb5 or 7.Nb3, black shall play Qxd1+!, which will give him an advantage.

r1bqkbnr/1ppp1ppp/p1n5/1B2N3/4P3/8/PPPP1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Nxe5
r1bqkbnr/1ppp1ppp/p1n5/1B2N3/4P3/8/PPPP1.x: The best move in this position is /4...axb5/ according to Stockfish but /4...Nxe5/ is more common.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/1B1pp3/4P3/5N2/PPPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...d5
r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/1B1pp3/4P3/5N2/PPPP.x:
This suspicious move offers White their choice of central pawns. This exotic gambit is generally bad for Black, but there are a few of traps White must avoid.

Black's main source of counterplay in this gambit is hoping to make an attack on White's kingside, where, if White leaves their knight in the centre before they have castled, Black tries to fork it and g2.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2np4/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...d6
r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2np4/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP.x:
3...d6 is the Steinitz defence or Old Steinitz. This is a passive move, a very minor sideline in tournament play but common in amateur games.

3...d6 appears to defend the e5 pawn, but the pawn was not at risk (Bxc6 dxc6 Nxe5 is met by Qd4!, forking the knight and pawn). Black actually reduces their control of the centre as 3...d6 created a pin on their own knight. Black allows his light square Bishop to become active, but at the same time his dark square bishop is getting blocked, so there isn't much of any gain in development.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2np4/1B2p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...d6/4. d4
r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2np4/1B2p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP.x:
White has two attackers on e5 and threatens to win it.

Black must either take the pawn first in trade, 4...exd4 5. Nxd4, or break the pin with 4...Bd7, so defending e5. In the latter continuation, Black may find themselves choosing between keeping the pawn protected and their development.

4...Nf6?!, counter-attacking e4, doesn't work out due to 5. dxe5 Nxe4 6. Qd5!, attacking the knight on e4. If Black defends well, they only lose a pawn: 6...Nc5 7. Ng5 (threatening Qxf7#) Ne6 (interposes between the queen and f7) 8. Bxc6+ bxc6 9. Qxc6+ (wins a pawn) Bd7 10. Qf3 (threatens Qxf7#) Nxg5 11. Bxg5 (trades knights).

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2pp2/4P3/5N2/PPPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5
r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2pp2/4P3/5N2/PPPP.x: The first thing to know about the the Jaenisch gambit, aka the Schliemann defence, is that it is not a gambit. Despite the apparent similarity to the Latvian gambit, Black's knight on c6 changes everything.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2pp2/4P3/2N2N2/PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. Nc3
r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2pp2/4P3/2N2N2/PP.x: 4...fxe4 is the only move - otherwise why bother attacking White's e-pawn?

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2p3/4N3/5N2/PPPP1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. Nc3/4...fxe4/5. Nxe4
r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2p3/4N3/5N2/PPPP1.x:
Black may now accept the invitation to build a classical pawn centre with 5...d5. If White were forced to retreat the e4-knight, this would be enough to put 4.Nc3 out of business. Alas, Black players at GM level have been scoring very badly out of the well-analysed complications that follow White's critical reply 6.Nxe5!

So Schliemann Defence champion Teimour Radjabov prefers the more sedate 5...Nf6, with the character of the resulting positions depending on whether White now exchanges on f6 voluntarily or has to be forced into it with 6.Qe2 d5.

r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1B2p3/4N3/5N2/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. Nc3/4...fxe4/5. Nxe4/5...Nf6
r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1B2p3/4N3/5N2/PPP.x:
Black has challenged White's unprotected e4-knight with another knight. This is a problem and an opportunity for White. In the 5...d5 lines this knight doesn't have the opportunity of gaining a tempo by swapping itself for a Black piece of equal value. Here, it does! So an obvious move here would be
* 6. Nxf6+, the Exchange Variation.

r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2N2/1B2p3/8/5N2/PPPP1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. Nc3/4...fxe4/5. Nxe4/5...Nf6/6. Nxf6
r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2N2/1B2p3/8/5N2/PPPP1.x:
6...Qxf6 is a useful developing move - many writers caution against bringing the queen out early, but without the b1-knight on the board she doesn't have to worry about losing tempos to Nb1-c3-d5 or Nb1-c3-e4 ideas. Any opening that features a quick ...e5 and ...f5 (looking at you, Latvian Gambit) will likely involve putting the queen on f6 and castling kingside to bring a rook to f8 and then mating White on the f-file.

6...gxf6 has been played by FM Danko Bokan. You get the same pawn structure as in the 6.Qe2 d5 7.Nxf6+ line but White still has the option of putting her queen on a square other than e2.

r1b1kb1r/pppp2pp/2n2q2/1B2p3/8/5N2/PPPP1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. Nc3/4...fxe4/5. Nxe4/5...Nf6/6. Nxf6/6...Qxf6
r1b1kb1r/pppp2pp/2n2q2/1B2p3/8/5N2/PPPP1.x:
Having avoided committing the queen to e2 on move 6, White typically puts it there anyway with 7. Qe2. This restricts Black's options, because now ...d5 would self-pin the c6-knight allowing White to capture the e5-pawn for zero compensation.

Viktor Kupreichik mixed things up a couple times with 7. O-O. If Black reacts the same way she would after 7. Qe2, with 7...Be7, White has a huge positive score with the plan of Bxc6 and Qe1. But alert Black players found 7...Nd4! to take advantage of the fact that the e-pawn isn't under any pressure.

r1b1kb1r/pppp2pp/2n2q2/1B2p3/8/5N2/PPPPQ.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. Nc3/4...fxe4/5. Nxe4/5...Nf6/6. Nxf6/6...Qxf6/7. Qe2
r1b1kb1r/pppp2pp/2n2q2/1B2p3/8/5N2/PPPPQ.x:
Attempting to defend the e-pawn with moves like 7...d6 or 7...Bd6 are ultimately futile. Either 7...d6 8.d4 or 7...Bd6 8.d4 (not allowing Black the trick 8.Bxc6 dxc6 9.d4 Bg4) just win it outright.

So instead Black gambits the pawn with 7...Be7. The compensation will be in the form of open lines for the rooks and an unopposed light-squared bishop.

r1b1k2r/ppppb1pp/2n2q2/1B2p3/8/5N2/PPPPQ.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. Nc3/4...fxe4/5. Nxe4/5...Nf6/6. Nxf6/6...Qxf6/7. Qe2/7...Be7
r1b1k2r/ppppb1pp/2n2q2/1B2p3/8/5N2/PPPPQ.x:
White accepts the gambit with 8. Bxc6, planning to capture on e5 once the guard is removed.

Castling kingside is still sub-optimal due to the ...Nd4 option (compare the position after 6...Qxf6).

r1b1k2r/ppppb1pp/2B2q2/4p3/8/5N2/PPPPQPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. Nc3/4...fxe4/5. Nxe4/5...Nf6/6. Nxf6/6...Qxf6/7. Qe2/7...Be7/8. Bxc6
r1b1k2r/ppppb1pp/2B2q2/4p3/8/5N2/PPPPQPP.x:
Here's an example of how chess opening theory moves with the times.
* 8...dxc6 was by far the more common move until the mid-2000s. It seems logical to open a diagonal for the bishop that it can actually use, right? The same exchange in the Exchange Ruy Lopez is always met with dxc6.
* But then along came Teimour Radjabov and revived the whole 5...Nf6 line based on the innovation 8...bxc6, and now every top player who tries this line - Zvjagintsev, Timmerman, Fressinet - goes 8...bxc6.
Why 8...bxc6 and not 8...dxc6? The intelligent answer is something to do with capturing towards the centre and pawn islands.

r1b1k2r/p1ppb1pp/2p2q2/4p3/8/5N2/PPPPQPP.x:
* 9. Nxe5 is the main line. White simply captures the free pawn with the nearest piece to hand.
* 9. Qxe5 has been played by Michael Adams, because being a pawn up and taking the queens off is usually what you want to do, but in this case simplifying hurts White's winning percentage as well as Black's. The queen enjoys being the most mobile piece on the board; if you exchange her off then that title would pass to the Black bishops, and there are two of them.
* 9. d4 is a fun idea of Swedish GM Emanuel Berg's, taken up by Alexei Shirov. It's not a gambit in that if Black grabs the pawn with 9...exd4, White shoves the queen away with 10.Bg5 and grabs it back.

r1b1k2r/p1ppb1pp/2p2q2/4N3/8/8/PPPPQPPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. Nc3/4...fxe4/5. Nxe4/5...Nf6/6. Nxf6/6...Qxf6/7. Qe2/7...Be7/8. Bxc6/8...bxc6/9. Nxe5
r1b1k2r/p1ppb1pp/2p2q2/4N3/8/8/PPPPQPPP/.x:
* 9...O-O looks like the best developing move Black has, immediately bringing the rook to the open f-file. What could be better than that?
* 9...Qe6 could be better than that. Catching the opposing king in the centre is half the fun of sacrificing pawns, and here 10.O-O?? would unprotect the White queen and so drop a piece to 10...d6.
** 10.d4 is surprisingly popular given that it doesn't actually get out of the pin! (It does help develop a piece though.) Black has tried various moves to claim some initiative; Radjabov's choice is 10...Bf6, 10...O-O is also obvious, 10...a5 prepares ...Ba6 hitting the queen, 10...c5 immediately challenges the d-pawn.

r1b1k2r/ppp1b1pp/2p2q2/4p3/8/5N2/PPPPQPP.x:
9. Nxe5 is the main line. White needs to capture the pawn now otherwise Black will play ...Bd6 and ...Bg4 and the window will be shut.

Why is it not a good idea to capture with 9. Qxe5, since White will be a pawn up with the queens off? Because Black doesn't have to obligingly exchange queens on e5. Instead she can play 9...Bg4 to exploit the brittle knight on f3, which won't have any good squares after 10.Qxf6 Bxf6, and if White has to play gxf3 her kingside pawn majority will be nobbled. (10.Qxc7? is suicide with White so under-developed. The simple 10...O-O! gives Black an irresistible attack.)

r1b1k2r/ppp1b1pp/2p2q2/4N3/8/8/PPPPQPPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. Nc3/4...fxe4/5. Nxe4/5...Nf6/6. Nxf6/6...Qxf6/7. Qe2/7...Be7/8. Bxc6/8...dxc6/9. Nxe5
r1b1k2r/ppp1b1pp/2p2q2/4N3/8/8/PPPPQPPP/.x:
9...Bf5 is a useful developing move. 9...O-O is also a useful developing move.

Why is ...Bf5 more popular than ...O-O? It comes down to a general principle of opening theory: postpone the hard decisions for as long as you can. Black in this position no longer has to decide where to put the c8-bishop. The White knight is hitting d7 and g4, and on e6 the bishop will be vulnerable to tactics like Nxc6 as soon as White gets a rook to the e-file. So it has to go to f5. That's an easy decision. Whether Black wants to castle queenside or kingside is a hard decision. Make the easy decision first!

r3k2r/ppp1b1pp/2p2q2/4Nb2/8/8/PPPPQPPP/R.x:
What happens next in this position depends more on what Black is planning than on what White's next move is.

Scenario 1: White and Black both castle kingside, Black attacks the e5-knight with ...Bd6, White defends it with d4 and possibly f4 too, Black swaps it off and gets a light-square bind to compensate for White's extra passed pawn.

There are three routes by which Scenario 1 can come about: 10. O-O, 10. d4 and, surprisingly, 10. d3. White loses a tempo in the 10.d3 line by playing d2-d3-d4, but Black also loses a tempo by playing Ra8-e8-d8. It all makes sense - see below!

r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1B2p3/4N3/5N2/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. Nc3/4...fxe4/5. Nxe4/5...Nf6/6. Qe2
r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1B2p3/4N3/5N2/PPP.x:
6...d5 is a beautiful freeing move in most 1.e4 e5 openings, and here Black gets it for free thanks to the awkward knight on e4.

6...Qe7 makes less sense, because if the queen is planning to capture on f6 then it's a waste of a tempo, and if the g-pawn is planning to capture on f6 then the queen isn't needed on e7 to defend the e-pawn because the new f-pawn will be defending it.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2n2n2/1B1pp3/4N3/5N2/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. Nc3/4...fxe4/5. Nxe4/5...Nf6/6. Qe2/6...d5
r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2n2n2/1B1pp3/4N3/5N2/PPP.x: Aron Nimzowitsch would have been proud of the move 7. Nxf6, a "liquidation with gain of tempo", in other words Black doesn't have time to make a normal developing move if you capture her knight with check. Plus, she's going to have to recapture with the g-pawn to protect e5, and then you can point and laugh at the hole in her kingside pawn cover (and hope that her brilliantly supported centre is not as solid as it looks).

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2n2N2/1B1pp3/8/5N2/PPPPQ.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. Nc3/4...fxe4/5. Nxe4/5...Nf6/6. Qe2/6...d5/7. Nxf6
r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2n2N2/1B1pp3/8/5N2/PPPPQ.x: It's check, and 7...gxf6 is necessary to regain the piece. 7...Qxf6 would be a bad way to sacrifice the e-pawn because White wouldn't be forced to give up the bishop pair in order to capture it (as she would after 6.Nxf6+ Qxf6 7.Qe2 Be7).

r1bqkb1r/ppp4p/2n2p2/1B1pp3/8/5N2/PPPPQP.x:
8. d4, threatening the e5-pawn, is the move that really gets to grips with Black's pawn centre - given that 8.Nxe5 straight away is not possible because the White queen is pinned after 8...fxe5 9.Qxe5+ Qe7.

Krum Georgiev tried 8. Nd4, not to show off how many Black pieces White has managed to pin, but to threaten a queen check on h5 that would deprive Black of castling rights. It's not such a threat though, as ...Qd6 solidifies the c6-knight and makes room for the king on d8.

r1bqkb1r/ppp4p/2n2p2/1B1pp3/3P4/5N2/PPP1.x:
8...Bg7 is a deceptive move. Yes, it defends the vulnerable e-pawn - but not by attacking the square it's standing on, which wouldn't actually work because it would still have three attackers and two (non-pinned) defenders. Instead it defends the e-pawn indirectly by allowing ...O-O, which will unpin the c6-knight and, more importantly, allow the king's rook to come to the e-file and make the white king and queen uncomfortable.

8...e4 looks impressive but it just freezes Black's central pawns into a block of ice. White can play around the block of ice with Nh4, Bf4 and Qh5, or can play c4 which hits the block of ice with a hammer.

r1bqk2r/ppp3bp/2n2p2/1B1pp3/3P4/5N2/PPP1.x: 9. dxe5 is consistent with the plan of attacking the e-pawn several times and then capturing it.

r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2n5/1B1pp3/4N3/5N2/PPPP1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. Nc3/4...fxe4/5. Nxe4/5...d5
r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2n5/1B1pp3/4N3/5N2/PPPP1.x:
This is a great time to dynamite Black's proud pawn centre with 6. Nxe5! White comes out of the resulting tactics in good shape.

6. Ng3 isn't exactly a bad move, and Black still has to do something about the threat to the e-pawn, but who wants to let Black play ...e5 and ...d5 in the first 5 moves and get away with it?

r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2n5/1B1pN3/4N3/8/PPPP1PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. Nc3/4...fxe4/5. Nxe4/5...d5/6. Nxe5
r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2n5/1B1pN3/4N3/8/PPPP1PP.x: 6...dxe4 captures 1 knight. All the other legal moves capture 0 knights.

r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2n5/1B2N3/4p3/8/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. Nc3/4...fxe4/5. Nxe4/5...d5/6. Nxe5/6...dxe4
r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2n5/1B2N3/4p3/8/PPPP1PPP.x: White ties the minor piece count at 3 with 7. Nxc6. It's a free knight because if Black recaptures with the b-pawn, Bxc6+ followed by Qh5+ gives Black big problems.

r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2N5/1B6/4p3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. Nc3/4...fxe4/5. Nxe4/5...d5/6. Nxe5/6...dxe4/7. Nxc6
r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2N5/1B6/4p3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.x: Black's queen is attacked, and capturing the attacker with 7...bxc6 will end in tears after 8.Bxc6+ Bd7 9.Qh5+! So we have to move the queen. Moving the queen to the fourth rank seems like a good idea, to try and neutralise the discovered check by hitting the b5-bishop, and at the same time cut out any of White's Qh5+ ideas.

r1b1kbnr/ppp3pp/2N5/1B1q4/4p3/8/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. Nc3/4...fxe4/5. Nxe4/5...d5/6. Nxe5/6...dxe4/7. Nxc6/7...Qd5
r1b1kbnr/ppp3pp/2N5/1B1q4/4p3/8/PPPP1PPP.x: Both of White's developed pieces are threatened with capture, so 8. c4 is necessary to distract the Black queen.

r1b1kbnr/ppp3pp/2N5/1B1q4/2P1p3/8/PP1P1P.x:
8...Qd6 is necessary to preserve the attack on the White knight. It's true that Black could have played 7...Qd6 in one move, but the move 8.c4 is hopefully going to prove to be a concession by White.

Horizontal queen moves like 8...Qg5 are inferior because the queen won't be hitting an undefended piece on b5 the way it would after 7...Qg5.

r1b1kbnr/ppp3pp/2Nq4/1B6/2P1p3/8/PP1P1PP.x:
9. Nxa7+ was first played in Gligoric-Heidenfeld 1960. It's not entirely clear how Black is going to punish White for simply grabbing a second pawn and holding on to it - on the contrary, White still has the threat of Qh5+ on the board, so it may be Black that gets the punishment.

9. Qh5+ was played against Günther Möhring, the originator of the 7...Qd5 variation, in two Hungarian tournaments in the 1980s. As is usually the case for loud forcing moves, it's actually a little more drawish than the alternative. Black will probably come out of the looming queen trade with castling rights still intact, which isn't the case in the 9. Nxa7+ line.

r1b1kbnr/Npp3pp/3q4/1B6/2P1p3/8/PP1P1PPP.x: Black isn't thrilled about the prospect of trading pieces when she's two pawns down, but the c8-bishop is coming off the board regardless, so it might as well be with 9...Bd7 which preserves Black's right to castle, rather than with the tempting 9...c6 which runs into 10.Nxc8 hitting the queen.

r3kbnr/Nppb2pp/3q4/1B6/2P1p3/8/PP1P1PPP/.x:
White's two threats in this position are Qh5+ and Bxd7+. It doesn't really matter whether White plays
* 10. Bxd7+, or
* 10. Qh5+
first, unless she wants to leave out Qh5+ entirely and just save the a7-knight with 10.Bxd7 Qxd7 11.Nb5. But that plan has a terrible score for White, despite the two extra pawns, because of Black's bind on the d-file and easy development.

r3kbnr/NppB2pp/3q4/8/2P1p3/8/PP1P1PPP/R1.x: 10...Qxd7 is a better recapture than 10...Kxd7, which would give up castling rights for no reason and leave the queen on a square where it would lose a tempo to Nb5.

r3kbnr/Nppq2pp/8/8/2P1p3/8/PP1P1PPP/R1BQ.x: The main line here is 11. Qh5+. White has the bread and butter of two extra pawns, and wants the jam as well (stopping Black from castling). Black can offer an exchange sacrifice in response, but White shouldn't accept it; the realisation that White isn't obliged to accept it was responsible for 11. Qh5+ taking over as the main line from:

r3kbnr/Nppq2pp/8/7Q/2P1p3/8/PP1P1PPP/R1B.x:
All of Black's moves in this position look terrible! 11...Qf7?? runs into 12.Qb5+. Moving the king out to e7 also loses at least a pawn to 12.Qe5+. The computer recommends 11...Kd8 as the least bad option, although White could then swing the queen over to a5 threatening Nc6+ and so forcing the king straight back to e8, while potentially saving a tempo by not having to move the knight immediately.

So the modern, active way of defending this position as Black is with 11...g6!? It doesn't sacrifice a whole rook, "only" an exchange, because White hasn't got time to capture on h8 and also save the knight.

r3kbnr/Nppq3p/6p1/7Q/2P1p3/8/PP1P1PPP/R1.x: 12. Qe5+ is necessary or Black will have a free move to capture on a7.

r3kbnr/Nppq3p/6p1/4Q3/2P1p3/8/PP1P1PPP/R.x: Black doesn't want the g8-knight to be hanging after a potential Qxh8, so 12...Kf7 is played to guard it. Black is planning to trap the queen in the corner with ...Nf6, so ...Ne7 would be a big mistake.

r4bnr/Nppq1k1p/6p1/4Q3/2P1p3/8/PP1P1PPP/.x: Because the queen gets trapped in the corner after 13.Qxh8 Nf6, after which Black can leisurely play ...Rd8, move the bishop, and force White to trade queen for rook. That wouldn't be a disaster for White, who would have two rooks and two pawns for the queen, in fact it's quite possibly a winning advantage still. But White's rooks would be stuck in the corners, and the Black queen would be running around in the middle of the board, and accidents can happen.

r4bnr/1ppq1k1p/6p1/1N2Q3/2P1p3/8/PP1P1PP.x:
Black's c7 and e4 pawns are threatened. 13...c6 saves one and, by kicking the knight, gains the necessary tempo to save the other.

Black still isn't worried about 14.Qxh8 which can be met by 14...Nf6 15.b3 Re8 16.Bb2 Bg7 or the quiet 16...Be7 ( 16...Bc5 is a well-known blunder because of 16.Qxf6+ Kg8 17.Qh8+ Kf7 18.Qg7+ Ke6 19.Qf6#) winning the queen for two rooks.

r4bnr/1p1q1k1p/2p3p1/1N2Q3/2P1p3/8/PP1P1.x:
It's now time for White to offer to take the queens off with 14. Qd4 and hope that the two extra pawns will be sufficiently healthy to win the day.

The retreat 14.Nc3 has been played too, but the attack on e4 is an illusion as long as the e-file is open for the a8-rook (14...Nf6 15.Nxe4? Nxe4 and now 16.Qxe4?? Re8 is a train wreck while 16.Qxh8 Nf6 is just a free piece for Black compared to the earlier Qxh8 lines) so the knight won't be well placed on c3.

r4bnr/1p1q1k1p/2p3p1/1N6/2PQp3/8/PP1P1PP.x: This is White's last chance to grab the h8-rook, otherwise Black is going to shut the door with ...Nf6. Alternatively, White can take advantage of the fact that Black has blocked the e-file with her queen, and go after the e4-pawn with 15.Nc3. This is a better move than 14.Nc3 would have been, because Black can't pin and win the queen with ...Re8 any more.

r3kbnr/Nppb2pp/3q4/1B5Q/2P1p3/8/PP1P1PPP.x: Black doesn't have an obvious way of escaping the check. 10...Qg6 would allow White with her next two moves Qxg6 and Bxd7 to a) ruin Black's pawns, b) swap off material when ahead and c) prevent Black castling. Fleeing to either d8 or e7 with the king followed by 11.Bxd7 Kxd7 12.Qb5+ would ship yet another pawn, as would 10...Ke7 11.Bxd7 Qxd7 12.Qe5+. The computer recommends 10...Kd8 11.Bxd7 Qxd7 as the least bad option, although White could then swing the queen over to a5 threatening Nc6+ and so forcing the king straight back to e8, while potentially saving a tempo by not having to move the knight immediately.

r3kbnr/Nppb3p/3q2p1/1B5Q/2P1p3/8/PP1P1PP.x: 11. Bxd7+ is necessary to free the b5-square if the knight is ever going to get out of a7.

r3kbnr/NppB3p/3q2p1/7Q/2P1p3/8/PP1P1PPP/.x: 11...Qxd7 is necessary to avoid losing another pawn to 12.Qb5+. It appears to lose a rook instead by unprotecting e5, but accepting the gift turns out to be fraught with danger.

r1b1kbnr/ppp3pp/2Nq4/1B5Q/2P1p3/8/PP1P1P.x:
9...g6 is the only safe move to block the check, because:
* 9...Qg6?? 10.Ne5+ wins the queen directly, and
* 9...Kd7?? 10.Qf7+ and the queen has to be shipped overboard with 10...Qe7, as either 10...Be7 or 10...Ne7 allow the pretty double check 11.Nb8+ followed by mate on e8.

r1b1kbnr/ppp4p/2Nq2p1/1B5Q/2P1p3/8/PP1P1.x:
The usual move here is
* 10. Qe5+, when after the forcing sequence 10...Qxe5 11.Nxe5+ c6 12.Ba4 Bg7 13.d4 exd3 White can simply recapture with
** 14.Nxd3 and try to untangle her queenside and convert the extra pawn, or alternatively: 
** 14.O-O (to meet ...Bxe5 with Re1 winning the bishop pair) and then 14...Bxe5 15.Re1 is simple enough, but with either 14...Be6 or 14...Bf5 Black can challenge White to the very very long variation:
*** 15.Nxc6 Bd7 16.Re1+ Kf8 17.Nd4! Bxa4 18.Ne6+ Kf7 19.Nxg7 Kxg7 20.b3 Be8 21.Bb2+ Nf6 22.Re7+ Bf7 23.g4 g5 24.f4 gxf4 25.g5 and White has at last won the piece back with, well, approximately a drawn position.
*** 15.Re1 is probably the sane option.

r1b1kbnr/ppp3pp/2N5/1B4q1/4p3/8/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. Nc3/4...fxe4/5. Nxe4/5...d5/6. Nxe5/6...dxe4/7. Nxc6/7...Qg5
r1b1kbnr/ppp3pp/2N5/1B4q1/4p3/8/PPPP1PPP.x: White turns the tables on Black with 8. Qe2, defending the b5-bishop and attacking the e4-pawn. The discovered check isn't as exciting as it looks thanks to the possibility of ...c6 in response. There's nothing to be gained by the panicked retreat 8.Nd4+ c6 9.Bf1, for example.

r1b1kbnr/ppp3pp/2N5/1B4q1/4p3/8/PPPPQPPP.x:
Black has to defend the e4-pawn, and does so with 8...Nf6, which has the additional benefit of covering h5.

8...Bf5 has a specific tactical problem: 9.f4! is a counter-sacrifice that White wants to play anyway, and with the bishop on f5 the pawn can't be taken: 9...Qxf4?? 10.Rf1 Qg5 11.Rxf5 Qxf5 12.Nd4+ is curtains. Plus, in the current position Black does have a secondary threat of ...a6 and ...Bd7 pinning and winning the c6-knight, which doesn't work if the bishop is away defending e4. Plus, f6 is almost certainly the best square for the knight anyway.

r1b1kb1r/ppp3pp/2N2n2/1B4q1/4p3/8/PPPPQP.x:
Now Black's attack against g2 is a real one. Defending g2 with moves like 9.0-0 or 9.Rg1 is too slow; Black will have time to execute her secondary threat of ...a6 and ...Bd7. The clever 9. f4 solves this problem by defending g2 with gain of tempo, while threatening to give the knight a beautiful square on e5 to retreat to, at the cost of restoring material equality (9...Qxf4 is the main reply).

9. Ne5+ c6 10.f4 as played by Gyula Sax is just the same moves in a different order.

r1b1kb1r/Npp3pp/5n2/1B4q1/4p3/8/PPPPQPPP.x:
9...Bd7 is the main line. Black preserves castling rights and denies the a7-knight the chance of exchanging itself on c8, which would be the coward's way out. It looks as though the move overworks the f6-knight, but in fact there are tactical reasons why grabbing the e4-pawn doesn't lead to any advantage.

9...Kd8 invites 10.Nxc8 and it looks like White has no problems, but Black has a glimmer of hope based on the fact that g2 is still hanging. German correspondence player Peter Leisebein is the main champion of this line.

9...c6? 10.Nxc6! means the c8-bishop will have to go to d7 anyway, but with one fewer Black pawn on the board.

r3kb1r/Nppb2pp/5n2/1B4q1/4p3/8/PPPPQPPP/.x: 10. Bxd7+ is necessary to give the a7-knight a retreat square.

r3kb1r/NppB2pp/5n2/6q1/4p3/8/PPPPQPPP/R1.x: 10...Nxd7 preserves castling rights for Black. Thanks to the precarious position of the a7-knight, it doesn't matter that it unprotects e4. The alternative 10...Kxd7? would allow the exchange of queens with 11.Qb5+ and the knight is saved.

r3kb1r/Nppn2pp/8/6q1/4p3/8/PPPPQPPP/R1B1.x:
* 11. f4 is the line adopted by all the top players who have had this variation as White, including Peter Svidler. As in the 9.f4 variation, White is defending g2 horizontally and hitting the Black queen, but now the circumstances are different: without the knight on c6, Black won't be obliged to chop f4 off simply to prevent the knight retreating to e5, and if she prefers to grab the c-pawn instead she can do that with 11...Qc5 (9.f4 Qc5? would have run into 10.d4 when everything is defended).
* 11. Nb5 allows 11...Qxg2 12.Qf1 Qxf1+ 13.Kxf1 O-O-O or 12.Rf1 O-O-O when Black's greater mobility compensates for the pawn.

r3kb1r/Nppn2pp/8/6q1/4pP2/8/PPPPQ1PP/R1B.x:
Black's queen is attacked by an unprotected pawn. There are two plausible queen moves:
* 11...Qxf4 accepts the gambited f-pawn, which then allows White to solve most of her problems with the developing move 12.d4 before the a7-knight needs to be extracted to b5. White remains a pawn up and although Black can point to a passed pawn on e4, it's isolated and immobile.
* 11...Qc5 attempts to imbalance the position a little by grabbing the c2-pawn instead of the f4-pawn, thus isolating White's d-pawn.

r1bk1b1r/Npp3pp/5n2/1B4q1/4p3/8/PPPPQPPP.x: 10. Nxc8 is the only move to save the knight, since White can't vacate the b5 square with tempo.

r1Nk1b1r/1pp3pp/5n2/1B4q1/4p3/8/PPPPQPPP.x: 10...Qxg2 is a crucial intermezzo, as recapturing the knight will allow White to get the thematic f4 move in.

r1Nk1b1r/1pp3pp/5n2/1B6/4p3/8/PPPPQPqP/R.x:
White has tried both ways of defending the rook: 
* 11. Qf1, after which Black can choose between 11...Qf3 and 11...Qxf1 12.Bxf1 Kxc8, and
* 11. Rf1, after which Black can choose between 11...Qxh2 and 11...Kxc8.
If Black doesn't capture the knight while it's on c8, White is going to go Nb6 and ruin Black's queenside pawns. Other than that, the tactics have subsided and Black scores terribly out of the resulting middlegame positions. Even in the line 11.Rf1 Qxh2 12.Nb6 cxb6 where material is level, Black's pawns look silly and White has the bishop pair on a very open board.

r1b1kb1r/ppp3pp/2N2n2/1B4q1/4pP2/8/PPPPQ.x:
9...Qxf4 is the main line, because why not take a pawn if White's going to leave them lying around.

9...Qh4+ is similar to the main line, in that the Black queen ends up on h3 via h4 in both lines, except without the bonus of having taken a pawn. A pawn is a pawn!

r1b1kb1r/ppp3pp/2N2n2/1B6/4pq2/8/PPPPQ1P.x:
White now has the simple plan of establishing a knight on e5 guarded by a pawn on d4 (which isn't going to get taken en passant because it'll go there with a discovered attack on the Black queen). The two possible ways of carrying out this plan of Ne5 and d4 are (you guessed it):
* 10. Ne5+ followed by 11.d4, and
* 10. d4 followed by 11.Ne5+.
The immediate 10.Ne5+ means that the Black queen will definitely go to h4 after 11.d4, whereas 10.d4 gives it the option of retreating to d6 instead. If she declines that option and goes to h4 anyway, the two lines merge into one.

r1b1kb1r/ppp3pp/5n2/1B2N3/4pq2/8/PPPPQ1P.x:
Black needs to defend against the check while keeping the knight on f6 to deny the White queen access to h5.

10...c6 is a sensible move that leaves two White pieces hanging.

r1b1kb1r/pp4pp/2p2n2/1B2N3/4pq2/8/PPPPQ1.x: White has two pieces hanging. 11. d4! defends one and gains a free tempo to move the other.

r1b1kb1r/pp4pp/2p2n2/1B2N3/3Ppq2/8/PPP1Q.x: With 11...Qh4+ Black's queen gets off the open f-file and attempts to win a tempo to capture the b5-bishop.

r1b1kb1r/pp4pp/2p2n2/1B2N3/3Pp2q/8/PPP1Q.x: As the b5-bishop is still hanging, 12. g3 is necessary to deny Black the crucial tempo to capture it.

r1b1kb1r/pp4pp/2p2n2/1B2N3/3Pp3/6Pq/PPP1.x:
The b5-bishop is finally forced to move, and 13. Bc4 threatens to revoke Black's castling privileges with a check on f7.

13.Nxc6 would be refuted by the same ...a6 and ...Bd7 trick, pinning and winning the knight, that we saw earlier.

r1b1kb1r/pp4pp/2p2n2/4N3/2BPp3/6Pq/PPP1Q.x: 13...Be6 is necessary to deny White access to the f7 square while keeping e4 nailed down. It has the pleasant side-effect of getting another piece off the back rank.

r3kb1r/pp4pp/2p1bn2/4N3/2BPp3/6Pq/PPP1Q2.x: For the first time since Black played 3...f5, White has no material hanging! So she has a major decision to make about where to develop the last remaining minor piece.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2pp2/4P3/3P1N2/PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. d3
r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2pp2/4P3/3P1N2/PP.x:
The move 4.d3 defended e4 but also threatened to snaffle the f5-pawn into the bargain, because now Black won't have the instant rejoinder ...e4.

4...fxe4 is the only move to justify the Black pawn thrust.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2p3/4p3/3P1N2/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. d3/4...fxe4
r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2p3/4p3/3P1N2/PPP.x: With the bishop already developed on b5, there are no clever gambits in this position - 5. dxe4 is played to recover the pawn.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. d3/4...fxe4/5. dxe4
r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP2P.x: 5...Nf6 is the only move. As well as attacking the e4-pawn, it's a case of making the easy decisions first: the g8-knight is the only Black piece that has an obvious square to go to.

r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. d3/4...fxe4/5. dxe4/5...Nf6
r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.x: There are a few minor moves here, but if White notices that the e-pawn doesn't need to be directly defended, then 6. O-O makes the most sense, avoiding a potential pin or check after 6... Bb4, which would allow Black to develop the dark squared bishop and play d6 more easily. 6... Nxe4? in response would be a tactical error, allowing 7. Re1 or Qe2 with a strong attack along the e file, as 7... d5 allows 8. Nxe5 with the c6 knight pinned.

r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. d3/4...fxe4/5. dxe4/5...Nf6/6. O-O
r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.x:
Time for Black to develop some more pieces. Spoiler: the pawn currently on d7 isn't going to make it to d5 at this point, because that would leave e5 hanging. So it'll have to go to d6 if the c8-bishop wants to get out.
* The immediate 6...d6 would shut in the f8-bishop.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2np1n2/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.x:
Now that Black is no longer vulnerable to Nxe5 tricks, the e4-pawn needs to be defended. The economical-looking 7.Re1, normally a very sensible move in the Ruy Lopez, would be dangerous in the Schliemann because it would weaken f2, the target of Black's future pressure along the f-file.
* 7. Nc3 develops an undeveloped piece to its natural square. Nothing wrong with that!
* 7. Qd3 is a move that's recommended against 6...Bc5, because after 6...Bc5 7.Qd3 O-O?? White simply wins a piece with 8.Qc4+, so Black is prevented from castling for a while.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2np1n2/1B2p3/4P3/2N2N2/P.x:
Having put the pawn on d6, the only square available for the f8-bishop is e7, so it might as well go there immediately with 7...Be7. The c8-bishop still has options, and the option of breaking the pin on the c6-knight with Bd7 may be particularly useful, so it typically stays put for now.

7...Bg4 is also played, inviting White to transpose to 7.Qd3 lines with 8.Qd3 which gets out of the pin.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2pp2/3PP3/5N2/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. d4
r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2pp2/3PP3/5N2/PPP.x: If Black takes the e-pawn, White's has two main options. 5. Nxe5 wins the pawn back, but runs into complications after 5. ... Nxe5 6. dxe5 c6. Now if the white bishop retreats, Black has 7... Qa5+ winning the e5 pawn and leaving Black better. (Note that in the Deferred Schliemann, because the white bishop is no longer on b5, c6 no longer comes with tempo, so this line is worse for Black. Thus, 5. d4 is the most common response to the Delayed Schliemann.) Thus, the most common line for white is 7. Nc3?!, a piece sacrifice. Play usually follows 7... cxb5 8. Nxe4 d5 9. exd6 Nf6, with an unclear position.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2pP2/8/5N2/PPPP1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. exf5
r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2pP2/8/5N2/PPPP1P.x:
Accepting the "free" pawn is inaccurate, as Black can regain the pawn with extra tempi and space.

After 4...e4, White's knight is kicked and is low on squares: g5 and h4 are controlled by Black'[s queen, while Black's knight controls e4 and d5. (The addition of this knight is the key difference between the Jaenisch and Latvian gambits accepted, 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 f5?! 2. exf5!) Un-developing the knight to g1 would be a big concession to Black.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B3P2/4p3/5N2/PPPP1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. exf5/4...e4
r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B3P2/4p3/5N2/PPPP1.x:
= Schliemann Defence Accepted =

/5. Ng1/ is an interesting move but best to keep a complex position

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B3P2/4p3/8/PPPP1PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f5/4. exf5/4...e4/5. Ng1

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n2p2/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f6
r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n2p2/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.x: Black defends their e-pawn with their f-pawn. This is non-standard as it weakens their kingside and prevents the knight coming to f6. It's also unnecessary for Black to defend the e-pawn again: the e5-pawn wasn't hanging because of the tactic Bxc6 dxc6 Nxe5? Qd4!, where Black recovers the material.

r1bqk1nr/pppp2pp/2n2p2/1Bb1p3/4P3/2P2N2/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...f6/4. O-O/4...Bc5/5. c3
r1bqk1nr/pppp2pp/2n2p2/1Bb1p3/4P3/2P2N2/.x:
In this line, White castles to protect the king and prepares to play d4 to gain more space in the center. Black develops the bishop to c5, which is a natural square for the bishop and also puts pressure on the f2-pawn. White plays c3 to support the d4-pawn advance.

The Main Line of the Nürnberg Variation is considered to be better for White, as White has more options and flexibility in the position. White can choose to play d4 immediately or delay it and play Re1, h3, or a4 first. White can also exchange the light-squared bishop on b5 with the knight on c6 at any time, creating a weakness in Black’s pawn structure.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1p1p/2n5/1B2p1p1/4P3/5N2/PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...g5
r1bqkbnr/pppp1p1p/2n5/1B2p1p1/4P3/5N2/PP.x:
An interesting move where Black threatens ...g4 to push the knight back, and to start a pawn assault if White castles.

4. d4! is the best move. This discovers an attack on g5 with the bishop while attacking the e5 square, the purpose being that now White is threatening 5. Nxg5 to just win the pawn, and if 4...g4? 5. Nxe5 is supported.

4. h3?! is more conservative, preventing ...g4 but is otherwise passive. 4. O-O?! allows 4...g4 5. Ne1 and White's position is far from comfortable.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1pp1/2n4p/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...h6
r1bqkbnr/pppp1pp1/2n4p/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.x: The h6 sideline in the Ruy Lopez is a rare and provocative move that aims to prevent White from playing Bg5 and pinning the black knight. It also prepares to play g5 and Bg7, creating a kingside fianchetto. However, it also has some drawbacks, such as:

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.x:
This is one of the two main branches of the Italian game. Black develops their kingside bishop ahead of the knight: this move order keeps control of g5 until Black is ready to castle. Compared to the Two Knights defence (3...Nf6), where Black develops while making an attack on e4, this is considered the slower and more positional continuation, hence the name which in Italian means "quiet game".

White chooses between two sorts of plans: to get their pawn to d4, or to content themselves with d3 (the hallmark move of the giuoco pianissimo, "very quiet game").

r1bqk1nr/pppp1Bpp/2n5/2b1p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. Bxf7
r1bqk1nr/pppp1Bpp/2n5/2b1p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP.x:
4. Bxf7+?? is the unhinged Jerome gambit. Though a Bxf7+ sacrifice works in many lines in the Italian, this is far too early and it is objectively woeful for White. However, it is sharp enough that White has some success at the club level.

The idea is 4...Kxf7 5. Nxe5+ Nxe5 6. Qh5+, and White hopes that between Black's exposed king and the skewering of Black's pieces on the fifth rank they will swindle compensation. e.g. 6. Qh5+ g6 7. Qxe5 d6?? (better is Qe7) 8. Qxh8.

r1bq2nr/pppp1kpp/2n5/2b1p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. Bxf7/4...Kxf7
r1bq2nr/pppp1kpp/2n5/2b1p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1.x: Black has a clear advantage. White will attempt to mate the black king with a series of checks, but with proper play black will come out ahead. His bishop pair and lead in development make it impossible to find enough compensation.

r1bq2nr/pppp1kpp/2n5/2b1N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. Bxf7/4...Kxf7/5. Nxe5
r1bq2nr/pppp1kpp/2n5/2b1N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PP.x: This move sacrifices another piece, but White will soon get it back with d4 or Qh5+. They will have gotten a second pawn for the piece, but would have lost the bishop pair and their own king would not be able to get out of the center. Therefore, the compensation is not nearly enough and Black is close to winning. Do not sacrifice unless you see reason. Here, White didn't have enough development to attack the king successfully.

r1bq2nr/pppp1kpp/8/2b1n3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. Bxf7/4...Kxf7/5. Nxe5/5...Nxe5
r1bq2nr/pppp1kpp/8/2b1n3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/.x:
This is the obvious response. It seems that black has won 2 pieces, but white will regain one. He will then be a piece down for two pawns with no compensation, however.
Since Black has many replies after 6.d4, all of which retain a winning position, the most popular move is 6.Qh5+.

r1bq2nr/pppp1kpp/8/2b1n2Q/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. Bxf7/4...Kxf7/5. Nxe5/5...Nxe5/6. Qh5
r1bq2nr/pppp1kpp/8/2b1n2Q/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.x: After this, Black has various good replies. 6...g6 and 6...Kf8 are enough to win, but the greedy and probably best 6...Ke6!? shows the unsoundness of White's attack. He simply is not developed enough despite the centralized Black king. He will just be down a piece for a pawn. Lines to avoid are: 6... Kf6?? 7.Qf5+ followed by Qxe5+ and Qxc5 with 2 extra pawns for White, or 6... Ke7?? 7.Qxe5+ with Qxc5 coming next, once again with two extra pawns for White.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. O-O
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.x: White chooses a quiet path, that tends to transpose to the Giuoco Pianissimo after white plays 5. d3.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/1PB1P3/5N2/P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/1PB1P3/5N2/P.x:
White offers a pawn to divert the bishop away from the centre.

White would like to play d4 and put both d and e pawns in the centre. At the moment, Black has too much control over the d4 square for that to be worthwhile. White can prepare d4 with c3, as in 4. c3, the classical variation. However, this gives Black extra time to develop and get ready to castle. The idea of 4. b4 is to achieve c3 and d4 with tempo instead.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/b3p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Ba5
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/b3p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/P.x:
5...Ba5 is the main retreat after the Evans Gambit 5. c3, and it is considered the best attempt to "refute the gambit." However, it is not as safe as the retreat 5...Be7. Now, the most aggressive move for White is to play /6. d4/, when Black has four options:

* 6...exd4
* 6...d6
* 6...Nf6
* 6...b5

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/b3p3/2BPP3/2P2N2/P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Ba5/6. d4
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/b3p3/2BPP3/2P2N2/P.x:
White takes the whole center, attacking the pawn on e5 aggressively. Black can choose from four options:
* /6...exd4/ is usually played.
* /6...d6/ is the most solid move.
* /6...b5/ is interesting.
* /6...Nf6/ is a mistake.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/b3p3/2BPP3/2P2N2/.x: Black counterattacks the e4 pawn with their knight, but this is not good. White should play /7. dxe5/ to exploit Black's mistake and set a trap.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/b3P3/2B1P3/2P2N2/.x: White exploits Black's mistake by taking the free pawn on e5. This also sets a trap. The most commonly played move is /7...Nxe4/, but that loses the knight to 8. Qd5!. Black should play /7...Ng4/ instead, but Black's position is still inferior.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/b3P3/2B1P1n1/2P2N2/.x: Black correctly avoided losing their knight with 7...Nxe4??, but their position is still inferior. White should strike with /8. Bg5/.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/b3P1B1/2B1P1n1/2P2N.x: White attacks Black's queen. The only good way to block the attack without losing material is /8...f6/. Although 8...Ne7? does not lose material, it unnecessarily cramps Black's position.

r1bqk2r/pppp2pp/2n2p2/b3P1B1/2B1P1n1/2P2.x: Black blocks the attack on their queen. White should now capture the pawn with /9. exf6/.

r1bqk2r/pppp2pp/2n2P2/b5B1/2B1P1n1/2P2N2.x: White takes the pawn on f6. As 9...Nxf6? loses the knight after 10. e5!, Black should play /9...gxf6/.

r1bqk2r/pppp3p/2n2p2/b5B1/2B1P1n1/2P2N2/.x: Black recaptures on f6. White should now save their bishop with /10. Bh4/.

r1bqk2r/pppp3p/2n2p2/b7/2B1P1nB/2P2N2/P4.x: White retreats their g5 bishop to h4. White is simply better as Black's kingside pawn structure is ruined and Black's king is weak while material is equal. This is why 6...Nf6? is a mistake.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/b3P3/2B1n3/2P2N2/P4.x: This move seems to regain the pawn, but instead loses the knight to /8. Qd5/!.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/b2QP3/2B1n3/2P2N2/P.x: White will win Black's knight on e4 as both it and mate on f7 is threatened (for example 8...Nxc3?? 9. Qxf7#). After Black plays 8...O-O or 8...Qe7, White will take the knight on e4.

r1bqk1nr/p1pp1ppp/2n5/bp2p3/2BPP3/2P2N2/.x: An interesting gambit, Black sacrifices their b7 pawn to White's bishop on c4. The idea is that after 7. Bxb5, Black can play 7...Nxd4 where White's c3 pawn is pinned to the king, and unlike 6...Nxd4?, Nxe5 wouldn't be possible as the bishop on b5 is also attacked.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2np4/b3p3/2BPP3/2P2N2/P.x: A solid move, defending the e5 pawn with their d7 pawn. White usually plays /7. O-O/ or /7. Qb3/. /7. Bg5/ is a sideline.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2np4/b3p1B1/2BPP3/2P2N2.x: An interesting sideline, White develops their c1 bishop and attacks Black's queen on d8. Black can choose from 7...Nge7, 7...Qd7, 7...f6 or 7...Nf6.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Bc5
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/.x: Black retreats their bishop to c5. This move is usually played by beginners, who believe this stops d4 when it does not. White should play /6. d4/, gaining tempo on the bishop and contesting Black's center.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2nb4/4p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Bd6
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2nb4/4p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/P.x: Black retreats their bishop to d6, defending the e5 pawn so d4 doesn't come with an attack on the pawn, but at the cost of blocking the d7 pawn. White usually plays /6. d4/ taking the center.

r1bqk1nr/ppppbppp/2n5/4p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/P2.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Be7
r1bqk1nr/ppppbppp/2n5/4p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/P2.x: Black retreats their bishop to the safest square. White usually plays /6. d4/, taking the full center and attacking Black's pawn on e5.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/P2.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Bf8
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/P2.x: Black retreats the bishop on f8. This is not good as it undevelops the bishop. White should play /6. d4/, taking the center.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. c3
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/.x:
White reinforces the d4 square, and prepares d4 in order to establish two pawns in the centre. It also stops any Nd4 by black, in the future.

White also prepares b4 to try and trap the Black bishop. White's secondary aim is to bring the queen to b3, thus intensifying the pressure on Black's f7-pawn.

A drawback to this move is that the pawn occupies a square that should be reserved for the queen's knight.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/2P2N2.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. c3/4...Nf6
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/2P2N2.x: The most common reply. It attacks the pawn on e4, develops the knight, and allows black to castle later on.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2BPP3/2P2N2.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. c3/4...Nf6/5. d4
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2BPP3/2P2N2.x: White attacks the center with 5. d4, attempting to create a strong pawn center with the d4 and e4 pawns. Black has to respond with exd4, or else surrender the entire center to White.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b5/2BpP3/2P2N2/P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. c3/4...Nf6/5. d4/5...exd4
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b5/2BpP3/2P2N2/P.x: Black takes the d4 pawn with the e5 pawn. White will respond by either pushing the e4 pawn forward to e5 attacking the Black knight, or recapturing the pawn with 6. cxd4, or by playing 6. b4!?.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b5/1PBpP3/2P2N2/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. c3/4...Nf6/5. d4/5...exd4/6. b4
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b5/1PBpP3/2P2N2/.x:
White sacrifices the d4 pawn for quick development and an open d file. White also attacks the Black bishop on c5, forcing it to move. Black can play either 6...Bb6 or 6...Be7.

In contrast to the Evans gambit, White doesn't sacrifice the b pawn. Because of this White has the threat of b5, forcing the knight to move to a5 or e7.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/1bn2n2/8/1PBpP3/2P2N2/P.x: Black retreats his bishop to b6. White cannot recapture the d4 pawn without hanging the b4 pawn. White can continue with 7. e5.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/1bn2n2/4P3/1PBp4/2P2N2/.x:
=The Egan Variation=

7. e5

White attacks the f6 knight and forces either d5 or Ne4.

r1bqk2r/ppppbppp/2n2n2/8/1PBpP3/2P2N2/P4.x: Black retreats the bishop to e7. This retreat is generally considered safer, as it blocks any checks on the e file and controls the g5 square. Black will give back the d pawn and try to achieve d5.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b5/2BPP3/5N2/PP3.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. c3/4...Nf6/5. d4/5...exd4/6. cxd4
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b5/2BPP3/5N2/PP3.x: White plays the natural recapture. Now the bishop will have to move to b4 or b6; in most cases, Black plays 6...Bb4+.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/1bBPP3/5N2/PP3P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. c3/4...Nf6/5. d4/5...exd4/6. cxd4/6...Bb4
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/1bBPP3/5N2/PP3P.x:
The bishop must move, and it did. This is actually the only not losing move. White has a couple options here.

7. Bd2 is a natural blocking move. Black can either trade and break the center with 8...d5, or immediately take with 7...Nxe4 which leads to complicated variations and the sacrifice of 8. Bxf7+!

7. Nc3 is a main line that sacrifices the e4 pawn. This is the Greco Gambit, where White then castles and gambits the pawn for development.

7. Nbd2 also exists. It was once very rare but has recently increased in popularity.

This is a weird-looking move that seemingly doesn't make any sense. White can no longer castle and the e4 pawn is undefended. But the compensation exists. White has got a massive center while Black has none, and White are more prepared to attack than Black. The Cracow Variation a tricky opening, Black has to find the only moves to not to get a bad position. Black has several options:

7...Nxe4. Black has grabbed an actually free pawn. White can strike in the center with 8. d5!, kicking the knight back. After 8...Ne7 White has 9. Qd4, grabbing even more space, or a tricky 9. Bb3 with a threat of 10. Qd4 which is somewhy often unseen.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/1bBPP3/2N2N2/PP.x: This is the traditional way to block the bishop check. With 7. Nc3, white does sacrifice the e4 pawn, but aims to get a dangerous initiative

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/1bBPn3/2N2N2/PP3P.x: Black accepts the gambit pawn, otherwise she will allow White to maintain a massive center. White follows her plan with 8. O-O

White castles her king. This unpins her knight to her king, causing the black knight on e4 to be hanging. Due to the open e-file creating complications should black retreat her knight, black generally exchanges on c3. While …Nxc3 is appealing to keep the bishop pair, it enters the rabbit hole.

Therefore, Black should play …Bxc3, where after exchanging, there is no hanging piece, giving her time to play …d5

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/3P1N2.x: With 4... Nf6, Black develops the king's knight to a good square where it pressures e4, controls the d5 square, and prepares to castle kingside.

r1bqk1nr/pppp2pp/2n5/2b1pp2/2B1P3/3P1N2/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. d3/4...f5
r1bqk1nr/pppp2pp/2n5/2b1pp2/2B1P3/3P1N2/.x:
With 4...f5!?, Black unleashes the Lucchini Gambit—an aggressive response to the Giuoco Pianissimo that breaks the symmetry and transforms a quiet line into a tactical battlefield. Named after Italian player Marco Lucchini, this gambit challenges White’s center and seeks rapid development at the cost of material.

After 5. exf5 d5, Black aims to blow open the center while White is still underdeveloped. If 6. Bb5 Ne7!, Black keeps the kingside flexible while preparing Bxf5 or even queenside castling in sharper lines. Even if White declines the pawn with 5. Nc3 or 5. O-O, Black can still build strong initiative with Nf6, d6, and Qe7.

r1bqk1nr/pppp2pp/2n5/2b1ppN1/2B1P3/3P4/P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. d3/4...f5/5. Ng5
r1bqk1nr/pppp2pp/2n5/2b1ppN1/2B1P3/3P4/P.x:
White chooses the aggressive 5. Ng5, eyeing an early attack on f7. This sharpens the game considerably and signals a tactical battle. Black must now decide how to respond to the dual threats of Nf7, forking the queen and rook, as well as Qh5+. If White is able to bring their queen, knight and bishop towards Black's weakened kingside, they'll be in trouble.

However, Black has 5...f4!, cutting off White's dark-squared bishop and threatening Qxg5, effectively inviting White to attack their f7 square.

r1bqk1nr/pppp2pp/2n5/2b1p1N1/2B1Pp2/3P4/.x: Black plays 5...f4!, the critical move of the Dubois Variation (named after Serafino Dubois, an 1850s Italian master). Here Black threatens Qxg5. Most often, White will continue to fork Black's queen and rook with 6. Nf7. Otherwise, they will force Black's king to move with 6. Bf7+?, a mistake. White's strongest move here is actually h4! to reinforce their knight and stop Black's queen from moving outwards.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1Bpp/2n5/2b1p1N1/4Pp2/3P4/P.x: After Black calmly sidesteps with 6...Kf8, White’s knight on g5 comes under immediate threat from ...h6, and there’s no safe retreat. For example, 7. h4 h6 8. Bxg8 hxg5 leaves Black with open lines on the kingside and a dangerous initiative down the h-file. Thus, 6. h4 or 6. Nf7 are much better options for White.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/2BbP3/5N2/PPP2.x: This capture is the best way for Black to proceed without entering the Haxo Gambit. White has nothing better to do than /5. Nxd4/ to open lines for their pieces.
