r1b1k1nr/ppp1qNpp/8/2bp4/2BnP3/8/PPP2PPP.x:
At this moment Black has already sacrificed a pawn and now sacrifices the other pawn and the rook on h8. Here White have only one move to not to lose on spot: 7. Bxd5. Taking the rook isn't the best option as after 7... Qxe4 8. Kf1 dxc4 black has an awesome position because of the trapped knight on h8 and amazing piece activity.

The main ideas for Black in this gambit is to open the e file by capturing the e4 pawn (if Black manages to do it, especially if White didn't castle, no matter of material, Black is victorious) and try to develop as fast as possible and open as much files as possible while attacking opponent's pieces.

r1b1k1nr/ppp1qNpp/8/2bB4/3nP3/8/PPP2PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. d4/4...Nxd4/5. Nxe5/5...Qe7/6. Nxf7/6...d5/7. Bxd5
r1b1k1nr/ppp1qNpp/8/2bB4/3nP3/8/PPP2PPP/.x: White has captured the d5 pawn with their bishop and didn't let Black take the knight on f7.

r1b1k2r/ppp1qNpp/5n2/2bB4/3nP3/8/PPP2PPP.x:
This is the only move for Black in this position. From now, white has 2 main options:

8. Nxh8??. This move looks natural because White had captured the rook that can be saved the next move, but this move is losing. Here Black can go 8... Bg4!. From now there is quite a lot of variations.

8. Bg5!. This move is much better. Now the knight on f6 cannot capture the bishop on d5 because it's pinned to the queen. But Black has a paradoxal move in this position: 8... 0-0! and after 9. Ne5+ Be6 there are also quite a lot of variations and all of them cannot be described in one article.

r1b1k2r/ppp1qNpp/5n2/2bB2B1/3nP3/8/PPP2P.x: This is the best move for White in this position. Now Black are unable to take the bishop on d5 because the knight on f6 is pinned to the queen. But here Black can carelessly castle.

r1b2rk1/ppp1qNpp/5n2/2bB2B1/3nP3/8/PPP2P.x: Despite the fact that the knight from f7 can retreat with check, it hasn't any dangerous for Black squares to go to.

r4rk1/ppp1q1pp/4bn2/2bBN1B1/3nP3/8/PPP2P.x:
Black has covered a check with their bishop. From this position there is a couple of variations:

10. Bxe6+??. This move is the most obvious one and the blunder. After a natural 10... Qxe6 move White don't have any way of defending both the knight on e5 and the pawn on e4.

10. Bxb7?. The fun fact is that after 10... Rb8 the bishop on b7 is dead. Trying to escape the attack by 11. Ba6? move is bad because of 11... Bd5! and black is victorious again because of the same reason as after 10. Bxe6+ move.

10. c3!. Black will go 10... Nc6 and after the only 11. Ng4! move, after a series of trades Black will end up in a more pleasant position.

r4rk1/ppp1q1pp/4Bn2/2b1N1B1/3nP3/8/PPP2P.x: How tasty this bishop isn't seem, this move is a big blunder. The fact is after Black taking the bishop with their queen White doesn't have any way of defending both the knight on e5 and the pawn on e4.

r4rk1/ppp1q1pp/4bn2/2bBN1B1/3nP3/2P5/PP3.x: This is the only not losing move for White. The knight now has to retreat to c6. White can't take this knight because of the move 10... Bf2+! and the bishop can't be captured because of 11... Nxd5+.

r4rk1/ppp1q1pp/2n1bn2/2bBN1B1/4P3/2P5/PP.x: The knight escaped an attack to it. Here White has the only not losing move 11. Ng4!, and after 11... Bxd5 12. Nxf6+ gxf6 13. Qxd5+ Kh8 14. Be3 Bxe3 15. fxe3 Ne5 Black ends up in a better position. Black's plan is there to create a massive pressure on g file.

r1b1k2N/ppp1q1pp/5n2/2bB4/3nP3/8/PPP2PPP.x:
Look at activities of each side. Black already has both knights, a queen and a dark-squared bishop developed, and the light-squared one is ready to join the party. White has only the light-squared bishop developed since they wasted a ton of tempos by capturing material (and also deactivated their knight). Black can go 8...Bg4!, bringing a new piece to the attack. From now, there are a couple of variations:

9. Qd3 - the most natural move. After that White can go 9... Nxd5, and after 10. 0-0 Nb4 11. Qd2 Nbxc2 Black will regain the lost rook with a bonus.

r3k2N/ppp1q1pp/5n2/2bB4/3nP1b1/8/PPP2PPP.x:
Black has attacked White's queen.

9. f3?? isn't the best move for White in this position as Black can safely take the bishop on d5. The bishop on g4 can't be captured because after 10. fxg4?? Black will go 10... Qxe4! with a forced checkmate.

9. Qd3! is a much better option. But after that the bishop on d5 will be captured.
So Black often chooses 9. Bf7! to remove their bishop from the danger with check. Black has to go 9... Kf8! and after 10. Qd3 Be2 11. Qh3 Qxe4 (or 11. Qg3 Nxe4) Black has got an overwhelming position.

r3k2N/ppp1qBpp/5n2/2b5/3nP1b1/8/PPP2PPP/.x: White removed their bishop from the danger with a check to Black's king.

r4k1N/ppp1qBpp/5n2/2b5/3nP3/3Q4/PPP1bPPP.x: Black has attacked White's queen. If the queen goes to h3, Black would take the e4 pawn with their queen, if White's queen goes to e2, the e4 pawn would be captured by a knight.

r4k1N/ppp1qBpp/5n2/2b5/3nP1b1/5P2/PPP3PP.x: This move looks logical: it saved White's queen, attacked the bishop on g4 and defended the e4 pawn, but Black loses because of the shocking 10... Nxe4!. The knight obviously cannot be captured, but if White captures the bishop, after 11... Ng3+ White will lose.

r4k1N/ppp1qBpp/8/2b5/3nn1b1/5P2/PPP3PP/R.x: Black bravely sacrifices the bishop on g4 for the e file to be opened. Accepting the sacrifice would be a fatal error because of the move 11... Ng3+! with a forced mate in 6. It's much better to go 11. Be3! and after the same 11... Ng3 either the bishop on e3 or the rook on h1 will be captured the next move.

r4k1N/ppp1qBpp/8/2b5/3nn1b1/4BP2/PPP3PP/.x:
The best attempt for Black to hold the position. But a simple move 11... Ng3 makes Black's victory inevitable. The knight obviously cannot be captured as after 12... Qxe3+ 13. Kf1 Nxf3+! Black aren't able to defend from the checkmate on f2.

If White try to defend their bishop with the move 12. Qd2, Black wouldn't take the rook on h1 but instead go 12... Nxf3+! 13. gxf3 Bxe3 White are forced to sacrifice their queen as there are no other good moves against 14... Bf4+.

r4k1N/ppp1qBpp/8/2b5/3nn1P1/8/PPP3PP/RNB.x:
After this move Black's victory is inevitable after the move 11... Ng3+!

12. Kf2 is a worse option as after 12... Ndf5+! White has to sacrifice a queen and the bishop and get checkmated on e3 with the queen.

12. Kd2 is a better option, but it doesn't save the game. Here Black out of nowhere goes 12... Nb3+!!, and after 13. cxb3 (13. axb3 leads to 13... Qe3#) Black is the whole 12 points of material down, but after 13... Rd8+ 14. Kc3 Bb4+ 15. Kc2 Qe4+ 16. Qd3 Qxd3# White loses.

r3k2N/ppp1q1pp/8/2bn4/3nP1b1/3Q4/PPP2PPP.x: Black has just captured an undefended bishop on d5. Black's ideas of either 10... Nb4 and 11..Nbxc2 or 10... Be2 and 11... Qxe4 are unstoppable. If White goes 10. Nc3, Black will trade off the knights and then go 11... 0-0-0!.

r3k2N/ppp1q1pp/5n2/2bB4/3nP1b1/5P2/PPP3P.x: This move looks logical: it saved White's queen from being attacked and also threatened the attacking piece. But here Black can simply take the bishop on d5 as the bishop on g4 is innocent (if the e4 pawn dies, White's king will do the same).

r3k2N/ppp1q1pp/8/2bn4/3nP1b1/2P2P2/PP4PP.x: This is the most tempting move for White: kicking a very active Black piece and unleashing the attack on the knight on d5 if the d4 knight runs away. But instead of moving away Black goes 10... Nxf3!! and after that White is likely to end the game being 13 material points up but with the king on a5.

r3k2N/ppp1q1pp/8/2bn4/4P1b1/2P2n2/PP4PP/.x: From here White is busted. Taking the knight with the queen would result in losing the queen, if the knight is taken by the pawn, after 11... Qh4! White's king will do a long race and get checkmated on a5 while White would be up 13 points of material.

r1b1k1nN/ppp1q1pp/8/2bp4/2BnP3/8/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. d4/4...Nxd4/5. Nxe5/5...Qe7/6. Nxf7/6...d5/7. Nxh8
r1b1k1nN/ppp1q1pp/8/2bp4/2BnP3/8/PPP2PPP.x:
One move earlier Black declined a pawn advantage in the sake of getting a giant piece activity, but in this position Black already takes the pawn on e4. Now a few things can happen:

8. Kf1 leads to 8... dxc4 and 9... Qxc2, so this isn't the best option, even with the fact of this move being suggested by a computer.

8. Be2 is a more popular and intuitive move, but after 8... Bg4 9. f3 Bxf3!! 10. gxf3 Nxf3+ 11. Kf1 Nd2+ 12. Ke1 Nxb1 13. Rxb1 Qxh1+ 14. Kd2 Qxh2 Black is victorious.

8. Be3?? is a very bad option because after 8... Nxc2+ 9. Kd2 Bxe3+ 10. fxe3 dxc4 either a rook on a1 or a rook on h1 will be captured.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/2BnP3/5N2/PPPP1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/2BnP3/5N2/PPPP1P.x:
Black violates an opening principle by moving his knight again. Black hopes to tempt White into taking the unprotected e5 pawn.

4. Nxe5?? falls into Black's trap. After 4...Qg5, forking White's knight the g2 pawn, White is in dire trouble. If White attempts to save the knight, (5. Nxf7?? Qxg2) then White has to give up the rook instead. If they try to hold onto their rook, then they must give up their queen or get mated. (6. Rf1 Qxe4+ 7. Qe2 (7. Be2? Nf3#) 7...Nxe2) 5. Bxf7+ is the only way to stay in the game.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/2BNP3/8/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4/4. Nxd4
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/2BNP3/8/PPPP1PPP.x: Instead of accepting the gambitted pawn, white declines it and instead trades the knights in the center.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4N3/2BnP3/8/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4/4. Nxe5
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4N3/2BnP3/8/PPPP1PPP.x:
This move looks natural, but it is a bad move as there is a strong double attack. It turns out that Black's pawn on e5 wasn't free.

After 4...Qg5!, both e5 and g2 are attacked by the queen. White is in a lot of trouble and has to give up a knight to have a playable game with either 5. Bxf7+ or 5. O-O, both with a better position for Black.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4N1q1/2BnP3/8/PPPP1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4/4. Nxe5/4...Qg5
r1b1kbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4N1q1/2BnP3/8/PPPP1P.x:
Accepting the gambit was a mistake, as Black now shows with the accurate 4...Qg5.

Attempting to hold on to the knight with 5. Nxf7?? will result in 5...Qxg2!, in which White will lose either the rook, attempt to hold on to the rook and lose the queen with 6. Rf1 Qxe4+, or get checkmated by attempting to keep both the rook and the queen with 7. Be2 Nf3#.

Better for White is 5. Bxf7+, which loses a piece for two pawns but keeps White in the game.

/5. O-O/ is another possible option. White castles and defends g2 while giving away the e5 knight to try and get development as compensation for the lost knight.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/6q1/2BnP3/8/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4/4. Nxe5/4...Qg5/5. Nxf7
r1b1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/6q1/2BnP3/8/PPPP1PPP.x: Here 5. Nxf7?? is a blunder. White would be better off losing their knight for two pawns with 5. Bxf7+, but Nxf7 loses a major piece or the game to 5...Qxg2.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/2BnP3/8/PPPP1PqP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4/4. Nxe5/4...Qg5/5. Nxf7/5...Qxg2
r1b1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/2BnP3/8/PPPP1PqP/R.x: Qxg2 is the accurate followup and the dream of Blackburne Shilling Gambit players. White has to give away a major piece to stop checkmate.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/2BnP3/8/PPPP1PqP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4/4. Nxe5/4...Qg5/5. Nxf7/5...Qxg2/6. Rf1
r1b1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/2BnP3/8/PPPP1PqP/R.x:
Rf1 seems like a defense to the gambit, but Black can play 6...Qxe4+ and White must sacrifice their queen or allow checkmate.

Better was 6. Ng5, which gives away the rook but moves the knight to safety and protects the e4-pawn. After 6...Qxh1+ White can play 7. Bf1.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/2Bnq3/8/PPPP1P1P/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4/4. Nxe5/4...Qg5/5. Nxf7/5...Qxg2/6. Rf1/6...Qxe4
r1b1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/2Bnq3/8/PPPP1P1P/R.x:
White is completely lost. Black plays 6...Qxe4+, which allows for two options.

The worse of the two options doesn't seem the worst, but 7. Be2? allows the smothered mate (7...Nf3#) where the bishop is pinned.

Therefore White must give away the queen with 7. Qe2 and play on without that queen.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/3nq3/8/PPPPBP1P/RN.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4/4. Nxe5/4...Qg5/5. Nxf7/5...Qxg2/6. Rf1/6...Qxe4/7. Be2
r1b1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/3nq3/8/PPPPBP1P/RN.x:
The worst of the two legal moves, but White was losing anyway.

Black can immediately win the game with 7...Nf3#.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4N1q1/2BnP3/8/PPPP1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4/4. Nxe5/4...Qg5/5. O-O
r1b1kbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4N1q1/2BnP3/8/PPPP1P.x:
White resists the temptation to take the 'free' pawn on f7 but instead calmly castles, sacrificing their e5 knight while defending g2 and relocating their king to safety.

5...Qxe5 is obviously the best move. Black captures the free knight and is now up 2 points of material, but they are only slightly better as White will get developmental compensation after 6. c3 followed by 7. d4.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.x:
With 3...Nf6, Black develops a knight and attacks the e4-pawn, getting one step closer to castling.

White has several ways to proceed from this position: defend the e-pawn, usually with 4. d3, attack f7 with the aggressive 4. Ng5 (taking advantage of the fact that Black's move 3...Nf6 blocked the queen's control of the g5-square), or sacrifice the pawn for an open centre and swift attack.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/2N2N2/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Bc4
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/2N2N2/.x:
White combines the typical Italian game bishop placement, Bc4, with the four knights game. This position arises most commonly in amateur games, from either the four knights or Italian games.

White seems to have made reasonable developing moves and is ready to castle. Their bishop on c4 targets f7 and White is ready to castle. However, Black has a tactical trick (4...Nxe4!) which has made masters shun away from this position.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p1N1/2B1P3/8/PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p1N1/2B1P3/8/PP.x:
4. Ng5!? is a sideline but the most common amateur move. This Romantic move is an attack on f7 with the bishop and knight, taking advantage of the fact that Black gave up control of g5 and cannot castle yet. However, it is unprincipled to attack before having finished development and Black equalises with best play.

Black needs to defend f7: otherwise, as in the common beginner blunder, 4...h6?? 5. Nxf7 Qe7 6. Nxh8, Black gets the house. If Black thinks to counter-attack instead, 4...Nxe4?, the Ponziani-Steinitz gambit, fails to 5. Bxf7+! Ke7 6. d4.

r1bqk2r/pppp1Npp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/8/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...Bc5/5. Nxf7
r1bqk2r/pppp1Npp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/8/PPP.x: White managed to fork Black's queen and rook as usual in the Fried Liver Attack, only to get hit by the shocking sacrifice 5...Bxf2+.

r1bqk2r/pppp1Npp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/8/PPPP1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...Bc5/5. Nxf7/5...Bxf2
r1bqk2r/pppp1Npp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/8/PPPP1.x:
The main idea of the Traxler Counterattack. Ignoring White's fork, Black aims to gain tons of space on the board and move all their pieces out to attack the wide open king. Impressively, Black will be able to gain their lost material if played correctly.

White can capture with Kxf2, but Black more easily be able to launch a counterattack, starting with Nxe4+. Thus experienced players generally prefer Kf1.

r1bqk2r/pppp1Npp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/8/PPPP1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...Bc5/5. Nxf7/5...Bxf2/6. Kf1
r1bqk2r/pppp1Npp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/8/PPPP1.x:
The bishop sacrifice is declined, not allowing Nxe4 with check. The position is now very unclear and both sides must play precisely to maintain their initiative. In addition, a fight for the center will likely play a big factor in the game for the next couple of moves.

Black should save their queen with its only move: 6...Qe7.

r1b1k2r/ppppqNpp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/8/PPPP1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...Bc5/5. Nxf7/5...Bxf2/6. Kf1/6...Qe7
r1b1k2r/ppppqNpp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/8/PPPP1.x: White must now take their one and only opportunity to complete their fork and capture the rook before the game gains some complications. Otherwise Black will set up a very dangerous file with Rf8 aiming down at the king.

r1b1k2N/ppppq1pp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/8/PPPP1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...Bc5/5. Nxf7/5...Bxf2/6. Kf1/6...Qe7/7. Nxh8
r1b1k2N/ppppq1pp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/8/PPPP1.x:
At the moment, White has a deceivingly uncoordinated attack on the Black king, but things can go very wrong very fast if Black allows moves like Bf7+ or Qh5+, preventing the Black king from ever castling to safety. For this reason, Black cannot afford a tempo moving their f2 bishop away or capturing with Nxe4. Instead, their best move is to cut off White's bishop with the move 7...d5.

This is not simply a free pawn, and leads to interesting offensive opportunities for Black.

r1b1k2N/ppp1q1pp/2n2n2/3pp3/2B1P3/8/PPPP.x:
There are two main moves for White in this position.

The first is 8. exd5, gaining a pawn but allowing Black to create an attack on the kingside.
The second is 8. Kxf2, trading the bishops in hopes of moving the king to relative safety on g1.

It should be noted that 8. Bxd5 is a mistake because Bg4 traps White's queen!

Black should now capture with 8...dxc4. A common mistake is Nxe4+ first, but after Kf1, White will be able to safely trade queens and play the game with a comfortable position.

After dxc4, Black will move out all of their pieces in an attempt to checkmate. However, with their deficit in material and solid defense by White, Black cannot force a win. They do, however, have many ways to attain a perpetual check and draw. (See the example game below.)

One trick White should be aware of is Black's potential knight sacrifice on e4. For example, after 9. d3 Bg4 10. Qd2, Black has 10...Nxe4!? because after 11. dxe4 Qh4+ 12. Kg1, 12...Rd8 threatens the dangerous Rd1 if the queen moves.

r1b1k2N/ppp1q1pp/2n2n2/3Pp3/2B5/8/PPPP1b.x:
This is the best way for White to maintain a slight advantage. However, they must play the precise, correct moves in order to deter Black's many threats. This is because despite White's huge material advantage, they have barely any pieces developed while Black has space for both of their bishops, knights, and queen.

The first of Black's threats comes after 8...Nd4, giving the White queen no safe squares to move to.

r1b1k2N/ppp1q1pp/5n2/3Pp3/2Bn4/8/PPPP1bP.x:
If it were Black's turn right now, they would love to play Bg4 to effectively trap White's queen.

There are two common mistakes when dealing with this threat. One is 9. Kxf2, but Black still has 9...Bg4!. If 10. Qe1, Black has 10...Nxc2 forking the rook and queen. If 10. Qf1, Black has the devastating Ne4+; Kg1 is White's best response and Ne2+ loses the queen. 10. Qg1 is somehow worse, giving Black checkmate in 4 moves.

The other mistake is 9. c3, still allowing 9...Bg4! because after 10. Qa4+ Nd7 11. cxd4 Bxd4, White faces the unavoidable Qf6+, with too many threats to deal with. 11. Kxf2 similarly deals with the same issue of Qh4+.

r1b1k2N/ppp1q1pp/3P1n2/4p3/2Bn4/8/PPPP1b.x: Taking with 9...cxd6 blocks Black's queen in and White can safely play 10. Kxf2. Thus 9...Qxd6 is the stronger move.

r1b1k2N/ppp3pp/3q1n2/4p3/2Bn4/8/PPPP1bPP.x:
At this point, White often prefers to play 10. Nf7. After 10...Qc5 11. d3, Black will be able to launch a strong attack on the White king, especially with an activated bishop pair after Bg4. White's strategy involves moving their king to safety on g1 at one point and trading off material. With perfect defense, Black can regain their disadvantage in material, but there is no forced checkmate.

10. c3 can also be played first with 10...Bg4 11. Nf7 but this is less concrete and likely favors Black. Additionally, 10...Bg4 11.Qa4+ leads to a perpetual check and draw with best play (see below).

r1bqk2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B1n3/8/PPPP1KP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...Bc5/5. Nxf7/5...Bxf2/6. Kxf2/6...Nxe4
r1bqk2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B1n3/8/PPPP1KP.x: Black plans to bring their queen out with Qh4 next move. To avoid any danger and move out of the open file, White has two sensible options: Kg1 and Ke3.

r1bqk2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B1n3/4K3/PPPP2.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...Bc5/5. Nxf7/5...Bxf2/6. Kxf2/6...Nxe4/7. Ke3
r1bqk2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B1n3/4K3/PPPP2.x:
This is the move which modern chess engines prefer.

Black continues their plan with Qh4.

r1b1k2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B1n2q/4K3/PPPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...Bc5/5. Nxf7/5...Bxf2/6. Kxf2/6...Nxe4/7. Ke3/7...Qh4
r1b1k2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B1n2q/4K3/PPPP.x: White must prevent Qf4+, leading to a swift checkmate. The only feasible option is 8. g3.

r1b1k2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B1n2q/4K1P1/PP.x: The Black queen and knight are double attacked. However, Black has Nxg3, opening a discovery attack on the c4 bishop.

r1b1k2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B4q/4K1n1/PPPP.x: White must capture back. A move like Nxh8 leads to mate in 2.

r1b1k2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B4q/4K1P1/PPPP.x: Black must be careful here. If 9...Qxc4, 10. Nxh8 and Black runs out of steam. If 9...Qxg3+, 10. Qf3 and the queens are traded. Therefore, 9...Qd4+ must be played first.

r1b1k2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2Bq4/4K1P1/PPPP.x: Black cannot be allowed to capture the c4 bishop with check so 10. Kf3 is the only move.

r1b1k2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2Bq4/5KP1/PPPP4.x: Here, Black's plan is to castle, targeting the knight, followed by d5, cutting off the bishop from the knight. It is actually impossible to save both minor pieces, and Black appears to be closing in on gaining back their -4 material advantage.

r1b2rk1/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2Bq4/5KP1/PPPP4.x: White must play 11. Rh4 to prevent d5 and Black's numerous checkmate threats.

r1b2rk1/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2Bq3R/5KP1/PPPP.x: Black can fortunately gain a tempo and protect their queen with 11...e4 here.

r1b2rk1/pppp1Npp/2n5/8/2Bqp2R/5KP1/PPPP4.x:
After Kg2, Black can finally capture with Qxc4 and the Traxler Counterattack is proved to have merit. Black has an obvious attack on the White king but White can finally start developing their pieces, starting with moving their f7 knight back.

Finally, it should be noted that 12. Rxe4 is a mistake because after 12...Ne5+ 13. Rxe5 Qxc4, White has no way to defend their knight.

r1b1k2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B1n2q/8/PPPP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...Bc5/5. Nxf7/5...Bxf2/6. Kxf2/6...Nxe4/7. Kg1/7...Qh4
r1b1k2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B1n2q/8/PPPP2P.x:
Checkmate with Qf2 is threatened. Surprisingly, the three strongest defenses, Qe2, g3, and h3 all give Black a perpetual draw (see below).

:*8. Qe2 Nd4 9. Qe3 Nxc2 10. Qe2 Nd4 11. Qe3 Nc2
:*8. g3 Nxg3 9. Nxh8 Nd4 10. hxg3 Qxg3+ 11. Kf1 Qf4+ 12. Kg2 Qg5+ 13. Kf1 Qf4+
:*8. h3 d5 9. Bxd5 Qf2+ 10. Kh2 Qg3+ 11. Kg1 Qf2+

This makes 8. Qf3 White's most popular move, although Black gains a strong initiative after Rf8 and with plans of rerouting their knight to g4.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p1N1/2BPP3/8/P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...Bc5/5. d4
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p1N1/2BPP3/8/P.x:
Rather than capturing the undefended f-pawn, White plays it safe and attacks the bishop while preventing the idea of Bxf2+.

Moving away the bishop is a mistake because after Nxf7, White captures a free rook and Black has no counterplay without the bishop sacrifice.

Capturing the d-pawn with the pawn or knight will similarly prevent the bishop sacrifice.

Another mistake is if Black captures with the bishop (5...Bxd4) and goes for the sacrifice anyway (6. Nxf7 Bxf2+). The difference between this position and if 5. d4 Bxd4 was never played is that White's queen and dark-squared bishop can protect key squares from Black's fierce counterattack.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/2bBp1N1/3PP3/8/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...Bc5/5. d4/5...d5/6. Bxd5
r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/2bBp1N1/3PP3/8/PPP.x:
Here Black can capture with Nxd5 and neutralize White's threat. Black is one pawn down but still has attacking chances, after 7. dxc5 Ndb4, for example.

Black can also try Nxd4!? here, allowing 7. Nxf7 because after 7...Qe7 8. Nxh8 sacrificing the rook, 8...Bg4! 9. Qd2 Nxd5 10. exd5 (trading the bishop for the knight) and 10...Bf5, the fork on c2 is inevitable and Black will win back the rook. However, if White plays 7. Bxf7 instead, Black will find themself down a pawn in an uncomfortable, albeit not losing, position.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/3np1N1/2B1P3/8/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...Nd5

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p1N1/2B1n3/8/PPPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...Nxe4
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p1N1/2B1n3/8/PPPP.x:
Not the best move for Black. Ignoring the threat of White's position, they grab the e-pawn. Black may imagine they are playing a centre fork trick: if 5. Nxe4? d5! forks the knight and bishop.

However, White can now capture Black's unprotected f-pawn with check: 5. Bxf7+ Ke7 6. d4! and Black cannot yet take on g5 without losing his queen.

5. Nxf7? is a mistake, as after 5...Qh4 Black gains an advantage even against White's best defence.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3pp1N1/2B1P3/8/PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...d5
r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3pp1N1/2B1P3/8/PP.x:
This is a pawn sacrifice, but it is necessary for Black to defang White's attack on f7.

White must capture the pawn, 5. exd5.

Any other move loses material, for instance retreating the bishop 5. Bb3? Nxe4!.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3Pp1N1/2B5/8/PPPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...d5/5. exd5
r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3Pp1N1/2B5/8/PPPP.x:
Taking the pawn is an automatic move as other moves lose material.

Black has a selection of interesting moves leading to diverse tactical positions.

The classical way to play, and one of the most popular continuations in amateur games, is 5...Nxd5?!. However, this is now known to be inferior. It allows 6. Nxf7+!, an audacious knight sacrifice known as the fried liver where Black's king is hounded into the centre of the board, or 6. d4, the Lolli attack and Bobby Fischer's preferred line.

r1bqkb1r/ppp1nppp/5n2/3Pp1N1/2B5/8/PPPP1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...d5/5. exd5/5...Ne7
r1bqkb1r/ppp1nppp/5n2/3Pp1N1/2B5/8/PPPP1.x:
Black retreats their knight and brings another attacker to the d-pawn.

White is very happy to play 6. Nc3 to defend the pawn.

A sharper line is 6. d4. Were White to play 6. d6? to open up the attack on f7 again, Black would be able to play 6...Ned5, and the knight, supported by the other one, obstructs the bishop's attack. Including 6. d4 first however means that if 6...exd4? 7. d6 Nebd5, White has 8. Qe2+, preventing Black's king from defending f7. If 6...Nxd6? 7. dxe5! with tempo.

r1bqkb1r/p1p2ppp/2n2n2/1p1Pp1N1/2B5/8/PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...d5/5. exd5/5...b5
r1bqkb1r/p1p2ppp/2n2n2/1p1Pp1N1/2B5/8/PP.x:
Black offers a pawn to deflect the bishop from control of d5 and pressure of f7, so that they may retake on d4 with the queen.

If White accepts the sacrifice, 6. Bxb5?!, this works out well for Black. 6...Qxd5 and both White's bishop and the g2-pawn are under attack.

If White trades, 6. dxc6?! bxc4, Black has equalised.

6. Bf1! is the surprising refutation. Un-developing the bishop guards g2, and though Black may retake the pawn with their queen, they'd be hit by Nc3 with tempo (6...Qxd5 7. Nc3), so the main line involves 6...Nd4 as in the Fritz variation.

r1bqkb1r/p1p2ppp/2n2n2/1p1Pp1N1/8/8/PPPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...d5/5. exd5/5...b5/6. Bf1
r1bqkb1r/p1p2ppp/2n2n2/1p1Pp1N1/8/8/PPPP.x:
6. Bf1! is a surprising move that un-develops the Bishop, but by guarding the g2 pawn with the bishop the threat of ...Qxd5 is nullified.

Now if 6...Qxd5?!, White can calmly answer 7. Nc3 with tempo, and once Black's queen is driven from the a8-h1 diagonal, e.g. after 7...Qc5, White can then snap up the pawn after all, 8. Bxb5!, and Black has no threats.

Though 6...Qxd5 may be off the table, Black's knight is still en prise and this must be resolved.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. c3/3...Nf6/4. Bc4
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/.x:
White leaves their e4-pawn undefended. This unsound gambit can easily be punished by Black if they know what they're doing. It may arise from the Ponziani opening or from the Italian game by transposition.

4...Bc5!? transposes into the classical variation of the Italian Game. This is the most common move in amateur play, but fails to punish White's inaccurate move order.

4...Nxe4 accepts the gambit. After 5. O-O!? d5! (gaining tempo on the bishop) 6. Bb5 Bd6 (defending e5) White is down a pawn for no compensation. Best is 5. Bd5 (attacking the knight) Nf6 (5...f5?! 6. d4 Nf6 7. Bxc6 dxc6 8. Nxe5 ) 6. Bxc6 dxc6 7. Nxe5 recovers the material, but Black is for choice with easier development.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2BPP3/5N2/PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. d4
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2BPP3/5N2/PP.x:
This aggressive move opens the queen's bishop for development while ignoring the attack on e4. Instead, White counterattacks Black's pawn. Black has their choice of pawns to capture.

4...exd4 is best, transposing into a line in the Scotch gambit. The usual continuation is 5. e5, and Black's knight is kicked to e4 either immediately, 5...Ne4, or after the tricky in-between move 5...d5 6. Bb5 Ne4 where Black first supports e4 with the d-pawn with tempo.

4....d6, simply defending the e-pawn, declines the transposition. White can answer 5. dxe5 dxe5 6. Qxd8+ Nxd8 7. Nxe5 Nxe4 and enter a queen-less middle game, or 5. d5, taking space and kicking away Black's knight.

r2qkbnr/ppp2ppp/2np4/4p3/2B1P1b1/2N2N2/P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...d6/4. Nc3/4...Bg4
r2qkbnr/ppp2ppp/2np4/4p3/2B1P1b1/2N2N2/P.x:
The White knight is somewhat pinned, however allows for the Legal Trap if White 'sacrifices' their queen with 5. Nxe5.

More sound, however, is first playing 5. h3. If Black mistakenly tries to maintain their pin with 5...Bh5, White can freely attempt Legal's Trap with 6. Nxe5! without worry of being down on material if Black captures their knight.

Legal's trap is named after the French player Sire de Legall, one of the best players of the 1700s. Although 5. Nxe5 is a losing move, as it leaves White's knight hanging, a naive opponent might capture White's queen with 5...Bxd1??. This leads to a mate in 2 for White (6. Bxf7+! Ke7 7. Nd5#).

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPPBP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Be2
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPPBP.x:
The Tayler Opening is a timid and less common response to 2...Nc6. Instead of going for an Italian, Ruy Lopez or Scotch, White chooses a quiet developing move that prepares castling kingside.

Black has multiple responses to this, such as:

* 3...Nf6, developing the knight and hitting the e4 pawn.
* 3...Bc5?, developing the bishop to an active square while eyeing f2, but allowing 4. Nxe5!
* 3...d6, reinforcing e5 even more and opening up the c8 bishop.
* 3...d5, aggressively attacking the center and opening the c8 bishop.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/4P3/2N2N2/PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Bc5
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/4P3/2N2N2/PP.x: Black chooses to develop their bishop instead of developing their knight with 3...Nf6. Now, White can play 4. Nxe5, the centre fork trick. Black's knight was not really defending the e5 pawn because after 4...Nxe5 5. d4! wins back the material with a fork. Black isn't down material, but it's a small positional mistake.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/3Np3/4P3/5N2/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Nd5
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/3Np3/4P3/5N2/PPP.x:
This is a tactical sideline. White undefends their e4 pawn.

If Black accepts the gambit, 4...Nxe4, the line 5. d4 exd4 6. Bd3 has transposed into a line in the Belgrade gambit.

This is a cunning move-order trick: through transposition, White has reached the same position as in the Belgrade gambit (after 4. d4 exd4 5. Nd5) where Black has played 5...Nxe4!? instead of the more critical 5...Nb4! or the main line 5...Be7, a quiet move that avoids complications.

In this line, White gives up two pawns but gets compensation in the form of activity and sets some traps for the unwary.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4N3/4P3/2N5/PPPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Nxe5
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4N3/4P3/2N5/PPPP.x:
White eliminates Black's central pawn, but gives up their knight to do so. The Halloween gambit is an offbeat line where White sacrifices their knight so they can expand in the centre with tempo. The gambit is considered to be unsound and is uncommon in tournament chess, but it is tricky and aggressive and affords White lots of practical chances.

4...Nxe5, accepting the gambit, is almost always played and is the most critical line. Generally, Black can choose to either hold on to as much material as possible or return the material for a more straightforward game. After White plays 5. d4 with tempo, Black has the choice of where to retreat their knight: 5...Ng6 or 5...Nc6.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/4N3/4n3/2N5/PPPP1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Nxe5/4...Nxe4
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/4N3/4n3/2N5/PPPP1P.x:
Black unusually declines the gambit and tries a flipped version of the Halloween Attack to counter White's own Halloween Attack. Although this recovers the pawn, it ignores the hanging knight and gives White back a drawish position, with higher winning chances for White.

There are usually 2 main moves White will most commonly try: 5. Nxc6, taking the black c6 knight and ignoring the hanging black e4 knight, and 5. Nxe4, taking the hanging black e4 knight, ignoring the hanging white knight on e5.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/3PP3/2N2N2/P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. d4
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/3PP3/2N2N2/P.x:
The Scotch variation of the four knights is a confrontational approach to remove the e5 pawn, opening the centre and preparing to develop White's remaining pieces. This resembles the Scotch game, 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4.

After 4...exd4, White may retake the pawn with 5. Nxd4 and the game transposes to the "normal" Scotch game after 5...Bb4 6. Nxc6 bxc6 7. Bd3. Alternatively, White has the option of 5. Nd5, the sharp Belgrade gambit.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/3pP3/2N2N2/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. d4/4...exd4
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/3pP3/2N2N2/PPP.x: Black accepts the d4-pawn. Unlike in the Scotch game (1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4), taking the d4-pawn comes with tempo on White's knight. White must retake the pawn or move the knight to avoid losing material.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/3N4/3pP3/5N2/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. d4/4...exd4/5. Nd5
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/3N4/3pP3/5N2/PPP.x:
White saves their knight but undefends their e4 pawn. This gambit is not completely sound and with best play Black equalises.

White is usually happy to see Black accept the free material, 5...Nxe4. A sharp but unsound idea is 6. Qe2!? (pinning the knight) f5 7. Ng5, where the most common amateur continuation is 7...Be7?? 8. Nxe4 fxe4 9. Qxe4 O-O 10. Bd3 , and White has the initiative and a strong attack. The modern move is 5...Bd3.

The main line is 5...Be7, a modest developing move that avoids complications and prepares to castle. White can snap up the bishop pair here but Black is better.

5...Nb4, threatening ...Nxd5, is the most testing move.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. d4/4...exd4/5. Nxd4
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP2P.x:
White recovers the pawn.

It is inaccurate for Black to initiate the trade of knights. 5...Nxd4?! 6. Qxd4 and White stands better: their queen is activated and Black cannot gain tempo on it. On the other hand, White is very happy to trade the knights on c6 with tempo on Black's queen, and does so in several lines.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/4P1P1/2N2N2/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. g4
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/4P1P1/2N2N2/.x:
* 4...Nxg4 Black accepts the pawn sacrifice.After 5. Rg1 Nf6 6. d4 exd4 7. Nxd4 White has compensation for the sacrificed pawn.
* 4...d5 strong move. Black fights for the center.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1p1p/2n3p1/3N4/3pP3/5N2/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...g6/4. d4/4...exd4/5. Nd5
r1bqkbnr/pppp1p1p/2n3p1/3N4/3pP3/5N2/PPP.x: The move order 4. d4 exd4 5. Nd5 after 3...g6 is the Steinitz-Rosenthal Variation and is a line for White which sacrifices a pawn for aggressive play in the center and active development.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4N3/4P3/8/PPPP1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nc6
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4N3/4P3/8/PPPP1P.x: Rather than try to recover the pawn (as in 3...d6 4. Nf3 Nxe4), Black invites White to trade knights. Black's plan after 4. Nxc6 is to take back with the d pawn, opening lines for their bishop and queen. They have entered the dubious but dangerous Stafford gambit.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4n3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nxe5/3...Nxe5
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4n3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.x:
Black captures the free knight and gains a big material advantage. However, they might still get caught by surprise if they do not focus or play too passively.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nxe5 Nxe5

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4n3/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nxe5/3...Nxe5/4. d4
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4n3/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.x:
White takes over the centre with tempo on Black's knight.

Black's knight has two places to go, 4...Ng6 or 4...Nc6, where after 5. d5 Ne5 6. f4, the knight ends up on g6 after all.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/1P2P3/5N2/P1PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. b4
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/1P2P3/5N2/P1PP.x:
An eccentric and rare reply where White offers up their b pawn to Black. The Pachman wing gambit is unsound and White does not get satisfactory compensation.

One plan is to win the e4 pawn: if Black declines (e.g. 3...Nf6?), White can kick the knight from defence of the e5 with 4. b5 then play 5. Nxe5. Alternatively, if Black accepts with 3...Nxb4?, White can take 4. Nxe5. The game is at best even.

However, most commonly and most critically Black accepts with 3...Bxb4, developing their bishop.

From there White may intend:

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/2P2N2/PP1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. c3
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/2P2N2/PP1P.x:
3. c3 is the Ponziani opening. White announces they are determined to achieve 4. d4. It also opens up a diagonal allowing the queen to reach a4. The cost of c3, supporting d4, is that Nc3 is unavailable.

By not having played Nc3, White's e4 pawn is loose. The strongest replies for Black therefore are those that target e4: either 3...Nf6 or 3...d5. After a move like 3...d6 or 3...Bc5? (a common amateur mistake), White plays 4. d4 and secures their two pawn centre with smug satisfaction.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/4P3/2P2N2/PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. c3/3...Nf6
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/4P3/2P2N2/PP.x:
3...Nf6, the Jaenisch counterattack, is Black's most popular retort to the Ponziani and most serious alternative to 3...d5. Nf6 targets White's e4 pawn, taking advantage of the fact that White cannot play Nc3 to defend it.

White may continue with 4. d4. This offers Black their choice of central pawns to take (4...Nxe4 or 4...exd4), after which White intends to push their other pawn to gain tempo and recover the pawn.

4. d3 to defend e4 is playable, but leaves White's pawn on c3 looking out of place and allows Black to take the centre with 4...d5. No other reply for White seems credible.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/3PP3/2P2N2/P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. c3/3...Nf6/4. d4
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/3PP3/2P2N2/P.x: With 4. d4, White ignores the attack on the e-pawn and counterattacks Black's central pawn on e5. Black's best moves are to choose a central pawn to capture, 4...exd4 or 4...Nxe4, though White has ways to recover the pawn. 4...d5 is also playable.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/3Pn3/2P2N2/PP3.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. c3/3...Nf6/4. d4/4...Nxe4
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/3Pn3/2P2N2/PP3.x: 4...Nxe4 takes White's undefended e4 pawn. This move is the main continuation at higher levels. Black's knight on e4 also pressures White's f2 pawn, which will become a serious threat if Black can get their bishop to c5. How White recovers their pawn with or without allowing ...Bc5 determines how the game proceeds.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/3Pn3/2PB1N2/PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. c3/3...Nf6/4. d4/4...Nxe4/5. Bd3
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/3Pn3/2PB1N2/PP.x:
White threatens Black's centralised knight.

Though Black can just defend it with 5...d4, the real point of this move is to develop White's kingside with tempo. This means that White can take the e5-pawn 6. Nxe5 Nxe5 7. dxe5, recovering the material, and answer 7...Bc5 (threatening to take on f2) with 8. O-O. Contrast with the line 5. Nxe5?! Nxe5 6. dxe5?? Bc5, where the threat to f2 is unstoppable.

5...Nf6?! allows 6. dxe5 to recover the pawn while gaining tempo on the knight.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/3Pp3/4n3/2P2N2/PP3.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. c3/3...Nf6/4. d4/4...Nxe4/5. d5
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/3Pp3/4n3/2P2N2/PP3.x:
White attacks Black's c6 knight. Black has two main options; going into a calmer continuation with 5...Ne7, saving the knight; or going into the extremely violent Vukovic Gambit with 5...Bc5!!, focusing on piece development with an attack on f2.

5...Ne7 is the mainline. This saves Black's knight but undefends e5, and White can recover the pawn. After 6. Nxe5, 6...d6?? falls into a common trap: 7. Bb5+, and Black cannot wrest control over the d7 and c6 squares without positional and material losses. Instead, Black redeploys the knight to g6, opening up bishop and the h file for their rook. 6...Ng6 7. Nxg6 hxg6.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/2bPp3/4n3/2P2N2/PP3.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. c3/3...Nf6/4. d4/4...Nxe4/5. d5/5...Bc5
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/2bPp3/4n3/2P2N2/PP3.x:
Black gambits their knight on c6 with 5...Bc5, the Vuković gambit or Fraser defence. Black's c5 bishop and e4 knight both target White's f2 pawn.

The Vuković gambit is so bloodthirsty that if Frankenstein and Dracula ever take a break from the Vienna game, expect to see them here. Accepting the gambit, 6. dxc6, is the engine recommendation but perilous. With best play from both sides, Black maintains a small edge by engine but huge success in practice.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/3pp3/4P3/2P2N2/PP1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. c3/3...d5
r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/3pp3/4P3/2P2N2/PP1P.x:
With 3...d5 Black threatens ...dxe4, taking advantage of the fact that, if 4. exd5 Qxd5, Nc3 is not an option to chase the queen away because White has played c3. 3...d5 is most chess engines' preferred move and the second most common response to the Ponziani by masters, behind the Jaenisch Counterattack with 3...Nf6.

Here 4. d4? would be a mistake, as White's e pawn is hanging. After 4...dxe4 5. Nxe5 Nxe5 6. dxe5 Qxd1+ 7. Kxd1 ∓, White's king is stranded in the centre and Black has the initiative.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/3pp3/Q3P3/2P2N2/PP1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. c3/3...d5/4. Qa4
r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/3pp3/Q3P3/2P2N2/PP1.x:
By pinning Black's knight on c6 to their king, 4. Qa4 undefends Black's e pawn and threatens Nxe5.

Were Black to ignore the threat and counterattack instead, 4... dxe4? 5. Nxe5! (threatens Nxc6 bxc6 Qxc6 winning at least one pawn) Qd6 6. Nxc6 bxc6 7. Qxe4+ wins a pawn.

Therefore Black must protect the e5 pawn. Their choices are:

4...Bd7, the Caro gambit, eliminates the pin. This protects the e pawn but, by obstructing queen's vision of d5, gives up Black's d pawn. After 5. exd5 Nd4 (discovered attack on the queen) 6. Qd1 Nxf3+ 7. Qxf3 Black has equalised.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2np4/4p3/4P3/2P2N2/PP1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. c3/3...d6
r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2np4/4p3/4P3/2P2N2/PP1P.x:
3...d6!? is a passive reply. It reinforces Black's e pawn, but there was not much threat to it and it hems in Black's dark square bishop. Black essentially passes a turn and allows White 4. d4, more space and easy development. White can even choose to push d5, kicking away Black's knight, and c4.

This is much more common at the amateur level than the master level where it is most often followed by 4. d4 exd4 5. cxd4 ±, Black giving up a central pawn for no compensation, after which Black may end up playing d5 anyway and wonder why they didn't play it on move three.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/4pp2/4P3/2P2N2/PP1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. c3/3...f5
r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/4pp2/4P3/2P2N2/PP1P.x: This is the Ponziani Countergambit. It sacrifices the f-pawn, but attacks e4 and prepares to develop the knight on g1. While 4.exf5 is a good move, 4.d4 is probably a better option. If White has studied against this, Black will have a bad time, but if not, both sides will be able to attack in an exciting game.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2np4/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nc6
r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2np4/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.x:
This is an uncommon way of playing the Philidor defence, as while the knight on c6 defends the e5 pawn, it may be pinned with Bb5. This position can arise in the Scotch game if Black declines to trade on d4 by playing 3...d6 instead.

White attacks e5 twice and Black appears to defend it twice. If White trades in the centre, 4. dxe5?! Nxe5 5. Nxe5 dxe5 6. Qxd8+ Kxd8 Black loses castling rights, but the queens are off the board and the position is close to even.

4. Bb5, pinning the knight to the king, removes a defender of e5 first. This is a transposition into the Old Steintiz defence in the Spanish game.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...exd4
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP.x:
Black takes the pawn the centre.

4. Nxd4, recapturing the pawn, is the main line. White centralises their knight, supported by their queen. Black has a chance to take the initiative and develop with tempo, attacking White's centre with 4...Bc5 or 4...Nf6.

Alternatively, White can gambit the pawn and not recapture it:

4. Bc4 is the Scotch Gambit. White leaves the pawn in peace and tries to establish attacking pressure with a lead in development.

4. c3 is the Göring Gambit. Similar to the Danish gambit, White offers one or two further pawns to get a lead in development.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/2BpP3/5N2/PPP2PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...exd4/4. Bc4
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/2BpP3/5N2/PPP2PP.x:
White temporarily forgoes recapturing the d4 pawn, instead developing the light-squared bishop to the most active square targeting the f7 pawn. There's no great way for Black to hold on to the pawn they are temporarily up.

4...Bc5, the Haxo gambit and second most common move, is the only way to add another defender to the pawn on d4. Though Black has two defenders to White's two attackers, after 5. c3 Black is best advised to give the pawn back.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/6N1/3pP3/8/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...exd4/4. Ng5
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/6N1/3pP3/8/PPP2PPP.x:
This line is dubious but sharp and can score well at low level.

If 4...h6, White plans to sacrifice their knight and draw out Black's king: 5. Nxf7? Kxf7 6. Bc4+, where they hope for the reasonable-looking 6...Ke8??, which leads to mate in six (7. Qh5+ g6 8. Qxg6+ Ke7 9. Qf7+ Kd6 10. Bf4+ Ne5 11. Qd5+ Ke7 12. Qxe5#). 6...Ke7 avoids this: Black's king is unsafe but they are up a knight for a pawn and should be winning, but the position is still very sharp.

4...Be7 is better, which attacks the misplaced knight on g5. If White continues with the same plan, 5. Nxf7? Kxf7 6. Bc4+, Black's king can step back to square vacated by the bishop, 6...Kf8!. If 7. Qf3+ Nf6 and Black's king is safe.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...exd4/4. Nxd4
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.x:
Black has now an opportunity to take the initiative that should not be wasted.

4...Bc5, the classical variation, attacks White's central knight on d4 and forces White to either move it or protect it. Black should expect replies like 5. Be3, 5. Nxc6, or 5. Nb3.

4...Nf6, the Schmidt variation, is most common. Black puts immediate attacking pressure on White's pawn on e4. Rather than defend it with 5. Nc3 Bb4 (pinning knight) 6. Nxc6 bxc6 7. Bd3, the main continuation is to trade off the knights and push it instead 5. Nxc6 bxc6 6. e5.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b5/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...exd4/4. Nxd4/4...Bc5
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b5/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP.x:
In the classical continuation of the Scotch, 4...Bc5 attacks White's central knight and puts indirect pressure on the f2 square.

White has three continuations of roughly equal popularity.

5. Be3 defends the knight and relieves the pressure on f2. It threatens a tactic to win a piece: if, say, 5...Nf6?? 6. Nxc6! (trades with tempo on Black's queen) dxc6 7. Qxd8+ Kxd8 8. Bxc5 wins a bishop. The main move is 5...Qf6, adding pressure to f2 and another attacker to White's knight, which White defends with 6. c3.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b5/3NP3/4B3/PPP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...exd4/4. Nxd4/4...Bc5/5. Be3
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b5/3NP3/4B3/PPP2P.x:
White defends the knight and relieves the pressure on f2.

White threatens a tactic to win a piece: if, say, 5...Nf6?? 6. Nxc6! (trades with tempo on Black's queen) dxc6 7. Qxd8+ Kxd8 8. Bxc5 wins a bishop.

5...Qf6 is the main move, adding pressure to f2 and another attacker to White's knight, which White defends with 6. c3. 6. Nb5?!, the Blumenfeld attack, which lays some traps and threatens Nxc7+ to win the rook, is inferior due to the continuation 6...Bxe3 (threatening 7...Qxf2#) 7. fxe3 Qh4+ 8. g3 Qxe4, and if 9. Nxc7+ Kd8 10. Nxa8 White's knight is trapped and Black can pick up a rook themselves with 10...Qxh1.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/3NP2q/8/PPP2PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...exd4/4. Nxd4/4...Qh4
r1b1kbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/3NP2q/8/PPP2PPP/.x: The main line is 5. Nc3 Bb4 6. Be2, which gives up the pawn after 6...Qxe4 7. Nb5 Bxc3+ (or 7...Kd8 8.O-O Bxc3 9.Nxc3 Qd4) 8.bxc3 Kd8 9.O-O Nf6, or 6...Bxc3 7. bxc3 Qxe4. White can reply with a powerful attacking idea 8. Nb5, with slight edge. +-

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/3pP3/2P2N2/PP3PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...exd4/4. c3
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/3pP3/2P2N2/PP3PP.x: Similar to the Danish Gambit, this opening sacrifices another pawn in return for faster development after 5. Nxc3.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5NP1/PPPP1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. g3
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5NP1/PPPP1.x: A rarely seen and usually illogical move, because the light squared bishop can already develop easily. White can fianchetto the bishop, but it is not always ideally placed here, and if he moves it along the f1-a6 diagonal, then the g2 and h3 squares easily become weak due to the compromised pawn structure.

rnbqkb1r/ppppnppp/8/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.x: An unorthodox and rare response to White's 2. Nf3. While it is seldom seen at high levels of play, this gambit seeks to confuse the opponent and create dynamic, unbalanced positions. Black's idea is to support a later ...f5 pawn push or prepare unexpected central play. White has several responses to take advantage of Black's unusual move:

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.x:
Rather than defend e5, Black counterattacks e4. This is the Russian game, aka Petrov's or Petroff's defence, a solid if drawish opening.

White's typical plan is to attack the centre, usually leading to a trade of pawns. Alternatively they may gambit their e4 pawn, or defend it and perhaps hope for a transposition.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/2B1n3/5N2/PPPP1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Bc4/3...Nxe4
rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/2B1n3/5N2/PPPP1P.x:
Black takes the undefended e4 pawn with 3...Nxe4. Now it would be unwise to continue with 4. Nxe5?! since after 4...d5! Black has a strong grip in the center, and white has to move the bishop to a less desirable location.

Instead white usually follows up with 4. Nc3 which is a gambit line known as the Boden-Kieseritzky Gambit, which resembles the Stafford Gambit with reversed colors, although the extra tempo gained by white with Bc4 does favor White greatly.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/2B1n3/2N2N2/PPPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Bc4/3...Nxe4/4. Nc3
rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/2B1n3/2N2N2/PPPP.x: This gambit can arise from the Russian or Vienna games. White invites Black to trade knights. White's plan after 4...Nxc3 is to take back with the d-pawn, opening up their queen's bishop, and threaten 5. Ng5 to win material. This is similar to Black's idea in the Stafford gambit, but here it's safer for White since, having played Bc4 already, they are effectively up a tempo. While the engine doesn't think this gambit completely sound (giving an evaluation of -0.5), it is a great weapon to use in faster time controls.

rnbqk2r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/1b2P3/2N2N2/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nc3/3...Bb4
rnbqk2r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/1b2P3/2N2N2/PPP.x:
3...Bb4 develops a piece and threatens to take or pin (should White move their d-pawn) the knight, thereby pressuring White's control of the centre.

4. Nxe5, taking the e5 pawn, is the main move. With their e4 pawn defended, White should feel confident that Black cannot take back immediately, and if Black thinks to remove the defender of e4 to take back the pawn, 4...Bxc3 5. dxc3 Nxe4?, this loses to 6. Qg4!, forking the knight on e4 and the g7 pawn. (6. Qe2, as in 3. Nxe5 Nxe4 4. Qe2, is also viable.)

rnbqk2r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/1bB1P3/2N2N2/PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nc3/3...Bb4/4. Bc4
rnbqk2r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/1bB1P3/2N2N2/PP.x:
Black has a few options here:
* /4... O-O/
* /4... d6/
* /4... Bxc3/

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P1n1/2N2N2/PPPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nc3/3...Ng4
rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P1n1/2N2N2/PPPP.x:
= Petrov's Defence, Vladimir Variation =

This is the Vladimir Variation of the Petrov's Defence. It is considered dubious for these reasons: It wastes tempo by moving the same knight again which is considered time-consuming. It also moves the knight to an awkward square, so it can easily be attacked. Finally, the knight on g4 isn't that effective and it is in danger of getting trapped.

1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. Nc3 Ng4

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5
rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.x: White picks up the undefended pawn. This is the classical continuation of Petrov's defence aka the Russian game. Before Black can recover the pawn, they must drive White's knight away, or else choose to gambit it.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2N2n2/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nc6/4. Nxc6
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2N2n2/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.x:
White, being up one pawn in material, trades knights.

4...dxc6 and Black recaptures while opening lines for their bishop and queen. Black will want to make an aggressive attack on White's kingside and try to swindle a win before the end game.

Taking back the other way, 4...bxc6, doesn't give Black developmental compensation and Black cannot then justify the pawn sacrifice.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2p2n2/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nc6/4. Nxc6/4...dxc6
r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2p2n2/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/.x:
Black recaptures with the d-pawn. This opens the d-file for Black's queen and the diagonal for Black's light square bishop. The g4-square is now covered by Black's light square bishop. Black is prepared for a lighting-fast attack on White's position. They want to play ...Bc5 and pressure f2 with ...Ng4 or ...Nxe4, or by forming a battery with the bishop with ...Qd4. To prove White's advantage, they must keep their head and play solidly, stalling out Black's momentum.

White's priorities are, in order:

# Find a way to protect their e-pawn to hold on to their material lead. 
# Find a way to prevent the knight from coming to g4.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2p2n2/8/4P3/2N5/PPPP1PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nc6/4. Nxc6/4...dxc6/5. Nc3
r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2p2n2/8/4P3/2N5/PPPP1PP.x:
5. Nc3 protects e4 with a natural developing move. White may have held off on d3 hoping to play d4 in one move, but will find that difficult without a knight on f3 or a pawn on c3 to support it.

Black's move is invariant: the standard Stafford idea, 5...Bc5, to coordinate with ...Ng4 and attack f2. White must prevent ...Ng4.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2p2n2/2b5/4P3/2N5/PPPP1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nc6/4. Nxc6/4...dxc6/5. Nc3/5...Bc5
r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2p2n2/2b5/4P3/2N5/PPPP1P.x:
5...Bc5 pressures White's vulnerable f2 pawn. This position should be winning for White but can be difficult for an unprepared White player to play. Black would like to follow up with 6...Ng4 to join the attack on f2.

If White allows ...Ng4, e.g. 6. Bc4?, a common club-level mistake, they can quickly become overwhelmed. 6...Ng4 7. O-O?? (to prevent Bxf2+) Qh4! then 8. g3?? Qxh2# or 8. h3 Nxf2 9. Qf3?? Nxh3 and Black has mate in 6.

For White to forestall the attack, they must control the g4 square.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2p2n2/8/4P3/3P4/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nc6/4. Nxc6/4...dxc6/5. d3
r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2p2n2/8/4P3/3P4/PPP2PPP.x:
White defends the e-pawn with 5. d3. This is White's most common continuation.

Black will almost always play the Stafford gambit's most thematic key move. 5...Bc5, developing the bishop and threatening the f2 square.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2p2n2/2b3B1/4P3/3P4/PPP2.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nc6/4. Nxc6/4...dxc6/5. d3/5...Bc5/6. Bg5
r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2p2n2/2b3B1/4P3/3P4/PPP2.x:
White thinks to pin Black's knight to their queen to prevent any shenanigans with 6...Ng4. However, this plays straight into Black's hand and it's already too late for White.

Black can play 6...Nxe4!, ignoring the pin and sacrificing their queen. If White takes it 7. Bxd8??, the most infamous Stafford trap is sprung: 7...Bxf2+ 8. Ke2 Bg4#. White can avoid checkmate but only at huge cost: their best move is to give up on Black's queen and retreat the bishop, 7. Be3.

It is critical Black play 6...Nxe4! here. For instance, 6...Ng4? and the knight prevents Black's bishop from coming to g4. 7. Bxd8 Bxf2+ 8. Ke2 Kxd8 and Black attack's fizzles out.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2p2n2/2b5/4P3/3P4/PPP1BP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nc6/4. Nxc6/4...dxc6/5. d3/5...Bc5/6. Be2
r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2p2n2/2b5/4P3/3P4/PPP1BP.x:
6. Be2 helps to control the g4 square. In addition, it adds a second defender to the queen, foiling the trap of ...Nxe4 dxe4 Bxf2+ to remove the guard of the queen.

Now 6...Ng4 leads to a trade of queens: 6...Ng4 7. Bxg4 Qh4 (7...Bxg4? 8. Qxg4) threatens Qxf2#, then 8. g3 Qxg4 9. Qxg4 Bxg4 and White is ahead, Black's threats mostly defused.

6...h5 is the most thematic response, where Black continues to fight for the g4 square. Black won't be able to keep their knight there, but they are optimistic that after ...Ng4 Bxg4 hxg4, they will be able to use the open h-file to their advantage, especially if White castles short.

r1bqk2r/ppp2pp1/2p2n2/2b4p/4P3/3P4/PPP1B.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nc6/4. Nxc6/4...dxc6/5. d3/5...Bc5/6. Be2/6...h5
r1bqk2r/ppp2pp1/2p2n2/2b4p/4P3/3P4/PPP1B.x:
Black defends g4 with the h-pawn. The idea is not so much to support a piece there but to open the h-file.

7. O-O?? may be tempting, if White thinks that their king will be safer away from the centre. However, it only serves to send the king into the danger. 7...Ng4 8. Bxg4 and rather than retake with the bishop, Black plays 8...hxg4 to open the h-file and bring their rook into the attack (though 8...Bxg4?! can also be tricky).

If 8. h3?! Qd6! threatens ...Qh2#. If White tries to defend checkmate by trading off the knight, 9. Bxg4? hxg4 opens up the h-file 10. e5 Qg6 Black has crushing pressure on White's kingside.

r1bqk2r/ppp2pp1/2p2n2/2b4p/4P3/2PP4/PP2B.x:
White's c-pawn supports playing d4, which would cut off Black's bishop's attack on f2 and, White hopes, end the threat of ...Nxf2.

The trickiest move is 7...Ng4!? anyway, where after 8. d4 Qh4 Black leaves their bishop hanging, but White can't take it because of 9. dxc5? Qxf2+ 10. Kd2 Bf5! 11. exf5?? O-O-O+, winning the queen. Instead, White must start with 9. g3 Qf6 (threatens ...Qxf2+ again) and the two lines are 10. f3 or 10. Bf3.

r1bqk2r/ppp2pp1/2p5/2b4p/4P1n1/2PP4/PP2B.x:
A sharp move. Both Black's knight and bishop are taking aim at f2.

8. d4 to cut off the bishop's vision of f2 is the best move. This (apparently) threatens to take on c5, and if 8...Bd6?! White is in time to play 9. h3. Black's knight has to retreat, else 9...Qh3, to pin the h pawn, fails to 10. g3! Qf6 and then White can pick up the free knight. After Black plays the disappointing concession 9...Nf6, their attack and initiative fizzles out.

r1bqk2r/ppp2pp1/2p2n2/2b4p/4P3/3P3P/PPP1.x:
White contests control of g4. This line is one possible refutation of the Stafford but remains sharp.

7...Qd4 threatens ...Qxf2#. After 8. O-O, Black is happy to sacrifice their knight on g4 if it means opening the h-file: 8...Ng4 9. hxg4 hxg4 10. Bxg4?? is a mistake because of 10...Qe5 and there are too many threats on the castled king, (e.g. 11. Bh3?? Bxh3 12. gxh3 Rxh3 13. Re1 Qh2+ 14. Kf1 Qxf2#). White can stabilise after 10. g3 instead.

8. Rf1 also playable, perhaps safer, with the idea of playing c3, d4, and e5 with tempi.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2p5/2b3B1/4n3/3P4/PPP2PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nc6/4. Nxc6/4...dxc6/5. d3/5...Bc5/6. Bg5/6...Nxe4
r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2p5/2b3B1/4n3/3P4/PPP2PP.x:
Black springs into action and offers their queen as sacrifice. Accepting it is poisonous for White, in fact Black has devastating continuations for all of White's moves.

If 7. Bxd8??, capturing the queen, Black has forced checkmate: 7...Bxf2+ 8. Ke2 Bg4#.

Unfortunately no other move for White is great either.

* 7. dxe4??, taking the knight, lets Black win White's queen. 7. dxe4?? opens the d file, and Black can force White's king away from protecting d1 to snap up their queen. 7...Bxf2+ 8. Ke2 Bg4+ 9. Kxf2 Qxd1 .

r1bBk2r/ppp2ppp/2p5/2b5/4n3/3P4/PPP2PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nc6/4. Nxc6/4...dxc6/5. d3/5...Bc5/6. Bg5/6...Nxe4/7. Bxd8
r1bBk2r/ppp2ppp/2p5/2b5/4n3/3P4/PPP2PPP/.x:
The Stafford Gambit player's dream. White mistakenly accepts their queen sacrifice and now will be checkmated in 2 moves.

Black checks with Bxf2 and after the White king moves up, Bg4 is Black's win.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2p5/2b3B1/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nc6/4. Nxc6/4...dxc6/5. d3/5...Bc5/6. Bg5/6...Nxe4/7. dxe4
r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2p5/2b3B1/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/.x: Recapturing the knight will leave Black's f-pawn too weak. Now, /7...Bxf2/ will force White to lose their queen.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2p5/6B1/4P3/8/PPP2bPP/RN.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nc6/4. Nxc6/4...dxc6/5. d3/5...Bc5/6. Bg5/6...Nxe4/7. dxe4/7...Bxf2
r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2p5/6B1/4P3/8/PPP2bPP/RN.x: Black has fully capitalized on their bishops. Taking the bishop with Kxf2 loses the queen immediately, otherwise 8. Ke2 Bg4+ still forces the king away from the White queen and Black is 4 points up in material with a clearly superior position.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2p2n2/2b5/4P3/2NP4/PPP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nc6/4. Nxc6/4...dxc6/5. d3/5...Bc5/6. Nc3
r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2p2n2/2b5/4P3/2NP4/PPP2P.x:
6. Nc3? looks like a normal developing move. However, it is a mistake as it allows Black to play 6...Ng4!.

6...Ng4! threatens the pawn on f2. The only move to defend it is 7. Be3, though Black can take on e3 with their knight and then bishop, recovering the pawn. 7...Nxe3 8. fxe3 Bxe3. Black is now even in material but holds a comfortable advantage because the bishop and threat of the queen swinging over prevents White from castling.

9. Qf3 is the continuation, but White must be mindful of other traps, e.g. 9. Qf3 Bd4 10. O-O-O? (thinking the king is best out of danger on the queen's side) Qg5+! 11. Kb1 Bg4 (pins queen to rook) 12. Qg3 (pins bishop to queen) Be5.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2p2n2/4P3/8/8/PPPP1PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nc6/4. Nxc6/4...dxc6/5. e5
r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2p2n2/4P3/8/8/PPPP1PPP/.x:
White defends their e pawn by moving it, and kicks the Black knight from its square at the same time. Black must move it:

5...Ng4? counter attacks the e5-pawn and pressures the pawn on f2. However, White has time to reinforce their centre with 6. d4 (also acting to prevent Black's bishop from coming to c5), then kick the knight again with 7. h3.

5...Ne4 is the usual move. This sets White up for a mistake with 6. d3?? 6...Bc5!, as in the 1950 Lowens v Stafford game, threatening mate and winning at least an exchange, or 6. f3?? Qh4+! winning at least rook. After 6. d4 Qh4 is trappy, but as long as White avoids playing g3?? they should be safe.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2p5/4P3/4n3/8/PPPP1PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nc6/4. Nxc6/4...dxc6/5. e5/5...Ne4
r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2p5/4P3/4n3/8/PPPP1PPP/.x: Rather than moving their knight back, Black plants his knight in the middle of the board. It aims at the weak f-pawn and White is tempted to remove the knight from the square. The inconspicuous move actually sets up a trap if White pushes their /6. d3/ or /6. f3/ pawn. Instead, a good response for White is 6. d4, creating a strong center in the middle of the board.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2p5/4P3/4n3/3P4/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nc6/4. Nxc6/4...dxc6/5. e5/5...Ne4/6. d3
r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2p5/4P3/4n3/3P4/PPP2PPP.x:
Although better than 6.f3??, the move gives Black a winning tactic. Instead of moving the knight away, Black has the move 6...Bc5!, sacrificing the knight.

Targeting the weak f-pawn, White's best move is blocking with 7. Be3. After the bishops trade 8...Qh4+ wins the rook for a knight, a common theme in the Stafford Gambit.

More commonly, White captures the knight with 7. dxe4. This allows 7...Bxf2+, sacrificing the bishop. If the White king captures the bishop, Black will capture the undefended queen. Otherwise, the White king will move up and 8...Bg4+ wins the queen.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2p5/4P3/4n3/5P2/PPPP2PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nc6/4. Nxc6/4...dxc6/5. e5/5...Ne4/6. f3
r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2p5/4P3/4n3/5P2/PPPP2PP.x: 6. f3 is a tempting move to kick out the knight from the center, but allows a devastating check from Black. After 6...Qh4+, 7.Ke2 immediately loses with a forced checkmate (see below). The other option is 7.g3 Nxg3, losing a rook for a knight and destroying the kingside.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2p2n2/8/4P3/5P2/PPPP2PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nc6/4. Nxc6/4...dxc6/5. f3
r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2p2n2/8/4P3/5P2/PPPP2PP.x:
5. f3 defends e4 and prevents Black's knight from coming to g4. White therefore achieves their first two priorities in refuting the Stafford gambit in one move.

5. f3 looks very unnatural because conventional wisdom is that moves like f3 or f6 weaken the kingside. However in this situation it is surprisingly sound, and a straight-forward way to refute the Stafford gambit.

If Black plays 5...Bc5?!, the usual Stafford move, White delays developing pieces still further and continues with 6. c3 O-O 7. d4 Bb6. White gets a huge centre and plenty of safe space to develop which Black, having removed their pawns from the centre, cannot contest. 8. a4 threatens to trap the bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1Npp/2n2n2/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nc6/4. Nxf7
r1bqkb1r/pppp1Npp/2n2n2/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.x:
White sacrifices their only developed piece for a pawn. After 4...Kxf7 White has the tenuous compensation that Black's king is now stuck in the centre.

Though objectively superior for Black, there is the potential for Black to misplay the position. A trap is:

5. Bc4+ d5 6. exd5 Nxd5?? allows 7. Qf3+ Ke8 8. Qxd5 Qxd5 9. Bxd5 . White is up two pawns in the endgame. Rather than recapturing with the knight on move six, a better implementation for Black is the intermezzo 6...Qe8+, which leads either to a queen trade or White abandoning the pawn.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4N3/3PP3/8/PPP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nc6/4. d4
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4N3/3PP3/8/PPP2P.x: Instead of playing 4. Nxc6 and accepting the Stafford Gambit, White chooses to take the center and defend their e5 knight. This refuses any of the traps the Stafford has in store. This is the second best move.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/4N3/4n3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nxe4
rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/4N3/4n3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.x:
A sideline. Black takes back on e4 immediately, but despite appearances, Black doesn't get to keep material equality this way. With best play for Black this line is a pawn sacrifice for which Black obtains some compensation.

4. Qe2 attacks the knight and sets up discoveries along the e-file that Black has opened. Black's best move is 4...Qe7, setting up a pin of their own after after 5. Qxe4. This leads to the Kholmov gambit: 5...d6 6. d4 dxe5 7. dxe5 Nc6 and Black wins the piece back at the cost of the d-pawn.

4. Qf3?! may be played, hoping for Black to defend their knight 4...d5?? 5. Qxf2# instead of 4...Nf6 or 4...Ng5.

4. d4 may transpose into a Classical attack after 4...d6 5. Nf3.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/4N3/4n3/8/PPPPQPPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nxe4/4. Qe2
rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/4N3/4n3/8/PPPPQPPP/R.x:
White threatens the black knight and sets up discoveries along the e-file that Black opened for them. Beginners often err here, but with best play by Black this is a pawn sacrifice with partial compensation.

* The classic beginner's blunder of saving the knight, 4...Nf6??, allows 5. Nc6+ discovered check, winning Black's queen. 
* 4...d6? to counter-attack White's knight allows 5. Nxf7! Kxf7 6. Qxe4 (White is up a pawn).
* 4...d5? to defend the knight does not resolve the pin. 5. d3 Qe7 6. dxe4 Qxe5 7. exd5 Qxe2+ 8. Bxe2 (White goes into an endgame up a pawn).

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4N3/8/8/PPPPQPPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nxe4/4. Qe2/4...Nf6
rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4N3/8/8/PPPPQPPP/R.x:
This appears to protect Black's knight, but in reality loses their queen. This famous trap, sometimes called the "copycat trap", has ensnared countless amateurs. Better was 4...Qe7, the Kholmov gambit.

The problem for Black is that 5. Nc6+ is both an attack on Black's queen and a discovered check. However Black stops the check, 5...Be7 or 5...Qe7, White's knight takes the queen next.

rnb1kb1r/ppppqppp/8/4N3/4n3/8/PPPPQPPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nxe4/4. Qe2/4...Qe7
rnb1kb1r/ppppqppp/8/4N3/4n3/8/PPPPQPPP/R.x:
Black allow White to take their knight but prepares to pin White's knight.

White will be ahead a pawn if he simply accepts the knight, so 5. Qxe4 is almost universally played. This pins White's knight to their queen, so Black can recover the piece for the cost of the d-pawn. 5...d6 6. d4 dxe5 7. dxe5 Nc6 and Black has partial compensation. White then usually gives back the pawn: if they cling onto it they can find themselves trapped.

rnb1kb1r/ppppqppp/8/4N3/4Q3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nxe4/4. Qe2/4...Qe7/5. Qxe4
rnb1kb1r/ppppqppp/8/4N3/4Q3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.x:
White takes the knight. This pins White's knight to their queen, so Black can recover the piece for the cost of the d-pawn.

5...d6 6. d4 dxe5 7. dxe5 is the continuation, offering non-trivial practical chances and partial compensation for the pawn. In fact, White's best line is then to give the pawn back, since they cannot hold onto it without getting a worse position and there are several traps for greedy players.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1qppp/3p4/4N3/4Q3/8/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nxe4/4. Qe2/4...Qe7/5. Qxe4/5...d6
rnb1kb1r/ppp1qppp/3p4/4N3/4Q3/8/PPPP1PPP.x:
Black attacks the pinned knight.

Preparing to retake on e5 is the most reasonable plan.

6. d4 is the main move: after the trades White will be up a pawn though should probably give it back on account of tactical fireworks.

6. f4 is also possible.

6. Qa4+?, attempting to unpin the knight, does not. 6...Bd7 and White's queen is hanging and their knight is still pinned, this time to the king.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1qppp/8/4p3/3PQ3/8/PPP2PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nxe4/4. Qe2/4...Qe7/5. Qxe4/5...d6/6. d4/6...dxe5
rnb1kb1r/ppp1qppp/8/4p3/3PQ3/8/PPP2PPP/R.x:
Black takes the hanging knight.

The main move here is 7. dxe5, keeping queens on the board.

7. Qxe5 is an alternative, going into an equal endgame (Black can recover the pawn without difficulty).

rnb1kb1r/ppp1qppp/8/4P3/4Q3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nxe4/4. Qe2/4...Qe7/5. Qxe4/5...d6/6. d4/6...dxe5/7. dxe5
rnb1kb1r/ppp1qppp/8/4P3/4Q3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.x:
White retakes on e5.

White has traded knights and is now up a pawn. The position is slightly better for White, but Black has some compensation and non-trivial practical chances. Black now intends to develop their queenside and castle long, and recover the pawn when convenient.

After 7...Nc6, White's best line is to give the pawn back, since they cannot hold onto it without getting a worse position.

There are several traps for greedy players. In rough order of likelihood:

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3pN3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...d5
rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3pN3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.x:
Rather than try to recover the e-pawn directly, Black offers their d-pawn to White as well in return for active play. This gambit is considered unsound.

4. exd5 accepts the free pawn, then the line continues 4...Qxd5 (threatening knight) 5. d4 Nc6.

After 6. Nf3 Bg4 7. Be2 O-O-O 8. c3, while Black has active pieces and a development lead, engine evaluation finds they do not have compensation for the pawn.

Alternatively, 6. Nxc6 Qxc6 7. Qe2+ Be7 8. Qb5 O-O 9. Qxc6 bxc6 cuts White's lead but steers into the endgame, stamping the life out of the position for Black.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...d6
rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PP.x:
White's knight is under attack and must be moved, then it is safe for Black to pick up the pawn.

4. Nf3 is the overwhelmingly common choice, and Black retakes the pawn with 4...Nxe5. This reaches the main junction of the Russian game where there are several theoretical continuations; the main line is 5. d4, the classical attack.

4. Nd3!?, the Karklins-Martinovsky variation has been tried occasionally, notably played by Magnus Carlsen in the 2018 World Chess Championship against Fabiano Caruana. Temporarily blocking the d-pawn, White's knight will eventually make way for it by rerouting to f4. 4...Nxe4 5. Qe2 Qe7 6. Nf4 Nf6 7. d4 Qxe2+ 8. Bxe2 Nc6 .

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p4/8/4n3/5N2/PPPP1PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...d6/4. Nf3/4...Nxe4
rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p4/8/4n3/5N2/PPPP1PPP/.x: Black captures the pawn and material is now equal. White would like to take some control of the centre, develop, and ideally force Black to move or lose their advanced knight. They have several options.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p4/8/4n3/2N2N2/PPPP1PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...d6/4. Nf3/4...Nxe4/5. Nc3
rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p4/8/4n3/2N2N2/PPPP1PP.x:
This is the Nimzowitch Attack of the Petrov's defense, often played if White wants to imbalance the position in the otherwise dull and symmetrical Petrov.

Usually Black takes the knight on c3 with 5...Nxc3, to compromises the White pawn structure, though if Black insists on keeping symmetry, he may also retreat the knight with 5...Nf6 instead.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p4/8/3Pn3/5N2/PPP2PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...d6/4. Nf3/4...Nxe4/5. d4
rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p4/8/3Pn3/5N2/PPP2PPP/.x:
= Petrov's Defense =
The Classical Attack in the Petrov is the most popular continuation to Black's natural 4...Nxe4. The overwhelmingly popular 5...d5 defends the knight and defends the center; White will attempt to attack Black's e4 knight and attack Black's d5 pawn with Bd3 and c4 respectively while Black will defend against White's ideas with all their might.

As mentioned above, 5...d5 is almost 20 times more popular than the second most popular move, 5...Be7, which often transposes into the main lines of the Classical Attack. Most Petrov lines have a higher than average draw percentage due to the highly symmetrical positions in the opening.
