rnbqkb1r/ppp2Npp/3p1n2/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...d6/4. Nxf7
rnbqkb1r/ppp2Npp/3p1n2/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/.x: White chose to exchange a knight against two pawns and an exposed king. While this gambit is considered as dubious, it can lead to a quick victory if Black doesn't know how to play it. Few of these games end in a draw.

rnbq1b1r/ppp2kpp/3p1n2/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...d6/4. Nxf7/4...Kxf7/5. d4

rnbq1b1r/ppp2kpp/3p4/8/3Pn3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...d6/4. Nxf7/4...Kxf7/5. d4/5...Nxe4
rnbq1b1r/ppp2kpp/3p4/8/3Pn3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.x: This is a grave mistake, allowing White to win back the piece. Other moves were better.

rnbq1b1r/pp3kpp/3p1n2/2p5/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...d6/4. Nxf7/4...Kxf7/5. d4/5...c5
rnbq1b1r/pp3kpp/3p1n2/2p5/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP.x: This move destroys White's center using the c-pawn. It also avoids Nxe4? Qh5+ when Black will lose a piece and still have an exposed King.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. d4
rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.x:
The chief sideline to 3. Nxe5, with 3. d4 White seeks to open the centre immediately and offers Black their choice of pawns to capture.

3...exd4!? is playable but less conventional as it allows 4. e5! to kick the knight. Typically this leads to trading both d- and e-pawns and opening the centre fully: the main continuation is 4...Ne4 5. Qxd4 (the Centre attack) d5 (defends knight) 6. exd6 e.p. Nxd6 7. Nc3, although there are some sidelines (5. Qe2 was advocated by Steinitz; 5. Bb4+ is the Tal gambit).

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/3Pn3/5N2/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. d4/3...Nxe4
rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/3Pn3/5N2/PPP2PPP.x: 3...Nxe4 is the main continuation. Black takes on e4 and is temporarily a pawn up. White will, now or soon, recapture on e5 and then it is a trade of pawns.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nf6

rnb1kbnr/pppp1ppp/5q2/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.x:
Black defends their e-pawn with their queen, but in doing so, Black prevents the natural development of their knight to f6, a critical square for knight activity in the opening. Conventional wisdom is against developing one's queen early: if it's attacked, then practically it must be moved, and this gives the opponent chances to develop with tempo.

This defence is rarely seen professionally as White is provided an advantage in development.

rnbqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/8/2p1N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...c5/3. Nxe5
rnbqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/8/2p1N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.x:
In the sequence 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 c5, the move 3. Nxe5! is a good move for White. Here's why:

After 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3, White is attacking the pawn on e5. If Black then plays 2...c5, this does not defend the e5 pawn. Therefore, White can capture this pawn for free with 3. Nxe5!, gaining material advantage early in the game.

This is a basic principle in chess: to take advantage of your opponent's mistakes. In this case, Black's mistake was not defending the e5 pawn, and White can capitalize on this mistake by capturing the pawn with 3. Nxe5!./3...f6/

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3pp3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.x:
Black ignores the attack on their e-pawn and tries to gain time and space. Black wants to open the centre and attack, however the gambit is unsound. Black will be on the back foot in an open position because they are a tempo behind White. If White plays accurately, Black does not get sufficient compensation for the sacrificed pawn, but the resulting positions can be sharp and it is sometimes used as a surprise opening for Black.

Capturing either pawn, 3. Nxe5 or 3. exd5, is winning for White, but the main move is 3. exd5.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3pN3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d5/3. Nxe5
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3pN3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.x:
Capturing the e-pawn is still winning for White but less common than 3. exd5.

If 3...dxe4 4. Bc4 and White has overwhelming pressure on the f7 pawn.

3...Bd6 is the main move. After 4. d4 dxe4 5. Bc4 Bxe5, White has the critical move 6. Qh5!, threatening Qxf7# and Qxe5. Black has to trade queens and White goes into an endgame with the bishop pair. 6...Qe7 7. Qxe5 Qxe5 8. dxe5⩲.

3...Nf6!? transposes into Jobava's gambit in the Petrov defence after 4. exd5. An advantage of this approach is that Black can meet either 3. Nxe5 or 3. exd5 in the same way: they transpose after 3...Nf6!? 4. exd5 or 3...Nf6!? 4. Nxe5 respectively.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3Pp3/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d5/3. exd5
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3Pp3/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP/R.x:
White accepts the gambit.

3...Qxd5?!, recapturing the pawn immediately, allows 4. Nc3 with tempo. Black has to move their queen again and they give White a development lead.

3...e4 is the main move. White's knight is hanging and moving it to 4. Ne5? or 4. Nd4? concedes the initiative to Black after 4...Qxd5!, attacking the knight again. Therefore the only move is 4. Qe2, pinning the pawn. 4...Nf6 5. d3! Qxd5 6. Nbd2 Nc6 7. dxe4.

3...Bd6 is the Maróczy gambit.

rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3qp3/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d5/3. exd5/3...Qxd5
rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3qp3/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP/R.x: This move regains the pawn, but leaves white with a huge lead in development after Nc3. Therefore, this line is not recommended. However, fans of the Scandinavian defence may find this line attractive.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3P4/4p3/5N2/PPPP1PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d5/3. exd5/3...e4
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3P4/4p3/5N2/PPPP1PPP/.x:
Black pushes forward with 3...e4, the Paulsen Countergambit. Named after Louis Paulsen, a 19th-century German master known for his deep opening ideas, this bold thrust kicks the knight and aims to seize the initiative.

By sacrificing a central pawn, Black hopes to disrupt White’s development and open lines for rapid piece activity. While objectively risky, this line can catch unprepared opponents off guard and lead to sharp, tactical battles. Precise play is required from White to avoid letting Black's central space advantage become dangerous.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PP.x:
Black defends their e5 pawn with 2...d6, sparing a piece from being saddled with the job.

Though solid, this is considered a more passive reply than 2...Nc6, as Black does not develop a piece and Black's pawn chain will get in the way of developing their dark square bishop.

3. d4 is the main line, threatening to immediately crack open the centre with dxe5. White imagines a continuation like 3...Bg4?! 4. dxe5 dxe5? 5. Qxd8+ Kxd8 6. Nxe5 Be6 +- (White is up material and controls the centre, while Black has lost castling rights).

rn1qkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4p3/2B1P1b1/5N2/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4/3...Bg4
rn1qkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4p3/2B1P1b1/5N2/PPP.x: This move is dubious, because it delays castling and knight development.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2PP.x: White attacks e5 again and threatens to win the pawn. Black must deal with the threat: trade, defend, or counterattack?

rn1qkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4p3/3PP1b1/5N2/PPP2.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Bg4
rn1qkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4p3/3PP1b1/5N2/PPP2.x:
3...Bg4?! may look like an attempt to defend the e4 pawn, but it doesn't succeed.

Though it appears that White's knight is pinned to their queen, after 4. dxe5 dxe5 5. Qxd8+ (trades queens and unpins the knight) Kxd8, White's knight is unpinned and can take back on e5 anyway. If 4... Bxf3 first, as in the Opera Game, 5. Qxf3 dxe4 6. Bc4 and White is threatening a crushing attack on f7.

Instead, after 3... Bg4 4. dxe5 Black can gambit the pawn with 4...Nd7, the Albin-Blackburne gambit. It continues 5. exd6 Bxd6, and Black has three pieces developed to White's one. They usually continue with Qe2 and long castles.

r1bqkbnr/pppn1ppp/3p4/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7
r1bqkbnr/pppn1ppp/3p4/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.x:
3...Nd7 develops a piece and defends e5. Though the knight controls less of the centre than it would on f6, on d7 the knight is safe from being kicked by d5 or pinned by Bb5. If 4. dxe5!?, Black can recapture with either 4...Nxe5 or 4...dxe5 (the knight on d7 prevents 5. Qxd8+).

The move is one of Black's main alternatives to the main line, 3...exd4. As it can be argued that opening the position with such an exchange is likely to benefit White due to a lead in development, Black hopes to keep the position closed and catch up.

White's options are to choose which piece to develop, or take more of the centre.

r1bqkbnr/pppn1ppp/3p4/4p3/2BPP3/5N2/PPP2.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4
r1bqkbnr/pppn1ppp/3p4/4p3/2BPP3/5N2/PPP2.x:
White develops their bishop to an active square, where it targets Black's weak f7 pawn.

This is a sharp position where several ordinary seeming moves become blunders, as White can take advantage of Black's comparatively passive play to extract material concessions.

4...Be7?, developing the bishop to its only available square, loses the pawn 5. dxe5, because any attempt to recapture it result in Black tactically losing a minor piece due to pressure on f7 (5...dxe5 6. Qd5! or 5...Nxe5 6. Nxe5 dxe5 7. Qh5).

r1bqk1nr/pppnbppp/3p4/4p3/2BPP3/5N2/PPP2.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4/4...Be7
r1bqk1nr/pppnbppp/3p4/4p3/2BPP3/5N2/PPP2.x:
This move, developing the king's bishop to its only available square, may look natural but is a mistake.

It immediately loses at least a pawn, because after 5. dxe5 retaking the pawn in either way (...dxe5 or ...Nxe5) fails and White wins a minor piece tactically. Black's position is simply too passive to defend against the tactical threats.

r1bqk1nr/pppnbppp/8/3Qp3/2B1P3/5N2/PPP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4/4...Be7/5. dxe5/5...dxe5/6. Qd5
r1bqk1nr/pppnbppp/8/3Qp3/2B1P3/5N2/PPP2P.x:
White threatens Qxf7#. Black can defend against the threat only by conceding a minor piece:

* 6...Nh6 defends the f7 square, but after 7. Bxh6 the threat is renewed. Black can defend the pawn with their rook (7...O-O or 7...Rf8) but is not in time to recapture the bishop. 
* 6...Bb4+ forestalls the mating attack while freeing the e7 square, from where Black's queen can defend f7. After 7. c3 Qe7 mate is prevented but Black's bishop is hanging.

r1bqk1nr/pppnbppp/3p4/4P3/2B1P3/5N2/PPP2.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4/4...Be7/5. dxe5
r1bqk1nr/pppnbppp/3p4/4P3/2B1P3/5N2/PPP2.x:
White opens the centre to capitalise on Black's passive development. This move comes with a specific tactical threat: by opening the d-file, White hopes to threaten f7, and so force Black to make material concessions.

5. dxe5?? is therefore a mistake, because it allows White to play 6. Qd5!, forming a battery and threatening Qxf7#.

5. Nxd5? is little better: after 6. Nxe5 dxe5 White could trade queens, but better is 7. Qh5 (threatening Qxf7+) g6 8. Qxe5 Nf6, winning two pawns.

The engine line is for Black to give up on recovering the pawn for now and focus on activating their pieces.

r1bqk1nr/ppp1bppp/8/4p3/2B1P3/8/PPP2PPP/.x: #REDIRECT Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4/4...Be7/5. dxe5/5...Nxe5/6. Nxe5/6...dxe5

r1bqk1nr/ppp1bppp/8/4p2Q/2B1P3/8/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4/4...Be7/5. dxe5/5...Nxe5/6. Nxe5/6...dxe5/7. Qh5
r1bqk1nr/ppp1bppp/8/4p2Q/2B1P3/8/PPP2PPP.x: This move forks e5 and f7. Since Black cannot allow Qxf7, the only sane move is 7...g6, allowing Qxe5. White is a pawn up, though the game is far from over.

r1bqk1nr/pppnbppp/8/4p3/2B1P3/5N2/PPP2PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4/4...Be7/5. dxe5/5...dxe5
r1bqk1nr/pppnbppp/8/4p3/2B1P3/5N2/PPP2PP.x: Apparently a reasonable move, to recapture the pawn, is instead a blunder. White played 5. dxe5 to open up their d-file, and can now reply 6. Qd5! and threaten Qxf7#. Black must give up a minor piece knight to defend it.

r1bqkb1r/pppnnppp/3p4/4p3/2BPP3/5N2/PPP2.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4/4...Ne7
r1bqkb1r/pppnnppp/3p4/4p3/2BPP3/5N2/PPP2.x: This move cramps Black's position even further and allows Ng5, when f7 cannot be comfortably defended. One example: d5 Qh5 (g6 Qf3 (Nf5 Bxd5) f5 Ne6 wins the queen) Ng6 Bxd5, and Black won't live very long due to f7.

r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/3p1n2/4p3/2BPP3/5N2/PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4/4...Ngf6
r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/3p1n2/4p3/2BPP3/5N2/PP.x:
Black develops a knight and controls d5, but this natural move loses a pawn.

White can capture 5. dxe5 and Black can't recover it and hold onto it.

* 5...dxe5 allows 6. Ng5! and Black has to give up at least a piece to prevent Bxf7 Ke7 Ne7!, trapping the queen. Black has to give up at least a piece to prevent it (6...Bb4+ 7. c3 O-O 8. cxb4), or accept two pieces for their queen (e.g. 6...Bb4+ 7. c3 Bc5 8. Bxf7+ Ke7 9. Ne6 Kxf7 10. Nxd8+ Rxd8).
* 5...Nxe5 is better, but allows White to seize the f7 pawn and trade queens (5...Nxe5 6. Nxe5 dxe5 7. Bxf7+ and e.g. 7...Ke7 8. Qxd8+ Kxd8).

r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/3p1n2/4P3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4/4...Ngf6/5. dxe5
r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/3p1n2/4P3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.x:
The critical move. White opens the centre and attacks Black's knight on f6.

The pawn must be retaken.:
* Simply moving the knight loses more material to exd6 and/or Bxf7+, e.g. 5...Ng4? 6. Bxf7+ Kxf7 7. Ng5+ Ke8 8. Ne6 (forking Q and B). 
* Black may think White's e-pawn is hanging and that 5...Nxe4?? kills two birds with one stone. However, 6. Qd5! threatens Qxf7# while forking the knight on e4. 6...Qe7 7. Qxe4.

These leaves Black with two ways to take the pawn on e5.

r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/5n2/4p3/2B1P3/5N2/PPP2.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4/4...Ngf6/5. dxe5/5...dxe5
r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/5n2/4p3/2B1P3/5N2/PPP2.x:
This seems to recover the pawn but loses tactically because the pressure White exerts on f7.

6. Ng5! launches a winning attack. White threatens Bxf7+ Ke7 Ne6 trapping Black's queen. 
* 6...Nb6 is the best attempt at defence. 7. Bxf7+ Ke7 8. Qxd8+ Kxd8 White is up a pawn in an endgame. Bb3 and Nf7+ forking the king, rook and pawn is threatened. 
* 6...Bb4+ at least allows Black to castle if they give up the bishop. 7. c3 O-O 8. cxb4.

r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/5n2/4p1N1/2B1P3/8/PPP2.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4/4...Ngf6/5. dxe5/5...dxe5/6. Ng5
r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/5n2/4p1N1/2B1P3/8/PPP2.x:
Black cannot guard f7. White threatens Bxf7+ Ke7 Ne6 and Black's queen is trapped.

6...Nb6 is the best attempt. 7. Bxf7+ Ke7 8. Qxd8+ Kxd8 White is up a pawn in an endgame. Bb3 and Nf7+ forking the king, rook and pawn is threatened.

6...Bb4+ at least allows Black to castle if they give up the bishop. 7. c3 O-O 8. cxb4.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4n3/2B1P3/5N2/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4/4...Ngf6/5. dxe5/5...Nxe5
r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4n3/2B1P3/5N2/PPP.x:
By recapturing the pawn with the knight, Black prevents 6. Ng5: this is because Black's knight is gaining time on White's bishop.

6...Bb3? concedes the initiative and gives Black time to develop. After 7. Bg4 pinning the knight, White still cannot play Ng5.

Therefore White must trade knights, 6. Nxe5 dxe5. This is to White's advantage as they will be able to leverage the open d-file to win a pawn (7. Bxf7+).

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4N3/2B1P3/8/PPP2P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4/4...Ngf6/5. dxe5/5...Nxe5/6. Nxe5
r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4N3/2B1P3/8/PPP2P.x: White trades knights. After Black recaptures 6...dxe5, the d-file will open and White has a tactical way of exploiting that to win a pawn.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/4p3/2B1P3/8/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4/4...Ngf6/5. dxe5/5...Nxe5/6. Nxe5/6...dxe5
r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/4p3/2B1P3/8/PPP2PPP.x:
Black recaptures on e5.

There are two tactical features that stand out for White in this position: the queens see each other, and White's bishop is threatening Bxf7+. It might seem that these moves could be played in either order to win a pawn, however 7. Qxd8+? Kxd8 8. Bxf7 allows Black to play 8...Nxe4 and recover the material.

The better order is 7. Bxf7+ Ke7 8. Qxd8+ Kxd8 and White is in time to play 9. Nc3 or 9. f3 to defend e4.

Despite appearances, 7. Bxf7+ Kxf7 is not a mistake due to deflection, as after 8. Qxd8 Black has 8...Bb4+ discovering an attack on d8 and guaranteeing they recover the queen.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2Bpp/5n2/4p3/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4/4...Ngf6/5. dxe5/5...Nxe5/6. Nxe5/6...dxe5/7. Bxf7
r1bqkb1r/ppp2Bpp/5n2/4p3/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/R.x:
White takes a pawn with check. This leads to a queen trade.

If 7...Ke7, to avoid the check while keeping contact with the queen, 8. Qxd8+ Kxd8. The queens have been traded and White is up a pawn.

If 7...Kxf7 8. Qxd8, for a moment White may think they have driven away the defender of Black's queen, but Black has 8...Bb4+ (discovered attack on White's queen) 9. Qd2 Bxd2 10. Nxd2. The queens and bishops are traded and White is still up a pawn.

r1bq1b1r/ppp2kpp/5n2/4p3/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4/4...Ngf6/5. dxe5/5...Nxe5/6. Nxe5/6...dxe5/7. Bxf7/7...Kxf7
r1bq1b1r/ppp2kpp/5n2/4p3/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/R.x:
Black takes the bishop. This moves the king away from defence of the queen: Black can tactically win it back, but only by giving back the bishop too, and White will be up a pawn.

8. Qxd8 discharges the tension between the queens. Black can take back via 8...Bb4+, discovering an attack on White's queen. White can defend the check and remove the queen at the same time: 9. Qd2 Bxd2 10. Nxd2. The queens and bishops are traded and White is still up a pawn.

If White avoids the queen trade, they are down a bishop for only a pawn.

r1bQ1b1r/ppp2kpp/5n2/4p3/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4/4...Ngf6/5. dxe5/5...Nxe5/6. Nxe5/6...dxe5/7. Bxf7/7...Kxf7/8. Qxd8
r1bQ1b1r/ppp2kpp/5n2/4p3/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/R.x:
White takes the queen. Black can recover the material, but only by giving back the bishop.

8...Bb4+ discovers an attack on White's queen. A move like 9. c3? blocks the check but doesn't deal with ...Rxd8. Fortunately for White they can play Qd2, allowing Black to recover the queen but only if they return the bishop.

r1bQ3r/ppp2kpp/5n2/4p3/1b2P3/8/PPP2PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4/4...Ngf6/5. dxe5/5...Nxe5/6. Nxe5/6...dxe5/7. Bxf7/7...Kxf7/8. Qxd8/8...Bb4
r1bQ3r/ppp2kpp/5n2/4p3/1b2P3/8/PPP2PPP/R.x:
Black discovers an attack on White's queen with check.

If White blocks the check with 9. Nc3??, 9. Nd2??, or by moving their king, they lose their queen back to ...Rxd8 and are down a bishop.

If 9. c3? to block the check while counter-attacking the bishop, then after ...Rxd8 cxb4 Nxe4! White has recovered the bishop but Black regains the pawn. The material and position is equal.

The best move is 9. Qd2: interposing the check, counter-attacking Black's bishop while also avoiding ...Rxd8. After 9...Bxd2+ 10. Nxd2 (defends the e-pawn), the queens and bishops are effectively traded and White remains up a pawn. good.

r1b4r/ppp2kpp/5n2/4p3/1b2P3/8/PPPQ1PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4/4...Ngf6/5. dxe5/5...Nxe5/6. Nxe5/6...dxe5/7. Bxf7/7...Kxf7/8. Qxd8/8...Bb4/9. Qd2
r1b4r/ppp2kpp/5n2/4p3/1b2P3/8/PPPQ1PPP/R.x:
White interposes the check while counter-attacking Black's bishop.

9...Bxd2+, recovering the queen, is the only good move of course. After 9...Bxd2+ 10. Nxd2 (defends the e-pawn), the queens and bishops have been traded and White remains up a pawn.

r1b4r/ppp2kpp/5n2/4p3/4P3/8/PPPN1PPP/R1B.x: #REDIRECT Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4/4...Ngf6/5. dxe5/5...Nxe5/6. Nxe5/6...dxe5/7. Bxf7/7...Kxf7/8. Qxd8/8...Bb4/9. Qd2/9...Bxd2/10. Nxd2

r1bqkbnr/pppn1ppp/3p4/8/2BpP3/5N2/PPP2PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4/4...exd4
r1bqkbnr/pppn1ppp/3p4/8/2BpP3/5N2/PPP2PP.x:
Black trades away White's d4 pawn. This allows Black to develop their knight and bishop without facing dxe5, which would open up a range of tactical possibilities for White.

White has two ways to recapture the pawn, with the knight, 5. Nxd4, or the queen, 5. Qxd4. Both are viable: if White intends to long castle, 5. Qxd4 might be preferred.

After recapturing, White is ready to castle and bring out their remaining minor pieces, and Black must catch up in development. Black intends ...Ngf6, ...Be7, then ...Nb6 to open up a line to develop the queen's bishop. While White's bishop is on c4, ...Nb6 comes with tempo.

r1bqkbnr/pppn1ppp/3p4/8/2BNP3/8/PPP2PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4/4...exd4/5. Nxd4
r1bqkbnr/pppn1ppp/3p4/8/2BNP3/8/PPP2PPP/.x:
The position after 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 Nd7 4. Bc4 exd4 5. Nxd4 is a complex one with various possibilities for both sides. This is the most common recapture and sets one more trap. Be7 is a blunder and should be substituted with Ngf6, when the minefield of traps has been safely crossed.

White primarily intends to castle (O-O), aiming to play Re1 or Nc3. This strategy is designed to counter Black's potential moves, such as Nb6, Ngf6, and Ne5. However, if Black plays Ngf6, creating a threat of Ne5, White is forced to castle, allowing Black to proceed with g6.

r1bqk1nr/pppnbppp/3p4/8/2BNP3/8/PPP2PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4/4...exd4/5. Nxd4/5...Be7
r1bqk1nr/pppnbppp/3p4/8/2BNP3/8/PPP2PPP/.x:
The position after 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 Nd7 4. Bc4 exd4 5. Nxd4 is a critical juncture for Black. The seemingly natural move 5...Be7? is a blunder, and 5...Ngf6 is a safer and superior alternative.

White can exploit the blunder with 6. Bxf7+!, intending to win the Black's queen with 7. Ne6 and 8. Nxd8+.

The move Bxf7+ is beneficial for several reasons:

* It sets up the Ne6 threat, prevents the defense of e6 with fxe6, and captures the black pawn on f7.

r1bq1knr/pppnbBpp/3p4/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.x: This move declines the sacrifice, but actually makes white's winning combination easier. The simple Ne6+ forks the king and queen.

r1bq3r/pppnbkpp/3pNn2/8/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7/4. Bc4/4...exd4/5. Nxd4/5...Be7/6. Bxf7/6...Kxf7/7. Ne6/7...Ngf6
r1bq3r/pppnbkpp/3pNn2/8/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.x: This is better than 7...Kxe6, but this is still losing anyway.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...exd4
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP/.x:
Black takes on d4, defusing the central tension. This is the main continuation.

White now recaptures, usually with the knight 4. Nxd4. Recapturing with the queen 4. Qxd4 is playable but allows Black to develop Nc6 with tempo.

Then, having resolved the issue of e5, Black must concentrate on developing their pieces, lest they fall too far behind White. This typically means Black plays ...Be7, ...Nf6, and castles short. Alternatives to dealing with the f8 bishop―...g7 to fianchetto (the Larsen variation) or ...d5 exd5 Qxd5 (the Paulsen attack)―have been tried but are probably too slow.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/8/2BpP3/5N2/PPP2PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...exd4/4. Bc4
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/8/2BpP3/5N2/PPP2PPP.x:
White declines to immediately recapture on d4, instead playing Bc4 and offering the pawn for rapid development and pressure on f7. This gambit, famously used by Paul Morphy to defeat the strong English player Thomas Wilson Barnes, exemplifies classical principles of rapid piece activity and initiative over material.

By inviting 4...Nf6 and responding with Ng5, White can generate swift threats before Black finishes development. If Black tries to hold the pawn with 4...c5 or 4...Nc6, they risk falling into a cramped and vulnerable position.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...exd4/4. Nxd4
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.x:
White recaptures the pawn with the knight.

4...Nf6 is the main move, attacking the e4 pawn, and is answered with 5. Nc3 to defend it. To bring more pressure to it, Black must bring the rook to e8, which requires the manoeuvre ...Be7, ...O-O, ...Re8 and ...Bf8.

Both sides develop their pieces: Black usually avoids playing ...Nc6 until after they have played ...c5 (with tempo on White's knight) to avoid blocking it in. ...c5 weakens the d6 pawn so committing to it too early can be a mistake, e.g. 4...Nf6 5. Nc3 c5? 6. Bb5+ Bd7 (prevents Q from seeing d6) 7. Nf5 Nc6 8. Nxd6+ Bxd6 9. Qxd6.

rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4pp2/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.x: The Latvian gambit is an aggressive counterattack. It is utterly unsound but sharp and has some practical chances against unprepared players. Rather than defend the attack on their e5 pawn, Black counterattacks and threatens ...fxe4. Black intends to prise open White's control of the centre, even at the cost of a pawn and the opening of the weakening e8-h5 diagonal. White can take either pawn and sharp play ensues.

rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4Np2/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Nxe5
rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4Np2/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.x:
White is threatening the fearsome Qh5+, which, supported by the knight on e5, can't be successfully defended by ...g6. There's also the incidental threat of exf5.

So that's the Latvian gambit refuted then? Most top players would say "yes". But there is a particularly optimistic breed of chess player that looks at the pawns on f5 and e4 and thinks that if the knight could just be driven away from e5, it's Black who will be capturing a pawn (fxe4), and possibly even defending it with ...d5.

And so the move 3...Qf6 was invented. Yes, it's not usual to move the queen so early, but then again, following up a wild lunge like 2...f5 with solid-looking moves is a recipe for disaster.

rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/5q2/4Np2/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Nxe5/3...Qf6
rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/5q2/4Np2/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.x:
Black's queen has come lumbering out to poke the e5-knight in the ribs. Should White hold the line, or retreat?

4. d4 is the (old) main line. It temporarily establishes a classical pawn centre (d4 & e4) allowing easy development of the remaining White pieces. If Black now wants to shift the knight from e5, they will have to play ...d6, shutting in the f8-bishop.

4. Nc4 is the Foltys-Leonhardt variation, recommended by Grandmaster Tony Kosten and now considered a more critical test of the Latvian than d4. White knows they can't prevent ...fxe4, so reserves the option of confronting that pawn with a d2-d3 advance when it arrives on e4.

rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/5q2/5p2/2N1P3/8/PPPP1PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Nxe5/3...Qf6/4. Nc4
rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/5q2/5p2/2N1P3/8/PPPP1PP.x: Black remains a pawn down, but White's knight has run off, so Black may now dream of playing …d5 in one move. That pawn on e4 will have to be cleared out of the way first, with /4...fxe4/. (If Black delays, White will play exf5 and retain the extra pawn.)

rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/5q2/8/2N1p3/8/PPPP1PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Nxe5/3...Qf6/4. Nc4/4...fxe4
rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/5q2/8/2N1p3/8/PPPP1PPP/.x: Black threatens to play ...d5 with beautiful development and only a slightly misplaced queen to worry about. But /5. Nc3/ covers d5 and gains further time by hitting the e4-pawn. Rarely do such delicate works as Black's encounter such a robust spanner as 5. Nc3.

rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/5q2/8/2N1p3/2N5/PPPP1PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Nxe5/3...Qf6/4. Nc4/4...fxe4/5. Nc3
rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/5q2/8/2N1p3/2N5/PPPP1PP.x: White's c3-knight is threatening to capture on e4 hitting the queen on f6, and taking advantage of this diversion to retreat safely to c3. Were the queen not on f6, Black could turn the tables after Nxe4 with ...d5! picking up a knight. So the queen must move again. In the old days of the Leonhardt Variation, /5...Qg6/ was the move, defending e4 and pressuring g2. The modern preference is /5...Qf7/, renewing the threat of ...d5.

rnb1kbnr/pppp1qpp/8/8/2N1p3/2N5/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Nxe5/3...Qf6/4. Nc4/4...fxe4/5. Nc3/5...Qf7
rnb1kbnr/pppp1qpp/8/8/2N1p3/2N5/PPPP1PPP.x: Black is planning ...d5 again. Now comes perhaps the only "unnatural" move with which a White player facing the Latvian must be familiar: /6. Ne3/. There's no other way to defend against ...d5.

rnb1kbnr/pppp1qpp/8/8/4p3/2N1N3/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Nxe5/3...Qf6/4. Nc4/4...fxe4/5. Nc3/5...Qf7/6. Ne3
rnb1kbnr/pppp1qpp/8/8/4p3/2N1N3/PPPP1PPP.x:
White has seemingly thwarted ...d5 yet again, and is now asking the Black army how they're going to save Private Ryan on e4.

There are two options for Black: abandon e4 and make another non-developing move with /6...c6/ to finally establish an iron grip over d5, or continue the charge with /6...d5/, the Atars Gambit, accepting the loss of the d-pawn and saddling White with only the minor inconvenience of having to come and capture it.

rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4pp2/2B1P3/5N2/PPPP1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Bc4
rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4pp2/2B1P3/5N2/PPPP1P.x:
White declines Black's gambit and instead develops a bishop, preparing Nxe5 with a threat on f7.

3...fxe4 is Black's best and main move, otherwise why would Black have bothered with attacking White's e4 pawn?

However Black has a few alternatives to consider:

* 3...Nf6?, the Morgado Defence, is the most common amateur move. It is usually played by people who are used to the Latvian gambit accepted. 
* 3...Nc6 transposes into the Rousseau gambit of the Italian game.
* 3...b5!? is the rare and dubious Strautins gambit, which triest to distract the White bishop from the a2-f7 diagonal.

rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4p3/2B1p3/5N2/PPPP1PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Bc4/3...fxe4
rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4p3/2B1p3/5N2/PPPP1PP.x: White's only move that makes sense is 4. Nxe5 to regain the pawn lost with fxe4 and attack f7, threatening Nf7 forking the queen on d8 and rook on h8.

rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4N3/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Bc4/3...fxe4/4. Nxe5
rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4N3/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PPP/.x:
Now White takes Black's pawn and threatens Nf7, which would fork Black's queen on d8 and rook on h8. Black can choose to defend this threat, ignore the threat or set a trap.

4...d5, the Polerio-Svedenborg variation, directly defends against the Nf7 threat by blocking the bishop on c4's vision of f7 and attacking it. This is the most common move by far.

4...Qg5!? sets a trap. It seems to blunder the fork 5. Nf7?!, but after 5...Qxg2! 6. Rf1 Bg4! Black has an attack where White has to be precise.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/5n2/4N3/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Bc4/3...fxe4/4. Nxe5/4...Nf6
rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/5n2/4N3/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PP.x:
= Latvian Gambit: Mayet Attack, Corkscrew Countergambit =
This gambit is utterly unsound but venomous if White doesn't know the refutation. It invites 5. Nf7 forking the queen on d8 and rook on h8, but Black will try to create an attack after 5...Qe7 6. Nxh8 d5, the Corkscrew Gambit. Black hopes for 7. Bb3? Bg4!, where White has to sacrifice a queen with 8. O-O Bxd1, or face an overwhelming attack with 8. f3 exf3+ 9. Kf2 Ne4+. However, if 7. Be2! is played instead, Black will find it hard to prove sufficient compensation for the sacrificed rook.

rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/8/4N1q1/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Bc4/3...fxe4/4. Nxe5/4...Qg5
rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/8/4N1q1/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PP.x:
= Latvian Gambit: Mayet Attack =
Black ignores the threat of Nf7 and instead counterattacks White's g2 pawn and e5 knight. 5. Nf7?! seems to win material; it forks the queen on g5 and the rook on h8, but leads to complications after 5...Qxg2! 6. Rf1 d5! where Black is starting an attack and White has to be careful not to be checkmated early.

5. d4! is the true test of Qg5. It gives up a pawn on g2, but when 5...Qxg2, named the Poisoned Pawn Variation, chaos will ensue after 6. Qh5+! g6 7. Bf7+!, where White may want to sacrifice material (probably a rook on h1 and a bishop on c1!) for an attack.

rnb1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/6q1/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Bc4/3...fxe4/4. Nxe5/4...Qg5/5. Nf7
rnb1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/6q1/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PPP.x:
= Latvian Gambit: Mayet Attack =
White believes they are winning material, forking the queen on g5 and rook on h8, but Black has other ideas. Black will now play 5...Qxg2!, taking a pawn and attacking the rook on h1. White has to be careful not to get checkmated early.

rnb1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PqP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Bc4/3...fxe4/4. Nxe5/4...Qg5/5. Nf7/5...Qxg2
rnb1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PqP/R.x:
= Latvian Gambit: Mayet Attack =
Black turns the tables on White by taking the pawn on g2 and attacking the rook on h1. White will definitely want to save the rook, so 6. Rf1 is the only move (6. Ke2?? Qf3+! forces the White king back to the first rank where the queen on d1 no longer see the rook).

rnb1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PqP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Bc4/3...fxe4/4. Nxe5/4...Qg5/5. Nf7/5...Qxg2/6. Rf1
rnb1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PqP/R.x:
= Latvian Gambit: Mayet Attack =
White moves their rook to safety. Black will now start an attack with 6...d5!. White will have to navigate safely. 6...Nf6 and 6...Nc6 are also playable but are risky. Any other move and the attack runs out of fuel.

rnbqkbnr/ppp3pp/8/3pN3/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Bc4/3...fxe4/4. Nxe5/4...d5
rnbqkbnr/ppp3pp/8/3pN3/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PPP/.x:
The best and most common move. Black now is attacking White's bishop on c4 and preventing Nf7. But 4. Nxe5 carried a second threat: 5. Qh5+!. However, if Black finds 5...g6!? to sacrifice the exchange after 6. Nxg6 hxg6 7. Qxh8 Kf7!, the position is objectively equal.

It's true that White can save the bishop with 5. Bb5+ or 5. Be2 (5. Bb3?? loses to 5...Qg5!), but it lacks the aggression and force of Qh5+, so 5. Qh5+ is more preferred.

rnbqkbnr/ppp3pp/8/3pN2Q/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Bc4/3...fxe4/4. Nxe5/4...d5/5. Qh5
rnbqkbnr/ppp3pp/8/3pN2Q/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PPP.x:
White brings their queen out and checks Black's king.

5...Ke7?? would lose to a forced mate in 9 after 6. Qf7+, so Black has to find the surprising 5...g6!?, sacrificing the exchange after 6. Nxg6 hxg6 7. Qxh8, but after 7...Kf7! White's queen is trapped in the corner and White's bishop on c4 is still attacked.

rnbqkbnr/ppp4p/6p1/3pN2Q/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Bc4/3...fxe4/4. Nxe5/4...d5/5. Qh5/5...g6
rnbqkbnr/ppp4p/6p1/3pN2Q/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PP.x:
Black blocks the check with their g-pawn. Now White has two pieces hanging: the bishop on c4 and the queen on h5, so retreating the queen would lose the bishop.

White's best and most common move is 6. Nxg6, where Black can choose between the sound exchange sacrifice, 6...hxg6 7. Qxh8 Kf7!, or the unsound (but playable!) queen attack, 6...Nf6, usually played by amateurs.

White can play 6. Bb5+, but gives Black the extra tempo of 6...c6 before 7. Nxg6, and so doesn't make as much sense to play.

rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/5p2/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PP.x:
Seeing the threat of Nf3, Black imagines they can protect their e pawn with 2...f6?. Unfortunately, f6's protection is only that: imaginary.

3. Nxe5 snaps off the pawn and opens up White's queen. Then if 3...fxe5? the typical refutation is 4. Qh5+! g6 5. Qxe5+ forking the king and Black's rook on h8.

Black can set a trap with 3...Qe7, hoping that White only half-remembers the refutation and proceeds 4. Qh5+? anyway, but this time 4...g6 and White has nowhere to go. (5. Nxg6 Qxe4+ 6. Be2 Qxg6 and Black is up a knight for a pawn.) Instead White should simply retreat the knight and give back the pawn, and be happy with their development lead. 4. Nf3 Qxe4 5. Be2

rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/5p2/4N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f6/3. Nxe5
rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/5p2/4N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/.x:
3. Nxe5 is the critical move that refutes the Damiano defence. White realised that f6 couldn't defend the e5 pawn because of the weakness of Black's kingside.

If 3...fxe5? then 4. Qh5+! exploits the open e8-to-h5 diagonal. Then if 4...g6 5. Qxe5+ forks the king and Black's rook on h8. After 5...Qe7 6. Qxh8 (6. Qxe7? and White only has two pawns for the knight) Qxe4+ 7. Kd1, Black has a knight and a pawn for the rook and two pawns they lost.

4...Ke7 does not fare better: 5. Qxe5+ Kf7 6. Bc4+ d5 7. Bxd5+ Kg6 and White has three pawns for their knight, their bishop developed, and Black's king on the run. The Chess Wikibook Sample Game follows the 3...fxe5 4. Qh5+ Ke7 line.

rnb1kbnr/ppppq1pp/5p2/4N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f6/3. Nxe5/3...Qe7
rnb1kbnr/ppppq1pp/5p2/4N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.x:
Black realises they cannot afford to take back with the f-pawn, and plays ...Qe7, skewering the knight and e4 pawn instead. This lays a trap for an unsuspecting White player.

The usual move, after 3...fxe5, is 4. Qh5+. If White only half remembers the refutation and plays 4. Qh5+? in this position then after 4...g6! White's queen and the knight are hanging. 5. Nxg6 Qxe4+ 6. Be2 Qxg6.

4. Nf3 is White's best move. This returns the pawn but White gets a big lead in development, and Black's pawn on f6 is permanently misplaced. 4...Qxe4+ 5. Be2 d5 6. Nc3 (kicking queen).

rnb1kbnr/ppppq1pp/5p2/8/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f6/3. Nxe5/3...Qe7/4. Nf3
rnb1kbnr/ppppq1pp/5p2/8/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.x: White retreats the knight to the safer square, where Black will play 4... Qxe4+, regaining the pawn with tempo. However, after 5. Be2, White is up in development and Black's queen is misplaced and will be kicked via 6. Nc3. Also, the pawn on f6 is permanently misplaced, and the development of the g8-knight is hindered.

rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RN.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f6/3. Nxe5/3...fxe5
rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RN.x:
Black is up material, at least for a while.

4. Qh5+ forks the king and the e5 pawn. After 4...g6 5. Qxe5+ wins Black's rook. 
4...Ke7 5. Qxe5+ Kf7 is no better. One continuation is 6. Bc4+ d5 (6...Kg6?? blunders mate in 11) 7. Bxd5+ Kg6 and White has three pawns for their knight, their bishop developed, and Black's king on the run.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1pp1/7p/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PP.x: The Truck Defense involves giving up the central pawn on e5, allowing the white knight to occupy the square. This defense is very rarely played and considered an offbeat opening. It is not commonly seen in high-level tournaments, but can be used to surprise your opponent, especially in casual play.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/7N/PPPP1PPP/.x:
= The Basman Attack =
The Basman Attack is an unusual chess opening named after the English International Master Michael John Basman who played the strange 2. Nh3 in a game versus John T Fletcher in 2013.

The Basman Attack is offbeat, but slightly playable for White. It is mainly used to avoid highly theoretical lines such as the Ruy Lopez or the Sicilian Defense: Najdorf Variation. White intends to play f2-f4 soon.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/5Q2/PPPP1PPP.x: The Napoleon Attack, or Napoleon Opening, is weaker than it sounds. Not only does it develop the queen too early, but it blocks the King's Knight from developing to f3, its best square.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P1Q1/8/PPPP1PPP.x:
White's 2. Qg4 breaks the chess opening principle of not moving the queen out early, as the opponent will gain tempos by attacking the exposed queen. Not only that, it does not threaten Scholar's Mate, unlike the other early queen attacks Qh5 and Qf3.

Black's best replies are 2...Nf6 or 2...d5, which both attack the queen and gain easy tempo. White might move the queen to g3, to keep an attack on e5 and g7.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p2Q/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/.x:
This is an aggressive opening move that violates an opening principle by bringing the queen out early. So long as Black doesn't fall into White's traps, they will be able to develop easily and play useful moves that gain time on White's queen.

2. Qh5 both attacks the pawn on e5 and puts pressure on f7. The f7 square is the weakest point in Black's position at the start of the game, because it is the only square guarded only by Black's king. White's usual plan is to follow with Bc4 and deal a swift, knock-out blow with Qxf7#, e.g. 2...Nc6 3. Bc4 Nf6?? 4. Qxf7#. This is called Scholar's mate or the four-move checkmate.

rnbq1bnr/ppppkppp/8/4p2Q/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/.x: Black makes a hideous blunder. They allow 3. Qxe5#, with red-faced spectators all about. This move is a curiosity as it leads to the fastest possible checkmate by White at only three moves.

r1bqkbnr/pppp3p/2n3p1/4pp2/2B1P3/5Q2/PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...g6/4. Qf3/4...f5
r1bqkbnr/pppp3p/2n3p1/4pp2/2B1P3/5Q2/PPP.x:
...f5 parries the threat of Qf7# by obstructing the queen's vision of the f7 square. It also attacks White's e-pawn, and if Black is able to remove it, they might be able to play d5 and take over the centre.

5. exf5?!, thinking to clear the obstruction, is inaccurate, ultimately because it gives up control of the d5 square.

Black can't play ...d5 straight away. If 5...d5?!, apparently with tempo on the bishop, then 6. fxg6! and Black doesn't have time to take the bishop because White's pawn now controls f7: 6...dxc4?? 7. Qf7#!.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1p1p/6p1/4p2Q/4P3/8/PPPP1PP.x:
1.e4 e5 2.Qh5 g6

=Wayward Queen Attack=
This move is a blunder as it allows 3. Qxe5+! creating a deadly fork to the king and the rook and thus loses that h8 rook. If, however, White blunders and Black plays well, the Queen may be trapped near h8, but this is unlikely.

Instead of playing 2…g6??, 2…Nc6 defends the e-pawn and gives Black a very slight edge due to White’s misplaced queen.

2…Nf6 attacking the Queen thus preventing the famous Scholar's Mate is another idea, though less common. Although this gives White the opportunity to capture on e5, Black in return gains tempos as White’s queen is far from her home and doesn’t have a clear way to get to safe squares such as e2 and d1 safely.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/1P6/P1PP1PPP.x: Charles' Opening is offbeat, but perfectly playable for White. It is mainly used to avoid highly theoretical lines such as the Ruy Lopez or the Scotch Game: Schmidt Variation, or to surprise the opponent. White intends to play Bb2 soon. After 2...c7-c5, the position is similar to an Anti-Sicilian.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/2P5/PP1P1PPP.x:
White wishes to build a big, two-pawn centre, and plays 2. c3?! to support pushing the pawn to d4.

This idea, c3 to support d4, is a common plan for White in many open games (games beginning 1. e4 e5): c3 after developing the knight is the Ponziani (2. Nf3 Nc6 3. c3), and it comes after developing the knight and bishop in the Italian and Spanish games (3. Bc4 Bc5 4. c3 or e.g. 3. Bb5 Bc5 4. c3). However, played on White's second move without any pieces developed, it is simply too slow.

Black can respond vigorously with 2...d5 to eliminate transpositional possibilities. After 3. exd5 Qxd5, there is no 4. Nc3 to chase the queen away and gain a tempo as the c3 pawn is occupying the square.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/2P1P3/8/PP1P1PPP.x:
White controls d5 another time with a pawn instead of developing a piece. This move is playable but slow. It concedes White's first move advantage and has the drawbacks of creating a permanent hole on d4 and blocking the f1 bishop from developing to c4 or b5.

Black has a wide range of reasonable options, including 2...Bc5, 2...Nf6, or 2...Nc6.

2...g6?! is called the Adorjan defence. This prepares to fianchetto, though the king's bishop could already develop along the a3-f8 diagonal, and invites 3. d4! exd4 4. Qxd4 with tempo on the rook on h8. 4...Nf6 5. Bg5 where 5...Bg7?? loses a piece to 6. e5.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/3P4/PPP2PPP/.x:
This insipid move is playable but concedes White's first move advantage.

Inferior to most other responses to 1. e4 e5, 2. d3 defends e4, though it was not under attack. While it opens a line for the queen's side bishop to develop, it closes the line 1. e4 opened for the king's bishop. Should White wish to play d4 in the future, they have lost a tempo here. White misses the opportunity to develop a piece to make an unnecessary pawn move instead.

Black is allowed easy equality with 2...Nc6 or 2...Nf6 followed by 3...d5. This can lead to a position like a Philidor defence with colours reversed: e.g. 2...Nf6 3. Nf3 Nc6 4. Be2 d5 5. Nbd2 is the reversed Hanham variation.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.x:
White plays 2. d4 to smash open the centre. White threatens to take on e5, but really they are provoking exd4, and planning to develop their pieces rapidly by opening up the d-file for their queen and bishop. White may yet gambit some pawns for even faster development. This is the explosive Centre game.

Black has some options, but almost always takes the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3pp3/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.x:
= Center Game: Beyer Gambit =
Black copies White's d4. Although this approach of pushing ...d5 can be plausible against the King's Gambit (in the Falkbeer Countergambit), here it is simply unfavorable for Black. With good play, White can gain a good and superior position.

The Beyer Gambit can be met with two responses. 3. exd5?! is not bad, but gives away White's advantage. After 3...Qxd5, Black's position is quite playable with no big problems and no material deficit.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4p3/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/.x: This is an inferior way to enter a Philidor. While White's best move is still Nf3, transposing into the Philidor, it gives the additional option of immediately entering an endgame with 3.dxe5 dxe5 4.Qxd8+ Kxd8 5.Bc4 (though engines have no trouble defending it for Black). Black would lose the right to castle, and White would have a lead in development. White can also enter a Chekhover-like position via 3.Nc3 exd4 4.Qxd4 with the intention to respond to Nc6 with a Bb5 pin, or alternatively drawing the queen back to d3 or e3 and simply enjoying a space advantage.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/3pP3/8/PPP2PPP/RNB.x:
Black takes White's d-pawn.

3. Qxd4 is the main move. This was Black to develop 3...Nc6 with tempo.

3. c3 is the Danish gambit. White offers to let Black keep the pawn in return for rapid development.

3. Nf3, the Kieseritzky variation, often leads to several transpositions. Black can transpose to the Scotch with 3...Nc6 or 3...Bb4+, to the Philidor with 3...d6, to Petrov's Steinitz variation with 3...Nf6, or to the Lewis Gambit of the Bishop's Opening with 3...Bc5 (followed by 4. Bc4 Nf6). An independent line is 3...Bc5 4. Nxd4 Nf6.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/2BpP3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. Bc4
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/2BpP3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.x:
White gambits their d4 pawn. After either 3...Nf6 or 3...Nc6, this will transpose into other openings.

3...Nf6 is Black's most common move, transposing to the Urusov gambit which is more normally seen from the Bishop's opening with 1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Nf6 3. d4 exd4.

3...Nc6 is another good move developing the queenside knight. This often transposes to the Scotch gambit after the normal and common developing move 4. Nf3.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/2BpP3/8/PPP2PPP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. Bc4/3...Nc6
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/2BpP3/8/PPP2PPP/.x:
Black develops their knight on b8. 4. Nf3 transposes to the Scotch gambit.

4. Nf3 is the most common move, which transposes into the well-known Scotch gambit, more often seen from the move order 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Bc4.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. Nf3
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP/R.x:
With this move, White brings another attacker to Black's d4 pawn. This often transposes to other openings, though independent lines exist.

3...Nc6 is the most common move, transposing to the Scotch game line, more normally seen from the move order 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 instead.

3...Bc5 is another normal move, developing the bishop. This can go two ways; 4. Nxd4 Nc6 transposes into the Classical Scotch game, while 4. c3 is the Lanc-Arnold gambit, an independent option.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/3QP3/8/PPP2PPP/RNB.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. Qxd4
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/3QP3/8/PPP2PPP/RNB.x: In the Center Game, White is happy with himself for knocking out Black's only foothold in the center square, e5. At the time, all four central squares are controlled by White. This may seem like a huge advantage for White, but if Black simply plays Nc6, the queen is forced to move. Conversely, it may seem like a bad idea to develop the queen before any other pieces; however, Black can get into trouble if careless.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/2B1P3/2p5/PP3PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Bc4
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/2B1P3/2p5/PP3PPP/R.x:
4. Bc4 gambits a second pawn. It develops the light-squared bishop to a place attacking Black's weakest square f7.

Black almost always accepts the second pawn with 4...cxb2, rather than offering a transposition to the Göring Gambit with 4...Nc6.

In one rare line, Black advances the pawn to c2, not wanting to let White develop the dark squared bishop onto the long diagonal.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/2B1P3/2p5/PP3PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Bc4/4...Nc6
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/2B1P3/2p5/PP3PPP.x: After Nc6, White will usually play 5. Nf3 offering the b2-pawn again and developing the knight to its best square. This transposes to the Göring Gambit.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/2B1P3/8/Pp3PPP/RNB.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Bc4/4...cxb2
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/2B1P3/8/Pp3PPP/RNB.x:
=Double Danish Gambit Accepted=
This time White has to recapture the pawn with 5. Bxb2 rather than give Black a second queen. (The sacrifice Bxf7 is an important idea in the Double Danish Accepted, just not yet.)

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3p4/2B1P3/8/PB3PPP/RN.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Bc4/4...cxb2/5. Bxb2/5...d5
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3p4/2B1P3/8/PB3PPP/RN.x:
By playing 5...d5, Black aggressively strikes back at the center, releasing the bishop to catch up in development, returning a pawn in the process. White main move is 6. Bxd5, and the main continuation is 6...Nf6 7. Bxf7+ Kxf7 8. Qxd8 Bb4+ 9. Qd2 Bxd2+ 10. Nxd2 with an equal position.

Alternatively after 6. Bxd5 Nf6, 7. Nc3?! is tried, but after 7...Nxd5 8. Nxd5 Nd7! (8...c6?? 9. Nf6+ gxf6 10. Qxd8+ Kxd8 11. Bxf6+ and White wins an exchange) Black has an advantage as he is still up a pawn and has the bishop pair, but accurate play is needed.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/4P3/2p2N2/PP3PPP/R.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nf3
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/4P3/2p2N2/PP3PPP/R.x:
This offers another pawn to Black. Black may take 4...cxb2, where White's idea is 5. Bxb2.

It is more typical for White to offer this gambit with 4. Bc4 instead, which develops the bishop to pressure f7. Delaying Bc4 with 4. Nf3 is less sharp. The difference can be illustrated in the lines

* After 4. Nf3 cxb2 5. Bxb2 Nf6 6. e5, Black has 6...Ne4, and 7. Bc4 is a bit too late. 7...Bb4+ and Black's knight and bishop combine to control the dark squares around the king. 
* Compare the 4. Bc4 line, 4...cxb2 5. Bxb2 Nf6 6. e5, where 6...Ne4? allows 7. Bxf7+ Kxf7 8. Qf3+ Ke8 9. Qxe4 .

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/4P3/2N5/PP3PPP/R1B.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/4P3/2N5/PP3PPP/R1B.x: This move was Alekhine's choice. This move regains the one of the lost pawns, thus keeping White's material deficit to a minimum. White now has a huge lead in development and a central pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/4P3/2P5/P4PPP/RNBQ.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. bxc3
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/4P3/2P5/P4PPP/RNBQ.x:
An error. White forgets why the sacrifice was offered in the first place: by retaking with a pawn, White does not develop their pieces in compensation for the sacrifice, and is left with weak and isolated a- and c-pawns to boot.

Black should have an easy game.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4PP2/8/PPPP2PP/R.x:
White attacks Black's pawn on e5 with the f-pawn, even though that pawn is itself attacked and undefended. White seeks to pry Black's pawn away from control of d4, so that they may place their own pawn there. In addition, White's trying to open the f-file so that once they have castled, their rook is activated on the open file immediately.

The king's gambit is a very aggressive opening that comes with severe trade offs. By moving the f-pawn so early, before they have castled, White has greatly weakened their kingside and exposed their king to danger.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4PP2/8/PPPP2PP.x:
2...Nc6, a way to decline the king's gambit, is much more common in amateur games than in tournament chess. 2...Nc6 develops a piece and prepares to recapture on e5, though Black's pawn was not actually hanging because 3. fxe5?? can be answered with 3...Qh4+!.

3. Nf3 is the main move, as in many king's gambit lines. This controls h4, therefore preventing the riposte ...Qh4+, and White actually threatens fxe5. Though the engine line is 3...d5 4. exd5 Qxd5 5. Nc3 Qe6, Black's usual idea is 3...f5!?, the Miles defence. 3...exf4 4. d4 transposes to the MacLeod defence.

3. Nc3 transposes to the Max Lange defence of the Vienna gambit.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3pp3/4PP2/8/PPPP2PP/R.x:
2...d5 is the most common way to decline the king's gambit (at least, for the moment: Black often takes the f-pawn later).

White has the choice of two centre pawns they may take, though 3. fxe5?? is a blunder as 3...Qh4+! 4. g3 Qxe4+ 5. Qe2 Qxh1 is most embarrassing.

3. exd5 is the main move, leading to a scramble for control of the d5, e4, and e5 squares. Black's traditional idea (called the Staunton line) is 3...e4, but more common today is 3...exf4 4. Nf3, transposing into the modern line of the king's gambit accepted, as if they had played 2...exf4 3. Nf3 d5 4. exd5.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3p4/4Pp2/5N2/PPPP2PP/.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. f4/2...exf4/3. Nf3/3...d5
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3p4/4Pp2/5N2/PPPP2PP/.x:
Black attacks White' e-pawn. As with 3...d6, the Fischer defence, moving the d-pawn opens the line for Black's bishop to develop. Moving it to ...d5 is more forcing, however, and by threatening ...dxe4, it compels White to capture the the pawn first, 4. exd5, and robs them of the time to make a developing move of their own.

4. e5? is inferior because after 4...g5 5. h4 g4, White has taken away the e5 square to where they would otherwise like to move their knight. White can end up transposing into the dubious Allgaier gambit.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3Pp3/5P2/8/PPPP2PP/RN.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. f4/2...d5/3. exd5
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3Pp3/5P2/8/PPPP2PP/RN.x:
Accepting the d-pawn is the main move. From here, Black has three choices:

3...e4!? is the traditional idea, but it has fallen out of fashion due to 4. d3!, the Charousek gambit. If 4...Qxd5 5. Nc3 (hits queen) Bb4. If 4...Nf6 5. dxe4 with complications that favour White.

3...exf4 is the main move today. 4. Nf3 (to prevent Qh4+) transposes to the modern king's gambit accepted.

3...c6!? is the Nimzowitsch-Marshall countergambit that offers material for development.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1p1p/2n5/4N3/2B1Pppq/8/PPPP.x:
= Salvio Gambit, Viennese Variation =
This accurate reply, named the Viennese Variation, deliberately gives up the f7 pawn to attempt to launch an attack on the White king on f1. White has multiple replies to this.

7. Nxf7 seems tempting — it wins the f7 pawn and traps the rook on h8. However, Black can start an attack on White's king with 7...b5! 8. Bb3 (8. Nxh8? bxc4-+ and Black is crushing white despite being down an exchange) Nh6! 9. Nxh8 Bc5! and White's king is struggling to survive.

7. Bxf7+ takes f7 with check but after 7...Kd8 8. d4 Nxe5 9. dxe5 Nh6 10. Bc4 Bc5 11. Qe1 g3! Black has a crushing attack on White's king that is survivable only with precision.

rnb1kb1r/pppp1p1p/7n/4N3/2B1Pppq/8/PPPP2.x:
= Salvio Gambit, Silberschmidt Defense =
Black chooses to defend f7 using their knight. This opening is called the Silberschmidt Defense. Despite the logicality and popularity of the move, this is not as accurate as the other main replies to 6. Kf1.

7. d4 is what most people play, taking the center and reinforcing the e5 knight. This is usually followed from the Black side by 7...d6 or 7...f3.

7. d3?? simply loses the knight to 7...d6!, trapping it as the d3 square is occupied by the pawn.

7. Nc3 is a minor try where after 7...d6 8. Nd3, Black has a slightly better position but White has more development.

= Muzio Gambit, Sarratt Defence =
Black defends their f4 pawn and f7 pawn while developing the queen and blocking the f-file. This is the most testing reply to the Muzio Gambit as it forces White to prove sufficient compensation for the knight sacrifice. Black also carries the threat of 7...Qd4+ winning the bishop on c4. White must not let their attack fizzle out; for example, the most common move at club level is 7. c3, but this is too slow. There are other, better options available for White.

With 4.Nc3, the Quaade Gambit, White indirectly defends against Black's threat of 4...g4 to kick away White's knight. Unlike the direct responses of 4.h4 and 4.Bc4, or the other indirect response of 4.d4, the move 4.Nc3 doesn't even seem to begin to defend against the threat of 4...g4, but it does.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1p1p/5n2/4N3/4PppP/8/PPPP2P.x:
There's a pawn on g4 if White wants to capture it, but it isn't a free gift: Black is counter-attacking e4.
* 6. d4 is the main line. White is attacking a pawn and Black is attacking a pawn, that's 1 pawn each, so rather than resolve either of those situations, White makes to 2 to 1 in her favour! This move also ensures that once Black kicks the knight away from e5 by playing ...d6, it will be able to retreat to d3 without blocking the d-pawn. Playing 6.d3 wouldn't have that advantage, and would also shut in the f1-bishop.
* 6. Bc4 was the move favoured by the world champion of the pre-World Championship era, Paul Morphy.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1p1p/5n2/4N3/2B1PppP/8/PPPP.x: Black has to do something about the attack by the White bishop and knight on f7. The bishop's diagonal must be blocked at the cost of a pawn with 6...d5.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2p1p/5n2/3pN3/2B1PppP/8/PPPP.x:
White's c4-bishop and e4-pawn are forked by the Black pawn on d5. 7. exd5 is necessary to remove the threat.

7. Bxd5 would be a positional disaster for White. It would give Black a powerful centralised queen after 7...Nxd5 8.exd5 Qxd5, it would bring White no closer to recovering the pawn, and it would give up the bishop pair for no reason. In the analogous position after 7.exd5, 7...Nxd5 would not oblige White to capture the knight.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2p1p/3p4/4N3/4PppP/8/PPPP2P1.x: 6. Nxg4 is the only sensible move, otherwise it's not clear how White will ever recover the pawn on g4.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2p1p/3p4/8/4PpNP/8/PPPP2P1/R.x:
6...Nf6 is the usual move. Black aims to come out with a lead in development after an exchange of knights on f6, that will compensate for her suspect kingside pawn structure.

6...Be7 is a move that lay gathering dust on a shelf for a century and a half, between Howard Staunton losing a famous game with it against Baron Tassilo von Heydebrand und der Lasa in 1853 and the computers rediscovering it in the 1990s. It's had a very positive score from a small sample size. Black threatens to take White's pawn on h4, because taking pawns means you have more of them than your opponent does.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1bp1p/3p4/8/4PpNP/8/PPPP2P1/.x:
White's h-pawn is doomed. The only move that saves it is 7.h5, but there's a subtle problem with that move. Black has the secondary threat that after 7...Bh4+ 8.Nf2 Nh6, the next move is going to be ...Ng4 winning the pinned knight on f2 (or at least forcing the h1-rook to sacrifice itself for the bishop). If the White pawn were not on h5, White could offer some defence with 9.Qh5, chasing the pinning bishop away before the knight arrives on the scene.

Doing nothing at all would be a better move than 7.h5, but that's not allowed, so how could White make some use of this spare tempo?

The Wagenbach Defence is an unusual response to the King's Gambit, defined by:1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 h5It was invented around 1991 by János (George) Wagenbach, an English club player (1936-2026) known for creative and chaotic play.

The idea of 3...h5 is to support a pawn structure with ...g5 and ...h4, aiming to hold onto the f4 pawn and complicate the game. Although it breaks standard opening principles, it can be effective as a surprise weapon.

The Breyer Gambit is considered a risky but aggressive opening that can lead to sharp and complex positions.

rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/5p2/4p3/4PP2/8/PPPP2PP/.x:
2...f6? is an inferior way to decline the king's gambit.

After 3. fxe5!?, recapturing with the pawn 3...fxe5? is a mistake. Despite appearances, the f-pawn is not able to defend e5 yet due to tactics involving Black's weakened king. 4. Qh5+! g6 5. Qxe5+ Qe7 6. Qxh8 wins a rook. This line is comparable to the Damiano defence, 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 f6?.

After 3. fxe5, Black's best continuation is 3...Nc6, the Soller-Zilbermints gambit. This adds an attacker to e5: the purpose is that Black now threatens 4...fxe5, as 5. Qh5? g6 and, in this line, the knight defends e5 so White doesn't have the option of Qxe5+.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/4p3/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.x:
1...e6 is the French defence. Black plans to gain space in the centre with their d pawn. If they were to play ...d5 immediately, White could take it, so first Black supports ...d5 with another pawn move. This way, they can recapture and keep a pawn on the d5 square.

The trade-off in supporting ...d5 with ...e6 is that it obstructs Black's queen-side bishop and makes it harder to develop. In the Caro-Kann on the other hand, 1...c6 is played to prepare the way for ...d5, where Black avoids the "French bishop" but with the trade off that ...c6 prevents developing ...Nc6, and Black has lost a tempo if they ever want to play ...c5.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/4p3/8/2B1P3/8/PPPP1PPP.x: 2. Bc4 this move is playable but allows black to play /2...d5/ and challenge the white center

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/4p3/8/4P3/2N5/PPPP1PPP.x:
This move has very little independent value, as it transposes into different opening lines.

After /2...d5/ this will transpose into a proper French defence. White can then play 3. d4, transposing into the Paulsen variation, or 3. Nf3, going into the Two-knights variation. 3. exd5 exd5 4. d4 is also possible, transposing into an exchange French. This is not that great for White however, since they usually want to defend the d4-pawn with c3 instead.

Black can also deviate from the French defence by playing /2...c5/, transposing into the Closed Sicilian instead.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/4P3/2N5/PPPP1PP.x:
Black puts their pawn in the centre. Play can transpose into the Paulsen variation after /3. d4/ or the Two-knights after /3. Nf3/.

/3. exd5/ transposes into the exchange French, but is somewhat inaccurate due to the knight blocking the c3-pawn, which would usually support the d4-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/3PP3/2N5/PPP2PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nc3
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/3PP3/2N5/PPP2PP.x:
3. Nc3 is White's most popular move against the French at the top level, and is considered the most challenging option. White develops a piece and defends the e4 pawn. In contrast to the 3. Nd2, the second most common line, this also pressures d5 and keeps the c1-h6 diagonal for the queen's bishop to develop.

Black has two main options, both of which leave the tension between d5 and e4 and develop a piece.

3...Nf6 is the classical approach. The main continuations are 4. e5, the Steinitz variation, leading to 4...Nfd7 5. f4 c5 6. Nf3 Nc6 7. Be3; and 4. Bg5, after which 4...dxe4, 4...Be7, and 4...Bb4 are all played.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/4p3/8/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.x:
White doesn't take up the centre with pawns and instead prioritizes piece development. This move is not as flexible for White, since it leaves them with a lot less options than 2. d4 would have. It does invite Black to play a Sicilian defence instead.

/2...d5/ continues to play in the style of the French defence. This is played most often, since most players playing e6 will be most comfortable with the French defence.

/2...c5/ is Black's second most common option. This steers the game into a Sicilian defence with e6, also known as the "French Sicilian."

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PP.x:
Black continues playing in the spirit of the French defence. White has a handful of options in this position, some better than others.

/3. Nc3/ enters the Two Knights variation where White continues developing pieces instead of pawns. Black has two responses: either kick White's knights around and grab a space advantage with 3...d4, or let White take over the centre after 3...Nf6 4. e5 Nfd7 in order to undermine it in a similar fashion to the advance variation.

/3. d4/ is the Perseus gambit. White gambits the e4-pawn and hopes to get compensation by putting their knight on e5 from where it can't yet be kicked by pawns (3...dxe4 4. Ne5 f6?? would lose to 5. Qh5+!).

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/4P3/2N2N2/PPPP1.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. Nf3/2...d5/3. Nc3
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/4P3/2N2N2/PPPP1.x:
This is a relatively rare sideline of the French defence, and for good reason. White's approach is not particularly ambitious, which gives Black a relatively smooth game. Black has two main responses.

3...Nf6 is the main line. This allows White to push 4. e5 and after 4...Nfd7 5. d4 c5 Black gets a fairly thematic French structure, while White's knights are in the way of the pawns. Similar positions can be reached from the Steinitz variation where White plays f4 instead of Nf3, or the Advance variation where White can keep their centre together with c3.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/3PP3/5N2/PPP2PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nf3
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/3PP3/5N2/PPP2PP.x:
With 3. Nf3, White gambits their e4 pawn, and after 3...dxe4 must move their knight again.

This at first seems like just a plain mistake for White. If White tries to recapture the pawn with 4. Ng5?, they will find they can't bring enough attackers (4...Nf6 5. Nc3 Bb4 6. Bd2 Qxd4 ∓).

Instead White plays 4. Ne5, hoping a nice central outpost for their knight is sufficient compensation.

This knight is hard for Black to remove: 4...f6?? to kick the knight is a trap, as it allows 5. Qh5+ g6 6. Nxg6 hxg6 7. Qxh8 +-. 4...Nd7, to trade off White's knight, is an option.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3pP3/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. Nf3/2...d5/3. e5
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3pP3/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP.x:
White advances the e-pawn into Black's side of the board, hoping to restrict Black's development.

The main move in this position is /3...c5/, taking control over the d4-square. This is usually a useful move in the French defence. Making it sooner rather than later allows Black to develop their queenside knight without blocking the c-pawn. Because this move is so common, White is likely to be familiar with the resulting positions, so Black can try to deviate by playing a different move instead:

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2ppP3/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. Nf3/2...d5/3. e5/3...c5
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2ppP3/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP.x:
This is Black's most natural and common move.

White usually plays this variation to respond with /4. b4/, the Wing gambit. While not objectively the best move, there aren't many reasons to use this move order to transpose into different French lines.

/4. d4/ transposes into the Nimzowitsch system of the French advance variation.

4. c3 is not an effective way to get into the advance variation, since Black can play the move 4...d4, resulting in completely different positions.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2ppP3/1P6/5N2/P1PP1P.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. Nf3/2...d5/3. e5/3...c5/4. b4
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2ppP3/1P6/5N2/P1PP1P.x:
White gambits the b-pawn in order to steer Black's c-pawn away from the centre. There isn't much theory in this line due to it being relatively rare. Despite being an unorthodox opening, it is a fairly sound way to meet the French defence.

/4...cxb4/, accepting the gambit, is the most principled move. White is usually quick to offer the a-pawn as well, but this sacrifice is less likely to be accepted by Black.

Black can also choose not to accept the pawn, and they might not even be worse off in doing so.

4...b6 tries to stabilise the centre and trade light-squared bishops. After 5. c3 Black has to respond with 5...Qd7 to not lose the bishop after ...Ba6.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/3pP3/1p6/5N2/P1PP1PP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. Nf3/2...d5/3. e5/3...c5/4. b4/4...cxb4
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/3pP3/1p6/5N2/P1PP1PP.x:
Black accepts White's gambit.

White usually continues with the immediate 5. a3, hoping for Black to take the pawn and allowing White some open lines. However, Black doesn't have to take and can simply develop with 5...Nc6 with the idea to recapture on b4 with the dark-squared bishop. This does help White by letting them build up their centre with tempo, so after 6. axb4 Bxb4 7. c3 Be7 8. d4 White gets a space advantage in the centre in exchange for a pawn and allowing Black a passed pawn on the a-file.

Black can choose to take back the a3-pawn too with 5...bxa3. White can simply continue with 6. d4 to build up the centre and delay taking the pawn for now.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/4p3/8/4P3/8/PPPPQPPP/R.x:
White develops the queen to e2. This line avoids the typical French defence continuations.

The queen pins the e6 pawn to Black's king. White's idea is that if 2...d5?! 3. exd5, Black cannot take back with the pawn. After 3...Qxd5 4. Nc3 White gets to gain time on Black's queen while developing.

If Black still wishes to play ...d5, first they may unpin the pawn with 2...Be7.

Otherwise, Black should look for ways to prevent White from achieving a two-pawn centre with both d4 and e4.

/2...c5/ is the most critical and common move. This leads to something like a closed Sicilian defence, where White ends up fianchettoing their king's bishop to avoid having to move their queen again.

rnbqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/4p3/2p5/4P3/8/PPPPQPPP.x:
The game takes on the appearance of a Sicilian defence. White cannot now play d4 because Black's c-pawn controls the square.

White's usual plan is to play 3. Nf3, with g3 and Bg2, in the manner of a closed Sicilian. Fianchettoing the kingside bishop avoids having to move the queen again to develop it

The move order 3. g3 is also fine. This reserves the option of f4 before Nf3.

rnbqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/4p3/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPPQP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. Qe2/2...c5/3. Nf3
rnbqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/4p3/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPPQP.x:
White develops the queen to e2, an active square that can attack the king later. c5 stops d4 while maintaining control of the center. Nf3 develops the knight to its natural square while making an e5 blockade impossible without d6.

A good move: Many viable options such as Nc6.

r1bqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/2n1p3/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP.t: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. Qe2/2...c5/3. Nf3/3...Nc6
r1bqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/2n1p3/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP.x: 4. g3 allows development of the f-rank bishop to g2 after playing Qe2 (in this variation, the queen takes a position that gives attacking possibilities later in the game that can allow the player to think outside the box a bit. For example: 4 ... g6 5. Bg2 Bg7 6. o-o and black can't always play d5, equal game.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/4p3/8/2P1P3/8/PP1P1PPP.x: The Steiner Variation is a counterattacking option against the French. It most often results in a trade of two pawns after /2...d5/ 3. exd5 exd5 4. cxd5 Qxd5 5. Nc3, where black is behind in development but has a stronger pawn structure. Another more infamous line is the Orthoschnapp Gambit after /2...d5/ 3. cxd5 exd5 4. Qb3!?, with the idea of Bc4, Nc3, and possibly sacrificing a pawn on d3.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2P1P3/8/PP1P1PP.x:
Black immediately challenges White’s central space. After 3. exd5 exd5 4. cxd5 Qxd5 5. Nc3, the game enters a symmetrical structure where White has a slight lead in development, while Black holds a sturdier pawn center. Alternatively, White can try the aggressive Orthoschnapp Gambit with 3. cxd5 exd5 4. Qb3!?, aiming for quick development and pressure on f7 and d5.

Though less common than 2. d4, the Steiner Variation can lead to sharp and non-standard French positions.
